Sports.title: 'Stick together, enjoy the ride and smile' - Haaland's message to Man City fans
Sports.content:
"Stick together, enjoy the ride and smile," is Erling Haaland's message to Man City fans.

The club have launched an appeal against the verdict of an independent commission finding them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.

City insist in their statement they are "innocent" and have described the judgement against them as "opinion" and claimed it "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

The independent commission found that between 2009/10 and 2017/18, Man City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

Amid all the off-field news, Haaland and his team-mates go to Anfield on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, to face Liverpool.

Liverpool

Manchester City Sunday 11th October 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

Asked what he would say to the City supporters ahead of that game, Haaland said: "They're going to have a good time.

"We have to stick together. We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile.

"So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game.

"We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile."

Haaland - the son of former City player Alf-Inge Haaland - says he considers himself a fan of City, too, and referenced his connection with Manchester.

"I care a lot about the city, I have to say. I care a lot about the fans because I'm a fan myself, and I feel with them as well."

City's matches with Liverpool became big rivalry games during the Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp eras at the two clubs and Haaland is looking forward to the occasion.

"It's always special to play against Liverpool. Especially with Pep and Klopp. I remember sitting in Salzburg and Dortmund and watching the games, how much they pushed each other. It's always special games there.

"I won there, I drew there, I lost. So it's always special, and every Premier League game is different, and every game against Liverpool is always special."

Maresca remains 'very calm' and 'trusts club completely'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Enzo Maresca speaks for the first time in a club interview over the guilty verdict

Man City boss Enzo Maresca has also spoken for the first time since the independent commission's verdict in an interview conducted by the club.

The Italian insists he is "very calm", "completely trusts" the club and that his players "don't care too much about the noise".

He told CityTV: "Personally, I'm very calm, to be honest. The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club.

"We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.

"The feeling is fantastic, to be honest. The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment, we are top of the league.

"The players are just focused on that. They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things.

"They know their profession and they know that the noise is there but they don't care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win at Anfield."

Maresca is set to be quizzed further on the guilty verdict at a pre-match press conference on Friday at 10.30am, which you can follow live on Sky Sports News ​​​​​​and digital platforms.

What did the independent commission find?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kaveh Solhekol explains how the other Premier League clubs are reacting to Manchester City's rule breaches ahead of the appeal process

Manchester City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

The club filed accounts that concealed the true state of its finances.

Manchester City were significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits and broke "well over 100" Premier League regulations.

Manchester City failed to co-operate and act in good faith towards the league during the investigation, with three out of four alleged breaches upheld and one charge not proven.

The commission also said it was "regrettable" that a decision had taken so long to reach, with the hearing having taken place between September and December 2024.

City: Process was not impartial

Following the publication of the guilty verdict on September 29, a Manchester City statement read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Manchester City's statement erroneously refers to a Premier League commission. It is an independent commission.

Why Man City's appeal could drag into 2027

Latest from Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol and Amar Mehta:

Manchester City's appeal could drag on into next year if they argue that the process should not be run according to Premier League rules which were introduced for this season.

City have filed their appeal and the new rules about appeals state that this part of the disciplinary process has to be concluded within 12 weeks and the appeal hearing can last no longer than five days.

City's lawyers could argue that they were charged in 2023 and a hearing was held in 2024 - when the rules about a speeded-up appeals process were not in the Premier League Handbook.

A legal expert told Sky Sports News Manchester City would have a strong case for arguing that the new rules should not apply in this case.

The new rules were introduced to ensure that clubs, where possible, were punished in the same season as relevant rule breaches.

Sports.title: Campbell would end retirement to fight Benn: 'He was insulting me!'
Sports.content:
Olympic gold medallist Luke Campbell would come out of retirement to fight Conor Benn without hesitation.

Campbell, who took gold at London 2012, fought at the highest level as a pro too, boxing Vasiliy Lomachenko and Ryan Garcia in an impressive professional career.

Benn incurred Campbell's wrath when he disparaged the Olympic champion's performance against Garcia.

Campbell hasn't boxed since that fight in 2021. But goaded by Benn, he would make a return.

"Once it's in your blood, it's in your blood," Campbell told Sky Sports. "I'm not officially making a comeback, but I'm in training as always and if there was an opportunity that presented itself then I would take it."

Image: Campbell won gold at London 2012. (AP Photo/Ivan Sekretarev)

Campbell is now the mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire. But boxing is remains on his mind. "I still think about it. There's combinations flying through my head all the time. Not as much it used to but still," he said.

"I think boxing's one of the only sports that brings you in the present moment. Your mind can't afford to drift backwards or forwards. You've got to be in the moment."

He wouldn't hesitate to fight Benn. "100 percent. If it came my way, definitely," Campbell said. "I haven't called anyone out. He was insulting me and I just responded to that.

"Everything's gone from there really. I would definitely entertain it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Toe2Toe, Barry Jones reflects on Conor Benn's defeat to Ryan Garcia.

Even now, after all these years out, Campbell, who boxed down at lightweight, is convinced he'd take out Benn, a welterweight looking to move back up through the divisions.

"I don't know what was going through his head or what level he thought he was at [when he fought Garcia]. I don't know what the boxing IQ was or what the game plan was," Campbell said.

"It would be the same result [with me as with Garcia], probably a knockout. I don't know if it would be two rounds but it would be the same result."

Sports.title: Russell, Antonelli to race with different specs amid Mercedes upgrade concern
Sports.content:
George Russell will race Mercedes' older-specification car, while Kimi Antonelli will run an upgraded package at the Singapore Grand Prix as the team bid to get to the bottom of why the updates introduced in Malaysia did not deliver the expected performance.

The world championship leaders brought their first big upgrade to their W17 cars since the end of May to last week's race but unexpectedly endured a challenging weekend on F1's return to Sepang, with Max Verstappen instead proving the dominant force and claiming Red Bull's first win of the season.

In an unusual move, Mercedes will now split their packages across their two drivers for the whole Sprint weekend in Singapore, with Russell - who will start at the back of Sunday's main race grid owing to an engine penalty, following his car's failure last Sunday - running the older aerodynamic package last raced in Baku and Antonelli the one that debuted with difficulty at Sepang.

Russell revealed he was the one who first floated such an idea, with the decision to do so ultimately becoming a "no-brainer" once they knew he was going to be starting last for the Grand Prix this weekend anyway.

"Well, actually, I instigated the conversation prior to the race on Sunday," revealed Russell, who slipped a season-high 84 points behind team-mate Antonelli after dropping out of third place with five laps to go at Sepang.

"So when the failure happened, it was kind of a no-brainer because we were kind of 50-50 about it pre-race.

"And I was more in favour to do it, even pre-race. Whereas now, it is a total no-brainer."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the F1 Show podcast, Naomi Schiff discusses what George Russell can do now after his 'gut-wrenching' DNF.

It means Russell will again race with the package he took to an impressive victory in Azerbaijan two races ago.

"It is back!" said Russell of the Baku-spec W17.

"Obviously, Malaysia was the worst weekend of the year for us as a team in terms of pace, qualifying result.

"Of course, we probably both would have been on the podium [had his power unit not failed], but it was a difficult one. And we don't know whether that was a Malaysia specific or whether that was anything to do with the upgrade.

"There's no major science telling us there's anything to do with the upgrade, but we don't measure performance in F1 on how much downforce a car produces, you measure it with a stopwatch, and the stopwatch wasn't great in Malaysia.

"So let's see this weekend. I'm very happy to be back on that package and do the compare. I'm not really in any sort of fight this weekend, or the championship for that regard, so it's the right place to do it."

Will front wing addition unlock new package's performance?

Russell also revealed that the newer package running on Antonelli's car will be boosted by the arrival of a front wing in Singapore that had originally been due to be part of the initial package at Sepang.

"I hope the upgrade that is on Kimi's side works as we expect, because as a team, we need that to be the case, and it would be slightly concerning for us if the new package we had in Malaysia is not working as we expected," he added.

"We have a front wing this weekend that Kimi's running that we didn't have in Malaysia. The package was meant to come with the front wing - maybe that was a reason why it wasn't working so well.

"There's nothing telling us it shouldn't work. But of course, the car I had in Baku, I won in Baku, Kimi won in Madrid. It's still a fast car, so hopefully we can have some good fun."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli shares hopes that a 'missing piece' will boost Mercedes' upgrades.

Asked about the new front wing, Antonelli said: "I hope [it makes the difference]! That's the question we will try to answer.

"George is going back on the old package, which we know works really well, especially on these kind of tracks. On my side we will try to find and answer for this package and hopefully we will understand it more and finally extract the potential of the package.

"Of course, we will have the front wing, even though it's just one front wing, but let's see. I think Sepang was overall a little bit of an outlier because of the tarmac, the temperatures, but hopefully this weekend we will be able to put the car in a better place and extract more from the package."

Image: George Russell and Kimi Antonelli will be in different-specification Mercedes W17s this weekend

Antonelli said he was happy to be sticking with the updated W17.

"We really want to understand this new package and try to strike the maximum out of it because the team has done a tremendous job," added the Italian

"They've put in so much work on this new package and it would be just a shame to write it off so early.

"I feel like I'm quite comfortable on keeping it and, actually, I really want to help the team out to understand it more and to try to extract the potential."

Antonelli also confirmed that he was "committed to the new package for the whole weekend", with no option to revert to the older-spec during the Sprint event should the older parts on Russell's car be proving more competitive.

Russell expects second grid penalty before season is out

While Antonelli will hope to contend for victory in both the Sprint and main Grand Prix at Marina Bay, Russell's hopes of fighting at the front are set to be restricted to the shorter-form race on Saturday ahead of his engine-change penalty being applied to Sunday's grid.

Russell will be running a fresh power unit all weekend, but it will not feature the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) upgrade Mercedes have been working on as that update is not in Singapore.

The ADUO upgrade will instead be introduced at a later race, with the United States GP next up in two weeks' time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater explains why George Russell's Singapore GP grid penalty could end his chances of a world title this season.

Mercedes had hoped to coincide the expected introduction on Russell's car of a penalty-triggering fifth engine of the season at the same race that the ADUO was deployed, but that will now not be possible.

Russell said: "We were waiting to take the engine penalty with the ADUO update but obviously unfortunately we've had to take it here.

"But with seven races remaining, that's longer than the engines are designed for. Unfortunately it means I'll be taking another penalty at some point between the next race and the end of the season.

"So, yeah, it feels a little bit one thing after another right now but that's just how the cookie crumbles."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell is OUT with a Power Unit failure in the closing stages of the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

Russell, who won last year in Singapore, has vowed to throw caution to the wind this weekend as he bids to salvage a strong result.

"Yeah, all-out attack, just trying to enjoy the weekend," he added..

"Obviously, if you could choose where to take the penalty in the season, this would be probably second bottom of the list after Monaco. But, unfortunately, we had no choice but to take it here.

"Singapore is a place I love and, yeah, I'll try and carve my way through the pack."

Sports.title: 'It wasn't good enough' - Hamilton reveals 'huge' talks over Ferrari blunder
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has revealed Ferrari held a "huge discussion" to reflect on a strategic error at the Bahrain Grand Prix that he says "wasn't good enough".

Ferrari fitted both Hamilton and his team-mate Charles Leclerc with slick dry tyres at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix, which was being hosted in Malaysia and started on a wet track that the Italian squad anticipated would quickly dry out once the race began.

The decision was proven wrong as Hamilton fell from his starting position of second to almost the back of the field in the opening stages, with the 14 of 22 drivers that started on the intermediate tyre gaining a huge advantage.

Hamilton ultimately produced a stunning fightback to finish on the podium in third, but having fallen 106 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, reiterated his desire to see improvement from his team ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Lewis Hamilton drop to P15 as Mercedes claim the lead at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia

"It wasn't good enough and we've had a huge discussion about it," Hamilton told Sky Sports F1.

"And we're going to try and work on how we can come to a better conclusion more consistently in the future."

Before revealing those talks, Hamilton had defended Ferrari from what he feels is disproportionate criticism the team receive compared to their F1 rivals.

McLaren also started the race in Sepang on dry tyres and suffered the same fate as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri slid towards the back of the pack.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit

"We do for some reason as a team get far more flack than anybody else," the seven-time world champion said. "McLaren made the same decision and no one even said anything about it.

"You know, they made some excuse of some sort. McLaren made the same mistake and the same call."

'The call didn't come from the strategist'

Hamilton also offered a specific defence of Ferrari's strategists, insisting they alone were not responsible for the starting tyre choice.

He added: "It was ultimately a mistake but it's not the strategists. I think, unfortunately, my strategy team gets the brunt of the (criticism for the) call.

"But in actual fact, the call didn't come from the strategist. The call comes from collectively, us working together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton recovers from P15 to podium places.

"(Team principal) Fred (Vasseur), (head of track engineering) Matteo (Togninalli), myself, my engineer, we make the decision together. And we discuss it and we put our input, we put all our ideas and information into the pot, whether that's good or not…

"I went into the pit lane, I'm like, 'it's wet'. I go to the pit wall, I'm like, 'it's wet'. Come back to the garage, I'm like, 'guys, we should be on the inters'.

"And then they all give a different perspective. And if you've got three people giving you a different perspective, you eventually get convinced by that. And you're like, 'OK, I'll go with what you suggest.' And that's how you work as a team.

"And you hope three are more right than one. But in some scenarios, it's the other way around. And you were right and your gut feeling was right. And then you're like, 'damn, I should have gone with my gut'. But everyone's generally trying to do the best they can."

'We're here to attack' - Hamilton hopeful of Singapore chances

Hamilton is hopeful Ferrari's car will be suited to the Marina Bay Street Circuit this weekend, with the track potentially providing the team with their best chance of victory over the final seven rounds of the season.

"I think with our car, it's generally good on street circuits, particularly when there's not particularly long straights," Hamilton said.

"If you look at the last races, we were quick through corners, not so quick on the straight line. This is a high-drag circuit, so I'm hoping the advantage others have on those long straights kind of comes down a little bit and we can start matching them through keeping up with them on the pace, through corners.

"I think for us, it's just making sure we've got a great, stable platform underneath us, particularly in the bumpy zones because it's bumpy here."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hamilton defends Vasseur but wants changes to Ferrari's F1 operation

With Singapore hosting a Sprint weekend for the first time, meaning there is only one practice session before Sprint Qualifying on Friday, Hamilton believes quickly finding a strong setup will be crucial.

He added: "We've looked at Monaco, we've looked at Montreal, we've looked at Baku's setup. We're coming here and it is requesting something different.

"I've been pushing the car in a certain direction, and I think we are slowly making gains and improvements.

"We're here to attack. Qualifying is key, and it would be really great if we could start tomorrow on the right foot and then just be attacking in qualifying, but we have to wait and see."

Leclerc: Singapore layout seems good for us

Leclerc is also hopeful Singapore could present an opportunity for he or Hamilton to add to their sole victories this season, but is taking nothing for granted.

Ferrari failed to meet pre-weekend expectations when many considered them favourites for victory in Monaco and Budapest earlier this year, but claimed surprise victories when Hamilton won in Barcelona and Leclerc at Silverstone.

Asked whether Singapore represented Ferrari's best chance to add another victory this season, Leclerc replied: "Maybe. It definitely is one of those tracks where the layout seems to be pretty good for us.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc says his Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton 'is driving at an exceptional level' and 'is having a great season'

"Whether this will pay off or not… Budapest and Monaco were strong layouts for us on paper and it didn't go well. Silverstone was a bad layout on paper and it went really well.

"I don't know if it tells the full story but we'll give our best. Historically we've been quite strong here but we cannot really rely on the past.

"We've got to do everything we can to be in the best possible situation. It's also true that the tendency lately has been that we've been losing a bit of performance compared to the guys in front, so to win will be very difficult."

Sports.title: Southampton boss Eckert welcomes 'clarity' after Spygate suspended FA ban
Sports.content:
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert says he welcomes the "clarity" provided by his suspended FA ban, admitting the Spygate saga has "changed my life" after more than four months of uncertainty.

On Wednesday, it was announced that Eckert has been handed a six-week ban, suspended until the end of the 2027/28 season, and fined £28,000 after admitting three FA charges relating to misconduct during Southampton's spying scandal. He will continue in his role and is now focused on Sunday's Championship clash with local rivals Portsmouth.

The German says the conclusion of the FA process has brought relief after more than four months of uncertainty and praised the Southampton board for standing by him.

"It's tough. It changes your life," Eckert said.

"It's been more than four months now, it's been quite a long time, and you go into a season and you push everyone aside because we have a job to do and we need to deliver.

"I'm very happy we go into Sunday and one of the biggest games we will have all season and we have clarity - and that's not just for me, that's for everyone at this football club."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News reporter Mark McAdam explains how Tonda Eckert will continue as Southampton boss after receiving a six-week ban and £28,000 fine over the Spygate scandal

Southampton were expelled from last season's Championship play-off final and handed a four-point deduction for this season after admitting multiple breaches relating to the unauthorised filming of opponents' training.

The EFL process could only sanction the club, with the FA subsequently charging Eckert with three breaches of Rule E3.1.

Eckert accepted responsibility for his actions and says he was prepared to accept whatever punishment followed.

"I've made a mistake and I've said that relatively quickly, then I think you have to accept whatever the consequence is," he said.

"The only thing that was up for me was to give my version of the story and I'm happy that the commission listened. But, in the end, if you make a mistake, it's not for me to judge the consequence, so I have to take whatever comes my way."

Eckert admits there was a possibility the outcome could have prevented him from continuing as Southampton boss.

"There was a fair chance the verdict went a different way," he said. "After such a long time... we've had a verdict from the EFL, we've had a verdict now (from the FA) and whatever you expect is not necessarily what you get in the end.

"For me, it's just to hold my hand up one more time, I've made a mistake and for me to take whatever the consequence is."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Wrexham co-owners, Rob Mac & Ryan Reynolds, poke fun at Southampton's Spygate saga in an advert for one of their sponsors

The 39-year-old also praised Saints owner Dragan Solak and the Southampton board for their backing throughout the saga.

"I think there's many football clubs that take a different decision in the summer and that is what makes this club special," Eckert said.

"That in times that are a lot tougher, especially with a lot of outside pressure, that we've come to a decision the way that we've done. It will be something to forever be grateful for."

Eckert believes the conclusion of the matter can now allow Southampton to focus fully on their promotion challenge.

"When I came in, I made a promise to the players to always give clarity and honesty - and the clarity that they deserve and everyone in the club deserves, I couldn't give for many months," he said.

"That is the reality and it's never easy to perform when you are not clear, when there's an uncertainty that doesn't allow you to look too far ahead.

"That is gone now, so we make sure we put our foot on the gas on Sunday and don't stop."

Asked what he would say to those who believe his punishment was not sufficient, Eckert simply replied: "Nothing."

He added: "It's good that we have clarity and I'm sure this is going to give us another boost going into a block of very important games."

Eckert insists Southampton's target remains promotion back to the Premier League.

"It's our goal," he said. "It needs a lot to do that because it's a strong league and there are so many tough games and a condensed schedule coming up, but if you have those goals in the end, you need to live that in every single moment, even more so on Sunday."

Hellberg: Eckert called me to apologise for 'Spygate' - everyone deserves a second chance

On Thursday afternoon, Middlesbrough boss Kim Hellberg was asked about the punishment and what he thought.

"I think for me, it ended after the first judgement," he told BBC Sport Tees.

Middlesbrough were the third side Southampton admitted to spying on during last season, following earlier incidents involving Oxford United and Ipswich Town.

Boro complained to the EFL after a Southampton analyst was spotted filming training from behind a tree close to their training ground in the days before the first leg of their Championship play-off semi-final.

"I'm not one to keep a grudge after that," Hellberg added. "They had their punishment in terms of that and we moved on.

"I talked to Tonda [Eckert] since that day. He called me, talked to me and apologised for those things.

"After the game, I talked about my point of view on it. I never said anything about a decision or a ban - I just talked about emotions and how I felt about it from my point of view.

"I think everyone is entitled to a second chance and I try to live by that in life every day."

Middlesbrough were reinstated to the Championship play-offs following Southampton's expulsion but were beaten 1-0 in the final at Wembley by Hull City.

Sports.title: Khaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City charges
Sports.content:
No one better understands the precarious tightrope Abu Dhabi walks when it tries to balance its relationships with western Europe while weighing the complex geopolitics of the Gulf region than Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. He was eight when his father, ambassador Khalifa Ahmed Abdel Aziz al-Mubarak, left the family’s Paris apartment for work on 9 February 1984, and was assassinated on the street by a Palestinian terrorist.

And no one outside the emirate’s royal family could be more wrapped up in the project of making and maintaining Abu Dhabi as a significant and secure world power and the dominant member of the United Arab Emirates, a nation state still only 55 years old. His paternal grandfather, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz al-Mubarak, was chair of Abu Dhabi’s Sharia judicial department and senior adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan, the founding president of the UAE. As such, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz was the James Madison of the UAE (the founding father, not the Spurs player) in that he crafted the Islamic legal framework of the new nation in the 1970s.

Khaldoon’s father was assassinated by a group led by Abu Nidal which, according to the CIA, was “the most dangerous and effective of all terrorist groups [and] the best organized of the radical Palestinian terrorist groups” before the emergence of Hamas. The murder was justified in a phone call saying that the UAE “had expelled Palestinian and Arab residents and was linked with American imperialism”. In essence, they were accused of being too soft on the west, not radical enough for Palestinians.

Both al-Mubarak’s grandfather and father have streets named after them in Abu Dhabi, with his father honoured as a martyr of the state. It is fair to say the City chair has honoured the family tradition as chief adviser to the UAE president and Abu Dhabi ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for whom he first worked after graduating from Tufts University in Massachusetts. Given his father’s martyrdom, the royal family is said to have looked out for al-Mubarak as a quasi-adopted son. According to a source in the Financial Times, al-Mubarak is “diplomatically in charge of the UK file as well as the China file … and he’s the main liaison with the US administration” and has diplomatic immunity in the UK. That said, he appears to have made a rare misstep with his belligerent tone on Manchester City.

According to Manchester City’s lawyer Simon Cliff, it was al-Mubarak who dictated the aggressive, confrontational stance City have taken with football authorities. As far back as 2014, when City were fighting their first Uefa charge, Cliff wrote, according to leaked documents first published by Der Spiegel: “Khaldoon says he would rather spend £30m on the 50 best lawyers in the world and sue them [Uefa] for the next ten years than agree a financial penalty.”

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon al-Mubarak with Pep Guardiola after Manchester City’s Premier League title win in 2021-22. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

He backed down on that occasion, along with the co-accused Paris Saint-Germain, both clubs agreeing a small fine and minor transfer restrictions with Uefa. It is extraordinary that City kept fighting thereafter, whereas the Qatar-owned PSG accepted their punishment, cosied up to Uefa – with the club’s president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, becoming chair of the European Club Association (now European Football Clubs) and chief opponent of the breakaway Super League – and built the most exciting and successful team in Europe, bringing admiration for the Qatari brand from observers willing to ignore human rights abuses. Al-Mubarak, in fighting to the end with City, appears to have broken an ambassador’s cardinal law: don’t embarrass your boss. Should City lose their appeal against an independent commission’s finding that they were guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, al-Mubarak may be instructed to organise the sale of the club.

“I’m sure that’s the case with Man City,” says Christopher Davidson, author of Abu Dhabi, Oil and Beyond. “More than that, I’ve been told by some [in Abu Dhabi] that it will be the case. I can’t see any reason why they would stick around and try to rebuild the reputation after this. It’s embarrassing the royal family now. I can’t think of any example where things have gone wrong [for Abu Dhabi] and they’ve just kept plugging money into it. I think they’ll play out the appeal – nothing to lose with that – but once that’s done, it’s all about how to get out before the owners are declared unfit, a far worse outcome. There are very clever people involved in Abu Dhabi who I’m led to believe will very strongly counsel this needs to be a quiet retreat because the longer they stay in the game, the more damaging it is and it will unravel any kind of soft power Abu Dhabi managed to gain.”

In June al-Mubarak said “these sorts of jewels, you don’t sell” and that there was “only intention to keep growing this”. As for the wider threat to UK-Abu Dhabi relations, Davidson believes it is overstated. “Some of the reporting perhaps has portrayed Abu Dhabi as a bit monolithic. There are entire big and growing sections of Abu Dhabi state economy that are outside al-Mubarak’s remit. Some of Abu Dhabi’s biggest investments in the UK in recent years have been in renewable energy and the windfarms of Scotland from Masdar energy, which is chaired by Sultan al-Jaber, who’s another key lieutenant of the ruler.”

Davidson also cites the International Holding Company (IHC), which has huge biotech, shipping, healthcare and retail investments in the UK, including the Ivy restaurants, and is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi and brother of the UAE president and Sheikh Mansour. “It’s inconceivable that these investments would be withdrawn,” says Davidson.

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon al-Mubarak (left) alongside City owner Sheikh Mansour at the then City of Manchester Stadium in August 2010. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters

In May this year the UK signed a free trade agreement with Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE which it said could be worth £3.7bn a year to the UK economy. “The UAE was a major force behind getting that and it was a major accomplishment on both sides, so there’s no prospect any of this is going to be interfered with,” Davidson says.

Al-Mubarak will probably emerge from this fiasco largely untarnished, because City are a tiny part of his portfolio. “He can’t possibly have known what’s going on in every part of his empire,” says Davidson. “My gut feeling would be that it’s the layers below him. It’s all about your legal counsel. I think the Qataris had very clever people working for them. This has been a case of poor advice being given to the senior Emiratis involved, a misreading of UK politics and a misreading of the Premier League and its bigger picture as a rules-based institution.

“I think the statements al-Mubarak has made, including the one early last summer that ‘We will not sell’, are the product of poor advice delivered to him and ultimately to Sheikh Mansour. It may be important to us in the UK but Man City has been a peripheral project [for Abu Dhabi].”

Sports.title: Sergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’
Sports.content:
An 11-year-old, second-hand VW Beetle with more than 300,000km on the clock pulls over on Clown Fofó Street in the heart of Vallecas. The music goes off, the Smiths silenced, and out gets Sergio Camello: movie aficionado with 156 films reviewed, part-time photographer, some-time drummer, Olympic gold medallist and the second top goalscorer in Europe’s top five leagues. Engulfed in graffiti, stickers covering the glass between metal bars in red, a single step up from the street, the small door into Rayo Vallecano’s ground is locked, but in 64 hours it will open for the first time this season. “It’s my home, it’s Vallecas,” Camello says.

Forced to abandon their place, on Saturday at 2pm the tenants return. With the Madrid council declaring Estadio de Vallecas unsafe, unfit for purpose, Rayo’s home matches have instead been played in Leganes, out of the city to the south and boycotted by fans. Walking the neighbourhood that is proud of its social conscience, its community and its team, Camello can’t wait to be back again. And not just for the football; maybe not even for the football. “It’s the pre-game, the post-game, the people,” he says, passing the bar where they’ll be waiting for him after, same as always.

View image in fullscreen ‘I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team’ – Sergio Camello at the door to Rayo Vallecano’s Vallecas ground. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Yet the football is good too, good as it’s ever been. Across the continent’s top five leagues only Raphinha has more goals than Camello’s seven in seven league games, and Camello himself has never had so many either. “I try not to think about it but my teammates keep reminding me,” he says. “‘Pichichi! Pichichi!’ It’s not Sergio any more.” Pichichi was the legendary Athletic Club striker whose name adorns the top-scorer award. No pressure, then. “None, I love it,” Camello replies, “and I love that they’re enjoying it.”

Two months into the season, this is already his best campaign in primera where the previous totals were five, three and six. And although there’s a tactical element, new coach Beñat San José altering his movement, Camello looks deeper for an explanation. Above all he looks inside, which is where, from the beginning, another conversation starts: a simple question prompts a complex, nuanced and human discussion, the striker talking calmly, thoughtfully and with startling unexpected honesty.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello celebrates after scoring against Barcelona in August. Photograph: Pablo Rodriguez/Quality Sport Images/Getty Images

Camello is that most unusual of footballers – prepared to speak on materialism, racism, or homophobia, social media “poison” or the housing crisis, that rare player prepared to use his platform, which he says was born of his upbringing but also learned being here in the barrio. This is personal, but at once universal too, something in his experience that is about everyone. Who knows, maybe there is something in what he has lived that can help, some reason to share it, the goals scored offering tangible proof of an intangible process.

So what has changed? “How I go on to the pitch,” he says. “I thought it would be much harder to change my mindset but I’m seeing that I can be myself: be free, connect with the Sergio I can offer Rayo. To feel liberated, to enjoy it – and it’s been a long time since I enjoyed all this like this.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello has been outscored only by Barcelona’s Raphinha so far this season. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“The first thing was to have many conversations with friends, people who truly know me. Especially my twin brother Gonzalo; there’s a connection that goes beyond the human. He could see I wasn’t enjoying it much, wasn’t myself. We talked and I tried to take that on to the pitch. Above all, to play without the pressure. Because pressure is horrendous. It makes it so that you don’t enjoy absolutely anything, puts you in a position where if things don’t work, that leads to frustration, frustration leads to pity, and suddenly everything is negative. There’s a point in the conversations where it’s ‘that’s it; it’s done’.

“This is a sport you chose before it was your job, because it’s what made you happiest. It’s about connecting to that kid again. I’d discussed this in therapy too; the idea of getting back to that kid.”

Somewhere that can be lost, not just failure you have to live with but also success. “The pressure can come from everywhere,” Camello says. “We’re young, the change happens so fast, no one prepares you for it. If you can’t manage that it can do a lot of damage and that happened to me. [Early on], I would even get a bit paranoid, have fixations. ‘They’re looking at me.’ The first day in primera, when I scored, the journey there had been normal – scooter, bus, metro, bus – but on the same journey home some kids followed me shouting ‘Camello! Camello!’ It was a shock. The night we returned from the Olympics I was in the usual bar, people crowded and I had a kind of anxiety attack and had to go. And, look, I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team. I can’t imagine what it is like for someone at Lamine Yamal’s level. I don’t envy that.”

“But it’s about seeing the balance, understanding,” Camello continues, “and football has given me so, so much. There are so many people who can’t enjoy their job, who don’t have the [financial] freedom. When you have bad moments, when the clouds come, when you feel that cycle of negativity, you talk.”

Camello looks across the room: it’s quiet, 25 chairs sitting empty. “One of my friends [Dani Fernández] is a musician about to do four sellouts at the Wizink [Centre]; when I met him, he wouldn’t have sold out this room,” he says. “We both got ‘caught’ in this about the same time and we talked a lot. When he had doubts, I was there; when I did, he was. A torch in the darkness. You think ‘I’d love to be a rock star’ and then someone you admire who is tells you how bloody shit it can be behind the scenes. You understand each other, you think: ‘Bloody hell, maybe I don’t have to analyse things so deeply.’ If in even those places you idealise, there is darkness, solitude, maybe I’m not so bad.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello says he his thriving by playing without pressure. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Otherwise you could go into a very dark place where you feel you have to escape this [football]. Even then the world wouldn’t end. And fortunately, the positive in football has always weighed much more heavily. And that’s been shown to be right. Those conversations give me perspective, make me conscious of how fortunate I am.”

Although Camello says doubts about the game itself are rarely shared in such depth in the dressing room – “football might be the most important thing in the entire world to your teammate” – something about this place helps. The club’s problems are significant, debilitating and should not be romanticised, he insists, and yet somehow they have made a success of it, built through solidarity. Besides, he says, “we’re also here because we want to be” and there is something about Rayo, something about breaking out of the bubble, that has been good for him, for all of them, as people as well as players. There’s a moment when he talks about everything that comes with being a footballer and says “it’s easy to be a dickhead”, but that’s diminished at a club not just in the barrio but of the barrio, one that’s “totally different” to anywhere else he knows, where “your feet are that bit more on the ground and you realise you’re not stars”.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello says the club and players have a unique connection with the Vallecas neighbourhood. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Rayo is the last team standing from football from another time, that’s what I like,” Camello says. “Even just parking here on the street right in front changes things. The same faces, every time. The least important thing about the football here is the football; it’s what they stand for every weekend, what the believe in, the connection. It’s Isi in the bar on the corner. Unai and his mates in the one down the bottom there. The bar we’ve taken over. That doesn’t exist anywhere else. To have those guys you were watching half an hour ago in the same bars, doesn’t happen. I’ve built relationships that are very sincere that I never expected. I’m a normal bloke who fulfilled mine and many kids’ dream. Like a superhero when they pull on the mask; I come here, I put on the kit, I’m the most competitive, most professional person you can be. But when I leave I take it off and forget about it.”

There is a release, refuge in something else. In the camera. In the drum lessons Camello admits have been slow and the guitar he’s abandoned, the ability God gave his feet denied to his fingers. In the films, in the indie rock music first heard in the family car, and the musician mates he has made. The music discouraged by reggaeton-loving teammates who control the stereo blaring out each morning. They wonder, he says laughing, why he’s not so keen on the gym.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello with the Action for Music charity. Photograph: Action for Music

The music that can make a difference, too; if there is anything that moves people, reaches them like football, it may only be that. “There’s something I’ve wanted to do for a long time and it’s really fun,” Camello says. “I joined a charity, Action for Music, which gives opportunities to kids to play music in humble neighbourhoods. They go to four hours of classes a week: percussion, strings, wind. The kids don’t pay a euro, everything’s free: the space, the teachers, the instruments. They have schools in Tetuán and Carabanchel. I’m getting involved, learning, and I want to set up a school in Vallecas next year.” He stops, grins. “Only I’m going to do it my way … with rock.

“I did a session with them the other day, me trying to play the drums after six months. There was a kid on sax: wow, what a vibe he had, he was just loving it. When you don’t know where to go, there’s a place, someone who believes in you, gives you an opportunity. Forty kids: put some drum sticks in their hand, a guitar, a sax, something that will give them so much. Tell them they can be good at something, feel good about themselves. Have fun, maybe find something inside they didn’t know was there. It’s a way of giving back to Vallecas everything it gives me. I’m so excited.”

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello stops to take a selfie with a fan while walking through the Vallecas neighbourhood. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Imagine them playing the Wizink. “I can be their manager,” Camello laughs. “The idea is to do concerts at the end of each year. Imagine those kids, coming into their first class … then going on stage. It’s good to see yourself up there, with an instrument. Their family there, people who have bought tickets to see them play, the applause. That feeling: ‘I’m worth it.’”

Sounds like scoring a goal. Camello’s eyes light up. “Yes, it is,” he says. “I’m still the same guy as I was when I didn’t score, eh. But at that moment when you’re standing there, there’s nothing else in your head, just a feeling that all this makes sense. When the ball hits the net, when you get a ground on its feet, all together, when they’re celebrating, it’s like it’s all worth it. You feel important, you’re good at something.”

Sports.title: Glasner urges quick end to Manchester City saga and fears damage to Premier League
Sports.content:
Oliver Glasner has said Manchester City being found guilty of arranging “sham contracts” has damaged the Premier League brand globally and believes the integrity of the English top flight is under threat.

The Nottingham Forest head coach said the league faces a job to repair its image and suggested supporters might switch off after City were found to have artificially inflated their income by more than £900m.

City have appealed against last week’s seismic judgment of an independent commission that they broke financial rules across a nine-year period. If City’s appeal fails, the panel could determine a range of sporting sanctions, including expulsion from the league and point deductions. Glasner said the case must be finalised “as soon as possible” to protect the competition’s integrity.

Glasner cited his experience of Crystal Palace being demoted from the Europa League at the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) last year for breaking Uefa’s multi-club ownership rules as an example of how legal processes can drag.

“Let’s wait until the final verdict is spoken, but my wish is just that this is quick,” Glasner said. “Because we didn’t know with Palace if we were in the Europa League or Conference League and then it was ‘you will hear on Thursday’ and then that became Monday, because it was always delayed. Then we got the final verdict 10 days before the Conference League started.

“And that’s why I think this must be [completed] as soon as possible. There is still damage for the Premier League, not just in England. It’s a big topic all over the world, especially in Europe. The most important thing is the integrity of the league because as soon as the fans can’t trust it, they won’t watch it any more.”

View image in fullscreen Manchester City are appealing against last week’s seismic judgment of an independent commission that they broke financial rules across a nine-year period. Photograph: Loannis Alexopoulos/Anadolu/Getty Images

Last week Aston Villa’s Unai Emery became the first Premier League manager to discuss the City case. “If other clubs had been artificially inflated and that were now coming to light, there would obviously be some damage,” Emery said, in an interview published with Spanish outlet Diario de Sevilla. “That is something for the courts and the relevant authorities to decide.

“I feel sorry because of the way that [City] team played. Under [Pep] Guardiola, there were times when they were unmatched.”

City deny wrongdoing and formally lodged an appeal last Thursday. “The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe,” a City statement read.

“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.”

Sports.title: Victor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency run
Sports.content:
Victor Montagliani has told Concacaf staff he intends to stand for re-election as the confederation’s presidentnext year, which will rule him out of going up against Gianni Infantino for the top job at Fifa.

The Canadian businessman is understood to have relayed the message to most of the 41 members of Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation.

Montagliani has been widely touted as a potential candidate to take on Infantino for the Fifa presidency, particularly among Uefa member associations, who are conscious a European candidate would have no chance of beating Infantino in a ballot of Fifa’s 211 members.

At a town hall meeting of Concacaf staff late last month, however, Montagliani is understood to have said that despite the Fifa governance crisis and calls for him to stand, he wants to continue serving members in the region.

Concacaf’s presidential election will take place in the first quarter of next year before the Fifa vote on 18 March in Rabat, with the similar timelines leading Montagliani to clarify his intentions to staff.

The 61-year-old was elected president on a reforming mandate 10 years ago after the corruption scandal that culminated in the arrest of then Concacaf president, Jeffrey Webb, after an FBI investigation. Webb admitted he had taken “bribes and kickbacks”.

Uefa will also hold presidential elections next year, with Aleksander Ceferin confirming his intention to stand at a meeting of Uefa’s 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday. Ceferin had said in February 2024 that he would not run for a fourth term at the helm but the likelihood that he would, after all, continue had long been an open secret. Previously, changes to the Uefa statutes had been passed that meant his first term, which began midway through the standard four-year cycle, did not count towards the standard three-term limit.

It raises the prospect of Ceferin, who took the presidency in September 2016, holding power for more than 15 years in total. That is seen among most European FAs as a positive amid the turmoil engulfing football’s governance while putting to bed any perception that Ceferin, who would have had a number of proponents, might be tempted to challenge Infantino for the Fifa role

Montagliani and Ceferin are expected to continue working together to bring about governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off scandal, which will be on the agenda at next Thursday’s Fifa council meeting in Zurich.

Fifa’s council has not met since Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan was exposed in July despite repeated calls from members for an extraordinary general meeting, with the summit their first meeting since Fifa congress in Vancouver last March.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Montagliani, Ceferin and the Asian Football Confederation president, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, are expected to use the council meeting to demand an independent review of FFE and call for broader governance reforms of Fifa, which would give a greater voice to stakeholders and formalise the council’s role in decision-making.

Previous calls from the trio, expressed in letters sent to Infantino last month, for Fifa to allocate a portion of its $6bn (£4.5bn) cash reserves to members will also be discussed.

Delegates at Uefa’s Berlin meeting discussed a framework for Fifa reform, whose key points were made public during the afternoon. Among the points listed were the need for “a president who leads, not manages”, “stronger ethics, disciplinary, audit and compliance”, and “a clear process for major decisions”.

Azerbaijan was an outlier in refusing to back Uefa’s reform proposals. The Azeri FA’s former general secretary, Elkhan Mammadov, now plays a key role at Fifa as its chief member associations officer and has been instrumental in Infantino’s attempts to keep wavering nations onside during the FFE crisis. Later this month, Azerbaijan will hold the first Fifa Under-15 World Cup, whose contestants will include Russia.

Sports.title: Wiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoff
Sports.content:
Sarina Wiegman heaped praise on Ella Toone for her positive reaction to being left out of England’s initial squad for their Women’s World Cup playoff against Greece, after recalling the Manchester United midfielder for Friday’s first leg in Heraklion, Crete.

An injury sustained by Lucy Bronze, described by Wiegman as “really small”, prompted the England right-back to return to Chelsea and Wiegman called up Toone, who travelled to Greece from Spain, where she had organised a training routine during the international window.

Toone has 69 caps and has scored 24 goals, including in the Euro 2022 final and 2023 World Cup semi-final, but Wiegman said when naming her squad that she had left out Toone and Chloe Kelly because “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch”. On Saturday, after starting Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, Toone took ownership of things, telling the BBC: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

Wiegman, asked whether she had been impressed with Toone’s response, said: “Yes, very much. I think when I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call. But she took that straight away. Of course [she was] very disappointed, but the first thing she did [was say]: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’ She has the support around her too.”

The head coach referenced Toone’s post-match comments when she said: “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good. And then getting everything ready to go to Spain instead, but go for training there, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

That will be music to the ears of Toone, whose experience is also understood to have been a factor in Wiegman picking her rather than a replacement right-back. She could feature on Friday, when the European champions will hope to build a strong first-leg lead before Tuesday’s reverse fixture in Leicester.

To qualify for next summer’s finals in Brazil, England must overcome Greece and win another two-leg playoff, against Slovakia or Ukraine, in December.

Quick Guide Greece v England: Wiegman's probable team for visitors Show (4-2-3-1) Hampton; Le Tissier, Morgan, Williamson, Greenwood; Stanway, Walsh; Mead, James, Hemp; Russo Greece v England, Pankritio Stadium, Friday, 5.30pm BST Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

The draw for the World Cup will follow on 11 December and it would feel inconceivable for the 2023 runners-up to miss out. They are in the playoffs despite winning five of their six qualifiers in a group with Spain, the defending champions, who pipped England to top spot by virtue of their stronger head-to-head goal difference.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Sarina Wiegman (centre), speaks to the players during a training session in Heraklion, Greece. Photograph: Naomi Baker/The FA/Getty Images

Greece have never qualified for a major tournament and, major underdogs against England, will probably set up in a low, defensive shape. The England defender Esme Morgan said she and her teammates would remain calm even if it takes time to break through: “It’s just [about] persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. I think a really good example of it was the away game we played against Ukraine [in qualifying].

“We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half – the keeper was making saves, I think we struck the woodwork a couple of times – but the messaging at half-time among the players and when Sarina came in to speak to us was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities. Not to start snatching or taking hot shots from distance, just trusting in the style of play that we have and in our ability to keep finding gaps in and around the defence. We came out for the second half after that and scored really, really quickly. So it’s just sticking to the gameplan, trusting in what we do and being patient”

Sports.title: Manchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000
Sports.content:
Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000.

The prodigy, who turned 16 this week, stunned the club when he asked for his registration to be cancelled last month, setting in motion a scramble among Europe’s elite clubs for his signature.

Under Premier League youth rules, Gabriel would have been able to leave for a rival for nothing in January if the club had not offered him a formal scholarship for next season. The Guardian can reveal that the offer has now been lodged with the player.

Whether he accepts it or not – and it appears unlikely he will stay at Old Trafford – any Premier League club must now negotiate a fee directly with United for the player. If one is not reached, compensation will be set by a Professional Football Compensation Committee tribunal.

At a tribunal, United would expect to receive in excess of £3m, plus a clause in the deal granting them 20% of his next transfer fee. In a previous tribunal for a high-profile academy player, Liverpool were required to pay Chelsea £2.8m up front – with an additional £1.2m in performance-related add-ons – for Rio Ngumoha, and a 20% sell-on clause was inserted in the deal.

A United team photograph released this week featuring Gabriel briefly raised fan hopes of a reconciliation. But a breakdown between his representatives and the club means the forward – who has been at United since he was 11 – is now almost certain to leave.

He was permitted under Premier League rules to sign a pre-agreement after his 16th birthday, but his camp were not prepared to enter discussions after a disagreement over first-team minutes.

His next move is yet to be decided, though it is believed he favours a move to Europe, where compensation would be significantly lower. Real Madrid are favourites to sign him, with Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain all monitoring developments.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

According to official Fifa compensation figures for a Category I academy, United would receive around £350,000 if he moves abroad. He would ordinarily have been prevented from transferring before his 18th birthday, but is eligible for an EU passport through his parents. The club will consider taking legal action if they believe recruitment rules have been breached.

Gabriel has not appeared at training for more than three weeks and, according to sources, the club has made multiple attempts to check on his wellbeing. To fast-track his progression into the first team, Gabriel had worked with specialist staff usually reserved for senior players.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Spygate: one of football’s stranger and more pointless transgressions
Sports.content:
RE-REWIND

The recent international break has proved to be a goldmine for punishment admin, nicely wrapped up on Wednesday night with the latest chapter of the Southampton Spygate saga. It sounds like a three-part Netflix documentary – and almost certainly will be one day – but for now, here’s a reminder of what went down; feel free to add your own haunting synth soundtrack … two days before the first leg of their Championship playoff semi-final, Middlesbrough staff spotted someone lurking on the perimeter of their training ground and the EFL confirmed “an individual associated with Southampton” was involved. Southampton won the tie and advanced to the final, but the storm kept building. After days of uncertainty and wild speculation, Saints were kicked out of the playoffs (and docked four points for the following season) and Boro went to Wembley. Their opponents, Hull City, threatened their own legal action, which by now we can safely assume is going absolutely nowhere.

Much like Marcelo Bielsa, who met similar accusations of spying at Leeds with a weary shrug and a cache of PowerPoint slides, Saints manager Tonda Eckert emerged as the central figure in the scandal. An independent disciplinary commission called the scheme “a contrived and determined plan from the top down”, where footage was captured of three opponents: Ipswich, Oxford and Boro. Amusingly, Southampton failed to win any of the relevant matches – but reports emerged that, in a tribute to Saints legend Kevin Keegan, the manager had “loved it” when presented with the footage. And who can blame him? His team had gone to Boro and got something. Eckert accepted “full responsibility” and proffered his wrist to authorities – but as a relative newcomer to English football, he also employed his own version of the Costanza defence. Was that wrong? Should I not have done that?

View image in fullscreen Tonda Eckert, neatly illustrating that par. Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PA

Eckert’s prospects looked bleak, but he was fortunate that Southampton had a supportive owner with a name straight out of a Bond film. Dragan Solak declared himself ready to “close the chapter and look ahead together”, pending final sanctions. Away fans kept bringing their binoculars to St Mary’s, but this gripping espionage tale lacked a final act until the latest verdict, when Eckert was hit with, er, a suspended six-week ban and £28,000 fine. The FA’s lawyers had targeted a potential nine-month suspension, later reduced to three months – but the independent panel found Eckert to be a “particularly impressive witness” who showed “genuine contrition”. So long as he can avoid concocting a similar scheme in future, Eckert will serve no ban at all; he will be in the dugout for Sunday’s derby against Portsmouth.

Despite the points deduction, Southampton already sit in mid-table and look a decent bet for promotion. Our preferred punishment – making this the permanent club crest – has also failed to materialise. A genuinely huge story at the time, Spygate will go down as one of football’s stranger and more pointless transgressions, its final act dwarfed by the news of Manchester City’s many, many charges. In the end, perhaps there was no point prolonging Eckert’s spell in limbo. Even if he was banned from attending Southampton’s training sessions in person, we’re pretty sure he would have found a way around it.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“It is difficult to recognise this team from the one that played just a few months ago. One might think that the [Geopolitics] World Cup was an illusion” – TV Azteca’s Álvaro López Sordo laments the end of Mexico’s honeymoon under new boss Rafa Márquez after a run of defeats that had one front-page headline audibly sighing: “¡Qué Horror!”.

double quotation mark Re: yesterday’s Football Daily. While enjoying the contrast between the departing Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, I’d politely draw your attention to two other veterans of the game: Robert Lewandowski and Luka Modric. They seem able to focus on what they are paid to do – play football” – Diana Brighouse.

double quotation mark This message may be later than a Mark Dennis tackle, but a comment on a recentish podcast about teammates with rhyming names reminded me of a Manchester United youth XI of the 1950s that featured Nobby Stiles, John Giles, Harold Batt and Tommy Spratt. This gem of information came from Tommy who owned the newsagent in Timperley village when I moved there in 1970” – David Campion [have any other former footballers given you similar tidbits of trivia? – Football Daily Ed].

double quotation mark Although I’m an England fan, I enjoyed seeing the picture of an ecstatic Gary Caldwell celebrating his winner for Scotland v France back in 2006 (yesterday’s Memory Lane, full email edition). I’m also a Wigan Athletic fan and poor Gary hasn’t had much to smile about this season, with the team firmly stuck at the bottom of League One, plus he’s had to deal with the desperately sad loss of his goalkeeping coach and good friend Kevin Miller. Here’s hoping the turnaround starts on Saturday at Stevenage. Up the [redacted] Tics!” – Adam Clark.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day goes to … Adam Clark, who wins a copy of Games of My Life by Sir Alex Ferguson. It’s out now and available in The Guardian Bookshop alongside loads of other great football titles. Terms and conditions for our competitions are here.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta’s new contract reflects where the power now lies at Arsenal | Ed Aarons
Sports.content:
If anyone doubts Mikel Arteta’s status as No 1 at Arsenal in the week he committed his future to the club until 2030, just ask Win the dog. The chocolate labrador who played a starring role in the celebrations when Arsenal were crowned Premier League champions in May has become part of the family at the training ground in Hertfordshire since being introduced by Arteta in May 2023.

Kai Havertz, David Raya and Mikel Merino, who issues commands in Spanish and has spoken about spending time with Win when out for three months with a foot injury, are particular favourites. But, according to sources close to Win, a therapy dog trained not to bark, there is no contest when it comes to her preferred human: Arteta.

The manager is understood to have taken Win home for Christmas last year, having been instrumental in her arrival a few days after his side had finished as runners-up to Manchester City for the first time. Cuddly replicas are available in the club shop. The real version spends most days at Arsenal’s training centre, with her primary carer a full-time member of staff based there.

“I carefully chose the dog and in my opinion it’s the perfect representative of who we are right now,” said Arteta in 2023. “Win needs accountability from us because we have to look after her as well; her emotions and what she needs.”

It is an example of Arteta’s attention to detail that has helped to transform Arsenal from also-rans into champions. Ominously for the rest, the Spaniard promised on Wednesday, when he signed a new four-year contract understood to be worth more than £20m a season, that this “is only the beginning” of what Arsenal hope could be a trophy-laden dynasty under his leadership.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta ended Arsenal’s wait for a Premier League title last season and has designs on further silverware. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

The length of deal was significant given that it would take Arteta, who will mark his seventh anniversary in the job in December, past a decade at the helm – even if he still has some way to go to match Arsène Wenger’s record of almost 22 years in charge. Wenger’s first day was 30 years ago last week and he quickly assumed control at the club. The influence of Arteta, made Arsenal captain by Wenger in 2014, has grown steadily since he was appointed after a stint as Pep Guardiola’s assistant at Manchester City.

Arteta, upgraded from head coach to manager in September 2020 having won the FA Cup six months after replacing Unai Emery, has seen various executives depart as his power has increased. The 44-year-old, who became the second-youngest manager after José Mourinho to win the Premier League, has a direct line to the co-chair Josh Kroenke and is able to exert a major say over most big decisions – on and off the pitch.

Arsenal’s announcement this week that they had decided against a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium came after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would be caused by a temporary move to Wembley or elsewhere. The owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment (KSE), is also thought to have been put off proposals to increase the capacity to 70,000 owing to the cost, despite agreeing a record $4bn (£3bn) deal to buy the MLB side Los Angeles Angels last month.

That did not stop KSE from making Arteta the best-paid manager in the Premier League with a hefty salary increase from the £10m plus £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League that he agreed in 2024. Only Atlético Madrid’s Diego Simeone is thought to earn more.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta is understood to have had the final say in the decision not to pursue interest in Malick Fofana after the Belgium forward was offered in the final days of the transfer window because he wanted to ensure the 16-year-old phenomenon Max Dowman would not be denied opportunities. He may regret not bringing in another forward after Christos Tzolis sustained a hamstring injury with Greece that is expected to keep him out for at least three weeks, but it is clear Arteta has been calling the shots even since the arrival of Andrea Berta as the sporting director in March 2025.

Such is the intensity Arteta brings to the job that it remains to be seen whether he can last as long as Wenger, although there are few signs that operating in such a high-pressure environment has affected him physically.

The odd grey hair aside, he barely looks different from the day he was announced in his first managerial role. With the twin motivations of making Arsenal back-to-back league title winners for the first time since the 1930s and European champions after coming so close last season when they lost to PSG in the final on penalties, Arteta appears to be here to stay.

Sports.title: Defiant Enzo Maresca insists players and staff 'completely trust' Man City despite guilty verdict and insists there are NO concerns in dressing room after Erling Haaland became first star to speak out
Sports.content:
Defiant Enzo Maresca insists players and staff 'completely trust' Man City despite guilty verdict and insists there are NO concerns in dressing room after Erling Haaland became first star to speak out

Enzo Maresca says he is 'very calm' despite Manchester City's seismic guilty verdict and has claimed the club's players 'don't care too much about the noise'.

The Premier League giants have appealed a devastating independent panel verdict that they broke competition rules over a nine-year period by illegally pumping in more than £900m, and are currently awaiting a sanction that could see them relegated, with trophies stripped.

Speculation has been rife that City's stars may soon be forced to seek an exit from the Etihad Stadium over what could be a potentially-crippling few months.

But Maresca, whose side return to action for the first time since the verdict was made public at what is sure to be a hostile Anfield on Sunday, believes City will prevail and has attempted to play down concerns.

In an interview with club media on a day when chief executive Ferran Soriano is understood to have addressed players returning from the international break, he sounded a defiant note.

'Personally, I'm very calm to be honest,' he said. 'The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club. We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.'

Enzo Maresca (pictured arriving to training on Thursday morning) insists he is 'very calm' about Manchester City's situation with the Premier League despite being found guilty

The City boss says he 'trusts' the club completely as they await their appeal against sanctions

Some have wondered what the impact of the verdict, which raises huge questions over a glittering period in City's history from 2009 to 2018, will have on the likes of Erling Haaland and Eliot Anderson.

However, the former Chelsea manager attempted to downplay any fears over the atmosphere within his dressing room. 'The feeling is fantastic, to be honest,' he said.

'The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league.'

Maresca added that his squad's concentration remained on the pitch, despite all of the noise around the club.

'The players are just focused on that (football),' he said. 'They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things. They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise.'

City are in for a noisy afternoon in Liverpool, with previously reporting how police on Merseyside have a plan in place while some fans are planning to provide a 'welcoming party' to the visitors as they arrive for the 4.30pm kick-off.

But Maresca, who will face the media on Friday, is hoping for a repeat of last year's victory.

'They (the players) are just focused in this moment on how we can bear Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield.'

Marc Guehi kept a low profile as he drove into Man City's training ground for the first time since September

Josko Gvardiol returned to Manchester after facing off with England for Croatia at Wembley

Summer signing Elliot Anderson arrived around lunchtime after returning from England duty

Antoine Semenyo and Ayyoub Bouaddi were also on parade as they returned to their club

When asked by if he had a message for City fans, he asked for their support.

NOTTINGHAM FOREST BOSS OLIVER GLASNER ON MANCHESTER CITY Oliver Glasner has urged football chiefs to wrap up the Manchester City case quickly or risk fans turning their backs on the Premier League. City were found guilty of all but one of their charges of breaking financial rules in a bombshell verdict that has rocked English football. The club have appealed against the findings that they artificially inflated commercial revenues by £830million through 'sham' contracts with a range of Abu Dhabi-based companies. City were charged with 115 financial breaches in February 2023 and three-and-a-half years passed until the verdict. Nottingham Forest boss Glasner is hoping for much swifter timeline now. Glasner said: 'Let's wait until the final verdict is spoken, but my wish is just that this is quick. When I was at Crystal Palace, we didn't know until 10 days before the European competitions started whether we would be playing in the Conference League or the Europa League. 'And that's why I think this must be [completed] as soon as possible. There is still damage for the Premier League, not just in England. It's a big topic all over the world, especially in Europe. The most important thing is the integrity of the league because as soon as the fans can't trust it, they won't watch it anymore.' Glasner was in charge of Palace when they beat Manchester City in the 2025 FA Cup Final. He takes his new club to Selhurst Park to take on the Eagles on Sunday. By Tom Collomosse

'Anfield away, we're going to bring our [patience], we're going to bring our gameplan. But for sure we need their voice, their [patience]. In the last two days I watched last year's game at Anfield and the celebration at the end was fantastic.

'We need to be all together. I said many times the reason why this organisation in the last 15 years was top was because from the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, the manager, players, fans, they are all on the same page. And this is fantastic.'

The Italian was also quizzed by the in-house team on whether the motto on the club's former crest 'Superbia in Prelio (Pride in Battle)' was particularly significant during these deeply troubling times.

'Yes, Superbia in proelio - Latin, Italian, we are quite close on that,' he said. 'It's what we need. We know that the next two games are going to both be battle, especially Anfield away.
