World.title: Nebraska Christian therapists sue city over ban on helping minors accept their biological sex
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Christian counselors are suing Lincoln, Nebraska, over an ordinance they say threatens therapists with jail, fines and professional consequences for helping minors who want to become comfortable with their biological sex or address unwanted same-sex attraction, even after the Supreme Court struck down a similar Colorado restriction earlier this year.

Thomas More Society Senior Counsel Matt Heffron told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that Lincoln's ordinance amounts to government "viewpoint discrimination," arguing counselors are permitted to help minors move toward gender transition but barred from counseling them toward accepting their biological sex when that is the client's stated goal.

"The government allows certain type of speech in therapy sessions, and it disallows other sorts of speech or viewpoints," Heffron said. "It's just a confirmation of government viewpoint, government-favored speech over disfavored speech."

FIRED SCHOOL COUNSELOR LOSES AGAIN AFTER FREE SPEECH FIGHT OVER GENDER-THEMED BOOKS IN HIS OFFICE

Heffron said Lincoln's ordinance prevents counselors from helping minors who want to become comfortable with their biological sex or address unwanted same-sex attraction.

He argued that a nearly identical Colorado restriction was found unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Chiles v. Salazar as viewpoint discrimination and that the Eighth Circuit subsequently reached a similar conclusion in a case involving Kansas City.

EXCLUSIVE: INDIANA SCHOOL COUNSELOR FIRED FOR SPEAKING OUT ON GENDER IDENTITY POLICY SETTLES LAWSUIT FOR $200K

Heffron said a counselor accused of having those conversations could face an investigation and potentially a misdemeanor charge, a $500 fine, a $100 civil penalty and the loss of professional licenses or credentials.

Heffron said Thomas More Society repeatedly asked Lincoln to repeal the ordinance or agree not to enforce it, but after the city declined to do so and stopped responding, the group filed suit.

DETRANSITIONERS REVEAL HOW DOCTORS PUSHED THEM TOWARD LIFE-ALTERING TREATMENT AS TEENS

"The stakes of this case as far as minors are concerned, is that there are minors out there, and a fair number of them is what I hear, who are perhaps faith-based or for other reasons, they are unhappy with same-sex attraction that they may be experiencing or they're unhappy with what used to be called gender dysphoria," Heffron said.

"And these minors go to a therapist, particularly a Catholic one like the one in this case, and they ask to be helped. It's awful, it's cruel to tell those children they can't be helped," he added. "In fact, the only thing that the statute or that ordinance allows is it will allow that therapist to help guide them into gender transition with all of the evils that include surgeries and hormones and that sort of thing. They can guide them into that. And they can make them comfortable with their same-sex attraction."

CATHOLIC NUNS CARING FOR DYING PATIENTS FIGHT NEW YORK TRANS RULE, FACE JAIL TIME

In this instance, Heffron said the government is policing speech.

"When an ordinance tries to say what sort of view is allowed, what sort of speech is allowed, that's viewpoint discrimination," Heffron said.

World.title: MAHA fractures deepen as some RFK Jr. followers turn to harsh critics
World.content:
Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides.

A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy’s campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy’s former chief speechwriter.

NBC News is first to report on the scorecard, which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives.

“We’re asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they’ve made to the MAHA movement, and we’ve seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face,” said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard.

About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF, a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn’t a primary reason for supporting the movement.

MAHA coalesced during Kennedy’s presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases.

But many of these advocates have become Kennedy’s harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration.

Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market. Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn’t put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S.

That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause.

“What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure,” said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration “has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

“After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy “remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability.”

“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government,” she said in a statement.

Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration’s actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy’s purview. But his time in the administration has done “obvious harm” to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy’s career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with.

“To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it’s probably working against his own inclinations,” Cianci said.

Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn’t fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump’s Cabinet because she knows “where his heart lies.”

“I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it’s something that he himself has criticized for years,” she said. “[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised.”

Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government.

Over time, though, MAHA’s main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement.

“What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals,” Lurie said.

Much of Cianci’s scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA’s decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises.

Phasing out food dyes

Several of the promises that were “partially kept,” according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration.

For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is “generally recognized as safe.” The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however.

Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but “never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?”

The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines, which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods.

It also does not address Kennedy’s vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.)

“If you’re going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it’s very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines,” Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said.

Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.”

But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections.

“The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump,” she said. “The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw.”

World.title: Trump’s pledge not to strike Iran before midterms fails to soothe oil markets
World.content:
The price of oil jumped early Thursday amid reports that President Donald Trump was weighing whether to resume large-scale U.S. military operations against Iran in the coming weeks.

That sharp rise in oil prices slowed, however, after Trump wrote on Truth Social that the United States, “Will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections.”

Brent crude oil rose as high as $105.92 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil rose to as high as $93.20 per barrel. Benchmark diesel futures jumped 8% in European trading. Heating oil, a proxy for jet fuel, was up more than 6%.

Following Trump’s post, oil prices remained higher on the day by more than 3%.

In addition to the elevated Iran risk, oil prices Thursday reflected traders’ concerns about reports of Iranian proxy attacks in Saudi Arabia.

Hurricane Isaias also figured into the price of oil. Major oil companies with rigs in the Gulf of Mexico announced that work had been suspended at several locations, and crews evacuated as a precaution.

Trump’s post appeared to be a direct response to reports from outlets, including NBC News, that he was considering strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms.

NBC News and others noted that Trump had not yet made a final decision, however.

Key bond yields also dropped following Trump’s post. The 10-year yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates fell to its lowest level since Monday.

Stocks rose to their highest levels of the day, but remained in negative territory. The broad S&P 500 trimmed its losses to just 0.2%. The Nasdaq Composite was still down by about 0.5%, while the Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium-sized companies, traded lower by about 0.6%.

With the midterm elections less than a month out and early voting underway, any substantial action by the Trump White House in the coming weeks would be likely to have at least some impact on voter attitudes.

A return to large-scale U.S. strikes on Iranian targets would represent a significant escalation in the war and an end to the uneasy stalemate between Washington and Tehran that has held for three months.

The prospect of U.S. forces resuming strikes on Iran was first reported Wednesday by The Atlantic.

Smaller-scale Iranian attacks on commercial shipping have reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for global oil supplies, to just a fraction of prewar levels.

From Sept. 28 through Oct. 4, daily traffic in the strait averaged fewer than 23 ships a day, according to data from MarineTraffic. Before the war, hundreds of ships per day passed through the waterway delivering crude oil and related products to global markets.

Oil and commodities market experts have repeatedly warned that any escalation in the fighting in Iran will cause oil prices to trend even higher.

“The market remains exposed to significant risks,” Bank of America’s head of global commodities, Francisco Blanch, wrote in early September. If skirmishes curbing oil flows continued into the year’s end, he wrote, Brent could trade in a $95-$120 per barrel range.

01:09 Trump eases restrictions on 'red-dye' diesel 00:00 00:00

“Meanwhile, a broader conflict resulting in major energy infrastructure damage may spike prices” as high as $150 per barrel, he added.

The cost to ship crude oil from countries that are not directly impacted by the closure of the strait has also reached new highs, as producers scramble to meet demand.

It now costs $77 million for a crude carrier to move U.S. oil to Asia, according to Bloomberg, which cited data from the Baltic Exchange in London. The average price for the same route in 2025 was just $9.2 million.

The continued elevation of crude oil prices has caused gas prices to remain higher for consumers, with just weeks until polls close in the midterm elections. On Thursday, the national average price for regular unleaded gas was $4.36 per gallon. That price is more than 45% higher than when the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28.

Diesel fuel prices have soared even more, spurred on by recent escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war. At $6.28 per gallon, diesel has risen almost 70% since Feb. 28.

World.title: Ithaca city council calls on Cornell to report sexual assault investigations to local police
World.content:
The city of Ithaca called on the Cornell University Police Department to turn over sex and violent crime investigations to the Ithaca Police Department, after the city council voted nearly unanimously in favor of the measure. The decision late Wednesday came as a gang-rape allegation by a former Cornell student took the campus and nation by storm last month.

The Cornell University Police Department has said it did not refer its investigation of the 2024 allegation to the Ithaca Police Department. The former student, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month detailing the allegations and what she said was a lack of appropriate response by the university and its police department.

The city council also voted on Wednesday to temporarily suspend affiliated student organizations at the university, such as fraternities, from new assemblies, parades and special events “due to public safety concerns.” The moratorium on events would expire on Nov. 5, unless the council were to take further action, according to a meeting agenda.

The resolution passed by a vote of 9-1. The council did not say how the measure would be enforced or what would happen if the university did not comply. Cornell declined to comment, citing pending litigation.

More than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a poll conducted last year. That figure was up from 23% in 2023, according to the university.

The university police department and the local district attorney are under intense scrutiny over how the investigation into Doe’s allegations was handled.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten previously said he based his decision not to bring charges based on a six-page summary made by Cornell police of Jane Doe’s initial interview with police. But, according to reports, that summary was missing some of Jane Doe’s strongest remarks to police.

CBS News New York, citing a transcript of a conversation between Jane Doe and investigators, reported that she told campus police three weeks after the fraternity incident that she had been raped.

“I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” Jane Doe is quoted as saying.

World.title: At least 30 people killed after Russia bombs two buses in Ukraine
World.content:
At least 30 people were killed when a Russian bomb struck two buses in the Ukrainian front-line city of Kramatorsk on Thursday, local officials said, as Moscow’s intensifying attacks grow ever more deadly.

Another 18 people were wounded when the bomb hit a street in the city at 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET), Ukraine’s National Police said in a statement.

Kramatorsk’s regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians, sharing images of a charred bus wreckage and bodies and body parts on the road next to it. Filashkin said he was shutting down public transport in the city and neighboring Sloviansk in light of “the sharp deterioration of the security situation.”

The bloody aftermath left debris and body parts strewn across a road in the eastern city. Ukrainian National Police

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement on his social media channels that Russia struck “an ordinary public transport stop” in Kramatorsk with an aerial bomb.

In a later post, he said doctors were fighting to save the lives of those injured and “some of those killed have still not been identified because of the severity of their injuries.”

Kramatorsk is close to the active front line and part of Ukraine’s industrial Donbass region, which has been central to Russian President Vladimir Putin war plans.

Civilian casualties have surged as Russia intensifies attacks across Ukraine, which is running low on air defense munitions.

Zelenskyy said in a social media post that it was important the country received “new packages for Ukraine’s defense” promised by its allies. “Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day,” he added.

00:25 Russian bombs hit Ukrainian public buses 00:00 00:00

His comments came as Ukraine has suffered from an uptick in daytime attacks in recent weeks, creating a round-the-clock threat to civilians.

Thursday’s strike came a day after a missile strike on a residential building in the north of the country killed 22 people, including five children.

Zelenskyy visited the site of that attack Thursday, saying in a Telegram post: “Over a hundred residential buildings were damaged, as well as educational institutions, kindergartens, shops, enterprises, and infrastructure that supports normal life in the city.”

Moscow has repeatedly denied that it deliberately targets civilians in Ukraine.

Elsewhere, Reuters reported Zelenskyy as saying that Ukrainian negotiators will visit the United States for talks Friday and Saturday.

Urging President Donald Trump to step up pressure on Russia, he said: “One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of... diplomatic stalemate.”

World.title: Over 290,000 in Nepal face extreme flood risk as Himalayan ice melts, study finds
World.content:
Long before a wave of water rushed down the Bhote Koshi river and its tributaries, researchers were working to calculate just how many people are living downstream and exposed to potentially catastrophic flood risk in the areas that drain from Nepal’s high mountain basins.

The number they came up with — about 294,000 and growing — shows just how many people are living in areas of extreme risk in a country where climate change is destabilizing the rock and ice holding Himalayan slopes together and where meltwater is pooling in an ever-growing catalog of glacial lakes.

“For Nepal, it shows that there’s a lot of development going on very close to the river channel in these potentially hazardous zones,” said Scott Watson, a senior research fellow at the University of Leeds in England who studies glacial lakes. “That’s driven by tourism and the trade routes. The recent disaster was on the main trade route between Nepal and the Tibetan Plateau.”

The August disaster — when a massive rock and ice avalanche plunged off an almost 24,000-foot peak called Langtang Lirung and caused a debris flow that traveled about 120 miles — killed at least 1,455 people, and at least 5,285 people are still missing, according to Nepali authorities. Nearly 14,000 people were rescued.

If nothing is done, researchers say the number of people exposed will only grow.

“Hopefully, for Nepal, it’s kind of a bit of a wake-up call, this unfortunate recent disaster, in that there needs to be obviously a lot more focus on thinking about early warning systems, but also land use zoning,” Watson said. “We show that there’s a lot of buildings, there’s a lot of people very close to the river channel that are exposed to these hazards.”

About 108,000 of those people are downstream of glacial lakes, the researchers found. Many of those glacial lakes are pools of water dammed by ice that could fail and release a flush of water all at once.

The researchers started putting together this analysis in fall 2025, but it spent months undergoing academic peer review. They published their findings for the first time in the journal Scientific Reports on Thursday. The research is best viewed as a rough draft of where flood risk exists near Nepal’s high peaks — more thorough analysis is still needed.

The researchers performed their analysis by building a map of all rivers that originate in the transboundary areas of Nepal along the border with Tibet and India. They isolated areas within 50 kilometers, or 31 miles, downstream of glacial lakes or the headwaters of a river basin. Then, they mapped what would be exposed to floodwaters in a flood with 50 meters, or 164 vertical feet, of rising water downstream.

World.title: Curtis Flowers, wrongfully convicted man who was on death row, dies at 56
World.content:
Curtis Flowers, a Black man from Mississippi who was wrongfully convicted multiple times when he was tried six times for the same crime by the same prosecutor, has died. He was 56.

Flowers' family confirmed that he died Wednesday at his home in Winona, Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told CBS News on Thursday.

No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers' legal team. CBS News has reached out to the coroner.

Flowers' struggle with the justice system began in Winona, Mississippi, on a July morning in 1996, when the owner of Tardy Furniture, a bookkeeper, a delivery man and a 16-year-old were shot in the head execution-style.

Flowers briefly worked at the furniture store that summer, but he was let go after he stopped showing up after only three days. Police questioned him after the murders, but didn't arrest him at the time. Flowers later moved to Texas to live with his sister, and he was arrested there in January 1997. He had no prior criminal history.

McDuff previously called Flowers' case "unprecedented in the history of the American legal system."

He told "60 Minutes" in 2021 that the first three convictions against Flowers were overturned "because of the prosecutor's misrepresentation of the evidence to the jury and because of his discrimination in the selection of the jury."

The murder weapon was never found, and there was no DNA or fingerprints linking Flowers to the crime.

In the first trial, an all-White jury convicted him after just an hour of deliberation. Flowers, then 27, was sentenced to death.

His conviction was appealed and overturned. But he was tried five more times for the same crime by the same prosecutor. He had three more convictions overturned on appeal, in addition to two mistrials.

The prosecutor was District Attorney Doug Evans, who in 2010 finally got a conviction to stick in trial six, and Flowers returned to death row.

Then reporters at American Public Media's podcast "In the Dark" looked into the case. Their investigation led witnesses, including one who said Flowers had confessed, to recant their stories.

"In the Dark" reporters and producers also analyzed decades of court data that revealed Evans had a history of excluding Black people from juries at a disproportionate rate. Across all of Flowers' trials, 61 of the 72 jurors were White. All 61 voted to convict.

In 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Evans and the state of Mississippi had violated Flowers' constitutional rights and overturned his conviction yet again. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that there was a "relentless, determined effort to rid the jury of Black individuals." Six months later, Flowers was released on bail, leaving jail for the first time in 23 years.

"And I'm telling you, I felt like I was floating. I was just ready to go," Flowers told CBS News in 2021.

World.title: Hurricane Isaias threatens Gulf Coast with rain, flooding. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Isaias is intensifying Thursday and expected to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle. It became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season after strengthening from a tropical storm late Wednesday night.

A hurricane warning is in effect for the northern Gulf Coast, from the Mississippi-Alabama state line, across southern Alabama, to Panama City, Florida.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in his state, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties. Government buildings will close in nine Alabama counties on Friday, Ivey announced.

The U.S. Coast Guard also said it was preparing for Friday's landfall and urged seafarers near the Gulf to stay informed and remain vigilant leading up to the hurricane's approach.

"Extremely high seas, heavy rains, and damaging winds that accompany tropical storms and hurricanes present serious dangers to the public," the agency said in a statement Thursday.

Maps show hurricane's path

Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," had maximum sustained winds of 85 mph at 2 p.m. ET, and its core was located about 355 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the National Hurricane Center. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 15 miles from the storm's center, and tropical-storm-force winds extended outward up to 90 miles.

Map shows the potential path of Hurricane Isaias as it heads toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

"Additional strengthening is expected through early Friday, and Isaias should remain a dangerous hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday night," the center said, emphasizing that "preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds along the warning area of the Gulf Coast should be rushed to completion."

Mandatory evacuations have been ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa and Walton counties, which took effect Thursday at 12 p.m. ET. Voluntary evacuations were in place for coastal spots in southeastern Alabama, with officials in the city of Gulf Shores urging non-residents to leave the area to "help reduce congestion, support emergency operations, and ensure the safety of those who may be most vulnerable during the storm."

Dauphin Island Mayor Jeff Collier told CBS News on Thursday that his biggest concern for the coastal Alabama community was whether its residents and visitors would heed official warnings.

"Because what inevitably happens is people hear the warnings, but they don't actually take any action until it's much too late," Collier said. "And oftentimes if it's really bad, first responders can't get out to people until things calm down a bit."

Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued from the southeast corner of Louisiana to Biloxi, Mississippi, plus in and around Apalachicola, Florida. A storm surge warning was issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeastern Louisiana, across the coasts of Mississippi and Alabama, into the Florida Panhandle. A storm surge watch was also in effect for parts of Florida's Big Bend region, along the Gulf Coast.

Map shows the strength of the wind Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring to the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 15 inches in some places along the coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see heavy rainfall.

Forecasters said rain could cause flooding, including in urban areas and around rivers, "some of which could be significant." Tornadoes may also materialize Friday night into Saturday in coastal parts of Alabama, Georgia and the Florida Panhandle, they added.

"There's a great chance that this will spin off tornadoes," said DeSantis at a Thursday news conference, noting how twisters can occur far from the center of the storm. "Please be on the lookout. Even if you're way outside the cone, you could still have tornado risks."

Map shows amounts of rain expected through Saturday in some regions of U.S. CBS News

The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.

The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late-June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early- to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

World.title: Space station crew returns to Earth with perfect splashdown
World.content:
Crew 12 dropped out of orbit and returned to Earth on Thursday, one day after undocking from the International Space Station, in a meteor-like fireball of concentrated reentry heat, safely splashing down in the Pacific Ocean west of Los Angeles to close out a 237-day mission.

Commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev enjoyed a final day in weightlessness while waiting for their orbit to line up with the southwest-to-northeast reentry trajectory.

Right on cue, their Crew Dragon capsule "Freedom" executed a nine-minute thruster firing starting at 10:46 a.m. ET Thursday, slowing the ship just enough to drop it out of orbit.

A SpaceX Crew Dragon spacecraft splashed down in the Pacific Ocean west of Los Angeles, bringing four space station crew members back to Earth after nearly eight months in orbit. SpaceX via NASA

In less than 12 minutes, the Crew Dragon's velocity was reduced from 17,000 mph at the start of the descent to just 15 mph at splashdown thanks to atmospheric friction and, finally, braking provide by four large parachutes. SpaceX via NASA

Thirty-six minutes later, still moving at nearly 5 miles per second, the spacecraft slammed back into the discernible atmosphere, rapidly decelerating in a blaze of atmospheric friction.

Eleven minutes after that, now descending at a sharply reduced 120 mph, the Crew Dragon's main parachutes unfurled and inflated, lowering the ship to a relatively gentle 15-mph splashdown at 11:34 a.m. ET, about 50 miles west of Los Angeles

A SpaceX team quickly moved in to stabilize the spacecraft, which was hauled aboard the company's recovery ship Shannon shortly after splashdown.

Flight surgeons were standing by to give the crew members initial medical checks as they began their re-adjustment to the unfamiliar tug of gravity. All four appeared in good spirits as they were helped out of the capsule and rolled inside the ship on reclining chairs. They were to be flown ashore by helicopter before continuing on to the Johnson Space Center in Houston for debriefing and physical therapy.

Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir is taken inside the recovery ship Shannon for medical checks, smiling and waving to supporters along the way. SpaceX via NASA

"I think the thing that I'm looking forward to most is seeing my 3 1/2-year-old daughter," Meir said earlier. "Of course, our loved ones are the things that we miss the most."

After family, she added, "I'm so looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves, experiencing all those things that we don't have up here. But I will very, very much miss being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have."

"Going home and being able to take a nice long hot shower will be very relaxing and very nice," Hathaway said. "And of course, I'm looking forward to seeing my family. But a hot shower is near the top of my list."

Meir and company blasted off from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station atop a Falcon 9 rocket on Feb. 13.

A pre-launch shot of the Crew 12 fliers during training. Left to right: Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, pilot Jack Hathaway, commander Jessica Meir and European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot. SpaceX/NASA

After replacing four other Crew Dragon fliers, the fresh crew settled in for an eight-month stay in space, joining a three-man Soyuz crew. Over the course of their mission, Crew 12 sailed through 3,792 orbits spanning nearly 101 million miles, carried out four spacewalks and welcomed a fresh Soyuz crew in July and their own replacements earlier this month.

And as with all space station flights, Crew 12 carried out station maintenance and, most important to NASA, operated scores of experiments and research projects for scientists on the ground.

And then there's the view from 260 miles up.

The combined crew of the International Space Station, made up of crew members assigned to the Soyuz MS-29, Crew 12 and Crew 13 ferry ships pose with a group hug, or "huggle," before the Crew 12 fliers returned to Earth. NASA

"Looking down at the ocean, oh, there are so many amazing things that you see," Meir said. "We all know that 75% of our planet is ocean, but you really understand that when you're up here looking down on it below, because most of the time, when you look out of the window, you see the ocean.

"You understand how big it is, how immense it is and how important it is for the entire ecosystem of our planet," Meir continued. "We drastically need to do everything that we can to protect our oceans."

Left in orbit aboard the space station were Crew 13 commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. They launched to the lab on Oct. 1 and plan to remain aloft for six months.

Also on board are Soyuz MS-29 cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, along with NASA astronaut Anil Menon. They launched from Kazakhstan on July 14 and are working through an eight-month stay.

World.title: Christa Pike has pneumonia, unable to move arms after botched execution
World.content:
Christa Pike's attorneys said she had pneumonia, a blood clot, couldn't swallow, and was unable to move her arms or hands once she regained consciousness in a Tennessee hospital, days after the death row inmate survived a botched execution by the state.

Pike was "taking limited steps," with help, by Thursday, according to her team. But they've also said the lethal drugs she received may have lasting consequences for her mobility.

"Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove," one of Pike's attorneys, Randy Spivey, told reporters at a Wednesday news conference. "It was extraordinary."

Spivey said he and Pike's other attorneys were told she was brain-dead on Monday and expected her to be removed from life support. But by the next day, she had woken up and started talking, he said.

The attorney said it was his understanding that Pike's first words were, "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"

"I don't have an explanation for what happened," Spivey told reporters after a hearing at Davidson County Chancery Court. He said that Pike was confused and disoriented at first, but she began to remember details of the execution attempt on Wednesday.

In addition to the lung infection, a blood clot in her arm, and an issue swallowing that had prevented her from eating, Pike's arms and hands are "tremendously swollen," said Spivey, adding that "we don't know what function she will regain."

Another attorney for Pike, Steve Ferrell, described her cognition as "foggy" and told CBS News partner BBC News on Thursday that she could suffer "permanent damage," although he said that he hasn't personally seen her since she was hospitalized.

Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S., according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Court grants request for evidence

Before Pike's attorneys shared updates on her health outside of the Davidson County court on Wednesday, they attended an emergency hearing in which they requested Tennessee's correctional department to preserve records and other evidence of her failed lethal injection.

Chancellor I'Ashea Myles granted the order and said the state would be mandated to preserve "relevant evidence" of its failed attempt to put Pike to death on Sept. 30, including "drugs, IV lines, needles, catheters, medical supplies, restraints, gurneys" and anything else in the execution chamber at the time of the procedure.

Myles said waste, such as packing supplies and labels, and all written or digital records, including records of communication through encrypted platforms, witness accounts, and correspondence regarding equipment or drug administration issues, must be preserved, too.

She explicitly directed the state "not to lose, misplace, accidentally delete, any information that may be pertinent to this litigation."

"To any extent that any information or any evidence has already been discarded, deleted, destroyed or no longer exists, I want [the Tennessee Department of Correction] to take an affirmative step to try to claw back that information and put in policies and procedures, while this incident litigation is pending, to ensure that no information is discarded or destroyed," said Myles.

Execution aftermath

Staff had given Pike, 50, two doses of a lethal injection drug, but her legal team confirmed shortly after the failed procedure that, in an unprecedented turn, she was alive and had been hospitalized. Her legal team said on Tuesday that she had regained consciousness and was speaking from her hospital bed.

Pike's attorneys also said Tuesday she was continuing "to receive critical medical care" as hospital workers attempted to clear her system of the lethal drug pentobarbital. Her prognosis remained unclear, they added, but she was expected to face, at minimum, "a long recovery."

The legal team has renewed its calls for Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike's death sentence, pushing him to change the sentence to life in prison without parole so that the state can't attempt to execute Pike a second time, which is the usual course of action after an inmate survives botched execution proceedings. However, while others have survived botched procedures before, Pike is the only known inmate in the United States' modern death penalty era to remain alive after actually receiving lethal chemicals.

"The state has made no promises that Ms. Pike will not be subject to a future execution," Luke Ihnen, one of Pike's attorneys, said in court on Wednesday. Evidence sought by the defense for the correctional department to preserve could help them build future arguments to prevent that from happening, Ihnen added.

Will Ayers, the assistant attorney general for the state of Tennessee, told the court that there's no pending execution order for Pike, and "there is no allegation that one is coming."

Attorneys for Pike had filed an emergency motion Friday asking that the correctional department be required to "preserve all relevant physical, written and electronic evidence" of the failed execution, which, they said, amounted to "evidence of TDOC [Tennessee Department of Correction] inflicting a cruel and unusual punishment on Ms. Pike through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol."

They accused correctional staff tasked with handling Pike's execution of failing to properly establish an IV line through which to administer lethal drugs, and then failing to realize she had a "blown vein," allegedly allowing pentobarbital to spread through her body and causing a painful, botched procedure. In court, Ihnen also referenced the secrecy that shrouds execution protocols and proceedings in Tennessee and elsewhere across the U.S., which makes arguing death penalty cases particularly challenging.

"We don't know what they have, because they won't tell us," Ihnen said in court. "And so the preservation order seeks the broadest possible preservation of evidence."

Case history

Lee had denied Pike's request for a commuted sentence before her execution date last week, rejecting her clemency petition in the days leading up to it. In its aftermath, he canceled the one remaining execution scheduled to take place in Tennessee by the end of the year and said an investigation would be conducted to determine what went wrong. The now-former Tennessee correctional commissioner stepped down from his post, although an official statement from the agency claimed it had followed protocols.

Pike was convicted in 1995 of the brutal murder of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Court filings show that Pike, then 18, tortured and killed Slemmer, slashing her with a meat cleaver and box cutter for up to an hour in a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus, with help from her boyfriend and a friend.

When Slemmer's body was found, she had pentagrams carved into her forehead and chest, and a piece of her skull was missing. Other students later told investigators that Pike had bragged about removing the piece of skull and revealed to at least one person that she'd kept it as a "souvenir."

Pike spent more than three decades on Tennessee's death row. As the only woman awaiting execution in the state for a vast majority of that time, she was alone for almost the entirety of her incarceration. She was the first woman Tennessee attempted to execute in more than 200 years and the first person the state attempted to execute in modern times for a crime they committed at age 18, 19 or 20.

Prior to Pike's botched injection, her case had garnered public interest as human rights leaders and advocacy groups rallied against her death sentence, raising issues with her age at the time of her conviction and long history of mental illness and childhood abuse. But those who strongly support her execution, including prosecutors and jurors in Pike's original trial as well as judges who presided over that case and many of her appeals, have countered that capital punishment is warranted given the horrific nature of her crime. Among them is Slemmer's mother, May Martinez.

World.title: FlyDubai co-pilot bashed women in thousands of "manosphere" X posts
World.content:
The FlyDubai co-pilot whose alleged violent attempt to crash a flight to Israel last week and kill everyone onboard has a history of writing and sharing misogynistic remarks on social media using the rhetoric of the so-called manosphere, CBS News has found.

Many posts written and shared by Hamam al Hamami on an X account that has since been deleted used derogatory language about women espoused by misogynistic online influencers. Some of his posts included violent rhetoric. In one, he threatened to "stamp on your head, wipe the floor with you, make you an example to others, and then release you." It is not clear if he was speaking about one person in particular, or referring to women in general.

Multiple sources familiar with the investigation into the alleged hijacking attempt told CBS News last week that al Hamami is an Omani national and was the co-pilot who attacked the plane's captain with a cockpit emergency ax as it approached Israel on Sept. 27. Passengers and crew managed to subdue him, according to their own accounts, and an off-duty flight crew on the jet made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

An Israeli security official told CBS News authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack. President Trump suggested a couple of days after the incident that the co-pilot could have links to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."

Passengers board a FlyDubai flight bound for Dubai before taking off from Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv, Sept. 30, 2026. Jack GUEZ/AFP/Getty

The co-pilot's posts on X, which were made between November 2021 and late October 2022, paint a picture of a man who, at least during that period, had a very skewed view of women and a low opinion of men who, in his words, "grovel" to them.

"No matter how much you grovel or 'lick their feet,' you can forget about ever being with them; you chose the cheap, easy route to approach the opposite sex instead of elevating your own value as a man," he said in one post, which CBS News found an archived version of online. The posts were written in Arabic.

The Financial Times reported Wednesday that it discovered some 3,000 misogynistic messages posted or shared by al Hamami as part of an investigation, including him calling women "rotten meat."

According to the FT, he also lauded flying as "the safest means of public transport."

CBS News has not independently reviewed all of the posts cited by the FT.

Al Hamami's posts mingled the rhetoric of extremist interpretations of Islam with that of the manosphere movement. The only woman he spoke of positively was his mother, whom he credited with raising him and his siblings "on religion, morals, and virtue."

In one archived post seen by CBS News, al Hamami uses the manosphere term "simp" to describe a man "who hangs around feminist circles, licking women's feet in hopes of gaining their approval and getting closer to them. Typically, only a low-value male resorts to this behavior, turning to foot-licking as the easiest way to ingratiate himself with women. Does this mean I have to lick women's feet? The only woman whose feet I would kiss is my mother. As for the 'simp,' he has no dignity; he licks the feet of any woman — worthy or unworthy — just in hopes of getting close to one of them."

Al Hamami said in January 2022, that he was hoping to get married and move out of his parents' home as he neared the age of 25, but that he would only consider a woman who met very specific criteria.

He turned to a Muslim dating website in the hope of finding a woman between 18 and 23, according to the FT, and said he was seeking a "religious Saudi from a tribal background" who was willing to wear a face cover, not seek work outside the home, and to live abroad.

His failed search led him to conclude, according to the X posts viewed by FT, that most women "care primarily about money" and are "skilled at pretense."

The posts seen by the British newspaper included more aggressive language, including the assertion that a woman's "only obligation is to lift her legs," and that women who seek a divorce deserve "a good thrashing."

Israeli investigators believe the co-pilot acted as a lone wolf in the alleged hijacking attempt at the end of last month, people familiar with the matter told CBS News. He is in the United Arab Emirates, where he is undergoing interrogation by Israeli and UAE authorities.

Speaking to Fox News last week, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"

Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.

One source told CBS News that he resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty, and then left the airline around 2024.

At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of planes belonging to Israeli flag carrier El Al airlines in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, the al Qaeda leader believed to have helped plan the Sept. 11 terror attacks on the U.S., who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.

Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.

It remains unclear how, despite his history of espousing both Islamic radicalism and misogyny — and questions over whether he should have been cleared to fly to Israel at all as an Omani national — he managed to become a pilot flying dozens of people to and from Tel Aviv.

World.title: Suicide is up among Black Americans. We need to talk about it.
World.content:
Suicide is up among Black Americans. We need to talk about it.

My brother took his own life on May 10, 2010. Rarely a day goes by that I don't think of him. But just because I thought about him, it didn't mean I could talk about him. For a long time, I couldn't.

Sometimes when the subject of suicide came up, I would want to — or literally have to — leave wherever I was. Not helpful if you're in the news business.

I've come to realize that I have to talk about it. We have to talk about it.

Why do we have to? Because our silence is not protecting us.

Sponsor Message

Suicide is a public health crisis for the country — but that crisis is becoming acute in the Black community. Black suicide rates are climbing, increasing more than 50% over about the past 10 years according to CDC data. And the suicide rates among Black youth are increasing particularly dramatically. The rate of Black youth suicides by firearms exceeded that of white youth in 2022.

At a time when government-sponsored public health initiatives are retreating from issues that impact different communities differently, we're going there with care, sensitivity and honesty.

I hosted an NPR's Morning Edition live event called Going There: A Matter of Life and Death. It brought together a panel of clinicians, lawmakers and people who have lived with this pain to talk about this epidemic, in front of a live audience who have also experienced it. Speakers include CEO emerita of BET Debra Lee, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-NJ, psychiatrist Dr. Paul Nestadt, retired NFL champion Vernon Davis, WWE superstar Ettore "Big E" Ewen and Rev. Johnny Parker, who is both a pastor and a counselor.

It was an attempt to try to find out why this crisis is happening, how it is affecting us, and most importantly, what we can do about it.

Sponsor Message

During the conversation, Super Bowl-winning tight end Vernon Davis shared his struggles with panic attacks and depression.

"I would have these episodes in the game," Davis said, "I would go sit on a bench and breathe hard. I just felt like, for a split second, that I didn't want to be here. I had nothing to live for. It happened so fast, and it was just so sudden."

Davis now says that focusing on his mental health is a daily priority. And, after Davis lost both his brother and sister in quick succession, he started speaking more openly about his experiences with mental health.

"There's people out there who are going through the same thing that I went through," he explained, "they just need to hear that there's someone else out there that is going through the same thing."

Dr. Paul Nestadt is a psychiatrist, medical director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Suicide Prevention, and a national authority on suicide. He notes that white people still account for the majority of suicide deaths, and the suicide rate has decreased slightly among white Americans. Meanwhile, the rate has gone up among Black Americans. Access to guns accounts for at least part of that increase.

"When that trend in young Black people, especially young Black males, started to go up was also a time when we saw a dramatic increase in firearm ownership in the Black community. That was in 2020, in the context of the pandemic, the murder of George Floyd, and a variety of other things," Nestadt said.

As a result, 2025 survey data shows the lowest rate of self-reported suicide attempts among young Black people in America in years. But, Nestadt said, "the death rate has gone higher than it's ever been. And that just comes down to the fact that when an attempt is made, now with so many more guns in the house, that attempt is fatal."

Sponsor Message

Nestadt emphasized that it is crucial to correct several prevailing myths about suicide: chiefly that only people with long-term mental illnesses are vulnerable and that mentioning that you are concerned that someone might take their own life plants the idea. Neither is true. He says suicide is often an impulsive act, and interrupting that thought can work.

Every panelist brought similar words of wisdom. Among the most important advice:



Reaching out to offer support to loved ones who seem like they might be struggling can be lifesaving.



Free and low-cost resources and treatment options are out there, and are effective.



Remembering those we've lost to suicide as the full people that they were can be healing to those left behind.

There's a lot we can do to support each other and take care of ourselves.

And if you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can reach someone 24 hours a day, just to talk or to help get access to care.

World.title: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
World.content:
New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture

toggle caption i Ariana Cubillos/AP

NEW YORK — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations.

Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation.

The updated indictment "alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable," New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power.

"This is the epitome of corruption," McDonald said.

The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."

Sponsor Message

Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.

A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations.

The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.

They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted.

Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.

Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores' lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest.

Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.

Alleged torture victims included U.S. citizens

The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.

Sponsor Message

While the indictment doesn't name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.

Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.

Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years.

In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed "El Tigrito."

"It's incredible to see a dictator in court," Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. "The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations."

Former first lady denied release for medical treatment

Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.

Sponsor Message

They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during her capture.

Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an "extreme" flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.

U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores' request. He noted, among other things, that she's unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.

He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she's already on medication for that.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

World.title: 4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space
World.content:
4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space

toggle caption i NASA via Anil Menon

Three astronauts and a cosmonaut of NASA's Crew-12 mission have safely returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station.

The crew, commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway with mission specialists Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency and Andrey Fedyaev of Russia's Roscosmos, splashed down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., on Thursday, aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule.

Their trip home started about 45 minutes before, at an orbital speed of 17,500 mph.

The spacecraft lit its thrusters to nudge it out of orbit, causing the capsule to plunge into the atmosphere, its ablative heat shield battling extreme temperatures (up to 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit) during the fiery reentry. Over the course of about half an hour, the capsule slowed to a few hundred miles per hour, and then four orange-and-white parachutes took over, easing the spacecraft to just 16 mph above the cool, blue ocean and a gentle plop into the water.

Sponsor Message

The Crew-12 mission was the 20th time SpaceX had sent humans into orbit, lifting off in February on a Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. It docked with the space station the next day. During the eight months in space, NASA said the crew completed dozens of science experiments and research, including studies of stem cells, how crystals grow in space and bone loss in microgravity.

Not all of their work happened inside the space station. Meir conducted four spacewalks totaling just over 27 hours to perform maintenance and upgrade the aging orbital outpost. Adenot performed three spacewalks.

Before departing, members of the Crew-12 mission were relieved by the three astronauts and cosmonaut of Crew-13, who arrived at the space station last week to start a six-month rotation.

During a pre-departure news conference on the station last month, Meir said she couldn't wait to be reunited with her 3 1/2-year-old daughter.

But there was something else she missed after all this time in orbit. "So looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves. Experiencing all those things that we don't have up here," she said.

The two-time space veteran said there were two things she'd miss about space: weightlessness and the wonderful views of Earth.

World.title: White House correspondent April Ryan reflects on reporting while under attack
World.content:
White House correspondent April Ryan reflects on reporting while under attack

Ryan has spent decades pressing presidents for answers. She talks about access, power, race and how asking questions put her in President Trump's crosshairs. Her new book is Notes on a Blacklash. Sponsor Message

World.title: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
World.content:
South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.

Sponsor Message

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.

North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.

Sponsor Message

It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.

Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.

South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,

World.title: South Korea test-flies its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon
World.content:
South Korea test-flies its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon

toggle caption i Jeon Heon-kyun/EPA POOL via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea flight-tested on Thursday its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, bringing Seoul closer to what it says could be game-changing weapons capabilities.

There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it's a major step in strengthening the country's conventional defense capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place.

Sponsor Message

The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and maneuvered both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the "Korean Peninsula theater of operations."

Lee stressed that South Korea "must secure our security through our own strength," and also inspected the country's most powerful Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile on Thursday, his office said. It did not mention any direct comments by Lee on the North.

Tensions between the Koreas have increased in recent weeks after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border.

The South's military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South's demands for an apology.

North Korea has also stepped up weapons testing activity as its leader Kim Jong Un expands his military nuclear program while taking an increasingly hard line toward Seoul.

Kim has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump's calls to revive their diplomacy that broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its "hostile" policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for its denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

Sponsor Message

The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favors engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric toward the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts.

Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea's conventional defense capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States, which unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with the South in August, with Trump citing his "very good relationship" with Kim.

In its latest weapons test on Oct. 3, North Korea launched what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that it said flew more than 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). Japan said the missile landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.

South Korea said it detected the missile flying more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), while Japan's Defense Ministry said it assessed that the missile flew about 680 kilometers (422 miles).

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, claimed the differing flight estimates by the two U.S. allies showed they are incapable of properly tracking such a missile during its flight and would therefore not be able to intercept it.

World.title: Isaias intensifies to hurricane. And, judge orders Pike execution evidence preserved
World.content:
Isaias intensifies to hurricane. And, judge orders Pike execution evidence preserved

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Tropical Storm Isaias intensified into a hurricane overnight and is forecast to make landfall as early as tomorrow night near the Alabama Gulf Coast and the Florida Panhandle. Coastal communities in its path are preparing for high winds and flooding by stocking up on supplies to board up windows and gather sandbags. Residents who live farther inland are also preparing for inches of rain and wind.

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images

🎧 State officials have declared states of emergency so they can stage equipment along the Gulf, Lauren Linahan of NPR network station WBHM tells Up First. They're coordinating shelters and warning people to be ready, even though, with landfall more than 24 hours away, the forecast could still change. Some non-essential workers from oil production platforms in the Gulf have been evacuated — a common occurrence during hurricane season. If the storm gets really bad, oil prices could be impacted, Linahan says. Big events are still scheduled for this weekend, including the Alabama-Georgia SEC football game in Tuscaloosa on Saturday night, which President Trump is expected to attend. If the storm maintains its path, its worst impacts will happen that morning.

Sponsor Message

Republicans currently have a slim majority in the House, holding 218 seats to the Democrats' 214. With less than a month until Election Day, an NPR analysis of both parties' campaigns highlights key races that will shape control of the House in 2027. The Cook Political Report lists 43 competitive districts, including 22 toss-ups. But both parties are pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into shaping a much larger electoral landscape.



🎧 Some districts that voted for Trump and a Democratic House representative, or vice versa, in 2024 are expected to be close again in the midterms. But NPR's Stephen Fowler says the political landscape has changed drastically since then. With an unpopular president, rising prices and strong anti-incumbency sentiments, many more districts are now competitive. The unpopularity of the current administration, particularly among Latino voters who supported Trump, could lead to new Republican-drawn districts electing Democrats. There's a massive amount of money involved in these campaigns; AdImpact reports half a billion dollars in House ads leading up to Election Day. Both parties are essentially throwing a huge amount of resources at the wall to see what sticks, Fowler says.

The Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville has ordered Tennessee prison officials to preserve all evidence related to the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike last week. This includes log books, medical waste and all communications from officials involved in the execution attempt. The court granted Pike's attorneys "liberal access" to her, requiring prison officials to respond to requests for in-person visits within two hours. Pike's attorneys said that she is now awake, speaking and receiving critical medical care after several days of unconsciousness.



Sponsor Message

➡️ Meanwhile, Trump has approved the execution of a former U.S. Army psychiatrist by firing squad. Nidal Hasan killed 13 people in 2009 during a shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. This would mark the first U.S. military execution in more than 60 years and the first by firing squad since World War II. Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced that Hasan will be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. The Pentagon's decision, including the choice of firing squad, remains unclear, but some experts that NPR spoke with say it may relate to recent concerns over Pike's botched lethal injection.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico are in federal court today to argue that Trump is infringing on their constitutional rights by blocking their access to the White House. The news outlets say that they have the right to determine how, what and where they can cover the president at any given time. A judge last month issued a temporary restraining order preventing the Trump administration from barring the outlets from the White House while the court considered the lawsuit.



🎧 NPR's David Folkenflik says the White House has inconsistently followed the judge's order, including not allowing CNN to do the work it typically does at smaller spaces, like Air Force One. Although the White House has the right to deny access to its grounds, once credentials are granted, they cannot be revoked for dissatisfaction with the speech. The White House has been saying these outlets report fake news and have cited national security concerns, referencing questions from the outlets about the bunker and areas below the East Wing's newly renovated ballroom.

Behind the story

by Cooper Katz McKim , The Indicator from Planet Money associate producer

toggle caption i David Zalubowski/AP Photo/David Zalubowski/AP

The cost of diesel fuel is breaking records left and right. The previous record was $5.85/gallon. A few weeks ago, it hit $6.53/gallon. If I drove a diesel car, I might stay home.

Sponsor Message

At the Indicator, we've been watching whether President Trump would try to lower prices by banning exports of diesel fuel. He did not do that, though he did make diesel cheaper by expanding the use of tax-exempt diesel for highway vehicles through the end of the year. Still, I wondered why diesel prices are so consistently higher than regular gas.

We have a weekly newsletter at The Indicator where we track what's driving the economy and how it affects your life. It was the right platform to ask: Is diesel fuel inherently more expensive than regular gas?

The answer: NO! Before 2004, diesel was actually cheaper. But step by step, the price got higher.

The first domino to fall: taxes. In 1993, the federal excise tax on diesel increased to 24.4 cents, 6 cents more than the regular gas tax.

Soon after, demand for diesel began to skyrocket. China and India were ramping up industrialization, agriculture and new infrastructure to new levels. The world saw diesel vehicles take off.

In the U.S., the last major domino to fall was air quality standards. In 2006, diesel fuel needed to have less sulfur, which required new — and more expensive — refining and distribution methods.

One lesson that stuck with me is how diesel is essential for the modern economy. It's needed in shipping, long-haul trucking, mining and backup generators. Whether the cost is high or low, the demand is there. Regular gasoline? Demand is a little squishier.

You can check out the full segment here. And if you liked this story, subscribe to The Indicator newsletter here!

Life advice

toggle caption i Anton Vierietin/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Are you feeling nervous about facing a high-stakes event, such as a race or a job interview?
