Well, get ready to face those challenges head-on with the help of psychologist Cindra Kamphoff, the author of The Confidence Habit: 7 Core Practices to Transform Self-Doubt into Self-Belief. She shared with Life Kit some of her creative strategies for managing fear and negativity to overcome anxiety and build confidence before, during and after big tasks.

Sponsor Message

🏃 Practice positive self-talk. Even small affirmations can boost your self-esteem. You can even write them on your arm to remind yourself during events like races.

🏃 Set a range of goals instead of aiming for one perfect outcome. This approach can help to reduce anxiety by lowering the pressure and encouraging you to focus on the present moment.

🏃 When negative thoughts creep in before your task, ask yourself: Is this thought true? Is it serving me? And what empowering statement can I replace it with? This approach pauses negativity and helps you refocus on the present.

For more advice on how to beat performance anxiety, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

Diaa Hadid/NPR

NPR's Diaa Hadid is sending greetings from the Lahore High Court in Pakistan for this week's installment of Far-Flung Postcards. She describes it as "a near-perfect example of British South Asian colonial architecture." Opal Lee, the Grandmother of Juneteenth, celebrated her 100th birthday at the future site of the National Juneteenth Museum in Texas. (via KERA) A remarkably intact fossil discovery has given scientists new evidence about when the ability to chew and swallow food emerged among mammals.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine's public buses leave 30 dead as blackouts worsen in Kyiv
World.content:
Russian strikes on Ukraine's public buses leave 30 dead as blackouts worsen in Kyiv

toggle caption i Evgeniy Maloletka/AP

KYIV, Ukraine — A Russian-guided bomb exploded next to public buses filled with passengers in eastern Ukraine, authorities said Thursday, killing 30 people as part of a wave of attacks that also worsened power outages in the capital.

The morning attack occurred next to a bus stop in the war-torn city of Kramatorsk in Ukraine's Donetsk region, prompting public transport to be suspended in the area.

"There is no doubt that Russia is cynically targeting civilians," Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the city's military administration, said, adding that the rescue effort had been hampered by subsequent Russian attacks using small drones.

Sponsor Message

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Russia has escalated its aerial attack in recent weeks, putting pressure on Ukraine as it prepares for winter and hitting the infrastructure keeping its war-battered economy afloat. Recent targets have included energy systems, key industries, railways, post offices, shopping centers, telecom networks, gas stations and grain exports.

toggle caption i Evgeniy Maloletka/AP

Thursday's attack followed a Russian missile strike a day earlier that killed 22, including five children, in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky. Rescuers were searching the rubble of a residential building. At least 54 people were wounded. Several survivors slept in heavily damaged apartments because they couldn't find anywhere else to stay.

Ukraine appeals for more defense support from NATO

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy traveled to Pryluky on Thursday with visiting British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who announced new sanctions on Russia.

Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries.

"It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine's defense," he wrote in an online post. "Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day."

Sponsor Message

In audio clips responding to journalist's questions Thursday evening, Zelenskyy said a Ukrainian delegation would meet in the U.S. with President Donald Trump's representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff for two days beginning Friday to discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses, among other issues.

Ukraine's energy company DTEK said national grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power outages in Kyiv. Regular, rolling outages that occur on a schedule across the country will be halted during these shutdowns.

Officials are urging families to prepare emergency kits, store drinking water and maintain backup power sources, as Moscow keeps up the intensity of its attacks.

Kyiv police said bomb disposal specialists defused two unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings. Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv's Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said.

Ukrainian attacks damage data center and oil refinery

Russian technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline.

Also Thursday, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.

Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said most of the drones were shot down by air defenses, but one "reached a northern industrial hub." He didn't elaborate. Russian independent news outlet Astra reported that the Omsk oil refinery was on fire after the attack. There was no official confirmation of the report.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his government presented proposals to both Russia and Ukraine aimed at protecting civilian shipping in the Black Sea, while warning that commercial trade and grain exports could be disrupted by escalating military offensives.

Sponsor Message

Separately, Lithuania deployed about 100 additional soldiers to help secure the NATO member's border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, the Baltic country's defense minister, Robertas Kaunas, said. Sandwiched between Lithuania and Poland, Kaliningrad is separated from mainland Russia and remains a major security concern for NATO's eastern flank.

World.title: Will Ottawa really take Stelco to court? Here's what happened last time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stelco Holdings has days to share a plan to save hundreds of Ontario steel workers from layoffs already underway — or it risks legal action from the Canadian government.

The clock is ticking on what lawyers say is a test of how foreign investors are held to account as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to lure more of them to Canada amid a bitter trade war with the United States.

So, how idle is the threat? And is it likely to save workers' jobs? Here's what we know from the last time the federal government took the U.S. steelmaker to court.

2 decades since Ottawa fought ex-Stelco owner in court

In 2007, Pennsylvania-based U.S. Steel announced a deal to acquire Stelco, then a publicly-traded company, for about $1-billion US, and the company was renamed U.S. Steel Canada.

Major foreign investments must benefit the domestic economy, per the Investment Canada Act. So, foreign buyers must give legally binding written commitments — called undertakings — to the federal industry minister to prove the deal provides a "net benefit to Canada."

At the time, U.S. Steel agreed to several such undertakings, including a three-year commitments to maintain Canadian employment levels, and increase steel production in Canada by at least 10 per cent.

However, when the 2008 financial crisis sapped global demand, U.S. Steel closed most of Stelco's Canadian operations and laid off over 1,500 employees.

WATCH | Union says layoffs have begun: Layoffs start at Hamilton Stelco plant, union says | Duration closed caption 7:19 Layoffs at the Stelco steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., are underway and expected to roll out over three weeks, says Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005. Stelco worker Jordan Williams says he received his layoff notice at the end of his shift on Wednesday.

The Attorney General of Canada filed a lawsuit against U.S. Steel in July 2009.

"As far as the public record shows, it is the only time Ottawa has gone to court over commitments like this," Toronto-based business lawyer Nassira El Hadri told CBC News.

According to a summary of court filings compiled by a lawyer at Toronto-based Torys LLP, Stelco argued the undertakings only required compliance at the end of their three-year term, not before.

Stelco also said that per Industry Canada guidelines its investors should not be held accountable for factors beyond their control, like the unfolding financial crisis.

WATCH | Stelco worker speaks about his layoff notice: Layoff uncertainty 'a roller-coaster' for Stelco workers | Duration 1:12 Steelworker Jordan Williams describes the frustration he’s feeling after receiving a layoff notice from Stelco. Cleveland-Cliffs — the Ohio-based company that owns Stelco — started issuing individual layoff notices as it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers and idle production at the Hamilton plant.

Last legal battle ended in deal to keep making steel

The Attorney General of Canada formally withdrew the lawsuit in late 2011, ending in an out-court-settlement before the court could make a judgment.

U.S. Steel agreed to keep production alive in Hamilton and Lake Erie, and to make $50 million in new capital investments by the end of 2015 to modernize its operations. It agreed to new undertakings with Ottawa, but those did not include minimum worker headcount requirements.

But before then, in 2014, U.S. Steel Canada filed for creditor protection, and the American parent company severed ties with its Canadian operations.

In 2016, a New York-based private equity firm acquired the steelmaker. The Stelco name was revived when the company returned to the Toronto Stock Exchange the next year.

The dispute prompted updates to the Investment Canada Act in 2009 and 2012 to make settlement negotiations easier, and strengthen enforcement. The government later raised daily non-compliance fines to $25,000, and tightened reviews for sensitive industries.

What's happening now at Stelco?

Flash forward to 2024, when Ottawa approved Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs' $3.4-billion cash-and-stock deal to buy Stelco.

The conditions included a promise to maintain at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers, according to a government statement at the time .

Last week, Stelco announced a plan to idle certain production in Hamilton, resulting in up to 500 layoffs company-wide. The union says layoffs are already underway.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves said the cuts are necessary and justified by the Canada-U.S. trade war, arguing that Stelco's ability to sell steel to the U.S. was an "underlying condition" of the deal.

But in a letter Monday to Stelco president Paul Simon, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly gave Stelco five business days to share a job plan, or face legal action.

And on Tuesday, Joly slammed Goncalves's public support of American steel tariffs.

"He's in favour of these U.S. tariffs against steel," she said. "They cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure."

Will Stelco fight Ottawa in court again?

El Hadri says the matter is "most likely going to end up in court."

She points out that Joly's letter does not ask Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs for an explanation about why they plan to lay off workers. It states the company's commitments "do not cease to apply simply because business strategy or market conditions have changed."

"It may end up in a settlement as well, but it all depends on the economic conditions, like what's going on inside Stelco," El Hadri told CBC News.

The court has "wide powers" at its disposal, she said, including putting a business up for sale.

"We could end up with new commitments, which is what happened with Stelco in 2009."

Sandy Walker, co-chair of the competition and foreign investment review group at the global law firm Dentons, says it's still possible that Stelco could reverse course on its full layoff plans to avoid going to court.

"That depends on how effective the Canadian government’s threats are," she said told CBC News.

"There are many reasons why [it] may not end up in court, but may end up with a variation of its undertakings, or otherwise settling with the Canadian government."

At the same time, Walker says those Industry Canada guidelines on factors beyond a company's control may let Stelco "off the hook" to some extent.

What does this mean for PM's agenda?

Both Walker and El Hadri agree the timing is somewhat awkward, given Ottawa's push for $1-trillion worth of investments across the country over the next five years.

Last month, Carney hosted hundreds of deep-pocketed investors at an investment summit in Toronto in a bid to spur deals, and cut reliance on the United States.

"We are giving a signal to the world that ... you have to respect our rules," El Hadri said.

"It's a difficult balance," Walker said. "The government has got to worry about looking weak."

World.title: Ottawa to provide $2B in rebates for homeowners who install heat pumps
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government is launching a $2-billion rebate program that it says will help homeowners in Canada lower their annual heating costs while reducing emissions when they install heat pumps in their homes.

The funding will provide rebates for up to 820,000 homeowners over the next eight years, saving them an average of $1,400 a year on their heating bills when they replace existing heat pumps or heating systems, officials speaking on background said Thursday.

"Homeowners can apply quickly for the rebate when their existing heating system breaks down and they decide to replace it with a new heat pump system," a background document said.

"They can also apply as their existing heating system approaches end of life, and they want to make the transition before a breakdown occurs."

The federal government said it will also work with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) to provide low-interest financing for apartment building owners to retrofit more than 280,000 homes over the next eight years.

"When fully taken up, these upgrades will save Canadian families more than $1 billion every year on their energy bills, that is a great return on investment," Carney said in Sherbrooke, Que.

The federal government is also providing $110 million in funding over three years starting in 2027-28 to renew the Deep Retrofit Accelerator Initiative.

That program provides funding for energy and emission reduction retrofits in commercial, institutional, and mid- or high-rise multi-unit residential buildings

Targeting emergency heating system replacements

The program, which will not begin until early next year, is targeting homeowners that need emergency replacements because their existing system has broken down.

The federal government said every year about one million Canadian households replace their heating system, with 80 per cent of those replacements taking place because their existing system broke down.

In the vast majority of cases, officials explained, people replace their existing system with the same one they had before. The officials explained the government wants to change that pattern.

Officials said the program is being announced months before it launches in order to give government time to consult with industry and allow installers to stock up on heat pumps.

Rebates and eligibility

The program will give rebates to households who earn below the median after-tax income in their province up to $10,000. Households earning over the median after-tax income in their province get a maximum rebate of up to $2,000.

Carney said the program can be combined with provincial grants and rebates for installing heat pumps which will result in further up-front savings.

Officials speaking on background explained the income cut-off will be calculated in the same way that it was for the now closed oil to heat pump program for low- and middle-income households launched in 2022.

That program was focused on replacing oil furnaces and only in some provinces. The new program not only covers households across the country, but also the replacement of other types of heating systems including natural gas, propane, diesel and electric.

WATCH | More about heat pumps: Why people in Ottawa are choosing heat pumps to warm their houses | Duration 3:06 CBC’s Stu Mills spoke with some homeowners who have installed heat pumps about their pros and cons.

"To qualify for the rebate, heat pumps must be on the Eligible Products List, an extensive selection of over 100,000 options at various price points and configurations, all suited for the Canadian climate," a government background document said.

People wishing to apply for the rebate can do so before their system is installed through an online government portal that will determine the level of eligibility within 24 hours.

Once the heat pump is purchased and installed, homeowners can return to the portal, upload their receipts and have their rebate approved within five days. The federal government will make a direct deposit into the homeowner's bank account.

The program only permits one rebate per person, which means that if a landlord installs a heat pump in a property they own, they can't get a rebate for installing one in their own home as well.

The government says homeowners do not have to get a pre or post energy audit for their home to take part in the program.

Opposition leader says rebate will cost Canadians

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said the rebate program was going to cost Canadians money by taking $2 billion out of their pockets, giving them only a small amount in return.

"Here's an idea: why don't you leave the $2 billion in the pockets of Canadians — people like you, whom I trust," he said while looking into the camera in Ottawa on Thursday. "And if you want to spend your money on a heat pump, then the government should leave the money in your pocket for you to do so.

"Rather, Mr. Carney would take the $2 billion out of your pocket, give it to the bureaucracy that gives it to big corporations, and you're supposedly going to get a rebate for some part of an expensive home transition that you might not otherwise make."

World.title: Sask., Alberta premiers reject Elon Musk's call for provinces to separate from Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan have rejected a suggestion by one of the world's richest men that the two provinces should separate from Canada.

Elon Musk, a trillionaire tech businessman who was formerly an advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, weighed in on his social media platform Twitter, now known as X.

On Wednesday, Musk said Quebec would benefit from independence, as would Alberta and Saskatchewan.

The tech tycoon was responding to a quote from Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who said the province's independence "will be realized one day."

On that same day Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one-word response to Musk in his own social media post: "No."

Moe was not available for an interview on Thursday and his office said he had nothing more to add to the post.

WATCH | Canada's future 'will be decided by Canadians': Carney on foreign interference: Canada's future 'will be decided by Canadians': Carney on foreign interference | Duration closed caption 0:58 Asked about whether he thinks Elon Musk's comments on Quebec sovereignty is an example of foreign interference, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada's future will be decided by Canadians' priorities. These priorities include living 'free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do,' he says.

According to the Canadian Press, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she also strongly disagrees with Musk's opinion.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was asked about Musk's comments Thursday while speaking in Quebec.

Carney said the future of Canada will be decided by Canadians, the priorities of Canadians and the people of Quebec.

"A strong Canada means more independent, more sovereign, more prosperous," Carney said, adding that Canada will be "free from foreign interference of foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do."

The state of play in each province

On Oct. 19, Albertans will head to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum on separation.

Smith has said she plans to vote to stay in Canada in the upcoming provincial referendum.

Moe believes Saskatchewan is stronger within a united Canada, but has previously said he would not stop a plebiscite if Saskatchewanians were able to secure enough signatures to trigger a referendum.

Moe has also enjoyed a much better relationship with Prime Minister Mark Carney than with his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

WATCH | Why Saskatchewan's premier says Trump's potash threats are 'not realistic': Why Saskatchewan's premier says Trump's potash threats are 'not realistic' | Duration closed caption 8:40 U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York that his country would stick with Canada as its potash supplier for the time being, while claiming Belarus is offering the U.S. potash at a much lower price. Power & Politics speaks to Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe about whether he thinks it's worth going back to the negotiating table with the Trump administration.

Moe has at various times refused to say Trudeau's name even after his departure from federal politics.

In Quebec, the sovereigntist Parti Québécois is back in power after a securing enough seats to form a minority government in Monday's provincial election.

Soon-to-be premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to hold a referendum.

World.title: The Democrats are surging as the U.S. midterms near. Here's the data that has Trump's Republicans spooked
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The upcoming midterm elections are a crucial test for U.S. President Donald Trump and the party he's dominated for the past decade — and early data points suggest it could be something of a bloodbath for the Republicans come November.

Poll after poll released in recent days suggests the Democrats are poised to make major gains among voters who, only two years ago, would have never given the party a chance.

Large swaths of the American electorate appear to be souring on Trump, who returned to power promising lower prices and no more foreign wars — but instead delivered higher prices and a war on Iran in the first two years of his second mandate.

Inflation is also running hotter than it was in January 2025, when Trump's second term began — which is significant because his predecessor, Joe Biden, also presided over an era of higher consumer prices.

Researchers say Trump's tariffs have only worsened affordability; without them, prices might have actually fallen slightly, affirming what many economists long predicted.

WATCH | Trump ramps up campaigning before midterms: Trump ramps up campaigning as midterm polls tighten | Duration closed caption 2:54 Donald Trump is hitting the campaign trail hard as Republicans face growing trouble in the midterms. New polls show Democrats making gains in key races, including some longtime Republican strongholds.

Oil and diesel costs have spiked partly because of the war on Iran and the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, the latter of which he promised to solve within 24 hours of taking office but has since struggled to help end.

After some early victories — stopping the surge of migrants with his border policies, and brokering peace deals — Trump's popularity has plummeted.

One number-cruncher says Trump is now the most unpopular Republican president since Herbert Hoover, whom historians generally regard as a failure given how he governed during the Great Depression.

"These are historically low approval ratings, like below Richard Nixon at the height of Watergate, and that really doesn't augur well for Trump and his party," said Asa McKercher, the Hudson Chair in Canada-U.S. Relations at the Brian Mulroney Institute of Government.

"Not only is Trump unpopular, but so are his policies, which have not borne out … any fruit."

That's why he is floating what McKercher calls "gimmicks" such as $5,000 cheques for every adult if the Republicans retain power in the midterms.

"There's a sense of desperation there," McKercher said.

Some Republicans distancing themselves

While Trump has repeatedly told his supporters to "pretend I'm on the ballot," thinking it will boost Republican fortunes in these congressional races, some of the party's candidates are distancing themselves given how toxic the president is in certain circles.

Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, who closely aligned himself with Trump in the past, released a new campaign ad Wednesday denouncing the president's trade war with Canada.

Just this summer, Rogers said Canadians "have not been good partners," but that was before polling showed the vast majority of Americans are opposed to tariffs on their northern neighbour. Politico found only 26 per cent of Americans surveyed think the Canadian tariffs are the right thing to do.

Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent running in Maine's tight Senate race, has said something similar about tariffs, while strongly suggesting she doesn't want Trump to campaign in her state.

"I’m not exactly his favourite senator," she said in a debate Tuesday.

More Americans now identify as Democrat

Perhaps the most revealing recent data point is the dramatic swing in how voters identify themselves when Gallup pollsters ask them to pick between the two parties.

For much of the last four years, Republicans held a clear edge.

Now, the Democrats hold a double-digit lead as some voters reject a party they thought would deliver better economic results, temper inflation and bring about peace.

Mark Bednar, a former spokesperson for House Speaker Kevin McCarthy who now works as a Republican strategist, said all is not lost for the party — Trump is still hugely popular among the MAGA base and he's defied the odds before.

But he said the party needs to urgently address what he calls the "enthusiasm gap," in which Democrats are much more motivated to turn out and vote than their Republican counterparts this year.

Bednar said there's one big bright spot for the Republicans that can help get those people fired up and off to the polls: a massive fundraising advantage.

Trump alone sits on a roughly $400-million campaign war chest that he can deploy in the closing weeks of this campaign to blanket the airwaves with ads and help boost candidates in tight races.

"The Republicans have a huge financial advantage and that gives them the opportunity to actually get out there, get your message on TV and tell your story as a Republican and prosecute the case against Democrats," Bednar told CBC News.

"The closer we get to these midterms, the closer the margins will be in some of these races."

U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the press at the White House. The Republicans have a huge financial advantage, which could help them close the polling gap with the Democrats. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty Images)

Reliably 'red' states in play, polls suggest

These midterm elections will decide who controls the balance of power in Washington.

Despite state-level efforts by Republicans to gerrymander the maps in their favour, polls suggest the party is poised to lose the House of Representatives — the final result could be relatively lopsided even with the creative map-making — and possibly the Senate.

On the face of it, the electoral map this year looks unfavourable to the Democrats, with many contests in reliably Republican states. (Only one-third of Senate seats are up for election every two years.)

But the most recent New York Times-Siena poll, which politicos watch closely given its past accuracy, shows states long thought of as "red" ones are in play.

Kansas, for example, hasn't returned a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but the Siena poll (and others) shows it could break that nearly century-old trend.

Farmers in particular have paid a dear price for Trump's trade war. Anyone who relies on a tractor or combine to get their products to market knows diesel prices have doubled on Trump's watch.

In the Republican crown jewel of Texas — where Trump beat Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the last presidential election by nearly 14 percentage points — new Siena data shows Democrat James Talarico has a six-point lead over the embattled Republican Ken Paxton.

Polls reveal why there has been such a dramatic shift in that historically ruby-red state: Hispanic voters are turning away from the Republicans.

According to exit polls from the 2024 presidential election, 55 per cent of Hispanics in Texas voted for Trump. But just 34 per cent of Hispanics surveyed say they will back Paxton in this campaign, according to YouGov.

About 64 per cent of Hispanics disapprove of the job Trump's done to this point.

This Hispanic shift follows nearly two years of immigration raids that rooted out many undocumented migrants, including some violent criminals, but also tore apart communities by removing people long established in the U.S.

But white voters in Texas, too, say they are much more likely to vote for Talarico, a political moderate and Presbyterian seminarian with a savvy social media presence, than they were for Harris two years ago.

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico pictured in Dallas on Sept. 9. A new poll shows Talarico with a six-point lead over his Republican opponent in the race for the Senate. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The inflation-battered economy has scrambled the electoral equation elsewhere.

In Ohio, a "Rust Belt" state that voted for Trump by wide margins three times, Democrat Sherrod Brown is leading his Republican opponent by three percentage points in the Senate race. Brown's pitch: "Life is too expensive."

As part of his recent campaign blitz, Trump visited both Ohio and Texas, but also Alabama and Oklahoma. This was an unusual move so close to a vote, when parties usually focus their leader's time on must-win swing states.

It suggests the definition of a "swing state" is much different now than in the recent past.

"This could be a perfect storm, where it's not just a blue wave but a blue tidal wave or tsunami for the Democrats," McKercher said.

World.title: Curtis Flowers, Black man whose conviction was thrown out after 22 years in U.S. prison, dead at 56
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the U.S. Supreme Court threw out his conviction and death sentence, has died. He was 56.

Flowers's family confirmed that he died Wednesday at his home in Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told The Associated Press Thursday.

No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers's legal team.

Flowers was 26 when he was arrested several months after the July 1996 shooting deaths of four people inside a Winona, Miss., furniture store.

At the time, prosecutors described him as a disgruntled former employee who sought revenge against the store's owner because she fired him and withheld most of his pay to cover the cost of merchandise he damaged. Nearly $300 US was found missing after the killings.

Tried 6 times for the killings

Flowers was tried six times in connection to the killings. He was convicted four times: twice for individual slayings and twice for all four killings. Two other trials involving all four deaths ended in mistrials.

Each of Flowers's convictions was overturned. In June 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court tossed out the conviction and death sentence from Flowers's sixth trial, which took place in 2010. Justices said prosecutors showed an unconstitutional pattern of excluding African American jurors in the trials of Flowers, who is Black.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the high court's 7-2 decision in 2019 that the removal of Black prospective jurors deprived Flowers of a fair trial.

During the sixth trial in 2010, Flowers was sentenced to death. There were 11 white jurors and one Black juror who considered the case after district attorney Doug Evans struck five Black prospective jurors from the case.

Flowers remained in prison for six months after the Supreme Court ruling because he was still under indictment. He finally was released in December 2019 after a judge set bond.

Mississippi dropped charges against Flowers in September 2020.

Flowers, centre, stands with his attorneys, Henderson Hill, left, and Rob McDuff, at a bail hearing on Dec. 16, 2019. (Rogelio V. Solis/The Associated Press)

'Free from the injustice'

"Today, I am finally free from the injustice that left me locked in a box for nearly twenty three years," Flowers said in a statement. "I've been asked if I ever thought this day would come. I have been blessed with a family that never gave up on me and with them by my side, I knew it would."

The legal team that represented Flowers for more than two decades said Thursday in a statement that each member feels "privileged to have called him a client."

"Later, in the years after his release and exoneration, we felt equally honoured to call him a friend," the legal team said. "No matter where he was — on death row, at home on his parents' porch with his feet up, singing in church, or fishing in a local pond — Curtis shared his light."

The trials stretched back more than 20 years. The records showed Evans's "relentless, determined effort to rid the jury of black individuals," with the goal of an all-white jury, Kavanaugh wrote.

Kavanaugh noted that Evans had removed 41 of the 42 prospective Black jurors over the six trials.

Flowers filed a lawsuit in 2021 against Evans and three investigators who worked with the district attorney. The suit claimed Evans and the investigators engaged in misconduct, including "pressuring witnesses to fabricate claims about seeing Mr. Flowers in particular locations on the day of the murders" and ignoring other possible suspects.

Earlier that year, a judge ordered the state of Mississippi to pay Flowers $500,000 US for wrongful imprisonment — the maximum under a state law that allows up to $50,000 US a year for 10 years.

Evans retired in 2023 after more than 30 years as district attorney. His jury selection tactics had been scrutinized for years.

Flowers's name is "etched into U.S. Supreme Court jurisprudence — about what it means to fight for a fair trial free from racial bias in the selection of jurors," Flowers's legal team said. "And also for that, but for so many other reasons, his name is etched into our memories, too — professional and personal. We will miss him."

World.title: This Ontario man won a court case for Stage 4 cancer treatment in the U.S. Then the province changed the rules
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Ontario man with Stage 4 melanoma says the province has effectively blocked access to public funding for out-of-country drug treatments in response to his attempts to urgently seek therapy in the United States.

Alex Shved, a 37-year-old father of two young children, took the province to court over Ontario Health Insurance Plan rejections. His cancer has spread to his lungs and his bones and he tried every avenue he could think of to ensure he is around for his daughters as long as possible.

He was successful in court but is now "incredibly disappointed and disheartened" to see the government further closing the door for patients in his situation.

"The courts concluded that the government's actions were unlawful, and the government's response was to change the law to make those same actions now lawful," Shved said in an interview.

OHIP had denied his oncologist's request for Shved to receive tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy in Florida at an approximate cost of US$600,000, largely citing the fact that the therapy is under consideration for public funding in Ontario.

The executive officer of Ontario public drug programs wrote in his denial that routinely funding out-of-country drug therapies while they are undergoing review in Ontario would "undermine the incentive structure that encourages manufacturers to participate in Canada's drug review processes."

WATCH | How often Ontario turns to international healthcare: This machine helps cancer patients. Why doesn’t Canada have one? | Duration closed caption 7:40 CBC News has obtained exclusive data showing how often Ontario turns to international healthcare, revealing proton beam therapy as one of the most commonly outsourced treatments. For The National, CBC’s Valérie Ouellet explores why this life-saving cancer therapy isn’t available in Canada and the toll it takes on families.

OHIP rejected treatment request 3 times

A Divisional Court ruling found that OHIP offered no real basis for that reasoning and ordered OHIP to reconsider.

Following that ruling, OHIP rejected Shved's request for a third time and Health Minister Sylvia Jones announced that the province has amended regulations to clarify that drugs will only be funded out of country if they are already funded within the province but access is temporarily unavailable or delayed.

"We're protecting Ontario patients and taxpayers from price-gouging and protecting their access to life-saving medications that would otherwise only be available in the United States or overseas," she wrote in a statement.

The government is also exploring a "mutually satisfactory resolution" in Shved's individual case, Jones wrote, but Shved said he is so far unclear on what that would entail.

Shved has tried various treatments since first discovering a growing mole in 2020 and his doctors say he would be a good candidate for TIL therapy. It involves doctors removing tumours, extracting immune cells that have infiltrated the tumours, multiplying them in the billions and infusing chemotherapy, then injecting the multiplied cells back into the patient to attack the cancer.

A version of TIL therapy called lifileucel was approved for sale last year by Health Canada, and is now undergoing reviews for consideration of possible funding by provincial drug plans, a process that could take years.

World.title: RCMP union raises concerns Liberals' proposed financial crime agency will hurt Mounties
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of the union representing thousands of Mounties says he's worried the Liberal plan to create a new financial crime enforcement agency will hurt the already-strained RCMP.

Rob Farrer, president of the National Police Federation, testified Thursday before a parliamentary committee studying Bill C-29, which would establish a dedicated Financial Crimes Agency (FCA).

The bill, introduced in the spring, is meant to address concerns that Canada falls short on investigating financial crimes including money laundering networks and online fraud, which historically have been investigated by the RCMP through its federal mandate.

If passed, the new agency would be a separate, specialized police organization with its own mandate and commissioner.

Farrer argued the RCMP could do that work if it had better resourcing.

"What these teams need is sustained staffing, modern tools and specialized support," he told MPs.

"We support stronger financial crime enforcement, but success must be measured by additional investigative capacity and better outcomes, and not simply the establishment of another organization."

WATCH | Liberals pitch financial crime agency in budget: Liberals pitch financial crime agency in budget | Duration closed caption 2:00 The Liberal government is pitching a new financial crimes agency to be introduced in the federal budget on Nov. 4 — an idea previously proposed during the 2021 campaign. Meanwhile, opposition parties are making budget demands with the Conservatives saying the deficit be no larger than $42 billion.

Union head says RCMP under-resourced

The union head, who represents some 20,000 Mounties, said one of his main concerns was that the proposed new agency would siphon off the national police force, which Farrer described as "absolutely" under-resourced.

The FCA is meant to be distinct from the RCMP, with its own police officers who would be able to execute search warrants and make arrests. However, the bill foresees Mounties being assigned to the new agency. The federal government has floated dedicating 150 RCMP personnel to tackle financial crimes.

"Our primary concern is workforce capacity. Experienced RCMP financial crime investigators cannot be replaced overnight," said Farrer.

"Assigning them to the FCA without qualified replacements will disrupt investigations, increase workloads and deepen retention pressures."

Long-documented recruitment, retention issues

He added that getting someone to the level of expertise needed to investigate these kinds of crimes "takes a very long time to develop."

The RCMP's recruitment and retention issues have long been documented. Earlier this year, the auditor general called out a worsening shortage of officers.

The proposed new agency is also expected to be staffed by civilian investigators, criminal and financial intelligence personnel, asset recovery experts and specialized prosecutors.

Farrer raised concerns about who is ultimately accountable for RCMP officers who are assigned to the FCA.

"Who manages safety, performance, discipline and disclosure?" he asked.

The union argued that any funding for the new agency should be new and not funding allocated to the RCMP.

It also urged Ottawa to make sure any Mounties assigned to it are backstopped by funded and qualified replacements and with a transition plan "that protects ongoing investigations."

World.title: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson awarded Nobel Prize in Literature
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded Thursday to Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.

Carson, 76, was recognized for "her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new ‌forms for contemporary literature," the award-giving body said.

The academy said Carson was in Reykjavik, Iceland, "listening to the wind" when its representatives made contact with her and she was surprised to learn she had won. The poet divides her time between Iceland and Ann Arbor, Mich., and holds Icelandic and Canadian citizenship.

Congratulations for Carson came from across the literary world and beyond, including from Canada's prime minister.

"With wit, imagination and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics," Mark Carney said on social media. "She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature."

Carson, sitting outside her home at Aegissioa in Reykjavik, Iceland, in October 2023. She divides her time between Iceland and Ann Arbor, Mich. (Kjartan Thorbjoernsson/Golli/Reuters)

The University of Toronto, where Carson earned her bachelor's, master's and PhD degrees in classics, also hailed the prize.

"This is a very proud moment for our global alumni community and for the entire university," Melanie Woodin, U of T president, said in a statement.

Poems as 'drawings'

Carson was born in Toronto but moved around small-town Ontario growing up as her father, a bank manager, relocated for work.

She has been a champion of the classics and has won a host of literary awards for her original, contemporary reimaginings of ancient Greek and Latin texts and stories.

Norma Jeane Baker of Troy — which mixes the life of Marilyn Monroe with stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides's play Helen — was awarded a 2020 Governor General Award in poetry.

WATCH | The moment Carson is awarded the prize: Canadian Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature | Duration closed caption 5:33 Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for 'her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new ‌forms for contemporary literature.'

'A writer of the great fires'

The following year, she received a career achievement award from the PEN America Literary Awards, who called her a "visionary, sui generis writer," with the judges announcing her honour in the form of a poem.

Carson's first book of poetry, Canicula di Anna, was published in 1984, and her reputation in Canada and beyond burnished two years later with the publication of her first collection of essays, Eros the Bittersweet.

"She is a writer of the great fires — love, fury, grief — but also of the quotidian. She amuses and shatters,” her agent, Nicole Aragi, told the New York Times in a statement.

Through the years, she has also been known for translating and performing Greek and Latin works, as well as pieces adapted for operas, including We Need to Talk and H of H Playbook.

"Making a poem is making an object," she previously told the CBC's Writers & Company with Eleanor Wachtel. "I always thought of them more as drawings than as texts, but drawings that are also physically enterable through the fact of language."

LISTEN | Anne Carson in conversation with CBC in 2011: Writers and Company 53:26 How writer and scholar Anne Carson used elegy to piece together fragments of her late brother

3rd Canadian-born winner

The Swedish academy also noted her strong work in the 1990s, including Glass, Irony and God, which it said "demonstrates the potential of the long poem where genre boundaries are seen to blur." Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, which reinterprets the ancient Greek poem Geryoneis through the eyes of a winged, gay teenager and became a cult favourite, "demonstrates her eminent ability to actualize the classical literary tradition," it said

In 2002, she became the first woman to win Britain's T.S. Eliot Prize for The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos.

Two years ago, in a London Review of Books essay, Carson revealed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

Just in! New Nobel Prize laureate in literature Anne Carson stands surprised in her kitchen in Reykjavík, Iceland. Stay tuned for our exclusive interview with her coming soon. Join us in congratulating our 2026 literature laureate - send your greetings in the comments. https://t.co/vateXOOBMp —NobelPrize

In addition to her published works, Carson has taught courses at universities in Canada and the U.S.

Joyce Carol Oates, the American literary polymath who taught for several years in the 1970s at Ontario's University of Windsor, recalled meeting Carson later in life at Princeton, the Ivy League school in New Jersey.

Carson possessed "truly an unclassifiable imagination — poet, translator, essayist, philosopher, observer of the vicissitudes of life," Oates said Thursday.

WATCH | Carson worked with the band Rheostatics: How Anne Carson and Rheostatics united for album The Great Lakes Suite | Duration closed caption 7:00 Canadian poet and Nobel Prize winner Anne Carson contributed spoken word tracks to the Rheostatics' most recent album, The Great Lakes Suite. Band members Dave Bidini and Kevin Hearn describe how their collaboration came to be and why her poems about water and swimming were the perfect fit for the album.

Rudyard Kipling, Ernest Hemingway, Albert Camus, Toni Morrison and V.S. Naipaul are among the notable writers to receive the award since its inception in 1901. Saul Bellow (1976) and Alice Munro (2013) are the previous Canadian-born writers to be awarded the prize, though Bellow moved to the U.S. as a child and launched his career there.

The committee has also occasionally awarded the prize to winners not foremost known as literary figures, including Winston Churchill and Bob Dylan.

The Nobel Peace Prize will be announced on Friday, with the Nobel's economics prize following on Monday. The Nobel prizes are presented to the laureates on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death.

Prize winners this year receive 12 million Swedish ‌crowns, or $1.7 million Cdn.

Nobel, the Swedish chemist and entrepreneur, dictated in his will that the bulk of his estate should be used to fund "prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind."

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Mayor from Colombia’s north claims De la Espriella’s armed men intimidated him
World.content:
The mayor of Sincelejo claimed Sunday that armed men intimidated him during a meeting with Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a video message, Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña said that armed men positioned themselves behind him while the president accused the mayor of corruption and threatened to pull municipal funds.

The accusations were partly published on the social media pages of the president, who accused Acuña of being “a person who, like you, faces 13 corruption charges, has a video in which he explains how to embezzle funds from the PAE, and, on top of that, is set to stand trial in the Supreme Court of Justice on charges of illicit enrichment.”

So let’s see what we do with Sincelejo, but I do not work under your scheme of corruption. And if you think you can continue engaging in those practices, know that someone has arrived who is going to prevent it and that I am going to concentrate on it. This money, mister mayor, I will take care of it, and to take care of it I have to keep it away from your control. President Abelardo de la Espriella

In his response, Acuña claimed that De la Espriella’s video “has been edited and digitally manipulated.”

I ask you, please, to show the full video, where you can see how disciplinary and criminal codes are being violated in Colombia, where you can see how a mayor is being intimidated with rifles in the hands of civilians. How can a mayor be constantly flanked—for the entire duration of an event—by a person armed with a rifle, with the sole purpose of intimidating him? Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

Investigative journalist Laura Ardila said on social media platform X that sources from the province confirmed Acuña’s allegations.

Sources from the department who were present say—fearing they might be named—that they left the scene terrified. They claim that Acuña was indeed surrounded by heavily armed men in civilian clothing, that the president’s office was recording the entire time, and that, based on details like these, they believe it was a scene staged in advance to go viral. Journalist Laura Ardila

The mayor subsequently pointed out that the investigations into his alleged corruption existed before the presidential campaign, during which the De la Espriella campaign may have violated electoral laws, according to Acuña.

Among other things, the mayor said that he had been approached by De la Espriella’s parents to support the far-right president’s campaign and that local print shops may have received unreported campaign funds.

Since this needs to be clarified, mister President, it would be a good idea for the oversight agencies to investigate whether any printing shops in Sincelejo incurred campaign expenses that have not yet been reported to the National Electoral Council, whether there was campaign financing, and where that campaign financing came from, Mister President. Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

The mayor also pointed out that two members of the De la Espriella administration are being investigated on corruption charges and that the president had ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

The president has repeatedly used corruption allegations to target political enemies.

World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Why Argentina's Falklands sanctions do not automatically reach Sea Lion's operator
World.content:
Why Argentina's Falklands sanctions do not automatically reach Sea Lion's operator

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:29 UTC Full article

Photo: Raphael WOLLMANN / Getty Images

The sanctions Argentina has imposed on companies involved in the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands target specific entities rather than entire corporate groups, so the subsidiary currently operating the field is not automatically covered, according to a legal analysis by specialist site Diplomacy & Law.

Argentina's Energy Secretariat declared Rockhopper Exploration plc's activities illegal in 2012 and barred it from operating in the country for 20 years in 2013. In 2022 it imposed a similar sanction on Navitas Petroleum LP. But the project's current operator is Navitas Petroleum Development and Production Ltd, a UK subsidiary of the Israeli group. “A sanction imposed on Navitas Petroleum LP does not automatically become an identical sanction against every affiliated company,” writes the author, Edmarverson A. Santos, unless the law expressly provides for it or a new measure is adopted.

Argentina's legal framework nonetheless reaches beyond licence holders. Law 26,659 of 2011 prohibits direct or indirect participation in hydrocarbon exploration or exploitation that the country regards as unauthorised on its continental shelf, with bans of five to 20 years. Subject to its conditions, it covers shareholders, service providers, financiers, logistics operators and technical advisers. Law 26,915 of 2013 added penalties for directors and companies.

The decree signed by President Javier Milei on September 3 designated the foreign ministry as the enforcing authority, set short deadlines for proceedings and required compliance declarations from those applying for the large-investment incentive regime or hydrocarbon permits in the country. That mechanism explains the effect on companies with business in Argentina: Halliburton, SLB and Baker Hughes have said they will not work on Sea Lion, and Halliburton said the authorities raised criminal and civil enforcement with it.

The analysis distinguishes between making rules and enforcing them. Argentina can deny permits and benefits and sanction those under its jurisdiction, but it cannot exercise coercive authority in the archipelago or another state without an independent legal basis or that country's cooperation. For companies with no ties to Argentina, the risk is mainly reputational or commercial.

None of these measures resolves the underlying question. “Falkland licences cannot establish British title to the islands, and Argentine administrative resolutions cannot establish Argentine title,” the author concludes. The United Kingdom maintains that the activity is legitimate and governed by the archipelago's legislation in accordance with international law; Argentina maintains its sovereignty claim and holds that the licences are invalid.

World.title: What could happen when Argentina's Sea Lion ultimatum to the UK expires
World.content:
What could happen when Argentina's Sea Lion ultimatum to the UK expires

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:18 UTC Full article

Milei ordered on September 28 the start of arbitration and said that, if London does not act, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea

The two-week deadline Argentina gave the United Kingdom to halt the Sea Lion oil project in the North Falklands basin expires around October 12. Its expiry will not in itself suspend the project or establish a British breach of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, according to a legal analysis published by specialist site Diplomacy & Law.

President Javier Milei ordered on September 28 the start of arbitration under Annex VII of the convention and said that, if London does not act, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The analysis's author, Edmarverson A. Santos, stresses that the deadline was set by Argentina and does not derive from the convention, and that the government's instruction and the formal start of proceedings are separate steps: arbitration begins with written notification to the other state, accompanied by the claim and its grounds. There is no record that this has been sent.

The Annex VII route reflects both countries' choices. Under Article 287 of the convention, Argentina chose the Hamburg tribunal as its first preference and the United Kingdom the International Court of Justice; where the parties do not coincide, the dispute goes to arbitration. Beforehand, Article 283 requires an exchange of views on how to settle the dispute, something a tribunal would have to assess.

If Argentina seeks provisional measures, the Hamburg tribunal could order them while the arbitral tribunal is being constituted, provided it considers that the latter would have prima facie jurisdiction and that the matter is urgent. Such measures would be provisional, not a ruling on sovereignty or the merits.

The main obstacle is jurisdiction. Convention tribunals can only rule on its interpretation or application, not on territorial title. In the 2015 arbitration between Mauritius and the United Kingdom over the Chagos Islands, the tribunal declined to rule on a claim whose real subject was sovereignty; in the 2020 case between Ukraine and Russia, it excluded claims requiring a decision on Crimea, though proceedings continued on the rest. In addition, both countries have made declarations under Article 298: Argentina excluded maritime delimitation disputes, among others, in 1995, and the United Kingdom made exclusions in 2003 and, according to the analysis, again in 2020.

“Argentina would need to formulate claims capable of adjudication under UNCLOS without requiring the tribunal to decide, expressly or implicitly, sovereignty over the Falkland Islands,” the author concludes.

The United Kingdom rejected the arbitration on September 30 and maintains that the activity is governed by the archipelago's legislation in accordance with international law. Sea Lion, developed by Navitas and Rockhopper, has had a final investment decision since December 2025.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro proposes constitutional reform to overhaul the courts and lower the criminal age
World.content:
Flávio Bolsonaro proposes constitutional reform to overhaul the courts and lower the criminal age

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:10 UTC Full article

The candidate said he intended to use his party's legislative weight to choose the presiding officers of both chambers and “amend the Constitution, to redemocratise the country”

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who will face Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil's presidential runoff on October 25, has said that if he wins he will use his Liberal Party's congressional bloc to push a constitutional reform that would change the judiciary, lower the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 and abolish presidential re-election.

On Tuesday, at an event in Goiânia, the candidate said he intended to use his party's legislative weight to choose the presiding officers of both chambers and “amend the Constitution, to redemocratise the country, so that institutions once again respect the Constitution”. Amid concern over the remark, he set out the scope of the reform in Brasília on Wednesday and responded to those fearing an authoritarian turn: “I've seen people saying that now, with a majority, Flávio will do what his father didn't. Stop that. Let's come back down to the real world.” His father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup.

A constitutional amendment in Brazil requires three fifths of each chamber in two votes: 308 of 513 deputies and 49 of 81 senators. According to the newspaper El País, the Liberal Party won 121 seats in the Chamber of Deputies on Sunday, 20% more than in 2022, and with its allies would hold around 50 in the Senate. Those elected include the former president's wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, and his son Carlos, as senators.

Bolsonaro this week won the backing of two first-round candidates. Ronaldo Caiado, a former governor of Goiás who won around 2.2% of the vote, endorsed him at the Goiânia event: “I'm here to defeat the PT.” Former Minas Gerais governor Romeu Zema, with less than 1%, did so on Monday. São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas, re-elected on Sunday, also attended.

Bolsonaro, who won 47% of valid votes to Lula's 45%, had already announced on Monday plans to cut the number of ministries and appoint at least four Supreme Federal Court justices. Lula held no public events on Monday or Tuesday and met his campaign team in Brasília, which has said the president will seek direct confrontation in the runoff.

World.title: Stuart Lawrence, for three decades a captain of Britain's Antarctic ships, has died
World.content:
Stuart Lawrence, for three decades a captain of Britain's Antarctic ships, has died

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 08:07 UTC Full article

He was awarded the Polar Medal in 1983 and appointed MBE in 1998. He retired in 2003 after 33 Antarctic voyages and 42 years at sea, with a farewell from the Ernest Shackleton in Stanley

Captain Stuart Lawrence MBE, who for more than three decades commanded the British Antarctic Survey vessels RRS Bransfield and RRS Ernest Shackleton, has died suddenly, according to the National Coastwatch Institution in Gosport, southern England, where he served as a volunteer watchkeeper.
