His calling began at the age of five in Grimsby, where he lived on the same street as a Cunard liner captain. He entered the HMS Conway training ship at 13 and spent his seventeenth birthday as a Canadian Pacific cadet. He was about to join the Royal National Lifeboat Institution when its head, Admiral Egg Irving, urged him instead to sail to the Antarctic. He joined the British Antarctic Survey in 1970 and remained until 2003.

After two voyages on the John Biscoe, he moved to the Bransfield, taking temporary command in 1972 and permanent command in 1974. He took her every year to Halley, the organisation's most southerly station, through the Weddell Sea. In 1984, the UK Antarctic Place-Names Committee named Lawrence Channel, on the Antarctic Peninsula, after him. From 1999 he commanded the Ernest Shackleton.

Days before the 1982 Argentine invasion, he hosted a reception on board in Stanley. He sailed on March 31 and, halfway to Tierra del Fuego, learned of the invasion from Patrick Watts' radio broadcasts and alerted the organisation's headquarters in Britain. By his own account, he later had to restrain part of the crew, who wanted to return and scuttle the ship at the entrance to Stanley Harbour.

Ships under his command were regular visitors to Montevideo on voyages to Stanley and Antarctica, according to those who sailed with him.

He was awarded the Polar Medal in 1983 and appointed MBE in 1998. He retired in 2003 after 33 Antarctic voyages and 42 years at sea, with a farewell from the Ernest Shackleton in Stanley. His wife, Sue, had died months earlier.

He later worked for the UK Hydrographic Office and as an ice master on cruise ships, and from 2017 volunteered at the Gosport coastwatch station. “A watch with Stuart would be one of professionally recording every detail and aspect of incidents at sea, interspersed with tales of the Antarctic and any number of anecdotes,” the institution wrote.

World.title: What was the world's largest penguin colony has lost nearly two thirds of its nests
World.content:
What was the world's largest penguin colony has lost nearly two thirds of its nests

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:54 UTC Full article

Photo: Nicole Richters

The chinstrap penguin population on Zavodovski Island, in the South Sandwich Islands, has fallen by almost two thirds since 2011, according to a study by the British Antarctic Survey. The island, described that year as the world's largest penguin colony, has lost that title.

Researchers recorded 63% fewer occupied nests in 2025 than in 2011. That year, the same organisation estimated that some 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nested on the island. For the new study, a team sailed for 15 days to Zavodovski, a volcanic island north of the Antarctic continent administered by the United Kingdom, and used drones, aerial photography, satellite imagery and tracking devices fitted to 20 birds.

According to the study's lead, Professor Norman Ratcliffe, the cause is ocean warming. “With waters warming, the krill the chinstrap penguins eat have moved southwards. Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food,” he said. The researchers believe the species may now qualify as officially endangered.

The team ruled out other explanations. The island's volcano, Mount Curry, last erupted significantly in 2016, while the decline has been steady since 2011. Nor do they attribute the fall to competition for krill from humpback whales, which in turn help boost krill production.

By contrast, the macaroni penguin population increased markedly. Tracking data show they forage in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where they are likely supplementing their diet with fish and other crustaceans. Ratcliffe described the shift as “the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica” and as “further evidence of how rapid warming is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems”.

The world's largest penguin colony is now at Cape Adare, in the Ross Sea, more than 5,000 kilometres away on the other side of the Antarctic continent.

The study comes days after Antarctic sea ice recorded its third-lowest winter maximum since satellite measurements began this year.

World.title: On the war's third anniversary, 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza
World.content:
On the war's third anniversary, 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:53 UTC Full article

Some 5,600 children are waiting to be evacuated from Gaza for medical treatment, according to the territory's Hamas-run Health Ministry, as three years pass since the group's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which killed around 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage and triggered the war.

To leave the Strip, patients need a referral from the Health Ministry, acceptance by a host country and Israeli security clearance. Among those recently evacuated is Raseel, a six-year-old girl injured at the al-Mawasi displacement camp in July, who travelled to Egypt in late September with support from the World Health Organization. Witnesses attributed the strike to an Israeli helicopter; the Israeli military said it had no record of a strike at that time and place.

Doctors warn that antibiotic-resistant infections are complicating the recovery of the wounded. A study shared with the BBC World Service, based on almost 80,000 bacterial samples collected at 11 hospitals between 2015 and 2025, found widespread resistance to key antibiotics. It was carried out by Gaza-based researchers with support from Imperial College London and the American University of Beirut; it has not yet been peer-reviewed and its findings are preliminary. “We will see the number of amputations rise, even if the war stops,” said Awni al-Jaafarawi, a Médecins Sans Frontières doctor at Nasser hospital.

The researchers link the problem to the destruction of water and sanitation. According to the UN, almost 90% of that infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged, and more than 80% of families face water insecurity. Cogat, the Israeli body that manages access to Gaza, says the water supplied exceeds the UN humanitarian threshold and that medicines, including antibiotics, enter without restriction.

Gaza's Health Ministry puts the number of Palestinians killed since the war began at more than 74,000, and at 1,421 since the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025. Israel disputes the figures and says it acts to minimise harm to civilians.

World.title: FAO Food Price Index rises in September amid weather concerns and transport disruptions
World.content:
FAO Food Price Index rises in September amid weather concerns and transport disruptions

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:37 UTC Full article

The FAO Cereal Price Index increased by 5.1 percent from August, averaging 17.2 percent higher than its September 2025 level.

FAO’s benchmark measure of world food commodity prices increased in September, due mostly to transportation disruptions and weather concerns that constrained availability as well as to higher quotations for crop-based commodity groups, according to new data released by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).

The FAO Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in the international prices of a basket of globally-traded food commodities, averaged 136.0 points in September 2026, up 1.5 percent from August and 5.8 percent from a year ago.

“We are seeing a persistent and increasingly broad based build up in global commodity prices, as disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea combine with climate shocks, putting pressure on energy, transport and key food commodities,” said FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero. “If sustained, these pressures will soon pass through to consumer food prices, especially in food and energy import dependent countries.”

The FAO Cereal Price Index increased by 5.1 percent from August, averaging 17.2 percent higher than its September 2025 level. World wheat prices increased by 6.3 percent, due to logistical constraints in the Black Sea region and dry weather in parts of North America ahead of sowing, while global maize prices rose by 5.6 percent from the previous month due to concerns over yields in the United States of America, reduced export availability in Brazil and disruptions to Black Sea trade. Ongoing uncertainty over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz provided additional support to prices of biofuel feedstocks such as maize.

The FAO All Rice Price Index increased by 1.4 percent, as Indica quotations rose amid weather concerns and seasonally tighter supplies.

The FAO Vegetable Oil Price Index increased by 0.9 percent from August, reflecting higher world palm oil prices associated with strong global import demand and concerns over the impact of dry weather on production prospects in Southeast Asia.

The FAO Meat Price Index declined by 1.1 percent, as pig and poultry meat prices fell amid abundant exportable supplies. Brazil’s bovine meat export quotations increased, supported by stronger import demand by United States, while ovine meat prices remained largely stable.

The FAO Dairy Price Index dipped by 0.1 percent in September, as declines in cheese prices slightly offset increases in milk powder quotations, and butter prices changed little.

The FAO Sugar Price Index increased by 6.1 percent from August, driven by expectations of tighter global sugar supplies in the 2026/27 season. Contributing factors included lower expected sugar production in Thailand, concerns over crop prospects in India due to below-normal rainfall and strengthening El Niño conditions, heavy rains in Brazil’s Centre-South growing region, and a decline in the area planted to sugar beet in the European Union.

World.title: British Army exploring military working horses: US used them against Taliban and Russia in Ukraine
World.content:
British Army exploring military working horses: US used them against Taliban and Russia in Ukraine

8th Thursday, October 2026 - 07:37 UTC Full article

When you hear of horses being used in battle, you could be forgiven for thinking back to the First World War or even the Napoleonic era. However, the British Army, specifically The Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment (HCMR), is exploring how Military Working Horses could contribute to future operations.

“We are platform agnostic. Whether it's a Challenger 2 or a horse, it doesn't really matter,” says Lieutenant Colonel Ben McNeil, HCMR's Commanding Officer.

The regiment is taking inspiration from other armed forces around the world, including Russia. In an era where drones are ripping up the playbook of modern warfare, the need for a war horse may seem redundant, however they bring many benefits.

For starters, horses and mules are an effective way of moving troops and cargo across rugged terrain. They can also carry more weight and travel further distances than troops on foot, saving soldier energy for the fight.

Horses are also low-cost, low-maintenance and can be procured even in remote locations – all qualities an armored vehicle or tank does not possess.

One of the big advantages horses and mules can bring to the battlefield lies in their genetics. They have a surprisingly small heat signature, making them great at evading drone detection.

Lt Col McNeil added: “A horse in a forest is a normal context to be in, and that plays to our advantage versus an armored vehicle, which has a very mechanical profile to it and thermal profile with it, as well as sound.”

These advantages are why we've seen horses used by Russia in the Ukraine war for frontline logistics and transport where regular vehicles are vulnerable. Videos circulating online even show Russian soldiers attaching Starlink terminals to horses to get internet on the frontline.

“It shows the utility of them,” said Lt Col McNeil. “Whilst we give our soldiers the opportunity to do something different and they really enjoy it and are enthused by it, it could grow into a capability that the British Army could use in the future.”

Forces closer to home use horses too. “We're learning an awful lot. Our Spanish, our Italian, our German colleagues, our French colleagues in the Gendarmerie, are using them in all sorts of ways, whether that's in ground-holding roles or whether that's in more reconnaissance-related or resupply elements.

”It's about applying a platform, as we are platform-orientated soldiers, into the environment that works.”

Household Cavalry soldiers split their time between the Mounted Regiment – the ceremonial side in London, which involves escorting the King. Then there's the operational side, which involves carrying out reconnaissance in tanks and, eventually, the Ajax armored fighting vehicle, if all goes to plan.

Should these horses ever be used in war, there could come a time when the troopers would need to engage the enemy from the saddle (Picture: MOD)

You don't have to look as far back as you might think for examples of horses used in war. US special forces from Operational Detachment Alpha 595 were sent to the mountains of Afghanistan to fight successfully against the Taliban on horseback, just after the 9/11 attacks in 2001.

Their efforts were depicted in the Hollywood movie 12 Strong and America maintains a mounted capability today.

The first experiment for The Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took place during their annual summer camp on Longmoor Training Area. Soldiers learned new skills like emergency first aid for horses and tested using camouflage nets on the animals.

As the experimentation continues, we could see the world-famous cavalry horses go from trotting up and down The Mall to finding enemy locations on military operations.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How many foreigners live in Mexico?
World.content:
How many foreign-born residents does Mexico have? Where in Mexico do they live?

We answer those questions in this “Mexico in Numbers” article, which is based on the recently published results of INEGI’s 2025 Intercensal Survey.

Let’s delve into the data.

Mexico has almost 1.2 million foreign-born residents

INEGI reported that 1,170,030 (1.17 million) foreign-born residents lived in Mexico in 2025.

That figure represents an increase of just 147 people — or 0.01% — from 2020, when the most recent census was conducted in Mexico.

Mexico’s foreign-born population represents just 0.9% of Mexico’s total population, which was 130.91 million in 2025, according to the results of the Intercensal Survey.

By contrast, foreign-born residents of the United States accounted for about 14.8% of the U.S. national population in 2024, according to the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, a large-scale survey of American households.

Just over half of Mexico’s foreign-born residents — 50.7% — have Mexican citizenship, according to INEGI.

Almost 60% of Mexico’s foreign-born residents were born in the US

Of the 1.17 million foreign-born residents of Mexico, 668,658 were born in the United States, according to INEGI.

Thus, 57.1% of Mexico’s foreign-born population was born in the United States. INEGI reported that 66.5% of U.S.-born residents are Mexican nationals.

INEGI also reported that:

75,826 residents of Mexico were born in Venezuela, a figure that accounts for 6.5% of the foreign-born population.

61,663 residents of Mexico were born in Cuba, a figure that accounts for 5.3% of the foreign-born population.

54,680 residents of Mexico were born in Guatemala, a figure that accounts for 4.7% of the foreign-born population.

309,203 residents of Mexico were born in “other countries,” a figure that accounts for 26.4% of the foreign-born population.

Just over one-fifth of the Venezuelan-born residents (21.1%) and the Cuban-born residents (22.6%) are Mexican nationals, according to INEGI.

Just over one-third of the Guatemalan-born residents (34.3%) are Mexican nationals. Among the more than 300,000 residents of Mexico born in “other countries,” 32.2% are Mexican nationals.

Baja California and CDMX have the largest foreign-born populations

A graph published by INEGI in its Intercensal Survey results report shows that two federal entities have more than 100,000 foreign-born residents: Baja California (131,221) and Mexico City (114,273).

Seven states have more than 50,000 foreign-born residents. They are:

Chihuahua: 98,785

Jalisco: 76,441

Chiapas: 73,711

México state: 71,703

Tamaulipas: 63,691

Nuevo León: 56,532

Quintana Roo: 50,325

According to INEGI, Tlaxcala has the lowest foreign-born population among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, with 3,758 residents born abroad.

Three other states have fewer than 10,000 foreign-born residents: Tabasco (6,429), Colima (6,802) and Campeche (7,595).

* This article is based on Intercensal Survey data published by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) in September. MND acknowledges that there are various estimates of the number of U.S. citizens living in Mexico, including a 2024 U.S. State Department estimate of 1.6 million. The State Department estimate could include U.S. citizens born in Mexico, whom INEGI, for obvious reasons, does not classify as foreign-born. Mexican-born people who moved to the United States, obtained U.S. citizenship, and subsequently returned to Mexico fit into this category. The State Department estimate could also include part-time residents (who may or may not have a Mexican residency permit and who may or may not have been in Mexico when the Intercensal Survey was conducted) as well as temporary residents on tourist visas, including digital nomads.

World.title: AIFA now serves 47 destinations, up from 7 in 2022: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

✈️ AIFA now serves 40 domestic and 7 international destinations : Airport director Isidoro Pastor Román said that since opening in March 2022, the Army-built airport has grown the number of destinations it serves from seven to 47. He also said more than 22 million passengers have used the airport, and highlighted that AIFA now handles more cargo than any other Mexican airport.

: Airport director Isidoro Pastor Román said that since opening in March 2022, the Army-built airport has grown the number of destinations it serves from seven to 47. He also said more than 22 million passengers have used the airport, and highlighted that AIFA now handles more cargo than any other Mexican airport. 🚓 García Harfuch reminds Querétaro governor that police academy collaboration with US must follow Mexican law : Sheinbaum said Security Minister Omar García Harfuch told Governor Mauricio Kuri that for any security collaboration with a foreign government, legal procedure must be followed. She said the same message was conveyed to U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson. Sheinbaum said both men committed to working “within the framework of Mexico’s Constitution.”

: Sheinbaum said Security Minister Omar García Harfuch told Governor Mauricio Kuri that for any security collaboration with a foreign government, legal procedure must be followed. She said the same message was conveyed to U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson. Sheinbaum said both men committed to working “within the framework of Mexico’s Constitution.” 🤝 Sheinbaum and Johnson to meet at National Palace today: Sheinbaum said the U.S. ambassador would accompany business leaders at a meeting on Thursday. She didn’t say whether she would raise the police academy project with him.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Passenger numbers at the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA), the Army-built airport north of Mexico City in México state, are still dwarfed by passenger numbers at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM).

However, information presented at President Sheinbaum’s Thursday morning press conference showed that the airport has made significant progress since opening in early 2022, attracting more airlines and expanding the number of destinations it serves. Since April, AIFA has been connected to central Mexico City by train, making the airport more accessible to residents of the capital.

Also of note at today’s mañanera — Sheinbaum’s 500th morning press conference as president — was the revelation that federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch spoke to Querétaro Governor Mauricio Kuri about the International Police Training Academy project in the Bajío region state.

The Querétaro government has been collaborating with U.S. authorities on the project, but that collaboration has not been approved by the federal government, as required by law.

Sheinbaum first spoke about the police academy project on Monday, three days after U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson attended an event in Querétaro at which the cornerstone of the facility was laid.

She questioned the establishment of the academy and the United States’ involvement in the project. In addition, Sheinbaum indicated that her government knew little about the project and declared that such an academy cannot be established without federal authorization.

AIFA now serves 40 Mexican and 7 international destinations

AIFA director Isidoro Pastor Román reported that the airport is currently serving 40 domestic destinations and seven international destinations, among which are Havana, Caracas, Bogotá and Santo Domingo. Five Mexican passenger airlines and two foreign ones fly to and from AIFA, he said.

Pastor said that 22.66 million passengers have used the airport since it opened in March 2022. Passenger numbers have increased gradually since the airport opened, reaching 7.1 million last year — equivalent to 16% of the 2025 total at AICM.

Pastor reported that 53 cargo airlines have used the airport. AIFA now handles more cargo than any other airport in Mexico, he said.

Pastor said that the “financial profitability” of the airport was achieved in the first quarter of 2024. He told reporters that the operation of the airport has created 18,000 direct jobs and 150,000 indirect ones.

Toward the end of his presentation, the AIFA chief displayed a range of information that showed how the airport has grown since it opened in early 2022. He reported that:

The number of passenger airlines serving the airport has increased from four to seven.

The number of domestic destinations served by the airport has increased from six to 40.

The number of international destinations served by the airport has increased from one to seven.

The number of cargo airlines using the airport has increased from two to 53.

García Harfuch reminds Kuri that Querétaro-US police academy collaboration must follow Mexican law

Sheinbaum told reporters that Security Minister García Harfuch spoke to Querétaro Governor Kuri about collaboration with the United States on the International Police Training Academy.

“Omar spoke to Governor Kuri and told him: ‘Remember that for any collaboration [with a foreign government] there is a law and a procedure,'” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the same message was conveyed to U.S. Ambassador Johnson.

“Both said, ‘Yes, we have to collaborate within the framework of Mexico’s Constitution,'” she said.

“… Governor Kuri even issued a message saying, ‘I’m not going to violate anything, but rather … I’m going to request permission … [for] collaboration [with the U.S.] when the academy starts operating,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum to attend meeting with Ambassador Johnson

A reporter referred to reporting — based on an X post by journalist Ioan Grillo — that U.S. Ambassador Johnson has sought to meet with Sheinbaum, but the president has declined.

Before the reporter could finish her question, Sheinbaum interrupted to say that Johnson would come to the National Palace on Thursday.

US ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson wants to be meeting with President Claudia Sheinbaum, but she is turning him down, possibly wary of how it will be reported/ wanting to keep distance, a US embassy official tells me. Sheinbaum talks with Trump by phone about once a month. — Ioan Grillo (@ioangrillo) October 7, 2026

“He’s coming today,” she said.

“He’s coming today because we have a meeting with businesspeople from the United States, from the American Chamber [of Commerce of Mexico]. Well, Mexican-Americans or Mexicans,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Various businesspeople are coming and the U.S. ambassador will accompany them. So he’s coming today,” she said.

Sheinbaum didn’t say whether she would raise the issue of the International Police Training Academy project with Johnson. However, at a meeting focused on business and investment, it would appear unlikely that the issue will be broached.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Mexico and My Money: Affordability is a growing problem in Mexico, too
World.content:
While Mexico has long been seen as an inexpensive country to live in (especially by those who don’t live here), the reality is more complicated.

Costs have been steadily rising due to geopolitical pressures such as the joint US-Israel war in Iran, supply chain disruptions, more extreme weather patterns tied to climate change and several factors unique to Mexico (more on that later).

Mexico’s headline inflation rate reached 3.4% in the first half of September 2026, accelerating from 3.26% in August. Excluding food and energy, the so-called core inflation rate is even worse, registering 3.8% in the latest period.

For context, inflation in Mexico has been above the central bank’s (Banxico) 3% target for 5.5 years (since March 2021), with prices up a cumulative 30% over this period. These persistent increases hit lower- and fixed-income residents the hardest.

These facts are not lost on Mexico’s long-term foreign residents. In our recent Mexico and My Money financial survey, 38% of respondents said that the rising cost of living was negatively affecting their lifestyle in Mexico.

Below, I take a closer look at where the pressure is coming from and some of the drivers behind this high inflation.

Essential services have seen rapid price increases lately

The reason that life feels much more expensive in Mexico lately is that some of the biggest price increases have been heavily concentrated in everyday necessities such as food, housing, healthcare and energy.

Food prices have been rising at a much faster rate than overall inflation in 2026, due to extreme weather, fertilizer scarcity and supply chain disruptions. According to INEGI, the national statistics agency, prices for fresh fruit and vegetables rose 3.4% in the first half of September, following massive increases in the first quarter of this year, when tomato prices surged 61%.

The cost of a basic food basket (canasta básica) containing ingredients necessary for a balanced diet is up roughly 4.6% year-over-year in urban areas. Dining out — whether in upscale restaurants or at humble taco stands — is seeing even greater price increases, putting considerable pressure on Mexican residents’ budgets.

Housing costs in Mexico are tracked as a service in official government data, and by most accounts, seriously understate the true level of inflation, according to experts.

According to INEGI, inflation in rent is around 3.5% this year, but data collected by private sources paint a more dire picture. While trends vary widely by city, years of rapid growth in places like Mexico City have left rents 64% higher there over the past five years, more than double the overall rate of inflation.

This phenomenon has been driven in part by an explosion in real estate prices. Last year, homes purchased with a mortgage increased in price by 8.7% nationwide, according to the Federal Mortgage Society, more than twice the rate of headline inflation.

Major cities like Guadalajara, Monterrey and Tijuana have seen real estate prices rise even faster, driven by rampant speculation and rising demand from foreigners, among other things. Lofty prices now keep many families stuck in the rental market.

Healthcare inflation is also a serious problem. An overstretched and underfunded IMSS system struggles to meet the public’s needs, which prompts many families to seek care from private sector providers. This situation has driven hyperinflation in the private health insurance market in 2026, which I wrote about earlier this year.

Energy is a rare bright spot. Since the U.S.-Israel war in Iran began earlier this year, the price of regular gasoline has remained nearly flat in Mexico, due to government interventions such as voluntary price caps and assorted fuel tax reductions.

State-owned Pemex has absorbed most of the price spikes, only raising prices for consumers on premium gas, which is not covered by the price caps.

Now, let’s look at a few lesser-known factors that contribute to Mexico’s higher cost of living.

Mexican sales taxes weigh heavily on consumer prices

The general sales tax across Mexico, known as the Impuesto al Valor Agregado (IVA), is a steep16% for most goods and services. This tax has been in place for the past 15 years (since it was raised from 10% to 16%).

Effectively a consumption tax that hits all Mexicans equally, regardless of their income, the IVA feels especially punitive in an inflationary environment for everyday goods.

Fortunately for those on a tight budget, food (excluding pet food), medicines and books are exempt from IVA. In addition, IVA was reduced to 8% back in 2019 for eligible taxpayers in the northern and southern border regions, to prevent consumers from shopping across international borders where taxes are lower.

Extortion compounds underlying pricing pressures in Mexico

Although food is exempt from IVA sales tax, there is another, less visible “tax” on fresh fruit and vegetables in Mexico, thanks to widespread extortion of agricultural producers.

Often referred to as derecho de piso (protection money), these nonoptional payments that Mexican farmers make to organized crime groups drive up product costs. While extortion affects myriad food products, those who cultivate so-called “green gold,” e.g., avocados, limes and agave, are a favored target.

Extortion in Mexico today does not look like the random shakedowns of years past. It has evolved into sophisticated, systematic coercion that affects the entire agricultural supply chain.

For small farms, extortion limits what they can produce. If squeezed beyond the breaking point, they may shut down entirely. At larger farms, these extra “operating” costs typically get absorbed and passed along to the consumer.

But things may be starting to change.

Omar García Harfuch, Mexico’s popular secretary of public security, has committed to taking on the problem. He recently launched a federal anti-extortion plan, the National Strategy Against Extortion, offering financial intelligence to states with the biggest problems. The initiative also encourages businesses to report extortion using a newly created hotline, as many are reluctant to report these crimes locally.

Your vices cost you dearly in Mexico

The Mexican government is heavy-handed with “vice” taxes, levying surtaxes on products it deems harmful, superfluous or undesirable. Known in Mexico as Impuesto Especial sobre Producción y Servicios, or IEPS, these vice taxes are levied on top of the standard 16% IVA, significantly increasing the prices paid by everyday consumers.

Here are several examples of products and services with IEPS taxes:

Cigarettes are subject to a 200% tax plus a fixed fee of around 0.65 MXN per cigarette.

Alcoholic drinks are subject to surtaxes ranging from 26.5% to 53%, depending on alcohol content and type.

Gambling is subject to an additional 50% tax. The tax is applied to physical casinos and foreign betting platforms.

Needless to say, it pays to live clean in Mexico.

Peso volatility compounds inflationary pressures

Exchange rate fluctuations are another source of anxiety for many expats in Mexico. If your income is derived from funds earned abroad, a weaker peso makes life more affordable in Mexico, while a strengthening peso makes life here more expensive.

Up until last week, a return of the “super peso” was exacerbating inflationary pressures for foreign residents. The peso’s abrupt 6.7% drop over the past month has brought some relief, as the currency is now up less than 2% against the USD in the past year.

All in all, Mexico’s cost of living is still roughly 40% cheaper than life in the U.S. or Canada, according to International Living. We can be grateful for that.

If Mexico’s rising prices are affecting your household, what are you doing to cope? Please drop your ideas in the comments below.

From tipping to moving money into Mexico from abroad, check out more from MND’s “Mexico and My Money” archive.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: The anatomy of Maya sacrifice: An interview with author Vera Tiesler
World.content:
Vera Tiesler is a Maya expert and professor of anthropological sciences at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in Mexico. During her career, she has published several books about ancient Mesoamerican culture. In today’s Q&A, Mexico News Daily sits down to talk with Tiesler about the newest book she edited, “Ritual Violence and Related Body Treatments in Ancient Mesoamerica,” which features contributions from 36 authors.

Tiesler takes us on a trip into a cosmovision where bloodletting was a sacred ritual practice, tells us about new forensic discoveries related to ritual instruments, and explores how ritual logic can still be observed today in cultural rituals in former Maya regions.

Your new book on ritual violence comes after more than three decades of research. What led you to this subject?

I began working on these subjects in 1992. Through collaborations with archaeological projects and access to many large skeletal collections, I was able to compare cranial modification and dental modification across regions. Then, in the field, we began encountering decapitated individuals in major Maya urban centers like Palenque and Calakmul. We could see the marks on the bones almost as one would in forensic work.

At the time, the question of heart extraction was still heavily debated: How was it done? How did they reach the heart? How did they open the trunk? We documented individuals sacrificed for the Red Queen and for Pakal who showed cut marks on the lower thoracic vertebrae, around the 10th through 12th vertebrae. We also documented cases in Calakmul and Becán.

“The marks led us to reconstruct the anatomy of the procedure. The most plausible route was an incision beneath the thorax, directly under the lower rib margin, using a flint or obsidian blade. That is anatomically the simplest way to reach the heart.”

When the heart is pulled out, it must be separated from the aorta and other structures; that is where the cut marks on the vertebrae at the back of the trunk can occur.

When we first published this interpretation, there was considerable pushback. But today we have many more cases of human sacrifice from across Mexico, including findings at the Sacred Cenote of Chichén Itzá, Templo Mayor and the major Mexica skull-rack Tzompantli tower, discovered in 2015. We can now discuss a much wider spectrum of sacrificial festivities and religious observances. That is why we felt the time was right for a new book.

Is the book primarily a forensic account of ritual violence?

No. Forensics is only one of several sources of information. We combine it with archaeology, iconography, inscriptions, ethnohistory, genetics, isotope analysis and archaeometry.

For example, we can use electron microscopy to examine the cut surfaces of stingray spines or obsidian blades that were found at the sacrificial site. What was once dismissed as merely a symbolic offering can now be tested for human red blood cells, muscle remains or any other human tissue. Researchers can identify if those objects were actually used as ritual instruments. We also examine how a victim would have had to be positioned in order for someone to open the thorax ergonomically, and which altars in archaeological contexts may have been used for that purpose.

When people hear about heart extraction, they may imagine an emotionally charged or chaotic act. But you describe the procedure as if orchestrated with anatomical and ergonomic precision. It makes the sacrificial ritual sound almost clinical.

It is a very good question. But it was not about performing the act carefully for its own sake. It was a human killing that had to be religiously theatricalized and dramatized; it had to be made meaningfully and effectively carried out by ritual specialists — a proper liturgy.

It could not be accidental or clumsy — “I missed,” or “I stabbed in the wrong place.” The rite had to be performed correctly. There are sources suggesting that specialists could face grave consequences if they failed in their ritual role, whether they were priests or musicians who performed incorrectly.

At the same time, these acts could be extremely forceful. There was an “overkill,” an excess. This pattern is documented in many societies where human sacrifice occurred. The point was an explosive release: bodily essences, understood as sublime substances, were released and communicated with the gods. The action had to be visually effective and choreographed, but it also required religious devotion, substantial knowledge and practical experience by the practitioners.

“So this was not uncontrolled, psychopathic violence. It was highly controlled, yet excessive violence, carried out within a ritual choreography, the highest expression of ritual debt making there was.”

The title of your book begins with the words: Ritual Violence. The word “violence” has a negative connotation in English and other European languages, as does the term “sacrifice.” Does that framing fit the Mesoamerican cosmovision?

If we worked through the Indigenous languages more carefully, sacrifice is the act of merit-making, debt payments, feeding, nourishment and sustenance.

The acts were described in direct terms: a person was cut; a person was opened. “Opened” is important. To sacrifice was to cut or open something so that bodily essences could be released, the trunk likened to the sacred mountain of the Indigenous cosmos.

Bloodletting was not simply a sign of brutality. It was the primary offering, the most sacred substance, surrounded by these bodily essences. It possessed great power. From this perspective, what we call violence was not necessarily understood as hatred, jealousy or uncontrolled aggression. It belonged to a different set of religious thoughts and a Weltanschauung, entirely different from our own Westernized views of existence.

Would ordinary people have participated in these human sacrifices, or were they reserved for elites?

Human sacrifice was the highest expression of religiosity, and it was generally institutionalized and centralized. It belonged to the inner political and religious structures of society.

Other people could be present as spectators. At a smaller level, households may have practiced rites involving deer, chickens or other animals. But human sacrifice was most probably not an ordinary household practice, except for times of extreme crises.

“The elite did not necessarily carry out every act themselves. A ritual specialist could perform the physical procedure, while a high-ranking person received the heart and offered it to the gods. That is simplified, of course. The details varied according to the period, region, Indigenous society and occasion.”

We must remember that Mesoamerica was not one uniform culture. It is more like speaking of Europe over a stretch of 3,000 years: You cannot say “the Europeans did this” as though every person, place and century followed one practice. Mesoamerica was a broad, highly complex cultural world.

Early Spanish accounts were often horrified by what they saw. How should we read those accounts?

The Spaniards were shocked, of course, but they were also impressed. They encountered highly developed societies knowledgeable of reading, specialized crafts, books, elaborate calendrical systems and complex political and religious structures.

There was fear of an enemy, but also a degree of admiration. These were not societies that can be reduced to a stereotype of “Indians” or to a single story of sacrifice. Their military disadvantage came from specific conditions — European weapons, horses and the wheel — not from a lack of sophistication.

In the Maya area, conquest also took much longer. Communities used guerrilla tactics, and in some areas, like the Central Petén, the Spanish could not fully penetrate the forested interior for around 150 years.

You suggested that some contemporary bull-related festivities in the Maya region may preserve elements of older ritual logics. What do you mean?

After the Spanish arrival, Indigenous communities were subjected to enormous pressure: violence, massacres and disease. Yet they also knew how to assimilate elements that had been foreign and make them their own.

Bullfighting came with the Spanish, but in some communities it was incorporated into local ritual systems. People no longer performed human sacrifice, but the bull could become the sacrificial being.

“Even today, bullrings in the Maya region used for patron-saint celebrations have a ceiba tree in the middle. This tree represents the axis connecting the sky, the human world and the underworld. It evokes centrality and communication by humans with the sacred realms of their cosmos.”

There are also elements such as the first drawing of the bull’s blood, removal of the heart, and the communal preparation and consumption of the entire animal. In Yucatán, for example, the dish chocolomo can be prepared using the animal in its entirety. This can be understood as part of incorporation or ritual consumption.

The Spanish may not have recognized these meanings, or they tolerated them.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Jalisco governor announces water-rationing plan for Guadalajara amid contamination crisis
World.content:
Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus has announced a water-rationing plan for the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area (ZMG) amid growing concerns over citywide water contamination.

“The city is going through an unprecedented drinking water crisis,” Lemus said in a video posted on his official social media channels. “And like in any crisis, the first step is to acknowledge it in order to solve it.”

The temporary measure, expected to last approximately six months in its first stage, will involve withdrawing up to 2.5 cubic meters per second from the distribution network by no longer using water from the Las Pintas dam and the old Chapala system.

According to the newspaper La Jornada, water consumption in the ZMG stands at between 10 and 11.5 cubic meters per second, so the decrease would represent around a quarter of the supply.

Gov. Lemus acknowledged in his video announcement that the move means less water during the rehabilitation project — hence the rationing — but what flows will be cleaner.

The plan does not mean that homes will be without water for six consecutive months. Rather, service rotations, low-pressure episodes, and interruptions during one or two days are expected in the most affected areas.

Further details about how the program will operate will be announced by the Intermunicipal Potable Water and Sewerage System (SIAPA) and the municipalities on Oct. 12.

State Chief of Staff Alberto Esquer told the newspaper El Informador that authorities are analyzing the volume of water that can be distributed without drawing from the Las Pintas source. This calculation will make it possible to determine service rotations and conditions while the planned works are being carried out.

“We call on residents for patience; we are working on this, and we acknowledge the problem,” Esquer said.

Poor water quality affects at least 342 metropolitan neighborhoods. Lemus attributed the problem primarily to the aging Chapala supply system and illegal discharges into the Las Pintas canal, where the water coming from Chapala mixes with the drainage from the south of the city.

To restore the supply, authorities will fast-track the La Calera diversion aqueduct and the first phase of the expansion of Water Treatment Plant No. 1 one in Miravalle. They will also establish a permanent working group with metropolitan mayors to monitor water supply and quality.

As a long-term solution, Lemus proposed building a replacement Chapala–Guadalajara aqueduct, with an estimated completion time of two years. He added that President Claudia Sheinbaum agreed that the federal government would carry out and fund the outstanding works required for the El Zapotillo system to operate at full capacity.

Lemus said that the announced measures would not entail public debt, increases in SIAPA rates, or privatization of the water service.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: No Atlantic hurricanes hit Mexico throughout September. That’s not normal
World.content:
The eastern coast of Mexico made it through September without a hurricane as the Atlantic basin recorded its first hurricane-free September in more than three decades.

On the country’s Pacific side, however, the storms kept churning.

Through Wednesday, the Pacific basin — which stretches from the Americas westward to the International Date Line — had produced 20 named storms and nine hurricanes during a 2026 season that began May 15.

Three of those hurricanes reached Category 5: Hurricane Genevieve, well off Mexico’s Pacific coast in July; Hurricane Lowell, which formed in the Eastern Pacific in August and moved toward Hawaii; and Hurricane Polo, which pounded the Baja Peninsula and the Sonora coast in September.

Meanwhile, no Atlantic storm had reached hurricane strength through Oct. 1, although the current Tropical Storm Isaias could change that.

A major driver is a “super” El Niño creating exceptionally warm equatorial Pacific waters.

According to specialists at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), warmer water from the central equatorial Pacific is shifted by El Niño toward the northeastern Pacific off Mexico, providing more energy for cyclones to form and intensify. Plus, El Niño tends to reduce vertical wind shear in the eastern and central Pacific, making conditions more favorable for hurricanes.

In the Atlantic, El Niño tends to increase vertical wind shear — changes in wind speed or direction with altitude — which can tear apart developing storms.

The contrast was forecast months ago, when Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) projected 18 to 21 tropical cyclones in the eastern Pacific and 11 to 15 in the Atlantic.

September further illustrated the contrast.

Historically the statistical peak of the Atlantic hurricane season, September was hurricane-free in the Atlantic for the first time since 1994.

The only other such Septembers since 1950 were in 1972 and 1962, according to Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.

All of that being said, the 2026 Atlantic lull might be over.

Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the southwestern Gulf of Mexico, north of Veracruz and west of the Yucatán Peninsula, and was forecast to become the season’s first Atlantic hurricane. Its maximum sustained winds were charted at 45 mph at 9 a.m. Mexico City time Wednesday.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) forecast Isaias to reach hurricane strength, with winds of at least 75 mph, early Thursday and peak early Friday at 110 mph, near the top of the Category 2 range.

Though increasing wind shear could weaken Isaias before landfall, the NHC expected it to reach the southern U.S. late Friday or early Saturday.

Before that, the storm could bring 5 to 10 centimeters (2 to 4 inches) of rain around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula.

Both hurricane seasons run through Nov. 30.

With reports from El Horizonte, Smithsonian magazine, KABC and BBC

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: State competitiveness, electric scooter rules and SIAPA director scrutiny
World.content:
This week we look at where and how Jalisco’s competitiveness ranking has fallen in 2026 in relation to other states, what the new SIAPA director has been up to in lieu of briefing the state Congress, and long-awaited new rules for electric scooter riders.

Jalisco falls to 6th place in state competitiveness rankings

Jalisco is losing competitiveness in its ability to generate, attract and retain investment and talent, according to the recently released 2026 Urban Competitiveness Index (ICE).

Prepared by the Mexican Institute for Competitiveness (IMCO), the ICE study ranks all 32 Mexican states for competitiveness, based on 53 indicators across six categories.

In 2026, Jalisco fell two spots to 6th place, down from 4th in the 2025 study. The state’s worst performance came in Political System and Government, at 16th out of 32 states (falling from 9th last year). Jalisco also did poorly in Law, ranking 15th, and Society and Environment, at 13th.

Weakness in the political system and government ranking this year is attributable to the public’s declining confidence in the public sector, with 86% of state residents believing that corruption is “frequent” or “very frequent” in Jalisco.

Another factor negatively impacting Jalisco’s competitiveness ranking this year is its poor performance in the Legal category — ranking 29th out of 32. Relative to other states, Jalisco’s notarial services are very limited, with only 1.3 notaries per 100,000 inhabitants.

Finally, Jalisco also underperformed in the Perception of Security indicator, ranking 18th. In 2026, the study found that only 21.5% of state residents over the age of 18 feel safe living here.

Offsetting these shortcomings, Jalisco performed well in its ability to develop and attract skilled labor, improving to 3rd place from 8th last year, and in economic innovation, where it ranked 3rd in 2026.

Commenting on Jalisco’s performance, Israel Macías López, an economics professor at the Pan-American University, told El Mural that the state cannot rely solely on its economic strengths any longer, adding, “This ultimately serves as a wake-up call for the state government.”

The top five states in the 2026 ICE rankings are Mexico City, Querétaro, Nuevo León, Coahuila and Baja California Sur, in that order. A year ago, the top five were Mexico City, Baja California Sur, Nuevo León, Jalisco and Aguascalientes.

With reporting from El Mural.

New regulations approved for e-scooter riders in Guadalajara

In recent years, walking or biking around the metropolitan area can sometimes feel like a death-defying maneuver, as scooter riders zoom every which way without warning. New regulations just passed by the Jalisco Congress seek to bring some order to the chaos.

A motion sponsored by two legislators of the Movimiento Ciudadano party, Alejandra Giadans and Mónica Magaña, passed with 20 votes in favor, 14 against, and one abstention.

The new law bans scooters from sidewalks as well as main avenues, tunnels, bridges and overpasses across the city, where traffic speeds exceed 50 km per hour. Scooter usage will now be limited to bike paths at speeds not to exceed 25 km per hour. In pedestrian zones, scooter users will be required to walk with the device instead of riding it.

According to Magaña, “This initiative incorporates elements to promote a cultural transformation towards a more humane and inclusive city, where the protection and safety of all people is a priority, considering pedestrians as the most vulnerable users.”

Each municipality covered by the new law will be responsible for defining penalties for the misuse of scooters in their jurisdiction. They now have a six-month window to adapt their local transit rules to the new law, with full enforcement expected to begin sometime next year.

With reporting from El Informador.

SIAPA’s new director yet to address Congress after 6 months on the job

Miguel de la Rosa Figueroa, leader of the Morena caucus, and deputy Mariana Casillas Guerrero, who oversees the Planning, Territorial Organization and Water Management Commission of the Congress, late last month called on State Water Ministry (SIAPA) Director Ismael Jáuregui Castañeda to attend a hearing before the Congress of Jalisco to talk about water quality issues and the agency’s plans to address them.

Jáuregui has been at the helm of the embattled water agency for almost six months and has yet to appear, despite numerous invitations from state legislators.

For his part, in a letter to Congress, Jáuregui cited the need to prioritize pressing hydraulic projects — such as work to overhaul the La Calera system and Miravalle Water Treatment Plant — over attending meetings with state officials. He has also indicated he would appear before the legislature only after Governor Pablo Lemus submitted a formal request for SIAPA’s new budget.

While Jáuregui clearly has his hands full, lawmakers’ frustrations are beginning to mount. Opposition groups have characterized his failure to appear as an act of disrespect and defiance in the face of the water quality crisis affecting Guadalajara.

With reporting from the University of Guadalajara press.

World.title: Latest Citi poll of Mexico-based analysts sees weakened peso through 2027
World.content:
The “super peso” that strengthened the Mexican currency’s exchange rate to under 17 per dollar for more than a week in late August and early September won’t be returning any time soon, according to the Citi Survey of Expectations published on Tuesday.

The prevailing opinion of the Mexico-based analysts consulted is that the peso will trade at 18 pesos per dollar at the end of 2026, a half peso weaker than was suggested in the early September Citi forecast, published at the height of the super peso. It is seen weakening further to 18.50 by the end of 2027, although some of the survey responders see it approaching 20 to the dollar.

If proof is needed that economics is not an exact science, one can note that predictions from the consulted institutions range from 16.80 to 18.80 pesos per dollar by the end of the year. Several financial institutions, including Barclays, BNP Paribas, Bx+, Citi, Bank of America, Santander México, and Itaú BBA, expect a more favorable outcome, while Masari Casa de Bolsa and Bankaool expect the peso to depreciate more quickly.

The analysts mainly agree on the peso weakening even further against the dollar in 2027, but not on how much.

“By the end of 2027, the consensus expects the exchange rate to be at 18.50 pesos per dollar, down from 18 pesos per dollar two weeks ago, with expectations ranging from 17.00 to 19.80,” the Citi Survey stated.

On Sept. 4, the peso traded at 16.89 pesos per dollar before depreciating throughout the rest of September, finally inching above 18 after losing 46 centavos against the dollar between September 28 and October 2. During September, the peso was the worst-performing currency against the dollar, falling 6%.

The dollar fell back under 18 pesos on Tuesday, but most analysts don’t foresee the peso remaining so strong, amid heightened global risk aversion and concerns about inflation and interest-rate differentials.

In the survey, 25 of 37 respondents said they expect the Bank of Mexico’s interest rate to remain at 6.5% through the end of 2027, a major factor in the pessimistic prognosis of the peso’s value.

Minutes from the U.S. Federal Reserve’s latest policy meeting, due Wednesday, could provide greater insight into interest rates and the U.S. central bank’s policy plans, informing future forecasts.

With reports from El Financiero, Informador and Reuters

World.title: Rubio Wants Europe Awake. Latin America Is.
World.content:
ANALYSIS · THE WEST AND POWER

Key Facts — The speech US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke on Wednesday, 7 October 2026, on the Pnyx in Athens, with the Acropolis behind him.

— The core line “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power.”

— The backdrop America has been at war with Iran since 28 February 2026, and Iran says the Strait of Hormuz stays shut until its conditions are met.

— Prediction markets Polymarket puts a US invasion of Iran before 2027 at 15.5% and a Democratic House win on 3 November at 90.5% (8 October, 2:32 p.m. ET).

— What it means for you Expect years of heavy spending on defense, chips, energy and factories, and more US pressure on allies to pay their share.

For three decades, the West believed trade and global institutions would make raw power old-fashioned. On a rock in Athens, Marco Rubio declared that era over.

On Wednesday, 7 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood on the Pnyx, the hill where ancient Athenians voted on war and peace, with the Acropolis behind him. He told the Western world that it had become ashamed of its own greatness, and that this shame now threatens its survival.

His message fit into one sentence: “Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power.” After thirty years of the globalization consensus, it marks the start of a new era in which the West intends to show its teeth again.

The Speech in Plain Words

Ancient Greece, Rubio said, gave the West its character: ambition, curiosity, a love of competition and the fighting spirit the Greeks called thumos. “Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive.”

Then he named what went wrong. The West opened its borders, shipped its factories abroad, let its armies wither and decay and handed decisions “to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control,” while rivals were “all too happy to fill the vacuum.”

His message to Europe was blunt but friendly. “We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber,” he said, praising Greece as “a model ally” and NATO’s 2025 pledge in The Hague to raise defense and security spending to 5% of GDP by 2035.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Marco Rubio Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Athens, and Why Now

The place carried a lesson. Around 483 BC, Athenians on this hill chose to spend a silver windfall on 200 warships instead of sharing out the money, according to the historian Herodotus. The ships were built for a war with the nearby island of Aegina, but three years later they formed the core of the fleet that crushed the Persian king Xerxes at Salamis.

Athens survived because it built power before it needed it. Rubio recalled the Athenians who defended the Acropolis to the last against the Persians, and today Persia’s heir is at war with America.

On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel struck Iran and killed its supreme leader, and Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world’s oil. A ceasefire collapsed in July, oil topped US$100 a barrel in September, and on the day of the speech President Trump said a deal was no longer something he wanted. A day later he said the United States would not attack Iran before the midterm elections.

Rubio’s attack on “the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes” sent Europe a clear signal: this war is yours too. He aimed at the regime, not at Iran’s roughly 90 million people, many of whom have risked their lives protesting against it.

Guests listen as Rubio speaks on the Pnyx on 7 October 2026, the hill where the citizens of ancient Athens met in assembly. (Photo: US Department of State, public domain)

In the Line of Truman and Reagan

Great American speeches to Europe have marked turning points before. In 1947 Harry Truman asked Congress for US$400 million to save Greece and Turkey from communism, and in 1987 Ronald Reagan stood at the Berlin Wall and said, “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!”

In Warsaw in 2017, Donald Trump asked “whether the West has the will to survive,” and in Munich in 2025 Vice President JD Vance warned Europe of “the threat from within.” Rubio’s own speech in Munich this February was the handshake; Athens is the battle plan.

Ronald Reagan speaks at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin on 12 June 1987, the speech in which he told Mikhail Gorbachev to tear down the Berlin Wall. (Photo: White House Photographic Office, public domain)

What is new is that Rubio no longer claims Western values belong to everyone. Truman, Reagan and George W. Bush spoke of universal freedom, but Rubio called heroism, honor and duty “the product of a distinct character,” echoing the Harvard scholar Samuel Huntington, who wrote in 1996 that the West is “unique, not universal.”

He also made power an explicit goal, joined to “prudence and diplomacy” and to “the credibility that you are willing to use it.” That is the classical rule the Greek historian Thucydides recorded 2,400 years ago: “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.”

Everyone Else Never Stopped

“War did not disappear simply because we preferred peace,” Rubio said, and the record proves it. China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and now makes close to 30% of the world’s manufactured goods, Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and Iran turned the world’s oil supply into a weapon in 2026.

Europe Is Living on an Inheritance

Europe’s comfort is real, but much of it was earned long ago: centuries of risk, conquest and invention, then the American security umbrella since 1949 and, until 2022, cheap Russian gas. That inheritance is shrinking, and the EU’s birth rate fell to a record low of 1.34 children per woman in 2024, far below the 2.1 needed to keep a population stable.

Migration is the most explosive issue. Some 46.7 million people born outside the EU lived in the bloc at the start of 2025, about one in ten, according to Eurostat, and the US National Security Strategy of December 2025 warned of Europe’s “stark prospect of civilizational erasure”; in Athens, Rubio praised the shared US-Greek ambition to “secure Europe’s borders from the threats of mass migration.”

Latin America Is Choosing Sides

The speech landed in a hemisphere that has already moved. Since October 2025, voters have elected right-leaning presidents in Bolivia, Honduras, Chile, Peru and Colombia, and more than a dozen countries in the region have joined the Shield of the Americas, a US-led coalition against cartels.

Of the region’s biggest economies, only Brazil and Mexico are still governed by the left, and Brazil may turn next. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, won 47.03% in the first round against 45.16% for President Lula da Silva and has promised to join the Shield if he wins the runoff on 25 October.

For the West, the region is a treasure chest. Chile, Argentina and Bolivia hold roughly half of the world’s identified lithium, Chile and Peru mine about a third of its copper, Mexico and Peru produce more than a third of its silver, Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves on earth, and Brazil leads the world in exports of soybeans, beef and coffee.

China noticed first: its trade with Latin America is worth more than US$500 billion a year, and a Chinese state company owns 60% of Peru’s new megaport of Chancay. The region can slide back into a colonial pattern of raw materials out and finished goods in, or become an indispensable partner in the West’s comeback, if its leaders use that leverage to build industry at home.

What the Critics Miss

The left says culture is “fluid” and that what binds nations is “material,” as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez argued in Munich, while Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum condemns anyone who praises Hernán Cortés, whom Rubio named beside Alexander and Caesar. None of these critics offers an alternative to power, and they argue about tone and history while Beijing, Moscow and Tehran keep arming, buying and building.

Why the West Must Show Its Teeth Again

Power never disappears; someone else simply picks it up. Athens built its fleet before Xerxes came, Truman armed Greece before communism could take it and Reagan rebuilt American strength before the Berlin Wall fell, and each time power came first and freedom followed.

Today only the United States can lead that comeback, because Europe has the money and the history but not yet the will. If Washington joins force with prudence and loyalty to its allies, the speech on the Pnyx will be remembered beside Truman’s and Reagan’s as the day the West decided to stand up again.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, the new doctrine means years of public money for defense, shipbuilding, chips, critical minerals and energy. For households, the Iran war is the immediate cost, because oil stays expensive as long as shipping through Hormuz is blocked or restricted, and in Latin America the war splits oil exporters from importers.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a US invasion of Iran before 2027 was priced at 15.5% on 8 October at 2:32 p.m. ET, and the Democrats had a 90.5% chance of winning the House on 3 November. The midterms are therefore the first big test of Rubio’s doctrine at home.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

Nobody knows yet whether Europe will turn its spending pledge into real ships and factories, or how the Iran war will end. Rubio has also said nothing about running for president in 2028, although some commentators read the staging as a sign of bigger ambitions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where did Marco Rubio give his Acropolis speech?

He spoke on Wednesday, 7 October 2026, on the Pnyx, the hill in Athens where the citizens of ancient Athens met in assembly. The Acropolis stood behind him.

What did Rubio mean by the unapologetic pursuit of national power?

He meant rebuilding industry, supply chains and defense and competing to lead in technologies such as artificial intelligence, chips and drones. He said real power needs both diplomacy and a credible willingness to use force.

Why did Rubio mention the Persians and Iran?

He opened with the Persian attack on Athens in 480 BC and later condemned the radical mullahs of Iran. The United States has been at war with Iran since February 2026.

How does Latin America fit into Rubio’s vision?

Most Latin American governments now lean right and work with Washington on security through the Shield of the Americas. The region’s lithium, copper, silver, oil and food make it essential to any Western comeback.

Sources: US State Department, Rubio remarks, 7 October 2026; Herodotus 7.144; Truman Doctrine; Reagan Library; Warsaw 2017; Foreign Affairs 1996; Eurostat population by country of birth; Eurostat fertility; TSE Brazil; RTP; Konrad Adenauer Foundation; USGS 2025; LatinFinance; Washington Times; CNBC; elDiario.es; Fox News; Polymarket Iran; Polymarket House (accessed 8 October 2026).

World.title: Canada’s NATO Path Needs US$112 Billion by 2035
World.content:
Canada’s NATO Path Needs US$112 Billion by 2035

CANADA · ANALYSIS

Key Facts — What is happening The Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO), Canada’s independent budget watchdog, says the NATO 5% pledge means core defence spending of C$159 billion (about US$112 billion) in 2035-36.

— Why it matters The PBO puts the extra deficit at C$63 billion (about US$44 billion) in that year, and the plan is a large, long-term procurement stream for US suppliers.

— The numbers A C$68.2 billion (about US$48 billion) gap over a 2%-of-GDP baseline in 2035-36, or about C$33.5 billion (US$24 billion) more a year on average over ten years.

— Who is who Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government made the pledge, David J. McGuinty is Minister of National Defence, and François-Philippe Champagne is Finance Minister.

— What to watch Multi-year defence appropriations, contract awards through the Defence Investment Agency, and the PBO’s next update on the fiscal plan.

— What it means for you US defence suppliers may gain from Canadian orders, but Ottawa wants Canadian industry to share the work.

Canada’s promise to spend 5% of its economy on defence by 2035 is now a priced budget item. Parliament’s independent budget watchdog says it would take about C$159 billion (US$112 billion) of core defence spending in 2035-36 and widen that year’s deficit by C$63 billion (US$44 billion).

Canada is the United States’ closest defence partner and a founding NATO member. This analysis explains what the pledge costs, who pays, and what it means for US investors and suppliers, building on our USA & Canada Intelligence Brief.

How Canada Got to the 5% Pledge

At the NATO summit in The Hague on 25 June 2025, allies agreed to invest 5% of GDP a year on defence by 2035. The pledge splits into 3.5% for core defence needs and up to 1.5% for related security spending such as infrastructure and resilience.

Canada joined that pledge under Prime Minister Mark Carney, and NATO data released on 26 March 2026 showed Canada had met the alliance’s earlier 2% benchmark. The hard part is the next step, lifting core spending from about 2% of GDP to 3.5% within a decade.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mark Carney Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Budget Watchdog Calculated

The PBO published its costing on 5 February 2026. It assumes core defence spending rises in equal yearly steps from 2.0% of GDP in 2025-26 to 3.5% in 2035-36.

This is a scenario, not a government plan, because Ottawa has not published detailed long-term projections. The government says the extra 1.5% is expected to be met under current planned spending, and the PBO holds it flat at 1.5% of GDP.

Core defence spending would reach about C$159 billion (US$112 billion) in 2035-36 on a cash basis.

(US$112 billion) in 2035-36 on a cash basis. That is C$68.2 billion (US$48 billion) more than if spending stayed at 2% of GDP.

(US$48 billion) more than if spending stayed at 2% of GDP. The path needs about C$33.5 billion (US$24 billion) more cash spending a year on average over ten years.

(US$24 billion) more cash spending a year on average over ten years. The deficit would be about C$63 billion (US$44 billion) larger in 2035-36, or 1.4 percentage points of GDP .

(US$44 billion) larger in 2035-36, or . The federal debt-to-GDP ratio would be 6.3 percentage points higher by 2035-36.

The PBO measures spending on a cash basis, as NATO does, then converts it to an accrual basis for the budget balance. A fast rise in equipment purchases lifts cash spending quickly, while the accounting expense shows up more gradually.

US$ values use the 8 October 2026 RT rate of about 1.42 Canadian dollars per US dollar, applied to the PBO’s future-dated figures. The conversion is indicative only.

Who Is Responsible

Budget 2025, introduced on 4 November 2025, proposed C$81.8 billion (about US$58 billion) over five years to rebuild and rearm the Canadian Armed Forces. That money is part of the government’s stated path toward the pledge.

David J. McGuinty has been Minister of National Defence since 13 May 2025, and François-Philippe Champagne is Minister of Finance. Between them they must decide how much of the extra spending is paid for by borrowing, new revenue or cuts elsewhere.

The government launched the Defence Investment Agency on 2 October 2025 to speed up procurement. Doug Guzman, a former deputy chair of RBC, was appointed its chief executive in November 2025, and its record on delivery will test whether money turns into capability.

The Business Stakes for US Suppliers

Canada’s likely shopping list covers areas where US firms already compete, including air defence, surveillance, communications, cyber and munitions. In our assessment, shared systems and the joint US-Canadian NORAD air-defence command give US suppliers an interoperability advantage.

Ottawa also wants more of the work done in Canada, so contracts may carry local-content or industrial-benefit conditions. US firms should expect to partner with Canadian companies or share technology to win large orders.

What It Means for US Readers and Investors

For investors in US defence and aerospace companies, the pledge points to years of steady Canadian demand rather than one large order. The C$33.5 billion (about US$24 billion) average yearly increase will arrive as many separate contracts across air, sea, land, cyber and space.

For US policymakers, Canada is a test of whether the 5% pledge can survive domestic budget politics. If a wealthy G7 economy struggles to pay for it, smaller allies will find it harder still.

For Canadian taxpayers and businesses, the extra deficit competes with health care, housing and other federal priorities. Readers who follow Canadian bonds or the Canadian dollar should watch how Ottawa chooses to finance the build-up.

What Is Not Known

Ottawa has not published a detailed long-term plan, so yearly spending, the mix of projects and the financing strategy are all still open. The PBO figures are an estimate of what a gradual path would require, not a forecast of what the government will approve.

It is also unclear which projects will count toward the 1.5% related-spending bucket. Disputes over dual-use airports, ports and telecoms could let Canada meet the number without matching gains in military capability.

What to Watch

The next federal budget is a natural place to look for multi-year defence appropriations rather than headline targets. Readers should compare any new figures with the PBO’s C$63 billion deficit estimate.

Major contract awards in aircraft, air defence, ships and cyber will show whether spending becomes delivered capability. Announcements from the Defence Investment Agency will show how quickly procurement moves.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Canada’s NATO defence spending target?

Canada has joined NATO’s pledge to spend 5% of GDP a year on defence by 2035, agreed at The Hague on 25 June 2025. It includes 3.5% for core defence and up to 1.5% for related security investment.

How much would the NATO target add to Canada’s deficit?

The PBO estimates the extra core defence spending would add about C$63 billion (US$44 billion) to the 2035-36 deficit, or 1.4 percentage points of GDP. The federal debt-to-GDP ratio would be 6.3 percentage points higher by then.

How much would Canada spend on core defence in 2035-36?

The PBO estimates about C$159 billion (US$112 billion) on a cash basis. That is C$68.2 billion (US$48 billion) more than keeping spending at 2% of GDP.

What does it mean for US defence companies?

Canada may buy more air defence, surveillance, communications and cyber systems, areas where US firms are strong. Ottawa is also likely to ask for Canadian industrial participation, so partnerships may be needed.

Is this an official government spending plan?

No. It is a PBO scenario with equal yearly increases, because the government has not published detailed long-term projections.
