World.title: Zambia and Its Neighbours in Southern Africa
World.content:
ZAMBIA · SOUTHERN AFRICA

Key Facts — The country Landlocked copper producer, 19.7 million people at the 2022 census.

— The neighbours Eight: DR Congo, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia, Angola.

— Who leads President Hakainde Hichilema, re-elected 13 August 2026, sworn in 1 September.

— What happened SADC, the regional bloc, elected Zambia’s president incoming chair, 17 August 2026.

— The bottleneck Road carried 95.8% of export value, January to July 2026.

— Still open No public completion date for Zambia’s 550 km Lobito rail link.

Eight borders, a shared Zambezi dam, rival railways to the sea and high copper prices shape Zambia’s ties with its region.

Understanding the Zambia neighbourhood starts with a map: eight countries border this landlocked copper producer at the centre of Southern Africa. Its copper reaches the sea only through neighbours’ roads, railways and ports.

That makes the neighbours central to Zambia’s economy, its electricity and its foreign policy. For US readers, the region is also where American-backed and Chinese-backed routes for critical minerals now compete.

Mapping the Zambia Neighbourhood, Eight Borders and No Coast

Zambia covers 752,612 square kilometres, a little larger than Texas, and counted 19,693,423 people at its 2022 census. The Zambia Statistics Agency (ZamStats), the national statistics office, calls it a land linked country rather than landlocked.

According to the census report, the Democratic Republic of the Congo lies to the north and Tanzania to the north-east. Malawi lies to the east; Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia to the south; and Angola to the west.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Ethiopia tells Eritrea to pull troops out of Tigray” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Zambia and Botswana meet on the Zambezi River at Kazungula. The Southern African Development Community (SADC), the 16-member regional bloc, calls it the point where Botswana and Zambia meet Namibia and Zimbabwe.

Five of these countries also share wildlife country. The Kavango Zambezi conservation area, known as KAZA, spans Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, according to Zambia’s Department of Immigration.

Rio Times explainers cover Congo, Angola, Zimbabwe and Tanzania, and daily news is on the Rio Times Zambia page.

Friends, Rivals and the Frontline Legacy

Many of Zambia’s regional friendships were formed in the liberation wars after its independence from Britain in 1964. Rhodesia, today’s Zimbabwe, declared independence unilaterally under white-minority rule on 11 November 1965.

Zambia then backed the liberation struggle as a frontline state, according to the official history of TAZARA, the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority. That history says Rhodesia tried to pressure Zambia by cutting its road and rail routes to South African ports.

Tanzania offered the alternative outlet, and China financed a railway between the two after Western lenders and the World Bank declined. Two jointly owned links, the TAZARA railway and the TAZAMA pipeline, still bind Tanzania and Zambia.

Zambia’s top diplomat in October 2026 was Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe, serving under President Hakainde Hichilema. Hichilema leads the governing United Party for National Development (UPND) and first won power in 2021.

Relations with Zimbabwe mix deep interdependence with occasional friction. The two countries run the Kariba Dam together, yet Zambian voices have also judged Zimbabwe’s politics in public.

In August 2023, while Hichilema chaired SADC’s security organ, a SADC observer mission led by Nevers Mumba watched Zimbabwe’s elections. Mumba is a former Zambian vice-president.

The mission’s preliminary statement of 25 August 2023 said some aspects fell short of Zimbabwe’s constitution, its electoral law and SADC guidelines.

Congo was Zambia’s biggest African customer in August 2026 and is also a rival for mining investment. It mined about 3.2 million tonnes of copper in 2025, against Zambia’s 940,000, according to US Geological Survey estimates.

Trade With the Neighbours, and Where the Copper Goes

In August 2026, refined copper earned US$1,098.2 million of Zambia’s US$1,748.4 million in exports, about 63 percent, ZamStats reports.

Imports that month came to US$1,396.4 million, leaving a surplus of US$352.0 million. From January to August 2026, the surplus totalled US$1,948.8 million.

The largest single buyer in August 2026 was Canada, with 32.0 percent of export earnings, mainly copper anodes sent for refining. Congo came second at 12.2 percent, ahead of China at 12.0 percent, Switzerland at 11.7 percent and Singapore at 10.6 percent.

On the import side, China supplied 25.5 percent and South Africa 25.3 percent of the bill. Congo, at 6.2 percent, was the only neighbour among Zambia’s five largest suppliers.

SADC members bought about 24 percent of Zambia’s exports in August 2026. They supplied about 37 percent of its imports, mostly from South Africa.

Neighbours matter most for non-traditional exports, the ZamStats category for goods beyond the traditional copper trade. Congo took 37.2 percent of these in August 2026, Malawi 8.6 percent and Zimbabwe 6.4 percent.

Refined copper exports reached 608,100 tonnes from January to August 2026, up 9.0 percent on a year earlier. The London Metal Exchange price averaged US$14,353.4 a tonne in August.

Migration and Refugees Across Zambia’s Borders

Zambia is overwhelmingly a country of its own citizens. At the 2022 census, 99.3 percent of residents were Zambian and 0.4 percent were foreign nationals.

Among those foreigners, 26.5 percent were Congolese and 13.0 percent Malawian, followed by Indians at 10.9 percent. Family was the most common reason for living in Zambia, at 37.5 percent, while 31.4 percent were refugees.

Families straddle the borders as well. Zambians holding a second citizenship most often also hold Congolese (15.2 percent) or Zimbabwean (14.9 percent) nationality, the census found.

The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, counted 83,225 refugees and 12,906 asylum seekers in Zambia at the end of 2025. Of the refugees, 64,792 came from Congo, with Burundi and Somalia next.

Entry rules for foreigners are set out in the Rio Times guide to Zambia visas, work permits and residency.

Shared Rivers, Kariba and the Zambezi River Authority

The Zambezi River carries much of the relationship with Zimbabwe. The Zambezi River Authority (ZRA), set up on 1 October 1987 by parallel laws in both parliaments, operates the Kariba Dam.

Zambia and Zimbabwe own the authority jointly and equally. Each runs its own power station at the dam: 1,080 megawatts on Zambia’s north bank and 1,050 megawatts on Zimbabwe’s south bank.

Full, the reservoir behind the dam holds about 185 billion cubic metres and stretches 280 kilometres. On 5 October 2026 its usable storage stood at 38.04 percent, against 14.30 percent a year earlier, ZRA data show.

Better 2025/26 rains allowed a 2026 allocation of 36 billion cubic metres for power, split equally between the two utilities. Because both draw on the same water, a dry year hits Zambian and Zimbabwean supplies together.

The next shared project is the 2,400-megawatt Batoka Gorge scheme, 47 kilometres downstream of Victoria Falls. First conceived in 1972, it was still at feasibility review and financing as of October 2026, according to ZRA.

Bridges, Railways and Pipelines to the Sea

Zambia’s trade still moves overwhelmingly by truck. Road carried 95.8 percent of export value from January to July 2026, while rail carried just 0.9 percent, ZamStats reports.

The Kazungula Bridge, a US$259 million crossing to Botswana, opened on Monday, 10 May 2021, with a one-stop border post. SADC says the 929-metre bridge replaced a pontoon ferry and should link Congo and Tanzania to the South African port of Durban.

TAZARA, the 1,860-kilometre railway from Dar es Salaam to New Kapiri Mposhi, began full operations on 14 July 1976. China built it with an interest-free loan, and Tanzania and Zambia own it jointly and equally.

On 29 September 2025, TAZARA signed a freight concession with China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), a Chinese contractor. TAZARA says the deal covers rehabilitation, new locomotives and wagons, and more than US$1.4 billion of investment.

A second link, the TAZAMA pipeline, runs 1,710 kilometres from Dar es Salaam to Ndola in the Copperbelt. It has carried finished diesel instead of crude oil since 16 March 2023, according to the company.

At Nakonde, on the Tanzanian frontier, the Zambia Revenue Authority already works with US scanner maker Astrophysics. The US Embassy says Hichilema commissioned that border post in June 2026, and a contract for Livingstone followed on 24 August 2026.

The newest route runs west, through the Lobito Corridor to Angola’s Atlantic port of Lobito.

Financial close on its Angolan rail leg, a 1,300-kilometre line to the Congolese border, was announced on 3 July 2026. The US$753 million package included US$553 million from the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), Washington’s development bank.

The Development Bank of Southern Africa added US$200 million, according to the Africa Finance Corporation, an adviser on the deal.

For Zambia’s own link, the African Development Bank approved a US$255 million loan and a US$10 million grant on 6 August 2026. The project covers about 550 kilometres of new railway towards Angola and upgrades to 105 kilometres of the Mwinilunga-Jimbe road.

In early October, Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane said financing for the corridor’s road links was sealed, the Lusaka paper News Diggers reported. The Rio Times covered the announcement in Zambia Says Lobito Corridor Road Financing Is Secured.

Regional Bodies, SADC, COMESA and the Free Trade Area

SADC, headquartered in Gaborone, Botswana, counts all eight of Zambia’s neighbours among its 16 members. At its summit in Durban on Monday, 17 August 2026, it elected South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa as chair.

The same summit elected Zambia’s president as incoming chair and noted that the next summit will be held in Zambia. Hichilema already chaired SADC’s Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation, its security arm, in 2023.

The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), a 21-member trade bloc, has its secretariat in Lusaka, the capital. Its 25th summit is due in Harare, Zimbabwe, from Monday, 19 October to Thursday, 22 October 2026.

Three neighbours, Congo, Malawi and Zimbabwe, belong to both blocs, and ZamStats tracks that overlap separately. Angola, Tanzania, Botswana, Namibia and Mozambique are SADC members outside COMESA.

Zambia ratified the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) agreement on 28 January 2021, African Union records show. By the AU’s list of 22 May 2026, all eight neighbours had ratified too, among 49 countries in total.

Where Zambia Leads and Where It Follows

Zambia punches above its weight in regional diplomacy: it hosts COMESA and will chair SADC next. It also had about 1,000 peacekeepers with the UN mission in the Central African Republic in June 2026, the US Embassy said.

Its elections have produced change at the top. In 2021, Hichilema defeated sitting President Edgar Lungu with 57.51 percent, Electoral Commission of Zambia results show.

He won a second term on Thursday, 13 August 2026, and took the oath at Lusaka’s National Heroes Stadium on 1 September. Times of Zambia, a Lusaka daily, reported the ceremony and a margin of over 1.1 million votes against opposition runner-up Brian Mundubile.

The Rio Times covered the vote in its Zambia election result report. The wider country picture is in Zambia Explained.

In copper, Zambia follows Congo, which mined more than three times as much in 2025 by USGS estimates. In trade, it depends on South African suppliers and on ports in other countries, from Dar es Salaam to Durban.

In power, it shares Kariba’s water with Zimbabwe under a joint authority. Lusaka can lead debates in SADC, but it cannot manage the Zambezi or reach the sea alone.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, Zambia is a copper supplier whose metal reaches the world through other countries. Border queues, port capacity and railway deals therefore matter as much as mine output.

Washington has a direct stake in that geography through the DFC loan for Lobito. The Millennium Challenge Corporation, a US aid agency, also signed a US$491 million compact with Zambia on 17 October 2024.

On Thursday, 8 October 2026, the two governments signed a five-year health memorandum worth US$2.49 billion, the US Embassy said. Washington intends to provide more than US$1.5 billion, and Zambia pledged US$975 million more in its own health spending.

The Rio Times has covered the earlier health negotiations and Zambia’s talks with the IMF on a new loan.

US citizens do not need a visa to enter Zambia, according to its Department of Immigration. The State Department rates Zambia Level 1, exercise normal precautions, in an advisory last reissued on 31 July 2023.

A KAZA UniVisa, valid for up to 30 days in Zambia and Zimbabwe, costs US$50. The kwacha traded at about K19.90 per US dollar on 8 October 2026, the Bank of Zambia’s mid-rate.

What Is Not Known

The African Development Bank’s approval notice gives no completion date or full cost for Zambia’s 550-kilometre Lobito rail link. It describes the US$255 million loan as a first tranche.

It is not known how much the road financing Musokotwane described is worth, or when construction will start. It is also unclear when the revitalised TAZARA will carry more freight.

The Batoka Gorge scheme has no announced construction start, and ZRA says its financing is still being secured. How the 2026/27 rainy season will affect Lake Kariba is not yet known.

No recent official count of Zambians living in neighbouring countries was found. The census counts residents of Zambia, not emigrants.

Official 2026 vote shares were not on the Electoral Commission of Zambia’s website as of 8 October 2026. State House could not be reached to confirm the inauguration details.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many countries border Zambia?

Eight: the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia and Angola. Zambia has no coastline, so all its sea trade crosses at least one of them.

Who is the president of Zambia in October 2026?

Hakainde Hichilema of the United Party for National Development. He won a second term in the election of 13 August 2026 and was sworn in on 1 September 2026.

Is Zambia a member of SADC or COMESA?

It belongs to both. COMESA’s secretariat is in Lusaka, and SADC elected Zambia’s president its incoming chair in August 2026.

How does Zambia get its copper to the sea?

Mostly by truck through neighbouring countries: road carried 95.8 percent of all export value from January to July 2026. Rail links run to Dar es Salaam via TAZARA, and a new line towards Angola’s port of Lobito is planned.

Who controls Lake Kariba?

The Zambezi River Authority, which Zambia and Zimbabwe own jointly and equally. In 2026 it allocated 36 billion cubic metres of water for power, split equally between the two countries’ power utilities.

Do Americans need a visa for Zambia?

No, US citizens are on Zambia’s list of nationals who do not need a visa. A KAZA UniVisa for US$50 covers visits to both Zambia and Zimbabwe for up to 30 days.

World.title: Ghana Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
GHANA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country About 34.4 million people in West Africa, per a 2026 official projection.

— Who governs President John Mahama of the NDC, in office since 7 January 2025.

— Parliament The NDC holds 185 of 276 seats; the NPP holds 87.

— What happened The NPP elected John Boadu national chairman on 3 October 2026.

— Still open Mahama cannot run again; the NDC has no 2028 candidate yet.

A term-limited president with a two-thirds majority faces an opposition that has already chosen its 2028 challenger.

Ghana politics in October 2026 revolves around a president who cannot run again and a governing party with two-thirds of Parliament. John Mahama, sworn in on Tuesday, 7 January 2025, is serving his second and final elected term.

Every president since Jerry John Rawlings in 2001 has respected the two-term limit, a government-appointed review committee noted in its final report.

How Ghana Politics Works Under the 1992 Constitution

Ghana’s 1992 Constitution makes the president head of state, head of government and commander-in-chief of the armed forces. Ghanaians call this order the Fourth Republic, and the current Parliament is its ninth.

A president serves four years from the day of swearing-in, and inaugurations fall on 7 January. Article 66(2) says no one may be elected president more than twice.

Mahama’s Constitution Review Committee found that the limit applies whether or not the two terms are consecutive. It proposed no change to that clause.

A presidential candidate needs a majority of valid votes in the first round, or a run-off follows. Parliament’s 276 members are elected on the same day, one per constituency.

Voters often split their ticket, a habit Ghanaians call “skirt and blouse” voting. The review committee warned that this can leave a president facing a Parliament run by rivals.

The system is a hybrid of presidential and parliamentary rule. Article 78(1) requires most ministers to be drawn from Parliament, and they keep their seats while serving.

The review committee said the rule has been blamed for weakening Parliament. Article 76(1) caps the cabinet itself at 19 ministers.

Below the national level, Ghana has 16 regions and 261 metropolitan, municipal and district assemblies. The president appoints a minister for each region.

The president also nominates each district chief executive, the head of a local assembly’s administration. A nominee needs approval from two-thirds of assembly members present and voting.

Article 276(1) bars chiefs from active party politics. A 2022 Supreme Court ruling lets them comment on policies but not endorse parties or candidates, the review committee notes.

The wider background on the country and its economy is in the Rio Times guide Ghana Explained.

President John Mahama and His Government

John Dramani Mahama of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) has held office since 7 January 2025. He previously served as president until January 2017, and before that as vice-president.

The Presidency calls him the first Ghanaian president democratically elected to a non-consecutive second term. Born in Damongo, in today’s Savannah Region, he was earlier an MP and communications minister.

The Electoral Commission’s updated declaration of 10 January 2025 gave Mahama 6,591,790 votes, or 56.42%. Mahamudu Bawumia of the New Patriotic Party (NPP) won 4,877,611 votes, or 41.75%.

That count covered 275 of 276 constituencies, with turnout of 63.97% among about 18.7 million registered voters there. The commission stressed that the outcome of the vote of 7 December 2024 was unchanged.

Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang is vice-president, the first woman to hold the post. A literature scholar, she was education minister from 2013 to 2017.

Key ministers as of October 2026 include Cassiel Ato Forson at Finance and Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa at Foreign Affairs. Muntaka Mohammed-Mubarak is Interior Minister, and Dominic Ayine is Attorney-General.

Kenneth Gilbert Adjei is Minister of Defence, the Ghana News Agency (GNA) reported in October 2026. Julius Debrah is Chief of Staff, and Felix Kwakye Ofosu is presidential spokesperson.

The defence post changed hands after a tragedy. On Wednesday, 6 August 2025, a helicopter crash killed Defence Minister Edward Omane Boamah, Environment Minister Ibrahim Murtala Muhammed and six others.

In late August 2026, Mahama brought two more lawmakers into the cabinet. Mahama Ayariga took Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, and Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings took Environment, Science and Technology.

Mahama told Agyeman-Rawlings to lead the fight against galamsey, the illegal gold mining that fouls rivers and forests. He called it one of the gravest threats to national survival.

The Presidency brands the government’s programme “Resetting Ghana”. Its 24-Hour Economy plan includes new model markets, such as 18 begun in the Volta Region in July 2026, GNA reported.

Parliament and the NDC Supermajority

The ninth Parliament was inaugurated on 7 January 2025. As of October 2026, Parliament’s website lists 185 NDC members, 87 NPP members and four independents.

That gives the NDC just over two-thirds of the 276 seats, one more than the 184 needed. Most constitutional clauses can be amended by two-thirds of all MPs without a referendum.

The governing party can therefore, in principle, carry such votes on its own. Entrenched clauses also need a referendum, in which 40% of registered voters must take part and 75% must vote yes.

Alban S. K. Bagbin is Speaker, an office that ranks third in precedence after the President and Vice-President, Parliament notes. Bernard Ahiafor and Andrews Asiamah Amoako are his deputies.

James Agalga leads government business as Majority Leader, with Rockson-Nelson Dafeamekpor as Majority Chief Whip. For the NPP, Alexander Afenyo-Markin is Minority Leader and Frank Annoh-Dompreh is Minority Chief Whip.

Because ministers keep their seats, much of the cabinet also votes in the chamber. Finance Minister Ato Forson, for example, has represented Ajumako-Enyan-Esiam since 2009, the Presidency says.

Bawumia and the Rebuilt NPP Opposition

The NPP governed from 2017 to January 2025 under President Nana Akufo-Addo, with Bawumia as vice-president. It is now the main opposition, and it has moved early to prepare for 2028.

On Saturday, 31 January 2026, party delegates chose Bawumia again as presidential candidate. He won 110,643 of 195,901 valid votes, about 56%, in a result declared by an Electoral Commission official.

Kennedy Ohene Agyapong, a former MP for Assin Central, came second with about 24%. Bryan Acheampong was third with about 19%.

On Saturday, 3 October 2026, NPP delegates in Kumasi elected national officers for the next four years. John Boadu, a former general secretary, became national chairman with 2,888 votes.

Justin Frimpong Kodua kept his post as general secretary with 4,486 votes, GNA reported. Kojo Fosu Boadu, Henry Nana Boakye and Nana Akomea are vice-chairpersons, and Daniel Nii Kwartei Titus-Glover is national organiser.

Bawumia has attacked the government on jobs, the economy and the justice system. He says Free Senior High School, the free secondary schooling introduced under the NPP in 2017, has deteriorated, citing school meals.

Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu rejected the claim on 7 October 2026, saying some problems were inherited, Citi Newsroom reported. Some NPP figures also call corruption cases against party members political intimidation.

In October 2026, NPP MP Kingsley Nyarko condemned the detention of Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah as intimidation. The Economic and Organised Crime Office, a state agency that investigates economic crime, had held him.

Baffour Awuah was later granted bail and charged with causing financial loss to a public body and money laundering. He pleaded not guilty, Citi Newsroom reported.

Smaller parties barely register. The Convention People’s Party of independence leader Kwame Nkrumah won 0.20% of the 2024 presidential vote.

The strongest independent candidate, Nana Kwame Bediako, won 0.76%. Four independents now sit in Parliament.

Courts, the Chief Justice and Constitutional Reform

The chief justice heads the Judiciary and is appointed by the president with Parliament’s approval. The president must first consult the Council of State, a constitutional advisory body.

On Monday, 1 September 2025, Mahama removed Chief Justice Gertrude Torkornoo under Article 146 of the Constitution. A committee examining a citizen’s petition had found grounds of stated misbehaviour, the Presidency said.

Paul Baffoe-Bonnie, acting chief justice in October 2025, now holds the post, the Judiciary’s reports show. At the opening of the legal year on Saturday, 3 October 2026, the Judiciary said his service ends later this year.

Supreme Court justices must retire at 70. On 10 September 2026, Mahama swore in three new Supreme Court justices, bringing the bench to 17.

They include Edward Amoako Asante, a former president of the ECOWAS Court of Justice, the court of the West African regional bloc. “Judicial independence is not a privilege granted to judges for their personal benefit,” Mahama said at the ceremony.

Constitutional reform is the other big institutional project. A review committee chaired by H. Kwasi Prempeh delivered its final report on Monday, 22 December 2025.

Prempeh led CDD-Ghana, a governance think tank, when Mahama appointed him. The government’s position paper, approved by the cabinet on 14 July 2026 and published on 30 July, accepts several big changes.

It backs five-year presidential and parliamentary terms, up from four, and a presidential vote in the first week of November. It also proposes lowering the minimum age for president from 40 to 35.

The paper would cap the number of ministers at 60. It rejects the committee’s call to bar MPs from serving as ministers.

Changes to entrenched clauses would go to a referendum, which the government wants held with the 2027 district assembly elections. The paper does not say when a longer presidential term would first apply.

Security Chiefs, Traditional Rulers and Local Power

Lieutenant General William Agyapong is Chief of the Defence Staff, the Presidency said in July 2026. He joined the Armed Forces Council in that role in April 2025, when he was a major general.

Christian Tetteh Yohuno is Inspector-General of Police, the head of the national police service. The Interior Ministry oversees policing, while the Defence Ministry oversees the Ghana Armed Forces.

Mahama has also used soldiers for civil tasks. In September 2026 he thanked the armed forces for helping clear waste from Agbogloshie, a dumping site in Accra.

Security worries are concentrated in the north. Mahama has called the long-running conflict in Bawku, in Ghana’s far north-east, a grave challenge to national peace.

In July 2025 he praised peace efforts by the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, king of the Asante. He also commended the Naa-Yiri, overlord of the Mamprugu kingdom, for his restraint.

Traditional rulers remain influential in Ghana politics, even though the Constitution keeps them out of party contests. In January 2025, days after taking office, Mahama pledged to involve traditional leaders in governance, especially in enforcing environmental laws.

Local power may shift too. The government wants every district chief executive elected, with voters choosing among candidates the president nominates and a panel vets.

The Road to the 2028 Election

The next general election is due in late 2028, with the new president sworn in on 7 January 2029. Under current practice the vote falls in early December; the 2024 election was on Saturday, 7 December 2024.

Mahama cannot stand, so the NDC must choose a new presidential candidate. As of 8 October 2026, it had not named one.

The party is led by national chairman Johnson Asiedu Nketiah and general secretary Fifi Fiavi Kwetey. In October 2026 it was holding constituency and regional executive elections, with national officer elections still to come.

Deputy general secretary Mustapha Gbande has said internal division, not the NPP’s new leadership, is the party’s biggest threat, Citi Newsroom reported. Youth Minister George Opare Addo urged the NDC not to copy what he called the NPP’s aggressive politics.

The Electoral Commission runs national elections and, under Article 46 of the Constitution, is not subject to any authority’s direction. Jean Mensa chairs the seven-member commission.

Two of its three most senior posts changed in 2026. Deputy chair Bossman Asare resigned from 31 July, and deputy chair Samuel Tettey retired; Mahama has nominated a successor.

The commission also faces a possible referendum on constitutional changes in 2027. Day-to-day coverage is collected on the Rio Times Ghana news page.

What It Means for US Readers

Ghana politics matters to Washington because power has changed hands through elections, under respected term limits, since 2001. With a projected 34.4 million people in 2026, Ghana is one of West Africa’s larger countries.

In foreign policy, the Mahama government is widening its options. On Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Foreign Minister Ablakwa said the cabinet had decided to apply to join BRICS.

BRICS is a bloc of emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. Ablakwa said Ghana would keep its traditional partners but “must have new friends”.

The details are in the Rio Times report on the BRICS bid.

Ghana also led a United Nations General Assembly resolution, backed by 123 countries, calling the transatlantic slave trade a crime against humanity. Ghana tabled it in March 2026 for the African Union and CARICOM, the Caribbean community.

Ghana’s Office of the Special Prosecutor has charged former finance minister Ken Ofori-Atta and seven others in a contract case. It has sent an extradition request to the US Justice Department, GNA reported.

Ofori-Atta, who is in the United States, also faces separate US immigration proceedings. INTERPOL deleted a Red Notice against him in February 2026, saying it appeared “of a predominantly political character”, according to his lawyer.

For investors, the Ghana Statistical Service puts inflation at 5.2% in September 2026 and economic growth at 6.0% in 2025. The figures are tracked in Rio Times coverage of September inflation.

The State Department rates Ghana at Level 2, “Exercise increased caution”, in an advisory issued on 7 July 2026. It advises reconsidering travel to the northern border areas and part of the Savannah Region, citing crime.

Washington’s trade, visa and security ties with Accra are set out in Ghana Geopolitics Explained.

What Is Not Known

The NDC has not named its 2028 presidential candidate. Its national officer elections had not taken place as of 8 October 2026.

No successor to Chief Justice Baffoe-Bonnie, whose service ends later in 2026, had been announced by the Presidency. Parliament would have to approve any nominee.

It is not known whether the constitutional amendments will pass, or when a referendum will be held. The position paper does not say whether a five-year term would apply to the president elected in 2028.

The outcome of Ghana’s extradition request for Ofori-Atta is not known. It is not confirmed whether both vacant deputy posts at the Electoral Commission have been filled.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the president of Ghana in 2026?

John Dramani Mahama of the National Democratic Congress has been president since 7 January 2025. His vice-president is Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang, the first woman in the post.

Can John Mahama run again in 2028?

No. Article 66(2) of the Constitution bars anyone from being elected president more than twice, and Mahama has now been elected twice.

Who leads the opposition in Ghana?

Former vice-president Mahamudu Bawumia is the New Patriotic Party’s 2028 candidate, and John Boadu is its national chairman. Alexander Afenyo-Markin leads its MPs as Minority Leader.

When is Ghana’s next election?

Presidential and parliamentary elections are due in late 2028, under current practice in early December. The government backs moving the presidential vote to the first week of November.

Who is Ghana’s chief justice?

Paul Baffoe-Bonnie is chief justice, after Gertrude Torkornoo was removed in September 2025. The Judiciary says his service ends later in 2026.

Is Ghana joining BRICS?

The cabinet has decided to apply, Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said on 6 October 2026. Membership would still need the bloc’s approval.

Is Ghana safe to visit for Americans?

The US State Department rates Ghana at Level 2, “Exercise increased caution”, in an advisory of July 2026. It advises reconsidering travel to northern border areas because of crime.

World.title: Nigeria Culture, the Key Figures to Know in 2026
World.content:
NIGERIA · CULTURE

Key Facts — The country Africa’s most populous nation, about 237.5 million people in 2025.

— The music Burna Boy, Wizkid and Tems hold four Grammys between them.

— What happened Behind the Scenes became Nollywood’s first film past ₦2 billion (US$1.5 million).

— The heritage UNESCO lists two Nigerian World Heritage sites and eight intangible elements.

— Coming up Headies in Toronto, 25 October; CAF Awards in Lagos, 7 December.

— US visas Washington suspended new Nigerian tourist and student visas from January 2026.

From Afrobeats and Nollywood to a Nobel laureate, Nigeria’s cultural figures now reach far beyond West Africa.

Nigeria culture reaches Americans mainly through Afrobeats, Nollywood films and novels. A fairly small group of musicians, filmmakers, writers and organisers carries much of that reach.

This guide names the key figures as of October 2026, from Grammy winners to festival founders. Daily news is in the Rio Times Nigeria section.

How Nigeria Culture Reached the World

Nigeria had about 237.5 million people in 2025, World Bank data show, far more than Ethiopia, the next most populous African country. That scale gives its artists a large home audience before they ever tour abroad.

Its music, films and books draw on Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and many other traditions. Lagos, the commercial capital, hosts most of the venues in this guide.

In the north, Kano is home to Kannywood, one of the country’s major film industries. In September 2026 the National Theatre held its creative summit there, its first outside Lagos.

Culture policy sits with Hannatu Musawa, the federal Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy. Obi Asika heads the National Council for Arts and Culture, the federal agency that promotes the arts.

The National Theatre in Lagos, renamed after the writer Wole Soyinka in 2024, reopened on 1 October 2025 after renovation. On 1 October 2026 it hosted the premiere of MKO, a documentary on the late politician Moshood Abiola.

How the state shapes daily life is covered in Nigeria politics explained. For one of the big traditions, see Igbo culture and language in Nigeria.

Afrobeats and the Musicians Who Took It Global

Two similar words describe two eras of Nigerian music. Afrobeat, without an s, is the style created by Fela Kuti, the bandleader and activist born in 1938.

The Recording Academy, which runs the Grammys, calls it a merger of Yoruba and other African styles with funk, jazz and rock. Fela, who died in 1997, paired that sound with outspoken political messages.

In 2025 his album Zombie entered the Grammy Hall of Fame. In 1998 his daughter Yeni Kuti launched Felabration, a week of events around his 15 October birthday.

In 2000 she and her brother Femi, a six-time Grammy nominee, opened the New Afrika Shrine in Lagos. Dates and venues for this year are in the Felabration guide.

Afrobeats, with an s, is today’s pop sound, blending African rhythms with R&B, hip-hop and dancehall. These are its leading names, with their Recording Academy record as of October 2026.

Burna Boy : one Grammy from 13 nominations. His album Twice as Tall won Best Global Music Album at the 2021 ceremony, and the Academy says he was the first African artist to headline and sell out major stadiums in the US and Europe.

: one Grammy from 13 nominations. His album Twice as Tall won Best Global Music Album at the 2021 ceremony, and the Academy says he was the first African artist to headline and sell out major stadiums in the US and Europe. Wizkid : one Grammy from six nominations, for the Brown Skin Girl video with Beyoncé and Blue Ivy Carter in 2021. His song Essence, with Tems, was nominated in 2022.

: one Grammy from six nominations, for the Brown Skin Girl video with Beyoncé and Blue Ivy Carter in 2021. His song Essence, with Tems, was nominated in 2022. Tems : two Grammys from eight nominations, for Wait for U with Future and Drake in 2023 and for her own Love Me JeJe in 2025.

: two Grammys from eight nominations, for Wait for U with Future and Drake in 2023 and for her own Love Me JeJe in 2025. Davido : five nominations and no win yet, most recently for With You, recorded with Omah Lay, in 2026.

: five nominations and no win yet, most recently for With You, recorded with Omah Lay, in 2026. Ayra Starr : two nominations, for Rush in 2024 and for Gimme Dat with Wizkid in 2026.

: two nominations, for Rush in 2024 and for Gimme Dat with Wizkid in 2026. Asake and Olamide : nominated together for Amapiano in 2024; Asake was nominated again with Wizkid for MMS in 2025.

: nominated together for Amapiano in 2024; Asake was nominated again with Wizkid for MMS in 2025. Rema: his song Calm Down, remixed with US singer Selena Gomez, won Top Afrobeats Song at the 2023 Billboard Music Awards.

The Grammys added Best African Music Performance in 2024, and Tems won it in 2025. South Africa’s Tyla took it in 2024 and 2026, so Tems is its only Nigerian winner so far.

Nigerian acts still filled three of the five nominations in 2026. At home, the top music awards are the Headies, founded by Ayo Animashaun, chief executive of the music channel HipTV.

The 18th Headies are set for Toronto, Canada, on 25 October 2026, with a watch party in Lagos. The money side is covered in how Afrobeats became a Nigerian export.

Nollywood, the Box Office and the Censors

Nollywood is the nickname for Nigeria’s film industry. Its box-office record holder is Funke Akindele, an actor, producer and director.

Her film Behind the Scenes opened in cinemas on 12 December 2025. The Nigerian Film Corporation, the federal film agency, says it was the first Nollywood production to pass ₦2 billion (about US$1.5 million).

By late January 2026 it had passed ₦2.4 billion (about US$1.8 million), according to Lagos governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu. The previous record, Everybody Loves Jenifa, was also hers, at ₦1.88 billion (about US$1.4 million), Premium Times reported.

Conversions use the Central Bank of Nigeria’s official rate of 7 October 2026, ₦1,331 to US$1. At that rate the record gross is modest by Hollywood standards, but it is large for a market priced in naira.

Films must be classified by the National Film and Video Censors Board (NFVCB), set up in 1993, before public release. Its director-general, Shaibu Husseini, has said the board wants to cut classification time to under 24 hours.

The board also polices content. In August 2026 it moved to block Living in Colours, an unclassified gay-themed web series on YouTube, Premium Times reported.

The industry’s big awards night is the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards (AMVCA), run by the pay-TV group MultiChoice. At the 12th edition in Lagos on Saturday, 9 May 2026, My Father’s Shadow won Best Movie.

Its director, Akinola Davies Jr., won Best Director. The historical epic Lisabi: A Legend Is Born won Best Indigenous Language (West Africa), for films in local languages.

For an Igbo-language example, see the box-office run of Ikenga: The Last Festival. Funke Akindele’s earlier record is covered in Behind the Scenes becomes Nollywood’s biggest film.

Writers Who Shaped How the World Reads Nigeria

Chinua Achebe came to prominence in 1958 with his novel Things Fall Apart. In 2007 he won the Man Booker International Prize for his body of work, the Booker Prize Foundation records.

Wole Soyinka, born in Abeokuta in 1934, won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Literature. The Nobel citation praised a writer “who in a wide cultural perspective and with poetic overtones fashions the drama of existence.”

Soyinka remains a public voice in his nineties. In October 2025 the US consulate in Lagos revoked his visa, and he told reporters he knew of no reason for it.

Ben Okri won the 1991 Booker Prize for The Famished Road. Okri has described the novel as the story of a spirit child in Lagos around the time of independence.

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie became a MacArthur Fellow in 2008, after Purple Hibiscus (2003) and Half of a Yellow Sun (2006). The foundation said the second book humanised “the Biafran tragedy,” Nigeria’s civil war over the breakaway Republic of Biafra.

Together these writers gave foreign readers their picture of Nigeria, from colonial rule to civil war. Since October 2025, Soyinka’s name has also stood on the National Theatre in Lagos.

Visual Artists and the Fight Over Heritage

In Osogbo, the Austrian artist Susanne Wenger and the New Sacred Art movement filled the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove with large sculptures. UNESCO credits that work with restoring the grove’s spiritual character.

El Anatsui, born in Ghana in 1944, has been based in the Nigerian university town of Nsukka since 1975. He won the Venice Biennale’s Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement in 2015.

The Biennale called him a leading member of the Nsukka School of artists. His Tate Modern commission, Behind the Red Moon, ran from October 2023 to April 2024, built from bottle tops sourced in Nigeria.

Nigeria’s pavilion at the 2017 Venice Biennale, How About Now?, showed work by Peju Alatise, Victor Ehikhamenor and Quddus Onikeku.

Heritage is also contested at home. In November 2025 Edo State’s governor, Monday Okpebholo, challenged Benin City’s new Museum of West African Art.

He said the project would be restored to its “original and rightful purpose” as a Benin Royal Museum. Days later, men described as armed thugs disrupted the museum’s preview opening.

Okpebholo then revoked the museum’s land title, saying the site would revert to the historic Benin Central Hospital, Premium Times reported.

Sport Icons From the NBA to the Super Falcons

Hakeem Olajuwon, born in Lagos in 1963, led the Houston Rockets to NBA titles in 1994 and 1995. The Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame, which enshrined him in 2008, lists his 3,830 blocked shots as an NBA record.

In football, Victor Osimhen won the Confederation of African Football (CAF) men’s Player of the Year award in 2023. Ademola Lookman followed in 2024, and Morocco’s Achraf Hakimi won in 2025, Premium Times reported.

The women’s team, the Super Falcons, hold a record ten African titles, CAF says. Goalkeeper Chiamaka Nnadozie was CAF’s women’s goalkeeper of the year in 2024 and 2025.

At the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco, they lost 1-0 to Cameroon in the quarter-finals. A 2-1 play-off defeat to South Africa in August ended their 2027 World Cup hopes, Premium Times reported.

The men’s Super Eagles reached the semi-finals of the Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco in January 2026. They did not qualify for the 2026 World Cup in North America.

Lagos will host the 2026 CAF Awards on Monday, 7 December. CAF’s executive committee approved the date on 2 October, Premium Times reported.

Media Figures, Festivals and Fashion

Behind the stars stands a layer of media entrepreneurs. Ayo Animashaun, chief executive of HipTV, founded the Headies, and MultiChoice’s Africa Magic brand runs the AMVCA.

Reality television also makes celebrities. In October 2026 Temi Nkem, season 11 winner of the reality show Big Brother Naija, received ₦90 million (about US$68,000) in cash.

Omoyemi Akerele founded Lagos Fashion Week in 2011. It won the 2025 Earthshot Prize, a global environmental award, in the Build a Waste-free World category.

Festivals are an easy way for visitors to meet Nigeria culture in person. These are the main ones, with their UNESCO status where it applies.

Osun-Osogbo Festival, Osogbo : a 12-day procession in July and August for Osun, the Yoruba goddess of the river. The grove has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005.

: a 12-day procession in July and August for Osun, the Yoruba goddess of the river. The grove has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005. Durbar in Kano : parades of horsemen in ceremonial dress at the two Eid holidays, inscribed by UNESCO in 2024. In 2025 security agencies banned Kano’s Sallah Durbar amid a dispute between two rival emirs.

: parades of horsemen in ceremonial dress at the two Eid holidays, inscribed by UNESCO in 2024. In 2025 security agencies banned Kano’s Sallah Durbar amid a dispute between two rival emirs. Argungu Fishing Festival : a fishing contest and cultural festival in Kebbi State, on UNESCO’s list since 2016.

: a fishing contest and cultural festival in Kebbi State, on UNESCO’s list since 2016. Sango Festival, Oyo : a festival in Oyo honouring Sango, a Yoruba deity, added by UNESCO in 2023.

: a festival in Oyo honouring Sango, a Yoruba deity, added by UNESCO in 2023. Calabar Carnival, Cross River State : a December street parade. The state tourism bureau counted more than 248,000 visitors and ₦17.4 billion (about US$13 million) in December 2025; see the Calabar Carnival guide.

: a December street parade. The state tourism bureau counted more than 248,000 visitors and ₦17.4 billion (about US$13 million) in December 2025; see the Calabar Carnival guide. Felabration, Lagos : a week of events at the New Afrika Shrine around Fela Kuti’s 15 October birthday.

: a week of events at the New Afrika Shrine around Fela Kuti’s 15 October birthday. Lagos Fashion Week: runway shows, usually in late October, with a focus on sustainable design; see Lagos Fashion Week 2026.

Nigeria’s other World Heritage site is the Sukur Cultural Landscape, listed in 1999. UNESCO’s intangible list also includes the Ijele masquerade, the Ifa divination system and Kwagh-Hir theatre.

What It Means for US Readers

The biggest practical issue is travel. Proclamation 10998, signed by President Donald Trump on 16 December 2025, took effect on 1 January 2026.

It suspends entry for Nigerians on immigrant visas and on business, tourist, student and exchange visas (B, F, M and J). Performer visas are not on that list, but consulates must shorten the validity of other visas issued to Nigerians.

Athletes travelling for major sporting events are exempt. Visa holders as of 1 January 2026 were not affected, the US Embassy said, according to Premium Times.

Commercially, the pull runs the other way. At an August 2026 workshop in Lagos, US Consul General Brandon Hudspeth called Nigeria’s music industry “a significant trade and investment opportunity.”

He named Universal Music Group, EMPIRE, Sony and Warner Music Group among labels helping Nigerian artists reach global audiences. Strong copyright protection, he argued, is what gives US investors confidence.

Washington has spent about US$1.2 million on cultural preservation in Nigeria over five years, the consulate says. A US$125,000 grant announced in August 2026 will document the Lejja iron-smelting site in Enugu State, dated to about 2000 BC.

The State Department rates Nigeria Level 3, “Reconsider Travel,” citing crime, terrorism, unrest, kidnapping and uneven health care. Festival visitors should read that advisory and its area-specific warnings before booking.

Fans in North America can catch the Headies in Toronto on 25 October. Nollywood titles also reach US screens through streaming, as with Akindele’s Finding Me on Amazon Prime Video in March 2025.

The wider business picture is in who runs Nigeria’s economy. Ties with Washington are covered in Nigeria geopolitics explained.

What Is Not Known

It is not known when, or whether, Washington will ease Proclamation 10998 for Nigerians. No amendment to it had appeared in the Federal Register by 8 October 2026.

No official body has published a final gross for Behind the Scenes. The last widely reported figure was ₦2.4 billion (about US$1.8 million), in January 2026.

How the dispute over the Museum of West African Art in Benin City ends is unclear. The size of the creative economy is also uncertain.

One widely quoted figure, ₦1.97 trillion (about US$1.5 billion) for 2025, came from a research group, not the statistics office. The winners of the Headies on 25 October and the CAF Awards on 7 December are not yet known.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Nigeria best known for culturally?

Afrobeats music, Nollywood films and writers such as Wole Soyinka and Chinua Achebe. The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove and the Durbar in Kano are also recognised by UNESCO.

What is the difference between Afrobeat and Afrobeats?

Afrobeat is the style Fela Kuti built from Yoruba music, funk, jazz and rock. Afrobeats is the broader pop sound of today’s stars, such as Burna Boy, Wizkid and Tems.

Which Afrobeats stars have won Grammy Awards?

Burna Boy and Wizkid have one each, both from 2021, and Tems has two, from 2023 and 2025. Davido has five nominations but no win as of October 2026.

What is Nollywood?

Nollywood is the nickname for Nigeria’s film industry. As of October 2026, its record holder is Funke Akindele’s Behind the Scenes, at over ₦2.4 billion (about US$1.8 million).

Who are the best-known Nigerian writers?

Wole Soyinka won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Literature, and Chinua Achebe wrote Things Fall Apart. Ben Okri won the 1991 Booker Prize, and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie became a MacArthur Fellow in 2008.

Which Nigerian festivals and sites does UNESCO recognise?

The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove and the Sukur Cultural Landscape are World Heritage sites. UNESCO also lists the Durbar in Kano, the Argungu fishing festival and the Sango Festival in Oyo.

Can Nigerian artists still perform in the United States?

They can apply, because performer visas are not among the categories suspended by Proclamation 10998. Consulates must shorten their validity, and tourist and student visas for Nigerians are suspended.

World.title: Cairo Jazz Festival Runs 5 to 7 November at Tahrir Square
World.content:
EGYPT · CAIRO JAZZ FESTIVAL 2026

Key Facts — The city Cairo, Egypt’s capital, hosts the 18th Cairo Jazz Festival.

— The dates Thursday, 5 November, to Saturday, 7 November 2026.

— The venue Two stages at the American University in Cairo, Tahrir Square campus.

— Tickets TicketsMarche: days about US$9.60 to US$15.30; full pass about US$19.10.

— Start times Seller lists 7 p.m. Thursday, 5 p.m. Friday, 1 p.m. Saturday.

— Not confirmed Hisham Kharma’s slot, Alexandria concerts, country count, three bands’ set times.

The Cairo Jazz Festival returns for its 18th edition on Thursday, 5 November, with two stages in downtown Cairo.

The Cairo Jazz Festival 2026 runs from Thursday, 5 November, to Saturday, 7 November, in downtown Cairo. Concerts take place on two stages at the Tahrir Square campus of the American University in Cairo, known as AUC.

For US visitors, entry costs little: TicketsMarche, the official seller, lists day tickets from EGP 500 (about US$9.60). The catch is paperwork, because Americans need an Egyptian visa and the campus requires photo ID for entry.

What the Festival Is

The festival began in 2009, according to its organisers, and the 2026 edition is billed as the 18th. Its stated aim is to raise awareness of jazz as culture and human experience before it becomes a music genre.

Pianist and composer Amro Salah founded it, Egyptian Streets, a Cairo news site, reported in 2015. The first edition drew about 2,000 people, the site reported, and the organisers said they aimed to develop Egypt’s music scene.

The organisers name the European Union and EUNIC, the network of European national cultural institutes, among their partners. Embassies, international organisations and cultural centres also fund the festival, they say.

The TicketsMarche page lists the organiser as a company called Agwa for event organizing. The festival’s own website does not name a company.

Besides concerts, the organisers promise workshops, Jazz Talks, jam sessions and after-hours club gigs. Jazzinino, a programme for children, includes a showcase by the Bandmakers music academy and a workshop called Colours of Sounds.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The 2026 Line-Up

The organisers’ programme page lists these set times, all on the Tahrir Square campus. Ewart Memorial Hall is a concert hall on the campus, and the Garden Stage is the second venue.

Thursday, 5 November: Nana Rashid (Denmark), 9:30 p.m., Ewart Memorial Hall.

Nana Rashid (Denmark), 9:30 p.m., Ewart Memorial Hall. Friday, 6 November: Warren Galea Trio (Malta), 5 p.m., Garden Stage; Michelangelo Scandroglio Quartet (Italy), 6 p.m., Ewart Hall.

Warren Galea Trio (Malta), 5 p.m., Garden Stage; Michelangelo Scandroglio Quartet (Italy), 6 p.m., Ewart Hall. Friday, 6 November, evening: ARIFA featuring Mohamed Sawwah (Netherlands, Turkey and Egypt), 7 p.m., Garden Stage; Hazem Shaheen (Egypt), 8:45 p.m., Ewart Memorial Hall.

ARIFA featuring Mohamed Sawwah (Netherlands, Turkey and Egypt), 7 p.m., Garden Stage; Hazem Shaheen (Egypt), 8:45 p.m., Ewart Memorial Hall. Friday, 6 November, late: Harfoush & The Egyptian Jazz Projekt (Egypt), 10 p.m., Garden Stage.

Harfoush & The Egyptian Jazz Projekt (Egypt), 10 p.m., Garden Stage. Saturday, 7 November: Bächlin & Elkholy (Switzerland), 8:30 p.m., Ewart Hall; Fathy Salama featuring Karima Nayt (Egypt and Algeria), 9:45 p.m., Garden Stage.

The organisers describe Nana Rashid as a Danish Grammy-winning jazz singer. They call Hazem Shaheen a leading Egyptian player of the oud, the Arab lute, as well as a singer and composer.

Fathy Salama is a composer, arranger, producer and pianist, and Karima Nayt is an Algerian singer, dancer and actress. Jazz vocalist Ahmed Harfoush founded The Egyptian Jazz Projekt in 2015, the programme says.

The festival homepage also lists the Guido Spannocchi Quartet, the Xavi Torres Trio and the Manuel Linhares Quartet. The ticket page puts all three on Saturday, but the organisers have not posted their set times.

The ticket page also bills Hisham Kharma with Nana Rashid at the opening concert. Ahram Online, the English-language site of the Al-Ahram newspaper, describes him as an Egyptian composer, pianist and arranger.

Kharma is known for combining Eastern and Western instruments, Ahram Online says. His name does not appear on the organisers’ own programme page.

The Venue and How to Get There

The American University in Cairo was founded in 1919 by Americans devoted to education and service in the Middle East. It is chartered and accredited in both the United States and Egypt, and keeps an office in New York.

AUC calls its historic Tahrir Square campus a landmark and cultural oasis in the heart of Cairo. The university gives the address as 113 Kasr El Aini Street, while the ticket seller lists 22 Mohammed Mahmoud Street.

AUC’s public events portal says a photo ID is required for entry and facial recognition applies at all times. The notice covers campus entry in general, so carry your passport.

The US State Department advises visitors to use taxis or hired drivers rather than drive themselves in Egypt. It calls public buses, microbuses, Nile taxis and trains unsafe, and says most Cairo traffic lights do not work.

The department also warns that driving in Cairo can be very challenging for foreigners used to strict traffic rules. Allow extra time to reach downtown.

Tickets and Prices

The festival’s own ticket page links only to TicketsMarche, an Egyptian online ticket platform. Buying requires a TicketsMarche account, registered with an email address and a phone number.

Each of the three days is sold separately, with prices listed from EGP 500 to EGP 800 (about US$9.60 to US$15.30). The seller does not say which seats or areas each price buys.

A full-access pass for all three days costs EGP 1,000 (about US$19.10). Three single-day tickets would cost at least EGP 1,500 (about US$28.70), so the pass is cheaper for anyone attending every day.

The page showed no sold-out notice on Thursday, 8 October. Conversions use open.er-api.com market rates updated on 7 October 2026, when US$1 bought about EGP 52.31.

Entry Rules for US Citizens

US citizens need a visa to enter Egypt, according to the State Department. Passports must be valid for six months and have at least one blank page.

The department says Americans can get a single-entry, 30-day tourist visa on arrival at Cairo International Airport for US$36 by credit card. At other entry points, it lists a US$30 visa paid in exact US dollar cash.

The official alternative is Egypt’s e-visa portal, visa2egypt.gov.eg, which asks for applications at least seven days before departure. The State Department warns that many unofficial sites offer e-visas, some at double the price.

Bringing more than US$10,000 into or out of Egypt is illegal, and the excess may be confiscated, the department says. No vaccinations are required unless you arrive from a yellow fever area.

Safety in Cairo

The State Department rates Egypt Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, citing terrorism, crime and health. The advisory was issued on 15 July 2025, when the level was lowered to 2.

Level 4, Do Not Travel, covers North and Middle Sinai and Egypt’s border areas, and the Western Desert is also flagged. Cairo itself is not on that list.

The advisory calls crime in Cairo and Alexandria moderate, but lists urban Cairo among possible terrorist targets. It warns that terrorists target crowds with little or no warning, including at tourist sites.

Protesting without a permit is illegal in Egypt, the State Department notes. It says people have been arrested just for being near protests, so walk away from any gathering.

The US Embassy is at 5 Tawfik Diab Street in Garden City, Cairo, on +20-2-2797-3300. The same number works after hours for emergencies.

What It Means for You

In Cairo between 5 and 7 November, this is an inexpensive night of live music on a historic campus. Buy through TicketsMarche, the seller the festival links to, rather than through resellers.

The EGP 1,000 pass (about US$19.10) costs the same as two of the cheapest day tickets. It makes sense if you plan to go on two or three evenings.

Apply for the e-visa at least seven days before you fly, and carry your passport to the campus gate. Use a taxi or hired driver rather than driving, as the State Department advises.

Check the organisers’ programme page before you go, because set times on the two official sites differ.

What Is Not Known

It is not clear whether Hisham Kharma will play the opening night, since only the ticket page lists him. Set times for the Spannocchi, Torres and Linhares bands have not been published.

The ticket page mentions extra concerts at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, the library in Alexandria, without dates. The organisers’ own site does not mention Alexandria.

The organisers’ homepage names eight participating countries, while the ticket page says 12. Egypt Independent, a Cairo news site, reported more than 12 countries and Alexandria concerts for the 2025 edition.

The ticket page may therefore repeat last year’s text on both points. It does not explain what separates the EGP 500 and EGP 800 tickets (about US$9.60 and US$15.30).

Venues and times for the workshops, Jazz Talks, jam sessions and Jazzinino children’s events are not yet listed. Age limits and gate opening times are not stated on either site.

What Comes Next

The festival opens on Thursday, 5 November, and closes on Saturday, 7 November. Watch the festival website for the remaining set times and the fringe programme.

A late change to the line-up would not affect visa or entry rules for US visitors.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the Cairo Jazz Festival 2026?

It runs from Thursday, 5 November, to Saturday, 7 November 2026. Concerts are on two stages at the Tahrir Square campus of the American University in Cairo, downtown.

How much are tickets, and where do I buy them?

TicketsMarche, the seller the festival links to, lists day tickets at EGP 500 to 800 (about US$9.60 to US$15.30). A three-day pass costs EGP 1,000 (about US$19.10).

Do Americans need a visa to attend?

Yes, US citizens need a visa for Egypt, according to the State Department. They can buy one on arrival or apply online at least seven days before departure through the official e-visa portal.

World.title: Aké Arts and Book Festival Runs in Lagos 19 to 21 November
World.content:
NIGERIA · BOOK FESTIVAL 2026

Key Facts — The city Lagos, Nigeria; the venue is in Ikeja, near the main airport.

— The dates Thursday, 19 November, to Saturday, 21 November 2026.

— The venue Silkwood Hotel Ikeja, 261 Sobo Arobiodu Street, Ikeja GRA, Lagos.

— Tickets Sold online by organiser Book Buzz Foundation via akefestival.org.

— Prices ₦20,000 (about US$15) online; ₦25,000 (about US$19) at the venue.

— Still open Daily programme, session times and opening hours are not yet published.

Nigeria’s Aké Arts and Book Festival returns to Lagos for a 14th edition, with US-linked writers on its guest list.

The Aké Arts and Book Festival returns to Lagos for its 14th edition, from Thursday, 19 November, to Saturday, 21 November 2026. The Aké Festival takes place at the Silkwood Hotel Ikeja, a short drive from the city’s main international airport.

Tickets cost ₦20,000 (about US$15) online and cover every festival event, according to the organisers, the Book Buzz Foundation. For American visitors, the draw includes Marvel comics writer Nnedi Okorafor and Nigerian-American filmmaker Roye Okupe, both on the 2026 guest list.

What the Aké Festival Is

The festival is run by the Book Buzz Foundation, a non-profit founded in 2012 to promote literacy and reading. Its board of trustees includes Lola Shoneyin, whom the literary site Brittle Paper describes as the festival’s founder.

The festival says it has brought together more than 1,000 writers, poets, musicians, filmmakers and artists since it began. Brittle Paper, an African literary magazine, calls it “Nigeria’s most beloved literary gathering.”

Over three days, the programme mixes panel discussions, book chats, poetry and music, the organisers say. Brittle Paper reported the November dates in April, when speakers and ticketing were still to be announced.

A Theme About Artificial Intelligence

The 2026 theme is Native Intelligence, which the organisers frame as a question about artificial intelligence and older ways of knowing. Their statement opens with the line “Long before the algorithm, there was the elder and the proverb.”

It argues that, across Africa, artificial intelligence is reshaping how stories are told, elections fought and truth reported. The question it poses is whose intelligence the future will be built on.

Who Is on the 2026 Guest List

The festival’s guest page lists more than 40 writers and artists under the heading Festival Guests 2026. Its programme page says the schedule is still in development and will be announced soon.

Nnedi Okorafor is the author of the Binti trilogy and of Marvel’s Black Panther: Long Live the King, Shuri and Wakanda Forever. Her festival profile lists Nebula, World Fantasy, Eisner and multiple Hugo awards among her honours.

Roye Okupe, a Nigerian-American filmmaker, created IYANU, an animated franchise streaming on HBO Max and Cartoon Network, his profile says. In 2021 he signed a 10-book publishing deal with Dark Horse Comics.

Chika Unigwe, born and raised in the Nigerian city of Enugu, is an associate professor at Georgia College in Milledgeville, Georgia. She founded the Awele Creative Trust, according to the festival.

Also listed is Wole Talabi, whose Shigidi and the Brass Head of Obalufon was nominated for Nebula, Locus and World Fantasy awards. Nigerian British author Irenosen Okojie, winner of the 2020 AKO Caine Prize, is on the list too.

The list also includes Wanjiru Koinange, a novelist from Nairobi, and Lagos-based author A. Igoni Barrett.

Tickets and Prices

The standard Aké Festival ticket costs ₦20,000 (about US$15) and has been on sale since Tuesday, 1 September. It includes the festival guide, the 2026 edition of the Aké Review, an ID card with lanyard and access to all events.

A venue ticket, sold at the door from Thursday, 19 November, costs ₦25,000 (about US$19) for the same package. A Green Room pass at ₦200,000 (about US$150) adds meals, refreshments and wi-fi, but is marked “available soon,” with ten places.

Tickets are sold through a Book Buzz Foundation page on Paystack, an online payments service, linked from the festival website. The payment page comes preset at ₦20,000 (about US$15), the online ticket price.

Conversions use the Central Bank of Nigeria’s central rate for Wednesday, 7 October, of ₦1,331.27 to US$1. Buy only through the festival’s own link, not through resellers or social media offers.

The Venue and How to Get There

The Silkwood Hotel Ikeja stands at 261 Sobo Arobiodu Street in Ikeja GRA, a residential district on the Lagos mainland. The organisers say Ikeja GRA is twelve minutes from Murtala Muhammed International Airport.

The airport, code LOS, lies in Ikeja itself, and the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria calls it the nation’s busiest. Delta Air Lines sells flights to Lagos on its US website.

The festival’s hotel page, last updated in August 2025, lists Ikeja GRA rooms with breakfast included. Its cheapest listed rate is ₦60,000 (about US$45) a night, at the Classio Hotel by House J.

The Ivy Emerald Hotel was listed from ₦95,000 (about US$71) a night. The Radisson Blu Hotel Ikeja was listed from ₦400,000 (about US$300).

For getting around, the State Department says app-based ride-shares are viewed as safer than traditional taxis, because drivers register with the company. It also urges extreme caution when driving between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m.

Entry Rules for US Citizens

US citizens need a visa for Nigeria and must apply before they travel, according to the State Department. The Nigeria Immigration Service website offers online applications for both an e-Visa and a regular visa.

Passports must be valid for six months beyond the arrival date, with a blank page for each stamp. All travellers older than nine months must show yellow fever and polio vaccination certificates on arrival.

Cash above US$10,000 must be declared on entry and on exit. Dual US and Nigerian citizens now need a valid Nigerian passport to leave Nigeria, the department says.

Safety in Lagos

The State Department rates Nigeria Level 3, Reconsider Travel, in an advisory issued on Friday, 12 June 2026. It warns that violent crime, including armed robbery, carjacking and kidnapping, is common throughout the country.

Lagos is not among the states rated Level 4, Do Not Travel. The advisory says kidnappings for ransom happen often and primarily target dual nationals visiting Nigeria, which matters for Nigerian-American visitors.

The US government has limited ability to provide emergency services to citizens outside Abuja and Lagos, the advisory adds. It recommends enrolling in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, which sends embassy alerts.

The US Consulate General in Lagos is at 2 Walter Carrington Crescent, Victoria Island. Its main and after-hours number is +234-201-460-3400.

Also in Lagos in November

Visitors planning a longer stay can also time a trip around ART X Lagos, an international art fair. Its website gives dates of Thursday, 5 November, to Sunday, 8 November, but lists no venue or tickets yet.

What It Means for You

For the Aké Festival, the online ticket at ₦20,000 (about US$15) is the cheaper way in and covers all events. Apply for a Nigerian visa early, because it must be issued before you fly.

Staying in Ikeja GRA keeps you close to the airport and the venue, but confirm current hotel rates directly. Ride-share apps are viewed as safer than street taxis, the State Department says.

Wait for the programme before booking around one author, since session times are not yet published. Nigerian-American dual nationals should carry a valid Nigerian passport so they can leave the country.

What Is Not Known

The daily programme, session times and opening hours have not been published, and the organisers say they will be announced soon. It is not known which guests will appear on which day.

The ticket page does not say whether US-issued cards are accepted, or whether tickets can be refunded. The Green Room pass is not yet on sale, and its release date is not given.

The festival’s hotel list dates from 2025, before the 2026 venue was announced, so rates and distances may differ.

What Comes Next

The organisers say the 2026 programme will be announced soon. Door tickets go on sale at the venue on Thursday, 19 November, and the festival closes on Saturday, 21 November.

A name on the guest page is not a confirmed session. Check the programme for a named appearance before travelling to see one writer.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the Aké Festival 2026?

The Aké Arts and Book Festival runs from Thursday, 19 November, to Saturday, 21 November 2026. It takes place at the Silkwood Hotel Ikeja, 261 Sobo Arobiodu Street, Ikeja GRA, Lagos.

How much do Aké Festival tickets cost?

An online ticket costs ₦20,000 (about US$15), and a ticket at the door costs ₦25,000 (about US$19). Both include access to all 2026 festival events, according to the organisers.

Do US citizens need a visa to visit Nigeria?

Yes. The State Department says US citizens need a visa before travelling, and passports must be valid for six months beyond arrival.

World.title: Kenya Tightens Ebola Checks at Nairobi Airport
World.content:
KENYA · EBOLA TRAVEL RULES

Key Facts — The country East African safari destination whose Nairobi airport is a regional hub.

— What happened First imported Ebola case confirmed Tuesday, 6 October; no outbreak declared.

— The new rule Arrivals from 10 African countries now pass through Gate 16.

— For US travellers Online travel permit from US$30 still needed; advisory stays Level 2.

— US entry rules CDC limits cover arrivals from Congo, Uganda and South Sudan, not Kenya.

— Still open Whether passengers changing planes in listed countries face Gate 16.

Ebola screening in Kenya has been tightened at Nairobi’s main airport after the country’s first imported case. For most US visitors, the entry rules and official travel advice have not changed.

Kenya has tightened Ebola screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) in Nairobi, the country’s main international gateway. Arrivals from 10 African countries now pass through a dedicated gate, Gate 16, for enhanced health checks.

The step follows Kenya’s first imported Ebola case, confirmed on Tuesday, 6 October. For US visitors flying in from outside Africa, the entry rules, the State Department rating and CDC guidance are unchanged so far.

What Changed at Nairobi Airport

Mary Muthoni, Kenya’s principal secretary for public health, announced the measures after touring JKIA on Wednesday, 7 October. A principal secretary is the senior civil servant who runs a ministry department under the cabinet minister.

Passengers arriving from 10 countries are now processed through Gate 16, Capital FM, a Nairobi broadcaster, reported. The list covers the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Angola, Zambia, Tanzania and the Central African Republic.

Under the protocols, arriving passengers must give verified health details and disclose any medicine taken in the previous month, Capital FM reported. The rule targets travellers who were ill before departure, because the Nairobi patient had reportedly been unwell and taking medication.

“Fill in the online form even before you land,” Muthoni said, to cut crowding at the airport. Kenya has also added health declaration forms for departing passengers, and she said exit screening may follow.

The government also asked people to avoid unnecessary handshakes and hugs, as during the COVID-19 pandemic. Muthoni stressed that Ebola spreads through contact with an infected person, not through the air.

Ebola screening in Kenya is not new: checks already run at 15 points of entry and have covered more than 652,000 travellers. Aden Duale, the cabinet secretary for health and in effect Kenya’s health minister, gave that figure.
