World.title: EU debates harsh working conditions for fishers: 'I had no other choice'
World.content:
"The food was in very poor condition and I could only drink seawater that had been filtered. I had no other choice, it was never properly clean," recalled Fredi Seprizal, an Indonesian who endured what he describes as "modern slavery" at sea and who spoke during the debate 'Boosting the social dimension of sustainable fisheries', held last week in the European Parliament.

 

Seprizal's was one of the most striking testimonies at the meeting, which took place on 30 September and was organised by Carmen Crespo (EPP), chair of the European Parliament's Committee on Fisheries (PECH), and Virginia Battu-Henriksson, a member of the cabinet of the Commissioner for Fisheries and Oceans, Costas Kadis.

The sailor told MEPs about the conditions he endured for 16 months on board a Chinese vessel. He explained that he worked between 16 and 20 hours a day and, at times, for 24 hours straight, with rest periods of between three and six hours. Seprizal also denounced the lack of adequate safety equipment and said he feared for his life while he was on the high seas.

The aim of the meeting was to examine fishermen's working conditions and the fight against forced labour. Survivors of labour exploitation, international organisations, trade union representatives and members of the fisheries sector came together to call for stronger guarantees for those working in the industry.

"Europe cannot compete by lowering its standards, but by turning them into its greatest asset," said Crespo, stressing that the European fleet must maintain its requirements on sustainability, safety and labour rights. "Defending a competitive fishing sector also means defending its workers against unfair competition and ensuring supply chains that are transparent, responsible and free from exploitation."

The need for "effective protection"

The experiences shared during the meeting, according to a statement (source in Spanish) by the Organisation of Associated Producers of Large Frozen Tuna Vessels (OPAGAC), are in line with the findings of a study presented by Sallie Yea, professor and researcher at Charles Sturt University, based on interviews with 121 fishers and 32 family members from the Philippines, Indonesia, Cambodia and Fiji.

According to her research, 94% of the fishers interviewed had at some point suffered non-payment of their wages, and all of them had seen their contracts changed to less favourable conditions.

In addition, one in every four fishers interviewed had witnessed the death of a fellow crew member, while deaths were recorded on one in every four vessels analysed.

"We need to move from purely formal compliance to the effective protection of labour rights, including checks on contracts and wages, arbitration mechanisms to resolve labour complaints, protection against reprisals and accountability mechanisms for recruitment agencies, and not only for fishing fleets and seafood companies," Yea argued at the meeting.

During the Fisheries Committee's round table, representatives from the International Labour Organization (ILO), the European Transport Workers' Federation (ETF), the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) and Oxfam called for stricter enforcement of labour standards.

Economist Tariq Haq, from the ILO, recalled that the Work in Fishing Convention lays down the minimum requirements for working on board, but has been ratified by only 27 member states.

The EU also has a regulation (source in Spanish) on forced labour, which will be phased in until December 2027. For OPAGAC, which promoted the meeting together with Hands for the Oceans, access to the European market should be made conditional on compliance with the same standards that apply to the European fleet.

"We hope that the EU rules on due diligence and forced labour can become a turning point," said Julio Morón, director-general of OPAGAC, to ensure that European consumers do not eat fish caught using forced labour and modern slavery.

In that context, Seprizal's words still resonate. During the debate he went so far as to say: "The thought of jumping off the ship or setting it on fire crossed my mind; but I could not escape because the captain kept hold of my documents. I even had to pay to get them back."

World.title: Mélenchon declares ‘Bastille retaken’ after major student rally in Paris
World.content:
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard left France Unbowed party took to X on Thursday to declare the Bastille had been "retaken", after students staged demonstrations across the country — including a major rally at Paris' infamous Place de la Bastille.

 

Thursday's major protests were part of the student-led movement which began on 17 September in the suburbs of Paris, before gradually developing into a broader campaign addressing issues including long school days, overcrowded schools, teacher absences.

The mass gathering which took place at the place de la Bastille started off peacefully, but clashes with the police later erupted, with tear gas and a water cannon fired at protesters.

Meanwhile, France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray said in an interview with broadcaster TF1 later that day that 3,000 substitute teacherswould be deployed to schools facing critical shortages.

Meanwhile, Mélenchon wrote "powerful demonstration by the youth who carry their demands in the most beautiful way possible! Immense pride. See you on Tuesday, October 13, at the call of the youth unions and workers."

The storming of the Bastille in 1789 marked a major turning point in the French Revolution and became a symbol of the people’s resistance to royal authority.

The leader of France Unbowed and his allies have been accused of stoking unrest and manipulating young people for political gain by their opponents. He has stated that despite the fact that his party supports the protest, they were independently organised by students.

The student and professional union coalition has called for another day of protests and strikes on 13 October, with a further major mobilisation planned for 17 October.

What did protestors say on the ground?

Cathy, a history teacher in a secondary school located in Paris told Euronews she had decided to accompany her students to the Bastille rally, because she backed their demands in favour of a change in France's education system.

"The students have demands that are very close to the ones teachers have been putting forward years. The system is degraded and it's because there has been no response for so long, that this is happening," she stated.

Meanwhile, one schoolboy warned that it was "normal" if violent outbursts occurred, if students' demands were "not be heard."

"All the revolutions in history have served a purpose. In 1789, there were a lot of deaths. We don't want to have deaths, but we could revert to violence as a means of expression. The goal is not to perpetrate violence to hurt people, but it's to use violence to change the system that harms us", he said.

Despite this, many other school pupils said they backed peaceful protests, instead condoning police violence.

Many students questioned by Euronews at the rally had not heard of the government's mass online consultation, which was launched earlier in the week in order to collate student opinions and drive possible policy proposals. France's Education Ministry said it surpassed 40,000 responses within days of its launch.

Breaking down the numbers

According to the Interior Ministry, 71,500 people took part in Thursday's protests, with 24,500 in Paris. Meanwhile, an estimated 55,000 people took part in protests outside schools, amid school blockades that were staged across the country.

The Education Ministry said 375 schools were fully or partially closed for the day.

Authorities also reported an increase in what they described as cases of "urban violence", saying they took place on the "margins' of peaceful student demonstration, acting as a 'stain on their legitimate expression.'

Police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when students, most of them under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, according to the Interior Ministry.

World.title: Drought: groundwater levels in France remain very low
World.content:
After a summer marked by exceptional drought, the situation beneath our feet remains highly worrying.

 

According to the latest bulletin from the French Geological and Mining Research Bureau (BRGM), published on Thursday 8 October, 66% of groundwater monitoring points are below seasonal norms (source in French) (source in French)as of 1 October.

More importantly, the situation is continuing to deteriorate: 81% of levels are still falling, compared with only 7% that have started to rise.

After their natural decline over spring and summer, autumn rains usually begin to seep into the ground and replenish underground reserves. This year, however, the recharge has been very slow to get under way.

Why are the current rains not enough to recharge the aquifers?

For groundwater tables to refill, rainwater has to infiltrate deep into the soil. At the moment, this process is being blocked by three factors:

The prior drying of soils: after a hot, dry summer, soils are parched. The first rains are used mainly to re-moisten the surface rather than feeding underground reserves.

Evapotranspiration: under the effect of warmth and vegetation, a large part of the rainwater evaporates or is absorbed by plants before it can reach deeper layers.

The accumulated deficit: light rainfall and high temperatures at the start of the autumn season have delayed the beginning of the recharge period, which normally starts around this time.

The situation is all the more worrying as it is already clearly less favourable than a year ago. On 1 October 2025, only 31% of monitoring points were below normal, compared with 66% today. The BRGM considers the 2026 situation to be "as worrying as in 2022", even if the aquifers concerned are not exactly the same.

According to the BRGM website, in 2022 an exceptional drought, combined with scant rainfall and heavy abstraction, led to an exceptionally severe low-water situation in aquifers, with below-normal levels across much of the country.

This year the problem is also affecting so-called "inertial" aquifers, which respond slowly to changes in rainfall. Some can take months, or even longer, to recover.

By contrast, "reactive" aquifers can rise quickly after several bouts of rain. For now, though, almost all of these are still declining.

The situation is not uniform, however. Levels are very low in Limousin, Morvan, Livradois, Forez, Vivarais, and in the east, from Champagne to Lorraine via northern Alsace and as far as the Jura. Conversely, several aquifers in the south-east of the country still show more favourable levels, as this BRGM map illustrates.

Map of groundwater levels in France in October 2026 @BRGM / www.brgm.fr

Autumn will be decisive

Aquifer recharge can still begin over the coming weeks, but it will depend on regular and substantial rainfall to infiltrate the soil. A few isolated episodes will not necessarily be enough to make up the accumulated deficit.

The BRGM believes that the slowest-responding aquifers will probably continue to fall until the end of autumn. For the others, everything will depend on the rainfall still to come.

In the most depleted areas, a wetter-than-normal winter may be needed to bring levels back close to normal.

The stakes are high: groundwater supplies nearly two-thirds of drinking water and more than one-third of the water used by agriculture in France, a sector whose activity has already suffered from the 2026 drought.

Seasonal forecasts nonetheless remain uncertain. Météo-France does not yet have a sufficiently clear scenario to say whether autumn in France will be generally dry or wet.

World.title: Astronaut Sophie Adenot returns to Earth after record space mission
World.content:
Sophie Adenot spent 235 days 400 kilometres above the Earth. After a day-long journey, the French astronaut splashed down on Thursday 8 October at 5:35 p.m. (French time), together with three other members of the International Space Station crew, in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.

 

The final minutes of the flight brought intense sensations for the Frenchwoman, Russian cosmonaut Andrei Fediaiev and the two Americans Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway: a high-speed plunge through the atmosphere, then a slowdown under powerful parachutes, all while communications were cut.

After exiting the spacecraft and undergoing a brief medical check-up, the four astronauts will be flown back to dry land in the United States, first to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, then on to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

A medical team from the European Space Agency (ESA) will then take charge of Sophie Adenot during the long return flight to Cologne, in Germany. There, the astronaut will be reunited with her loved ones and will begin a recovery programme lasting several weeks.

Sophia Adenot, French ESA astronaut at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, on 13 February 2026, as part of a mission to the ISS. (AP Photo/John Raoux)

Thirty years after Claudie Haigneré, Sophie Adenot became in February the second Frenchwoman to cross the Karman line, the internationally recognised boundary between the atmosphere and outer space. She also became the first French woman to venture into the vacuum of space, during three spacewalks on 18 and 25 August and 1 September.

With 237 days spent in space, the eleventh French astronaut now holds the record for the longest European spaceflight. The previous record-holder, Italian astronaut Luca Parmitano, spent 201 days in orbit in 2019–2020.

World.title: Italy probes gaming giant Activision Blizzard over in-game spending by children
World.content:
Italy’s antitrust authorities have launched an investigation into Microsoft-owned gaming company Activision Blizzard amid claims it has used predatory game monetisation such as “loot boxes” and pay-to-progress designs in its popular mobile games Diablo Immortal and Call of Duty Mobile to target and exploit children and other players.

 

Italy, supported by consumer protection authorities in Norway and Denmark, is first seeking to find if the games company’s practices constituted a “widespread infringement” of EU consumer protection rules following player and public backlash in recent years.

Activision Blizzard is one of Microsoft's most well-known game publishers, known worldwide for genre-defining game series Call of Duty, Warcraft, StarCraft and Diablo, among others, and was bought by the big tech company in 2023 for $75.4 billion (€67.29bn)

Should the company be found in breach of the Italian Consumer Code it could face fines of up to 4% of its annual turnover in each of the affected countries, according to the European consumer law framework.

FILE - An illustration of the Call of Duty®: WWII Fear Not Pack produced to support the placement of veterans into high-quality jobs. Distributed by AP via Business Wire. Copyright Business Wire 2018.

Italy’s investigation is part of a wider EU coordination launched at the end of September by the European Commission’s Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network, with actions set to launch across the EU with the aim of strengthening the protection of gamers’ rights targeting nine video games companies.

The CPC Network is coordinating action against Activision Blizzard UK Limited, Crytek GmbH, InnoGames GmbH, King.com Limited, Mojang AB, Plarium Europe S.à.r.l., PLR Worldwide Sales Limited, Riot Games Limited, Supercell Oy and Ubisoft EMEA SAS.

Italy’s investigation is the first step of this EU-wide approach.

Chief among the Italian authorities’ concerns is how the company’s practices have targeted children who are more at risk of gaming addiction and unable to understand or keep track of how much they are spending, especially as the company relies on virtual currencies paid for with real money to make purchases of in-game items, benefits and features.

Authorities highlighted the “lack of transparency and fairness in the use of virtual currencies” within the games, said the Authority in a statement.

The move is part of a wider drive at European and global level against tech companies over concerns their platforms’ and games’ designs negatively harm young people’s mental health, following a spate of suicides.

Just last month, the European Commission unveiled a proposal to protect children online known as the EU Kids Act, which aims to introduce a requirement for digital service providers to first prove that their platforms are “safe by design” and age-appropriate before children can use them.

The proposal specifically targets video games, including a ban on loot boxes — virtual mystery packages containing random items such as equipment and cosmetic gear — for children, as well as a requirement to clearly display real currency costs for in-game purchases and purchase alerts.

The proposal also aims to curb addictive behavior in children including banning “streak” mechanics that require players to login regularly or even daily as well as notifications encouraging children to resume or keep playing longer than they want.

The EU-wide action follows an open dialogue launched by the CPC Network with the video games industry last year, which the organisation diplomatically saying that it “did not bring satisfactory results,” especially in addressing monetisation and virtual currencies practices.

FILE - The Activision Blizzard Booth is shown on June 13, 2013 the during the Electronic Entertainment Expo in Los Angeles. Copyright 2019 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Parallel to these actions, the Commission is expected to present an EU Digital Fairness Act later this year, with measures including banning “dark patterns” (manipulative designs and false urgency), unfair personalization practices and subscription traps.

The CPC Network is also investigating Activision Blizzard UK Limited to see if they are complying with EU consumer law in their games.

“Roughly half of Europeans play video games… With that reach comes responsibility. The industry must ensure that its games do not expose players — especially children — to harmful or unfair practices,” said Michael McGrath the EU’s consumer protection commissioner.

“The game must be fair, and the rules must be respected. National authorities, with the support of the Commission, will make sure they are enforced,” he added.

Many gamers have also complained over the years over what they see as pay-to-win mechanics being employed more frequently by video game publishers.

These mechanics reward players who have spent more money in game, giving them an unfair advantage over players who have not despite them being more skilled.

This reduces the game to a battle of bank accounts rather than skill or merit. Games companies have often defended this decision by saying their games are free to play, and that paying is optional.

In a July 2022 interview with the Los Angeles Times, the former head of Blizzard Entertainment Mike Ybarra defended their gaming business model saying the company “gives a free Diablo experience to hundreds of millions of people, where they can literally do 99.5% of everything in the game".

He also claimed the vast majority of players had not spent any money and that players could complete the game without paying.

World.title: Podcast: AI in France, translators fight back, musicians' mentor
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is everywhere in France but who's using it, and how? We also look at its impact on translators and how they're striving to keep humans at the helm. And Nadia Boulanger – the pioneering French composer and conductor who taught generations of musical greats.

Advertising

AI is widely used in France, despite many peoples' misgivings. Tech consultant Frederic Cavazza says adoption is being driven by individuals, rather than a coherent or systemic approach. That results in a paradox: the technology is everywhere, but guidance and confidence in it is lacking. (Listen @2'40'')

One field that is heavily impacted by generative AI in France – and the non-English-language world – is translation. Low-cost translation agencies are increasingly using machines to deliver first drafts and relying on humans for ungratifying, poorly paid "post-editing". But translators are fighting back. The En chair et en os collective and the recently-launched STEF union for translators in publishing marked last week's World Translation Day with symbolic strike action. They gathered to find collective ways of keeping humans at the heart of the translation process, including an initiative to "sabotage" the post-editing system. (Listen @17'50'')

The story of French musician Nadia Boulanger, a talented composer and the first woman to conduct some of the world's top orchestras. Today she is best remembered for teaching an extraordinary number of the 20th century's most famous musicians, from Aaron Copland to Philip Glass, Burt Bacharach and Quincy Jones. (Listen @10'30'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: South Africa: Anti-migrant protests turn violent
World.content:
A court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications reignited violent protests against immigration in South Africa.

Anti-migrant protests erupted in South Africa on Thursday as tensions over immigration were reignited by a court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications.

Some of the protests turned violent, according to local media reports. This included incidents in the coastal city of Durban and the Soweto township of Johannesburg, where cars were set on fire and gunshots were heard.

What do we know about protests in South Africa?

The unrest in Durban reportedly followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. About 10 vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.

Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.

At least nine vehicles were torched, said Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television.

"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," he said. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."

Police fired rubber bullets when clashes erupted between protesters and foreign nationals in Durban Image: Rajesh Jantilal/AFP

What has the court decided?

The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.

The court explained that this was because the provisions prevented individuals from accessing the asylum system on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.

Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.

On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa".

Immigrants in South Africa pushed out of their own shops To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Xenophobic sentiment in South Africa

South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.

Amidst international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.

Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.

Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.

World.title: US will not resume strikes on Iran before midterms — Trump
World.content:
President Donald Trump said the US will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterm elections on November 3. High gas and grocery prices are top concerns for voters.

US President Donald Trump said he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.

Trump's announcement on social media on Thursday came after two US media outlets reported that he was weighing options to strike Iran.

The Atlantic magazine reported that the thinking was Trump would want to maintain the period of relative calm in the war with Iran until after the elections to keep the deeply unpopular war out of the news. The US has not struck the country in recent weeks.

A Pentagon official told Axios that the Department of Defense's job was to be ready for possible strikes on Iran if the president ordered them.

War abroad, soaring prices at home: is Trump in trouble? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran war, gas prices, and US midterms: What to know

The US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire agreement in April, but that agreement didn't hold as both countries resumed fighting in the months that followed.

Trump said at the UN General Assembly that he could yet escalate the war with Iran.

But gas and fuel prices remain high in the US, with many voters already feeling the pressure of high prices for groceries and other goods — factors that have weighed on candidates in Trump's Republican Party.

Plus, the economy remains one of the top concerns for voters this midterm, when US citizens are going to be electing members of Congress.

In his social media post on Thursday, Trump also said his team has been "having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran."

That came after Trump, at the end of September, publicly rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — the vital waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed — to commercial shipping if the US met necessary conditions.

Then Iran last week said it had received a counterproposal.

Pentagon deploys more resources to the Middle East, WSJ reports

Trump's post also came as the military dispatched more resources to the Middle East, according to a report the Wall Street Journal .

US officials said a third aircraft-carrier strike group, and its thousands of troops, would arrive by the end of November, according to the newspaper.

World.title: France: Police clash with protesters at Paris student rally
World.content:
Police fired tear gas at protesters in Paris again as students continue to voice grievances about school conditions across France. The education minister has said 3,000 substitute teachers will reach schools soon.

Thousands of students demonstrated near Bastille Square in Paris on Thursday afternoon, as France's nationwide student protests continue.

Crowds of students climbed the famous Bastille Monument. Some waved the French flag and sang the national anthem.

Footage from Reuters TV showed riot police charging at protesters with batons as they moved in to clear the square.

Across France, some 71,500 people took part in Thursday's protests and police detained more than 500, the Interior Ministry said.

France will send 3,000 substitute teachers "within the next hours" to struggling high schools, the education minister said Thursday.

"Within the next hours, 3,000 teachers will be joining these institutions," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the evening news on the TF1 television channel.

Geffray said they would be at schools between Friday to Tuesday.

Protesters marched toward the Place de la Bastille during a demonstration in Paris Image: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP

Students barricade high school

Earlier on Thursday, students barricaded Helene Boucher High School in northeastern Paris with trash bins before police broke up the protest with tear gas.

As students gathered at the school, riot police assembled in the side streets. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid identification.

The school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests on Thursday.

Although the rallies have largely been peaceful, some demonstrators have set fires and vandalized bus shelters.

Since the beginning of the protests in September, the French police have made more than 6,600 arrests Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

In response, the police have used tear gas, batons, and blast balls. Human rights groups and children accuse officers of using excessive force.

Following an incident in which a teenager's hand was blown off, the government suspended the use of stun grenades for crowd control on Wednesday.

Since late September, when students, most of whom are under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, police have made more than 6,600 arrests, according to the Interior Ministry.

France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Government promises response

On Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised that the government would present "concrete, quick, and fully funded responses" to the protests by the end of October.

Nevertheless, student protest leaders said this was not good enough and called for more marches.

In a televised address, Lecornu also lamented the "violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults."

World.title: US prosecutors add new torture charge against Maduro
World.content:
US prosecutors have added a new charge to their case against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing the couple of conspiring to commit torture.

US prosecutors have announced new charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents and US citizens.

The new charges against the couple are in addition to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced, according to a revised indictment released Thursday.

Both Maduro and Flores have denied the previous charges brought against them.

Maduro's lawyer Barry Pollack said in a statement, "President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks ​forward to his day ‌in court."

Revised indictment adds pressure on Maduro

The revised indictment alleged that the couple committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.

High tensions between the US and a socialist and oil-rich Venezuela were a constant during Maduro's 13 years in power.

Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but Thursday's indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

"He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," the indictment said.

The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.

Maduro's wife seeks release from New York jail

Meanwhile, the 69-year-old Flores is due in Manhattan federal court on Thursday. She is expected to ask a judge to release her from jail and place her under house arrest, citing health problems.

Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11.4 kilograms) in custody, suffers from dizziness and shortness of breath and may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.

They have proposed that she live at a New York residence under 24-hour security.

Media reports said prosecutors are also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing US nationals [FILE: March 26, 2026] Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

Prosecutors, however, oppose the request, arguing that Flores poses an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released.

They said she has received hospital treatment when necessary while in custody.

Trump vs. Maduro

Maduro, 63, and Flores are being held at a federal detention center in Brooklyn as they await their trial in June next year.

The couple was captured during an unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid on their Caracas home on January 3, which was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation."

Critics have accused Trump of operating outside international law.

They were subsequently brought to New York, where they face existing drug trafficking and firearms charges.

Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Meanwhile, in August, Trump announced that the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, which Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez also termed "historic."

World.title: EU pulls sponsorship from Disinfo2026 event in Lithuania
World.content:
The EU's diplomatic service, Canada and host nation Lithuania all pulled support from a disinformation event in Vilnius. Amid reports of US pressure, the EU said it was "uncomfortable with the framing" of some panels.

The European Union on Thursday offered its reasons for withdrawing sponsorship for a disinformation event in Lithuania, following media reports claiming that it did so after pressure from the US government.

The EU's foreign affairs division, the European External Action Service (EEAS), and the governments of Canada and Lithuania all pulled their support from the event at short notice. Sponsors' logos on flyers and placards at the event were hastily covered over with paper strips.

They withdrew participation in Disinfo2026 after pressure from the US State Department, according to reports in several media outlets, including the British newspaper The Guardian.

What did the EU say about its decision?

EU spokesperson Christian Wigand made no mention of the US or external pressure on Thursday but also did not repudiate the reports.

"We were not comfortable with the framing of some of the discussions at the event," he told reporters in Brussels.

"The organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU," he said.

He refused to discuss details of which discussions or what framing had perturbed the EEAS. He also would not comment on whether there had been talks with US officials on the matter.

"I'm not commenting on diplomatic exchanges as a matter of principle," he said.

What signs of potential controversy at Disinfo2026 were visible?

While a number of the sessions planned on the event's website across two days at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius appeared to have the potential to perturb more sensitive members of Donald Trump's administration, the opening two sessions on Wednesday morning stood out.

The opening of the conference was an interview with Kimberly Prost, a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has come under sustained and heavy fire from Trump and his administration during his second term.

This was followed by an hourlong session entitled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back," using the acronym for Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference. One of the planned speakers was a former CIA officer.

Strong US free speech safeguards in the First Amendment to its Constitution mean the US has maintained a comparatively hands-off approach to combating disinformation — both in the political and legal spheres. This has arguably intensified, however, under President Donald Trump's leadership, with critics alleging it's partly because of his own often uneasy relationship with the truth.

World.title: How the Houthi-Saudi conflict is affecting countries on Africa's Red Sea coast — and beyond
World.content:
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which Yemeni government forces are trying to take back from the Houthis, is located not far from Djibouti and other African states.

In September, one of the major conflicts in the Middle East came within sight of Africa, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Yemen's Perim Island.

The island forms the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the southern entrance of the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It is roughly 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Djibouti and 20-minutes by air to Ethiopia.

In early October, Yemen's armed forces and their Saudi allies launched a counteroffensive. TheIran-backed Houthis have been firing on merchant ships since the start of the Gaza war in 2023.

The economic consequences for Africa is coupled with a refugee inflow

African economies are already suffering from crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, which is making particularly fuel and fertilizer scarce and more expensive.

If the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also becomes impassable, the situation could deteriorate further. Shipping companies would have to make detours via the Suez Canal, which is controlled by Egypt or the southern tip of Africa, as some already do. The additional costs would be passed on to consumers.

The human cost of the escalation in Yemen hit Djibouti almost immediately. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), at least 3,700 refugees have crossed from Yemen into Djibouti since September 10. Most of those who made it to the country's northern Obock region are women and children.

The UNHCR is preparing to assist another 10,000 people who have not yet crossed into Djibouti. But Obock, which is on the border with Eritrea, is extremely dry and this is causing other issues.

"We don't have much water here; there's no groundwater at all," Alessandra Roccasalvo, the UN Development Program (UNDP) representative for Djibouti, told DW. "Everything has to be desalinated."

Thousands flee to Djibouti from Yemen's war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Djibouti is a strategic military hub

Despite its small size, Djibouti — a Muslim-majority Horn of Africa country with a population of just over a million — is a major player in the region. Its position at at the entrance to the Red Sea makes it an attractive commercial and military shipping hub.

The United States, China, France, Italy, and Japan all operate military bases in Djibouti. The German Bundeswehr was also present until 2021, as part of a naval mission to combat maritime piracy.

The country's civilian ports serve as transshipment, or intermediate, hubs for global shipping cargo, goods and containers. So far, the Houthi advance has not led to empty docks in Djibouti.

But there are still potential consequences, said Roccasalvo: "Basically, there's an economic upswing here — which means, as in any country experiencing an upswing, building materials are needed: cement, raw materials, and other things."

Less of that money is now coming in because ships have to pay nearly twice as much for insurance and reinsurance as they used to. "Many ships no longer want to pass through the Suez Canal; many no longer want to pass through the Red Sea."

Knock-on effects for landlocked neighboring Ethiopia

Ethiopia — the world's most populous landlocked country — handles about 95% of its imports and exports through Djibouti's ports. Price hikes resulting from higher war-risk shipping insurance premiums are affecting the country greatly.

Shortly after the Houthis seized Perim, Ethiopia's economy faced another, even more immediate threat: On September 23, fighting broke out in the country's northern Tigray region.

Since then, the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) have reportedly made gains against the Tigray-led rebel coalition that aims to overthrow the national government. The rebels briefly advanced toward the main corridor used for transporting goods between Djibouti's ports and the Ethiopian hinterland.

Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to certain experts, the ENDF's advances have since reduced the threat of yet another trade blockade — but as long as the conflict remains unresolved, the situation could potentially deteriorate again.

For months now, Ethiopia has suffered more than almost any other African country from the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and has already had to ration fuel at times. In the long term, the country aims to reduce its dependence on imports, for example by powering vehicles with domestically generated electricity instead of imported gasoline.

In early 2024, Ethiopia became the first country in the world to impose a ban on the import of internal combustion engine vehicles Image: Shewangizaw Wegayehu/DW

Can the conflict in Ethiopia affect Bab el-Mandeb access?

Ethiopia and its northern neighbor, Eritrea, have severed diplomatic ties; other regional powers such as Sudan, Egypt, and Somalia may find themselves siding with Eritrea rather than with Ethiopia.

Eritrea sees itself as facing a threat that Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has reiterated on several occasions: With Ethiopia deprived of access to the sea since Eritrea's independence, Abiy has often alluded to rectifying this perceived injustice — either through a political agreement, as was once sought with Somalia's breakaway region of Somaliland, or by force.

The port of Assab is located on the edge of Eritrea's panhandle — and is often described as the most likely target should Abiy choose the path of aggression. If the fighting within Ethiopia further escalates into a full-blown regional war, this could also lead to additional restrictions on safe passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the surrounding waters.

Experts have also raised concerns about the Shiite Houthis increasingly collaborating with the Sunni terrorist group Al-Shabab, which is based in Somalia. Although their ideologies are fundamentally different, they are particularly united by their hostility toward Israel and the US.

Inside Somalia's arms smuggling network To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What tools are at the disposal of African countries to help remedy the situation?

The three African non-permanent members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia — held an emergency meeting in mid-September, jointly calling for free shipping lanes and endorsing the demand that the crisis in Yemen be resolved under the auspices of the UN.

Liberia's UN Ambassador Lews Garseedah Brown formulated joint principles with his counterparts from Somalia and the Congo: the African nations are hoping for a UN-led diplomatic solution for Yemen Image: Bianca Otero/ZUMA/picture alliance

The situation at Bab el-Mandeb and in northern Ethiopia once again demands flexibility from Africa. In fact, some African economies could also benefit from relocation activities: Ports inKenya and Tanzania, for example, are becoming increasingly attractive for transshipment.

And while many countries are suffering from high oil prices, Nigeria's Dangote Group has announced an initial public offering and a new refinery in Kenya.

This article was originally published in German. It has been updated.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

World.title: Rodrigo Duterte ruled fit to stand trial by ICC judges
World.content:
Judges at the International Criminal Court said Rodrigo Duterte was fit to understand the charges at his trial, which is set to begin in November. His legal team argued that he suffers from cognitive deficiencies.

Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) said Thursday that former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is competent to stand trial on charges of crimes against humanity.

Duterte walked into the courtroom for his first-ever in-person appearance at a hearing last month after a year of having been detained at The Hague, where the global court is located.

Judges at the court this April confirmed charges against him, accusing him of murder and attempted murder for his alleged role in the killings of dozens of people during his "war on drugs."

Duterte's trial is set to begin on November 30. He faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.

Filipino woman who lost family to drug war takes on Duterte To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Duterte makes his first appearance in court after being arrested

Duterte did not speak at a hearing last month but sipped water throughout the proceedings.

His legal team has argued that he suffers from cognitive decline that affects his memory and daily functioning.

ICC judges in January said his health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court. He had missed several hearings or attended those via videolink.

Now, the ICC's ruling, dated September 28 and made public on Thursday , clears the road for his trial to get underway.

The court ruling said an independent panel of experts found Duterte "has the capacity to understand the charges" and follow the proceedings, including the implication of entering a plea — which he will be asked to do when the trial opens.

He also is mentally fit to understand evidence and discuss his defense with his lawyers, the panel of experts said.

Families of victims of Duterte's war on drugs followed the hearing in Manila. Their banner reads, "Hold Duterte and his accomplices accountable" Image: Joeal Calupitan/AP Photo/picture alliance

Duterte's violent anti-narcotics campaign

Duterte was arrested last year on accusations of crimes that took place during his "war on drugs" campaign when he was president between 2016 and 2022 and before that, when he was mayor of Davao City.

The charges against him are tied to brutal killings that took place on his watch between November 2011 and March 2019.

Duterte's campaign to wipe out the use of illegal narcotics in the country ended with the deaths of thousands of people as police systematically targeted poor and defenseless people, according to Amnesty International .

Prosecutors alleged that police and hit squad members carried out dozens of murders at Duterte's behest starting in 2011, motivated by the promise of money or to avoid becoming targets themselves.
