World.title: Renewed push to trial pet-friendly train, metro carriages in NSW
World.content:
A campaign to trial a pet-friendly carriage on trains and metro services in NSW is gaining traction, despite similar calls falling flat in previous years.

More than 6,500 people have signed a petition in support of the two-year trial, which would require pet owners to keep their dogs on a lead or in an approved carrier if riding in designated animal-friendly carriages.

Current public transport guidelines prohibit people from bringing dogs into train and metro stations and onto carriages across the state.

Dogs in carriers may be permitted on buses, ferries and light rail services with the permission of the driver or crew.

Different rules apply to accredited assistance animals, which can accompany their owners on all NSW metro, train, bus, ferry, light rail and taxi services.

Accredited assistance animals are permitted on all public transport in NSW. (Supplied: Transport NSW)

According to the petition, the current rules disadvantage people who do not own a car, including apartment residents, older people, low-income earners and some people with disabilities.

Petition organiser Rosemary Lee runs a social club for small dog owners in Sydney, saying some had difficulty attending events due to being unable to take their pets on public transport.

"We have a government that's very pro-taking public transport to events ... but dog owners can't use it, we're banned from it," she said.

"That makes no sense to me whatsoever."

Rules differ between states

Public transport guidelines around passengers carrying pets differ across the country, with small animals allowed on buses, trams, trains and some V/Line services in Victoria.

Ms Lee pointed to Victoria as evidence of the success of pet-friendly public transport policies.

"What we're asking for is one pet-friendly carriage on all New South Wales trains and for a two-year trial to see how it goes," she said.

Ms Lee says pet-friendly carriages have proven successful in Victoria. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

She acknowledged some may have concerns about the proposal.

"At the moment, pets are travelling on trains. They're just not doing it legally and [pet owners are] risking getting a fine," she said.

"This [proposed trial] restricts all those animals into one carriage, they will have to be on a lead, they will have to be muzzled.

"So it actually removes any chance you've got of sitting beside a dog or an animal ... if you do have an allergy or a concern.

"The only people that should be in the pet carriage are people that like pets or people that have got a pet."

Ms Lee acknowledges some may be concerned about the proposed trial. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

Ms Lee recognised some had also raised concerns about the implications of having pet-friendly carriages during peak travel times.

"What we're asking for is exactly the same as what we have with the present quiet carriages. People haven't raised that as an issue with the quiet carriages, saying 'now there is one less carriage for me who likes to talk'," she said.

"It's up to Transport for NSW to ensure that there's always enough carriages made available."

A Transport for NSW spokesperson said the department was aware of the petition and "welcomes community feedback on any issue related to public transport."

Pets may be allowed on light rail services if the driver or staff give permission. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Similar campaigns have proved unsuccessful in previous years, with the City of Sydney backing a petition to allow pets on public transport in 2023.

Lord Mayor Clover Moore at the time said public transport must serve everyone's needs.

"People with pets are still often made to feel like second-class citizens through unnecessarily restrictive policies about pets on public transport," she said in a statement at the time.

The current petition is open until November 4, with at least 20,000 submissions required for the proposal to be debated in NSW parliament.

World.title: Would the Griffins approve of Canberra's proposed waterfront stadium?
World.content:
A waterfront stadium was part of the original plan for Canberra, but a historian says a new proposed venue could "knock out parts" of the architects' legacy.

A stadium in Canberra's CBD has long been a topic of discussion in the nation's capital.

The notion was catapulted back into the limelight this week, when the Canberra Airport unveiled a proposal to build a stadium in the city centre near Commonwealth Park.

The airport's CEO and a consortium of business owners are proposing to purchase land owned by the Catholic Church along Commonwealth Avenue to clear the way for a 25,000-35,000 seat venue to host sporting and musical events.

The proposed location of the stadium in Canberra's CBD. (Supplied: Canberra Airport)

The airport said it was "willing to contribute to the proposal's development" but was not seeking ownership and would have no ongoing financial interest in operating the stadium.

After meeting with the airport's chief executive yesterday, ACT Planning Minister Chris Steel said the render for the stadium looked "incredible", but further study was needed to examine its potential impact on transport and parking.

Griffins' stadium vision 'quite different'

A lakeside stadium was part of the Griffins' plan for the city, but the current proposal is quite different to what they drafted. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

The idea of a stadium in the capital's CBD was floated more than 100 years ago when the design for Canberra was entered into a competition, which received more than 130 entries.

The coolest things in the Griffins' Canberra plan that never were Marion Mahony Griffin and Walter Burley Griffin designed the original plan for Canberra, but much of it was never realised.

American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin won the competition in 1911.

In the award-winning blueprint, the Griffins imagined a cultural hub by the lake, dotted with baths, a gymnasium, zoological gardens and a stadium.

In the 1912 departmental board design, a stadium could be seen in what is now Kings Park. In later designs, the stadium still featured, but had been moved to Rond Terrace at the end of Anzac Parade.

"The stadium for general assembly faces the waterway, and is recessed into the slope of the bank, where it does not interrupt the continuous vista along the land axis," the Griffins' plan stated.

Canberra historian Tony Maple says the proposed stadium could significantly encroach on the Griffins' original plan. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Tony Maple, of the Canberra and Region Heritage Researchers network, said the stadium Walter Burley Griffin had in mind was "quite different to what is being proposed now".

"It was going to be a place for general assembly of people, and it was going to be a flat structure, really like the Rond Terrace that's there now," he said.

He said the stadium the Griffins imagined was not a multi-storey structure that could be as high as 30 or 40 metres tall.

"I think that site would encroach significantly on the Canberra plan, the legacy of the Griffins, and it would likely take over a significant part of Commonwealth Park," he said.

Walter Burley and Marion Mahoney Griffins' winning design for Canberra intentionally included a large amount of parkland. (National Archives of Australia)

Mr Maple said the proposed stadium was a "dominating thing" that had the potential to "whittle away" the city's parks and gardens.

He stressed that it could take over a large space of the intended environment surrounding Lake Burley Griffin.

"I'm concerned about the potential to knock out parts of the Griffin legacy," he said.

The National Capital Authority, which has planning control over the area close to the lake, has said it would work alongside all parties "as the concept evolves and following the processes and requirements of the National Capital Plan".

World.title: Amount of people barred from working with children in Qld nearly doubles
World.content:
Thousands more people are being barred from working with children in Queensland, according to reporting from the state government.

Annual reporting from Queensland's Department of Justice showed in the last financial year, 6,403 people were denied working with children checks under Queensland's blue card system.

An anonymised Queensland Blue Card required for working with children. (Supplied)

It's nearly double the amount previously refused, with 3,712 people prevented from holding the passes in the 2024-2025 financial year.

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said it was the sign of a strong system.

"Queensland has one of Australia's strongest working with children screening systems, with robust safeguards in place to protect children and young people," they said.

Increased refusals don't mean safer kids, academics warn

Twenty-five years since it was introduced, more than 1.4 million people are monitored through the blue card system, a figure up by about 100,000 people more than last year.

The government expanded the scope of roles requiring blue cards in December, following a landmark report into failings in the child safety sector.

The report, prompted by the serial offending of paedophile, Ashley Paul Griffith, found the blue card system had functioned as intended but offered no meaningful protection to children.

The University of Queensland's Tamara Walsh said blue card refusals didn't mean a safer system.

University of Queensland law professor Tamara Walsh said a higher number of blue card refusals did not mean a more protective system.

"A lot of discretion is given to decision makers when they're deciding whether to give someone a blue card or not," she said.

Professor Walsh said someone charged with drug possession when they were young could be prevented from working in the youth justice space in the future, for example.

"We're actually preventing people from getting blue cards who we would want to have blue cards, so the system is not being strengthened in the ways in which we'd all hope.

"What we're doing is capturing a whole lot of people who don't pose a protective risk to children and we're missing people who do."

The department had a 98 per cent clearance rate at the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal last year, despite a 25 per cent increase in lodgements, the government report said.

Queensland's Attorney-General Deb Frecklington said a rigorous and fair framework was in place. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Further changes on the way

In August, Queensland's Attorney-General and Justice Minister Deb Frecklington introduced legislation for a new Child Protection Commission.

The centralised commission would coordinate agencies and departments — including blue card services — to share intelligence and investigate concerning behaviour that may not meet the threshold for police investigation.

Queensland Attorney-General and Minister for Justice and Integrity Deb Frecklington said the system was making kids safer.

"The safety of children remains the paramount consideration in Queensland's Blue Card system," she said.

"The Crisafulli Government will continue to support a framework that is both rigorous and fair."

World.title: Unique Rite of Passage ritual alive and well in Inala's Indigenous community
World.content:
On the outskirts of Brisbane, a group of First Nations youth are embracing the western tradition of the debutante ball, while celebrating their own heritage.

One by one, girls in white ball gowns glide across the stage, taking the hand of their partners dressed up in suits.

They are stand on the precipice of their adult lives, as they turn to present themselves to an audience filled with family members.

For two decades, young Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Inala have taken part in the Rite of Passage Ball.

The community in Inala has taken part in the Rite of Passage for two decades. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

"It's pretty unique, I haven't heard of much people my age who get to do stuff like this," said 15-year-old Lilee Randall.

Lilee is one of dozens who have just completed the program, which is designed to help First Nations youth prepare for their transition into adulthood.

"It's a big thing in our culture, like coming of age, so it's really celebrated," she said.

From public speaking to ballroom dancing

Program coordinator with Inala Wangarra, Frances Lomas, leads the teenagers through eight weeks of workshops.

Frances Lomas leads the group as they prepare for the Rite of Passage Ball. (ABC News)

"A lot of the kids come here and start the program very shy, they don't engage with a lot of the other kids. In this setting, our first workshop is a lot of team building," Ms Lomas said.

The workshops gradually incorporate public speaking and traditional Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander dance lessons, before the young ones try their hand at ballroom dancing.

"At the beginning, they're just like girl boy germs, and at the end they're just loving it," Ms Lomas said.

Waltz, progressive swing, and cha cha are some of the dance styles they pick up.

The group dances to several different styles. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

"I'm nervous about messing up and stuff like that, hopefully other people know their steps, but overall I'm excited," Lilee said.

The importance of ritual

The origin of the debutante ball can be traced back hundreds of years, where opulent parties were held to introduce young women from affluent families to high society.

But coming-of-age ritual dates much further back for First Nations Australians.

Chelsea Watego is a Munanjahli and South Sea Islander writer and academic, who has researched the survival of Indigenous peoples locally and globally.

"From birth to death, we walk with our community throughout all stages of life," Professor Watego said.

It is often an emotional evening for the family members watching on. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

"We recognise the importance of these traditions, to have something to look forward to, but also to counter the prevailing social imagining about our people in our community.

"This is not just an event. This is a process of building up our young people in the community for the long term."

Professor Watego, who is a founding member of Inala Wangarra, has also seen all five of her children participate in the Rite of Passage Ball.

"It's interesting that it has a real colonial feel to it, like the old debutante ball, but we bought it back some years ago at the request of young people on our Youth Advisory Committee," she said.

"So, it's a colonial tradition, but it was Indigenous kids in Inala who said, 'we want to have this for ourselves.'"

Twenty years after its introduction, now multiple generations of Inala-based families have taken part in the Rite of Passage Ball.

The Indigenous community in Inala say the Rite of Passage is their culture. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

"I've been waiting for this my whole life since my siblings done it," said 15-year-old Taleii Brady.

"My dads done it, my older siblings done it, I'm the last one to do it now."

Ms Watego said the Rite of Passage Ball had allowed for cultural identity to persist in the modern day society.

"So mob are still identifying in relation to place … even here in suburban areas like on the outskirts of Brisbane.

"That culture is still alive, our kinship systems still operate.

"They've changed a bit, because of course they have, but our mob have always kept our culture alive."

World.title: Woman wins $460k child sexual abuse case after cross-examining abuser
World.content:
A legal expert says a woman who won a civil sexual abuse case after cross-examining the man who abused her as a child is "extraordinary" and rare.

Judge Gregory Sirtles, SC, awarded the woman more than $460,000 in Sydney's Supreme Court last week for psychiatric injuries caused by Rex Thomas Osbourne, who worked as a school grounds keeper.

Judge Sirtles found the now 85-year-old sexually assaulted her when she was between the ages of four and seven in the NSW Central West town of Parkes.

The woman represented herself in the proceedings.

Senior law lecturer at the University of New South Wales, Henry Kha, said it was "very rare" for a plaintiff to represent themselves seeking compensation for historic sex offences against the perpetrator.

"The extraordinary nature of the case is worth emphasising," he said.

"It would have been very difficult to demonstrate that these allegations had occurred given the significant length of time that had transpired between when the abuse was alleged to have occurred and the court case itself."

Rex Thomas Osbourne sexually abused the woman during walks on council grounds in the town of Parkes between 1986-1987. (Supplied: NSW Government)

Judge Sirtles noted that the woman said she first met Osbourne at the school canteen at the age of three, where her mother and his wife worked together.

He concluded the abuse happened "multiple times" during walks on council grounds in the Christmas school holidays of 1986–87.

Judge Sirtles noted that Osbourne pleaded guilty in 1987 to 10 counts of indecent assault against four children.

Three of those charges related to the woman.

He was sentenced to a two-year good behaviour bond and a 300-hour community service order.

Henry Kha says it is rare for a person to represent themselves and seek damages for historic child sexual abuse. (Supplied: University of New South Wales)

Judge Sirtles said he used the guilty plea and contemporaneous accounts she gave as a child to help determine his findings that the abuse occurred.

Cross-examining former grounds keeper

Judge Sirtles observed the woman's decision to represent herself without legal qualifications caused "some difficulties" while she cross-examined her abuser.

"It was apparent to me that the plaintiff found that exercise deeply confronting," he said.

"Although the plaintiff seemed at times frustrated or truculent when speaking, I regarded this as an expression of her anxiety and the stress of representing herself in such a painful matter.

"At no point did I doubt the authenticity of her efforts, both in making submissions and cross-examining Mr Osbourne," he found.

"I draw no adverse inference from her conduct."

Mr Kha said it was an intimidating experience for any self-represented litigant to cross-examine someone, let alone their abuser.

"It is understandable that the plaintiff was emotional, and those emotions were reflective of the plaintiff's past history of trauma," he said.

Judge Sirtles found Osbourne "tarnished" the woman's youth. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

"The judge would have to provide some accommodations to the plaintiff to ensure that they are not going to be re-victimised or re-traumatised in the court process."

Mr Kha observed that there were typically more people representing themselves in family law matters.

"Interestingly, in the Family Law Act, a person who is accused of family violence, they are not allowed to cross-examine their former partner," he said.

"That rule doesn't apply in civil cases in tort law."

Damages won

Judge Sirtles found that the abuse largely caused the woman's depression, gambling disorder, drug use and post-traumatic stress disorder.

He said those psychiatric issues have also impacted her ability to work.

"It is clear that Mr Osbourne betrayed a fundamental trust reposed in him by the plaintiff, who was only a child when he sexually abused her," he said.

"While I do not doubt the plaintiff may have some fond memories of childhood, Mr Osbourne tarnished the plaintiff's youth."

Judge Sirtles concluded that Osbourne's sexual abuse caused the majority of the woman's psychiatric injuries. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

He awarded the woman $461,046.02 in damages and aggravated damages.

The woman had also sued the State of New South Wales but settled the matter out of court and received $150,000.

Mr Kha said although the woman was successful, there were "significant barriers" for people representing themselves, such as understanding the law of court procedure.

He observed that she had a "head start" with some legal representation at the beginning of the case before continuing alone.

"The odds are stacked against self-represented litigants," he said.

"It's still a wise idea to have legal representation in order to improve one's chances of succeeding in a case."

World.title: Historic club's closure reveals sad new truth about Footscray
World.content:
The pale faded blue of Gary Tomlins's eyes is an almost perfect chameleonic colour match for the dusty pool cue tip he has spent so much of his life peering over.

For 45 years, the limber 78-year-old has held court at the pool table by the windows of the Footscray Club.

Gary Tomlins is rarely without a pool cue in hand. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

As the light waned on Sunday afternoon, he tried to eek out just a few more games before the club shut its doors for good.

"It's sad. It's 132 years of history," Tomlins said.

"It's a wonder I haven't got tears running down my eyes. Maybe those will come later. I'm just hiding them at the moment."

Tomlins says he doesn't know where he'll go now the Footscray Club is closed. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

The Footscray Club has survived in some form since 1894.

It couldn't survive this moment.

Like so many community cornerstones around the country, the working-class members club, perched atop 33 narrow steps in Melbourne's inner-west, has become overwhelmed by the new economic reality.

Neil Lewis, president of the Footscray Club, in Melbourne's west. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"We've been holding on to all this for as long as we can," the club's 73-year-old president, Neil Lewis said.

"We've tried everything. We're not closing because of choice."

'It's a family sort of thing'

An old stamp for the Footscray Cycling Club, first founded in 1894. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Lewis recently found an old stamp that gives a clue to the club's origins.

A picture of a bicycle with the letters F.C.C. — Footscray Cycling Club — harks back to its earliest 1890s iteration, before it broadened to an (initially male-only) members club.

What that has meant in more recent times is a club for people — typically in their 50s-70s — to gather, grab a soft drink or $7 schooner and feel some sense of belonging.

An archival photo of the Footscray Club found in an old magazine. (Supplied: Footscray Hotel)

"It's a family sort of thing," Lewis said.

"There's not many pubs around where you can leave your wallet on the bar or table and walk away and come back and [it's still there]."

It is, by no means, a model business for modern times.

The Footscray Club has prided itself on being welcoming to all. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

The room is unremarkably furnished.

The offering, limited.

There used to be cheap plates of hot food, but that had to be wound up.

"We kept getting hassled by the health department and the council, it just wasn't worth it," committee member Steven Bartlett grumbled.

Steven Bartlett used to work as a bartender at the club and has been a member for decades. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

The club instead relied on drink sales to remain viable, but found itself pinched at both ends.

As inflation has nudged the word 'recession' back into public debate, recent ABC analysis found the cost of beer has risen 23 per cent since the COVID-19 pandemic.

The tension of soaring costs and a shrinking member base with less money to spend has become unsustainable.

An older member and former service member at the Footscray Club. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"We don't put the price of beers up or the price of drinks up because if we do that, we're going to lose those members," Lewis said.

" It's an older clientele and they just haven't got the money to spend as they used to. "

The steep stairs to the club have become a problem for some older members. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Club regular and local Cameron, a comparatively younger member at 49 years-old, can feel the cost-of-living crisis changing the community around him.

"Sometimes you've got to cut things out that you can't afford," he said.

"This shouldn't be one of the places."

Crime on the doorstep

Long Huynh used to pay rent to the Footscray Club to run a bakery in the space beneath it.

He now owns the whole building.

Long Huynh at the Footscray Club on the last day of trading. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

When the club badly needed an injection of funds, they sold up to Huynh, who has rented it back to them for almost two decades.

"I want to keep this club," Huynh said.

"But at the moment, Footscray is very bad."

Community safety has become a major issue in Footscray. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

In an economically depressed moment, signs of disadvantage — of homelessness and drug use — are visible from the club's doorstep.

In August, amid growing concerns about community safety, Mayor Mohamed Semra was himself threatened with a knife in the nearby mall, remarkably while waiting to meet the minister of police.

Last year a man with a knife was shot dead by police just metres from the Footscray Club, prompting significant community backlash.

Can Australia still afford...? From our coffee addiction to a trip to the pub, some of the simple pleasures many Australians have taken for granted now feel like luxuries.

As Victoria approaches a state election where crime looms as a central issue, Huynh has never seen his suburb of 40 years like this.

"You see how many shops in Footscray now, they're closed," he said.

"I think business now in Footscray is very hard. You're lucky to cover the rent."

Former in-house bartender and decades-long member Bartlett conceded anxieties around safety contributed to the club's closure.

The club said some members have begun staying away over safety fears. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"People just won't come into Footscray because of that atmosphere that is around the place," he said.

"They just don't feel safe."

Last drinks

Even as members contended with losing something dear to them, the club's final afternoon was less a funeral and more akin to a boisterous wake.

An 87-year-old member on the final afternoon of the Footscray Club. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Manager Roula Glavas had endured an "emotional week," but was a flurry of activity about the room and behind the bar.

"I'll still keep in touch with all the boys. I'll definitely be calling one of them once a week and [plan to] catch up with them every now and then," the 52 year-old said.

"They're definitely part of my family.

" It's the only family most of us all have. "

Footscray Club president Neil Lewis and building owner Long Huynh. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

In its heyday, you could scarcely manoeuvre your way to the bar amid the heaving crowds, according to the club's president Lewis.

As he sought to sum up 132 years of history in a closing speech, he once again found himself surrounded by a crowd — this time amid the dozens of members who had come to say goodbye.

"Thank you for being part of the club's history," Lewis said to those in the room.

"You made this as a community, you made it as a family.

"I hope to see you around."

World.title: Family day care shrinks as parents opt for centre-based care
World.content:
Debbie Macleod's job encroaches on her home.

A section of her neat brick house on Melbourne's western fringe is lined with organised learning material, blocks and colourful toys.

A play kitchen intersects her dining room and there is a small library of picture books near the dining table.

Three-year-old Zayne Jardine loves going to family day care at Debbie Macleod's place. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Outside, her courtyard has been made child safe and is home to climbing frames, scooters and seesaws.

"I'm really proud to be able to say that a child comes into my care, I learn their personalities and their interests, provide program planning, experiences, and activities to promote their learning journey," she said.

"It's very rewarding."

A family day care educator for 37 years, she says her job has become increasingly difficult and bureaucratic, which has left her feeling undervalued.

"I'm all for qualifications and I'm all for providing learning but I'd like to put the family back in family day care," she said.

"We're actually qualified and we do a lot of paperwork, administration, program planning, observations, reflections and we have to journal everything and have evidence for government bodies to prove that we are doing our job."

Debbie Macleod says there is a misconception that family day care is "just babysitting". (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

She said she made less money than a worker in a childcare centre, partly because of the long hours of admin that is part of running the business herself.

Services like Ms Macleod's need to meet the same national regulatory requirements that large childcare centres do.

"We get lobbed in with centre-based care and that's a whole different business model to family day care," she said.

"We've got a uniqueness."

Family day care educators work in their own homes with groups of no more than four children under school age, at any one time.

Educators can either be employed by, or contracted to, an approved provider.

In Ms Macleod's case, she contracts to Wyndham Early Learning Family Day Care which conducts regular visits to monitor children's development and provides support.

'Not just babysitters'

A national Deakin University study of 200 family day care educators found many feel professionally isolated and unrecognised.

All of the respondents in the study were women who were generally older than centre-based educators and had more years of experience.

Three-year-old Zayne Jardine loves coming to family day care. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

But they reported being perceived by outsiders as "just babysitters" or a lower-quality option to centre-based educators.

"We're just not babysitters," Ms Macleod said.

"It's very frustrating to be labelled that when we achieve so much more and I feel I'm worth more."

Lead researcher Professor Andrea Nolan said workers in the sector felt misunderstood.

"It's anything but babysitting. These educators are sole traders, so they're doing everything," Professor Nolan said.

"Their work doesn't finish when the children leave, which could be as late as six o'clock, and then their family comes home.

"They're the ones that are doing the administration, the relationship building and the planning."

That heavy workload is having an impact on the workforce.

Figures from the industry regulator, the Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority, show the number of approved family day care services declined from 7 per cent in 2016 to 2 per cent this year.

Andrea Nolan has surveyed 200 family day care educators, all of whom were women. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

"I am worried that family day care might disappear in Australia," Professor Nolan said.

"And that is a concern because it is a viable option for many families and children."

Professor Nolan said the fact it was a feminised profession meant the work was devalued.

"It is just assumed that this is women's work and this is what women naturally do. They're nurturers, this comes naturally to them," she said.

She said there was a misconception that preschoolers were just playing at family day care and that there was a "total ignorance to what is really going on".

Making the effort for family day care

Erica Jardine loves family day care.

Her three-year-old son Zayne was previously enrolled at a childcare centre but she has committed to driving her son one hour each way from their Geelong home to Ms MacLeod's service.

"He kept getting quite sick from being in child care and he didn't really have really any relationships with the educator," she said.

"So, I decided to get him into family day care and it's been great."

Erica Jardine drives an hour to access family day care. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Initially she had questions about how safe the environment would be, but said she was now happy this was the right option for Zayne.

"I feel much safer sending my child to someone I know and someone I can trust," she said.

"As a mum, I feel much happier with my child being in this kind of environment, a home environment."

Debbie Macleod says her work does not finish when the children leave. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

The childcare industry has been under renewed pressure after cases of abuse in childcare centres were uncovered in July last year.

A Victorian government review found delays to revocations of Working with Children Checks, poor cross-agency information sharing, and underfunded regulatory oversight.

In response, education ministers agreed to a National Early Childhood Worker Register and mandatory national child-safety training which started in February.

Ms Macleod said she was all for protecting kids but the system was unfair to small operators.

"When they make a rule or regulation, they're making it with a centre in mind where there's more than one person," she said.

"If I have to program plan or attend meetings, a lot of the time that's in my own time and I'm not paid.

"The government doesn't give us the same amount of funding."

The number of family day care services across Australia is declining. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

In June the federal government agreed to extend funding for a 15 per cent pay rise for childcare workers for an extra 18 months.

The pay rise affects about 200,000 workers and will cost $3.6 billion, but family day care workers who are contractors miss out.

A regional trial

The Australian government began a "capability trial" of family day care in 860 regional areas in 2024 to provide support and resources to educators.

The trial, run by Family Day Care Australia, will inform any changes to the family day care model and is due to finish at the end of this year.

Family Day Care Australia chief executive Andrew Paterson said the industry had come a long way.

"The sector started as a cottage industry 40 to 50 years ago and is now a sector that's made up of early education professionals," he said.

Andrew Paterson says family day care can be the only viable option in regional communities. (Supplied: Andrew Paterson)

Mr Patterson said family day care can be the only viable option in some communities.

"Family day care plays an incredibly important part in the entire early childhood education and care landscape, but particularly in a lot of areas across regional, rural and remote Australia," he said.

" The sector does lag in its funding from commonwealth and states and territories, and I think that puts viability strain on the sector as well. "

The federal government's "capability trial" aims to improve access to flexible child care and education in regional areas of need.

Ms Macleod said she would like to see family day care recognised as a different business model to centre-based care.

"I would like the government to provide more funding which would make our work-life balance better, because at the end of the day, we all just want what's best for the children," she said.

World.title: Veterans sue government over 'mass and routine' medical data sharing
World.content:
A class action has been launched against the federal government over allegations of "mass and routine sharing" of veterans' medical records over 20 years.

On Wednesday, Gordon Legal served the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) with a privacy breach claim, following a two-year investigation into a health program which accessed thousands of Australian military veterans' data.

Medicines Advice and Therapeutics Education Services (MATES) was administered by the now-defunct University of South Australia (UniSA) under contract from 2004 to 2024, when the Veterans' Affairs Minister shut it down after an ethics review.

Gordon Legal partner Seb O'Meara, who worked on the Robodebt class action settlement, said anyone who used a DVA healthcare card while MATES operated — around 300,000, including bereaved spouses – could register for the lawsuit.

Lawyers for the plaintiff will alleged most veterans were "not aware of the MATES program" and "did not provide consent … for the disclosure of their personal information".

The firm will seek damages for breach of confidence in the Victorian Supreme Court.

Gordon Legal estimated more than 300,000 veterans and family members with DVA healthcare cards had been auto-enrolled in MATES. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

Case about 'what government can do with our information'

DVA's website said MATES was about "preventing adverse health outcomes, such as hospitalisations or unwanted side effects, for veterans who take multiple medications".

Their DVA healthcare card payments — equivalent to Medicare data — were periodically sent to UniSA, including their name, address, accepted medical conditions and treatments.

The patient's identity was initially obscured, but if health risks were found, "a restricted and small number" of staff identified them and contacted their GP.

"In these instances, the data accessed was limited to the veteran's name, address and targeted patient feedback … this may have included prescribed medicines, prescriber details and potential risk factors," the website said.

Mr O'Meara said the legal issue was that DVA enrolled participants without seeking their informed consent about who would see their personal information and where it would be stored.

Seb O'Meara said at least 6,000 people have expressed interest in joining the class action. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"At the heart of this case is what our own government can do with our personal information, and in particular … of a reasonably vulnerable cohort of people," Mr O'Meara said.

"A lot of these people have pretty complex medical histories.

"They include complex psychiatric and psychological conditions, and for many of them, learning of the disclosure … has caused them pretty significant distress."

A DVA spokesperson said it was aware of the class action but it would "not be appropriate to comment" while the matter is before the courts.

"Throughout its operation, the program was conducted under ethics approvals and formal contractual arrangements, including data security requirements," they said.

"As this matter is the subject of active legal proceedings, it would not be appropriate to comment further on questions relating to program governance, consent arrangements, data handling processes, or allegations made by parties."

DVA previously said MATES prevented 930 hospitalisations and 140 deaths.

Adelaide University, an institution created during a merger between UniSA and University of Adelaide, declined to comment.

Veteran wants 'accountability'

Vietnam War veteran Alan Ashmore, who has "significant health issues" stemming from deployment, is among at least 6,000 who have expressed interest in joining the action.

Mr Ashmore, of Melbourne, is helping others use Freedom of Information to access their MATES files, following a recent swell of interest.

Alan Ashmore was sent to Vietnam as part of his national service. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

He was "staggered" to discover his own contained 25 pages, including health conditions and prescribed medications.

"If this happened to the Prime Minister's family or the Veterans' Affairs Minister's family, how would they feel?" he said.

"They would be angry, they would shut the program down, and they would want heads to roll.

"Here is a third party wanting to liaise with a veteran's GP … what does that say about the doctor-patient relationship?"

The anonymised data also ended up in academic papers, according to Gordon Legal, but how many remains unclear.

The British Medical Journal has flagged at least two with "expressions of concern" about participants' consent.

Julie Anderson was awarded a Medal of the Order of Australia in 2020 for her service to veterans and their families. (ABC News: Matthew Holmes)

Veterans' advocate Julie Anderson, whose husband joined the class action, questioned the program's intent and said "most [veterans] had never heard of it".

"[It] seemed on the surface not to be a bad idea, but the reality was, it never worked that way," she said.

"To me, it was a program that was set up for researchers to access a massive pool of data, under the guise of it being used to help those veterans."

DVA declined to respond to this claim.

No date has yet been set for a court appearance.

World.title: Chaos in Sydney’s CBD after alleged carjacking, crash outside Queen Victoria Building
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

A man has been arrested after allegedly carjacking a vehicle in Sydney’s CBD and driving erratically down George Street before hitting a pedestrian and crashing into a police car in front of stunned Thursday night shoppers.

The 36-year-old man appeared covered in blood and was wearing only his underwear when he was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building about 9pm on Thursday.

A man was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building after an alleged carjacking. TNV

Police allege the man bundled a woman aged in her 20s out of her Mazda sedan at the intersection of King and Pitt streets in Sydney’s CBD, then drove along George Street before crashing into a ride-share vehicle near the intersection of Market Street.

The vehicle then allegedly crashed into a marked police car parked near the light rail tracks at the Queen Victoria Building. Footage from the scene shows the Mazda crashed head-on with the vehicle, next to the light rail stop, while the man was treated by police and paramedics on the nearby footpath.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Trump rules out fresh strikes; Christa Pike ‘up and walking’; closing statements in murder of Perth brothers in Mexico
World.content:
A judge is expected to hear closing statements before handing down his verdict in the trial of three men accused of killing two Australians and their American friend in Mexico in 2024.

The men – Jesús Gerardo, known as “El Kekas”, and two others identified as Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús – have faced court in the coastal Baja California city of Ensenada over the past month.

They are accused of killing Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, along with their American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, in an alleged robbery gone wrong while the trio was on a surfing holiday.

Loading

After multiple delays, the boys’ mother Debra Robinson requested last week that a verdict be delivered before a pre-booked return flight home to Australia.

The judge agreed closing arguments would be heard on October 8, US time, with the verdict delivered the following morning. Any sentencing would likely take place the following week.

In the closing statements are expected from both lawyers, the Robinson parents and Jack Carter Rhoad’s fiancee. Nine also reported the three accused may be given the chance to provide a final statement.

World.title: He was just 21 when he joined Miles Davis on stage with no rehearsal. He’s never looked back
World.content:
CultureMusicWhat’s on He was just 21 when he joined Miles Davis on stage with no rehearsal. He’s never looked back John Shand October 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The first time Dave Holland played with Miles Davis, he had no rehearsal, no set list, no sheet music and no prior discussion. The young British bassist, replacing Ron Carter in Miles’ famed 1960s quintet, watched the trumpeter approach the microphone, and start playing a song at breakneck speed that Holland at least recognised: Agitation – an apt title for the situation. Davis had heard Holland play in London only weeks before, in 1968. Dave Holland was in his very early 20s when he played with Miles Davis. “The next thing I know, here’s Miles Davis asking me to go to New York to play a gig with him,” Holland, who this month will play shows with the band Aziza in Sydney and Melbourne, tells this masthead via Zoom from his New York home. “I had no expectation of being a part of the band … We did three weeks in New York, and at the end of that, I was told we were heading out on the road the week after, and it went on until I finally left the band in 1970.”



Few non-Americans had cracked New York’s jazz scene at this point, and yet here was Holland, at 21, immediately reaching its pinnacle – albeit initially sleeping on the couch of his close friend, the exceptional drummer Jack DeJohnette. Holland, however, wasn’t thinking about any pinnacles, he was consumed with decoding the bandstand dynamics. Holland is playing shows with Aziza in Australia this month. “My focus was on trying to figure out how to play with musicians who had played together for five years,” says Holland, now 80. “When you have a band that is working so consistently, the music becomes a language that’s developed over that time. To connect into that takes a while. So I just had my antennae full on, trying to figure out where we were going. And I thought, ‘I’ll make the most of this. Maybe I’ll last for a week, maybe I’ll last for a day. I’m going to enjoy the ride while I’m here’.” Before Miles’ call-up, Holland had moved from Wolverhampton to London at 17, and his reputation soon spread. He divided his time between playing jazz (including with touring Americans) and studying classical music at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. It added up to what he calls “about the best start I could have possibly wished for”. After three acclaimed studio albums with Miles (Filles de Kilimanjaro, In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew), and many tours, including the band’s appearance before 600,000 people at the 1970 Isle Of Wight Festival, Holland quit. He’d found himself playing bass guitar more than double bass, and wanted to return to his primary instrument.



His first album as leader, Conference of the Birds (1971), announced Holland’s arrival as a composer of substance, as his pieces were often characterised by striking melodies, while shifting between visceral and cerebral. Since then, while simultaneously leading his own groups, he’s lent his brilliance to hugely diverse projects, from Anouar Brahem’s Tunisian-flavoured music to Betty Carter’s inimitable vocal gymnastics, and the supple Gateway Trio with DeJohnette and guitarist John Abercrombie. He even immersed himself in flamenco with the late Pepe Habichuela. “That was a profound experience,” Holland says. “It really affected me: the power of the music, the integrity of it, the passion of it.” Whatever the project, Holland emphasises that the music is not about individuals, but collectives. “Certainly, there are individuals who make great contributions,” he concedes, “but the music only exists out of the chemistry of what’s going on between the people. When the chemistry’s right, the magic happens.” To mark Holland’s 80th birthday on October 1, Edition Records released a six-LP (three-CD) set, The Freedom Call, which presents previously unreleased live recordings of Holland’s sextet, quintet and the quartet Prism. The sextet is essentially the most composition-focused, Prism is the most daring and freest, and the quintet lies in between.



Both sextet and quintet feature virtuoso saxophonist Chris Potter, a long-term Holland colleague who was the impetus behind forming Aziza, with astonishing drummer Eric Harland and shape-shifting guitarist Lionel Loueke. This is the band with which Holland comes to Australia this month, still at the height of his powers, despite the bass’s physical demands. Related Article Literature Sylvester Stallone has a memoir out this month – and yes, those famous steps get their moment “I find I have to practise more now, just to keep on top of it,” he says, before relating how a recent arm injury necessitated adjustments to his technique which he found interesting, perhaps offering a foretaste of how his relationship with the instrument might evolve. He’s certainly far from morose in his twilight years. “Nothing lasts forever, and we come, and we go,” he says, and quotes a Native American saying, “While you live, be with the living”. He continues: “The important thing is to stay engaged in life while you’re here … So I try to make new friends and have new associates in the music. Of course, I sometimes wish it could go on. But the reality is what it is. I don’t push back on that. I embrace it.” Aziza, Hamer Hall, Melbourne, October 25; City Recital Hall, Sydney, October 28

World.title: This bridge is a missing walking and cycling link – and it was supposed to open this year
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandCross River Rail This bridge is a missing walking and cycling link – and it was supposed to open this year Felicity Caldwell October 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This huge walking and cycling bridge is even longer than the popular Kangaroo Point Bridge – and it was supposed to open this year. But authorities have provided no clues about its launch date. Construction on the 480-metre long Yamma Bridge, described as a “game-changer for the local community”, began four-and-a-half years ago, and the bridge will link a new Boggo Road train station, Park Road station, the Princess Alexandra Hospital precinct and the busway at Dutton Park. An aerial image of the Yamma Bridge in Dutton Park, taken in September. Cross River Rail Delivery Authority Yamma Bridge is part of the Cross River Rail project, which had its launch date pushed out to 2029, but advocates say the bridge’s opening should not be delayed until then.



It would provide safe connections to the Princess Alexandra Hospital Bikeway, Veloway, Brisbane South State Secondary College and The University of Queensland, using the Eleanor Schonell Bridge. Related Article City life A new leafy pedestrian boulevard has opened in the heart of Brisbane Cyclists argued nearby Kent Street at Dutton Park, the current route, remained unsafe and confusing, including a footpath leading to a narrow 90-degree turn. They also say there are issues with ramps, unclear signs, and no traffic-calming for vehicles turning into Cornwall Street, where riders must cross. A Cross River Rail Delivery Authority spokesman said construction of the bridge continued. But he did not provide an opening date. “The community will be kept updated on construction activities and will be notified well in advance of the bridge opening,” he said.



“A specific opening date is yet to be determined, and a timeline for opening will be developed in conjunction with the Department of Transport and Main Roads.” This week, this masthead was told work yet to be finished included installing bridge deck waterproofing, safety screens, passenger lifts, way finding and mechanical and electrical systems, such as CCTV and emergency communication systems. Safety testing, compliance certification and surrounding precinct work would need to be finished before the bridge can be used. An aerial image showing Yamma Bridge and the Ecociences Precinct, taken in September. Cross River Rail Delivery Authority One year ago, Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said work yet to be done included surface works, line painting, kerb patching, canopy roofing, vertical transport work, electrical and lighting installation, pathway and landscape works and CCTV installation.



It took three years to build the Kangaroo Point Bridge, just under two years to build the Kurilpa Bridge, 1.5 years to build the Eleanor Schonell Bridge and 18 months to build the Goodwill Bridge. In 2022, Labor’s then-transport minister Mark Bailey said construction on the Dutton Park bridge would start in March and take about 18 months. In May 2024, before the Cross River Rail deadline was pushed out to 2029, the Cross River Rail Delivery Authority said construction on the Dutton Park bridge was “well progressed” and was expected to open in line with the whole project in 2026. The Queensland CFMEU inquiry has this week heard evidence about an escalating campaign by the CFMEU against major contractor CPB at the Cross River Rail Dutton Park station site, including a blockade in 2024.



A ramp obscured by a high kerb at Kent Street, Dutton Park. Chris Cox, supplied Mary Doolan, from the Brisbane South Bicycle User Group, said Kent Street was not safe, logical or easy to navigate. “Until this connection is fixed, we continue to seek a safe alternative, which could be Yamma Bridge,” she said. “Many, but not all riders, will then be able to avoid the safety issues on Kent Street. The same ramp from a different angle.



“This bridge could easily be opened when it is structurally finished and deemed safe to use. “We hope the minister approves this safe and logical approach and does not put more people at risk for another two years.” Labor Transport spokesman Bart Mellish said the bridge had been substantially completed for some time. “It’s clear this government has dropped the ball on all Cross River Rail-related projects after they’ve delayed the overall project by three years,” he said. “This government needs to just get on with the minor works needed to get it finished and get it open.”



Mickelberg was contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Where’s the honesty?’ Zelensky accuses US of inaction after deadly Russian bus strike
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Where’s the honesty?’ Zelensky accuses US of inaction after deadly Russian bus strike Updated October 9, 2026 — 5:40am ,first published 10:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, with authorities describing it as a targeted strike on civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow. Another 18 people were wounded in one of the largest single attacks this year, which took place on a street where police said two city buses were operating at the time of the strike. President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a bus stop. A bus burns following a Russian air strike in the city of Kramatorsk. Press service of the National Police of Ukraine Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. “For them (the Russians), a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app.



There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022. The two-day death toll from the recent wave of Russian strikes is more than 70. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, left, and British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, second right, at the site of a deadly attack in Pryluky on Thursday. Ukrainian Presidential Press Office via AP Hours after the news of the bombing, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the conflict was at a “dangerous stalemate”. “We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal.



He added that the US would continue to try to facilitate a settlement to end the conflict. But Zelensky accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine, criticising Washington’s effort to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made the comments during a joint press conference with Portugal’s Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel on in Lisbon on Thursday. Mark Schiefelbein/POOL AP via AP Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to accede to his requests to expand Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers. “Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly – give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table,” he said in an emotional statement.



Ukraine has in recent months aimed to wrest the battlefield initiative from Russia, whose gains have slowed this year, but is still suffering from Moscow’s increasingly brutal air war. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Russian drones attack Kyiv as Merz meets Zelensky “So where’s the truth here, where’s the honesty? Where’s the stalemate? ... That’s called unwillingness,” he said, referring to Rubio’s comments. “One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate,” Zelensky said. Moscow’s forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region.



Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do. The pace of Moscow’s battlefield gains in the region has significantly slowed this year. Filashkin said he had ordered city authorities in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, another key fortress-belt city, to halt public transport, saying “we have no right to risk” citizens’ lives. Thursday’s attack came a day after dozens were killed in a massive Russian air attack across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country’s power grid. Separately on Thursday, three people were killed and 14 wounded in morning drone strikes on the capital Kyiv, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Russian forces have unleashed frequent waves of attacks on Kyiv amid a shortage of Ukrainian air defences. World.title: The artists who want to inject ‘anger, life force, joy, passion’ into the ’80s AIDS crisis
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows The artists who want to inject ‘anger, life force, joy, passion’ into the ’80s AIDS crisis Kayla Olaya October 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The first thing Jeremy Lloyd told his then-boyfriend when he found out he was HIV-positive 10 years ago was: “You can break up with me”. He hid the diagnosis from his parents for four years and equates telling people he has HIV to feeling as though he is “coming out again”. “I would relate it to levels of self-worth,” Lloyd said. “And whether I was capable of loving myself and seeing myself as valid or worthy in multiple scopes – and that’s in the modern day 21st century.” (Left to right) Jeremy Lloyd, Fraser Morrison, Sean Landis, and Jonny Seymour at the Seymour Centre. The four are the creatives behind Sydney theatre show Cruise, which celebrates queer nightlife and pays tribute to a generation affected by the AIDS crisis. Sitthixay Ditthavong Lloyd, the movement director for the upcoming Sydney production of Jack Holden’s acclaimed play Cruise, a one-man show set in the 1980s at the height of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, said the production had allowed him to connect his story to another narrative. Cruise director Sean Landis said the “heart of the story” is a conversation between a young gay man who works for an LGBTQ+ helpline and an older queer man who lived through the heart of the AIDS crisis in Soho, London, who rings in.



“This older character, Mikey, sharing his story of coming of age in ’80s London … [he] is around for the introduction of house music to London, and how that really transformed the queer scene,” Landis said. The production is back at Sydney’s Seymour Centre and Melbourne’s Theatre Works in October after premiering in 2025. Sitthixay Ditthavong “The fact that it is a manageable health condition now doesn’t take away the carnage it has wreaked on the queer population, on gay men, on the world, and I think that with any historical tragedy is important that we honour and recognise it, and it’s not something that is widely talked about or taught in schools.” The production returns to Sydney’s Seymour Centre and Melbourne’s Theatre Works in October after premiering in 2025. The latest iteration features 31 characters played by a single actor, Fraser Morrison, alongside a heightened score and reworked dance pieces. Morrison said portraying that many characters can be “a bit overwhelming” but an exciting challenge – particularly when pushing forward queer stories about the AIDS crisis.



“I feel like sometimes there is a tendency with stories centred around the AIDS crisis to look at it with a reverence and a sadness that can be passive,” Morrison said. “Our interest in coming back into it is how to push against that. It was such an activated time in history, and [there wasn’t] hindsight that we have now looking back at those stories … to inject anger, a life force, a joy, a passion.” LGBTQ+ icon, Jonny Seymour, who consulted on the production, said he had seen his community evolve over his three-decade DJing career in Sydney and there were many parallel themes with the play. “The culture [Cruise is] tapping into with the setting of the play and how it parallels with Sydney’s nighttime communities … it has a universal theme of caring for each other in nocturnal spaces that’s existed and still exists today.” For movement director Lloyd, despite being diagnosed with HIV decades on from the AIDS crisis, the diagnosis continues to carry a pervasive stigma.



“Being openly HIV, for a lot of people they go like ‘You’re the first person that I know that’s just spoken about this so freely,’ … and I’m like, yeah, and I’m healthy, and I’m successful, and I’m in love, and I have prospects,” Lloyd said. “This show that we do – there is such celebration. Like not to say that we don’t pull our punches … [but] we dance, and we love, and we celebrate ... That’s the big thing that propels audiences to come back to this story and watch it.” Cruise, Seymour Centre, October 9-31.

World.title: ‘No face-to-face visits’: Banned Sydney church school flagged 15 times for harm without inspector visit
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPrivate schools ‘No face-to-face visits’: Banned Sydney church school flagged 15 times for harm without inspector visit Emily Kowal October 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Sydney private school run by a church banned from caring for children was flagged nearly two dozen times in reports that children were suspected of being put at risk of significant harm, but has never been visited by authorities, new documents reveal. A parliamentary inquiry into Redeemer Baptist School in Parramatta – triggered by a joint investigation by The Sydney Morning Herald and 60 Minutes – has revealed multiple failings in the state’s child protection agencies. Redeemer Baptist School in North Parramatta. Wolter Peeters The reports detailed allegations that the acclaimed school denies teachers wages and enforces extreme control over members, dictating student’s underwear choices and forcing children to live with staff. Former staff and students told the ongoing inquiry they suffered sexual, physical, emotional and spiritual abuse, urging the government to classify the school and its associated church as a system of group-based coercive control. Some alleged in the inquiry it was a cult.



In answers to questions on notice, the Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ) revealed it had received 15 risk of significant harm (ROSH) notifications involving children from the school since 2004 but not a single report ever triggered an on-the-ground, face-to-face field assessment. Instead, the department relied on phone assessments and referrals to other agencies to clear child welfare reports at the school, despite whistleblowers and former students alleging systemic control, abuse and forced communal living. Under NSW law, a child is deemed at risk of significant harm if there are safety or welfare concerns for a number of reasons, including assault, sexual abuse, psychological harm and neglect. The DCJ declined to confirm under which categories the ROSH reports fell, confirming only that they involved children enrolled at the school. Alexandra Garth came forward after escaping from the Redeemer community. Steven Siewert It follows revelations by this masthead that in 1981, Redeemer Baptist Church was banned from providing out-of-home care for foster children due to concerns over isolation and family separation.



At least 50 children, some of whom gave evidence to the inquiry, have lived on the school grounds, including in elders’ homes. The ban followed the case of Elizabeth Bradbury, who said she was dragged by her hair by members who limited her access to her biological mother. Despite the ban, state educational authorities granted the community school registration and accreditation two years later. Asked if the Department of Youth and Community Services, now the DCJ, ever notified education authorities of the ban, executive director of child protection Nicholas Backo said the department could not confirm due to the age of the records. A spokesperson for Redeemer Baptist School said the institution took its child safety obligations extremely seriously and held an “unblemished record of compliance with both state and federal regulators” over its 45-year history.



The spokesperson said the school and church were “separate entities and should not be conflated” – a claim repeatedly contested in submissions made to the inquiry. Related Article Exclusive

Private schools Inside the Sydney private school that dictates students’ choices right down to their underwear “Redeemer Baptist School and Redeemer Baptist Church were inseparable,” one former student wrote in submissions to the inquiry. Another submitted there was “no meaningful distinction between spiritual authority, educational authority and community authority”. In a statement, a Redeemer community spokesperson said that while there were “differences of view” regarding foster care placement models in the early 1980s, its relationship with the DCJ has “remained co-operative”, and the department later resumed placements with Redeemer families. However, historical records show that in 1983 only a single exception was made allowing a previously placed child to remain with two parents in the church community, on the condition the community not be used for future substitute care placements.



In its responses, the DCJ confirmed there was no evidence the ban was ever revoked, noting a subsequent request by Redeemer to overturn the decision was declined. Asked whether the 1981 ban surfaced during later child protection reports, Backo said the DCJ has since taken steps to merge legacy databases into its current system, though some historical records remain accessible only via the state’s record-keeping regulator. World.title: Sandpapergate: The tough questions about who knew what that never got asked
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Sandpapergate: The tough questions about who knew what that never got asked Darren Kane Sports Columnist October 9, 2026 — 5:30am

October 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Over the last fortnight, so many of us have been enthralled in a game of “Remember When” regarding a blizzard of rude recollections about the Sandpaper-gate events of 2018 in South Africa. Remember when, indeed … Australia’s Test team is back in South Africa this week, where that imbroglio kicked off eight years and seven months ago. Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were all banned over the scandal. AP Back then, I wrote that the Australian players needed to lawyer-up and demand a fair hearing; such was the schemozzle of their head-spiking. A year later I opined that they’d been bashed up too hard.



In 2022, I dared to write that David Warner’s lifetime leadership ban constituted moral policing ham-fistedly disguised as the metering-out of discipline. Nothing Cricket Australia (CA) has done since gives me the slightest inclination to deviate from these views. There’s my remember when … On the Saturday of the Cape Town Test, Cameron Bancroft was filmed comically shoving sandpaper into his underpants. The next day, CA’s then chief executive James Sutherland fronted the media, without consulting the captain, Steve Smith. Cameron Bancroft stuffs a piece of sandpaper down his trousers in the infamous Test eight years ago. Nine By Tuesday, CA scrambled a two-man squad to arrive in South Africa, to investigate. The probe was completed inside 100 hours. Only selected witnesses had their chains rattled.



By the following day, Smith and Warner had been handed 12-month bans from all cricket, Bancroft nine months. Smith was barred from leadership roles for a further year. Warner was banned from leading for life. By Thursday, they were on their way home. Within days, each had cried on camera, blubbering their scripted “messaging”. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images Within a fortnight, they had accepted everything. Nobody appealed. Smith’s admissions were that he’d been party to a premeditated, orchestrated and juvenile plan to cheat. You can’t remain captain after that. Nobody has sensibly prosecuted the alternate case.



None of the players were charged by CA with wilfully or unfairly changing the condition of the ball under law 41.3 of the Laws of Cricket. That’s the on-field offence, and the only body competent to prosecute it is the International Cricket Council. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith front an infamous press conference at Newlands. Getty Images The ICC dealt with Bancroft under 41.3; he copped a small fine and some demerit points but no suspension. The ICC dealt with Smith for conduct contrary to the spirit of the game; he copped one

Test match and his match fee. That’s it. Warner, supposedly the evil puppet master; the ICC didn’t touch him. And the umpires didn’t even change the ball. The sandpaper failed.



CA instead reached for article 2.3.5 of its Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. That’s the archetypal catch-all: conduct contrary to the spirit of the game, unbecoming, harmful to the interests of cricket, blah blah. Disrepute is of course an elastic concept; it stretches to fit whatever the outrage demands. The players weren’t banned for sandpapering a ball. They were banned for the embarrassment CA suffered when the calamitous scheme was detected, and for the fibbing that followed. Loading They could’ve copped the sanction; admitted the charge but contested the severity before an independent Code of Conduct commissioner; or denied it and appealed. The sanctions were announced as settled fact before any commissioner had been appointed, let alone sitting in judgment.



Each player was frogmarched to a microphone by CA to make admissions, in harrowing circumstances, before any of them had so much as a phone call from a lawyer. I’ve advised plenty of clients to run dead on questions from journalists for this reason; honest answers given under duress become legal potholes. And then there’s the thing nobody at CA will utter aloud: selection of a national cricket team is discretionary. A player who takes his employer to an independent hearing and succeeds in getting a reduced penalty must then present himself to that same employer for selection. Warner and Smith didn’t appeal because they did the calculus: winning the battle meant being banished. That calculation was rational. A right you’re too frightened to exercise isn’t a right.



So some tough questions about who knew what never got asked. How did the bowlers using that ball form no suspicion it was being attacked with an abrasive? Was Cape Town the first time, or just the first time anyone got caught? What did coach Darren Lehmann know, and when? How does Smith’s instinctive blurting about a “leadership group” square with the official narrative? When Bancroft stated in 2021 that the bowlers’ knowledge was “self-explanatory”, CA invited him to provide evidence; the bowlers issued a denial. Since then, nothing.



Compare the process other athletes have been afforded. The 34 Essendon players who sat out the 2016 AFL season after being found guilty of anti-doping rule violations copped a comparable penalty, but they got there via a full hearing before the code’s Anti-Doping Tribunal. Former Bulldogs NRL star James Graham copped 12 matches for biting Billy Slater’s ear in the 2012 grand final. Sandpaper on a ball that the umpires didn’t bother replacing drew a sanction roughly four times longer. CA also announced that any future leadership for Smith and Bancroft would be “conditional on acceptance by fans and the public”. How was that meant to be measured? No disciplinary system in any sport, or any court, conditions the restoration of a person’s standing in a popularity contest. That sentence told you everything about what the window-dressing exercise really was about.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Sandpaper series was radioactive from the start. Then a USB stick was delivered to my room Yes, they broke the rules – they admitted it; they didn’t appeal; and anyway the organisation has since reformed. But CA’s treatment of Warner, Smith and Bancroft in 2018 was shameful. In late 2022 the CA’s Code of Conduct was changed to allow long-term sanctions to be reviewed, only because Warner had asked for his lifetime leadership ban to be revisited. The review panel then insisted on a public hearing that would’ve retried Cape Town from scratch. Warner withdrew from a procedure considered by some to be akin to a lynching. He wasn’t wrong.



The ban was quietly lifted in November 2023, weeks before he retired from Test cricket, at the precise point it no longer mattered. That’s not redemption. That’s an institution abandoning a position it knew wouldn’t survive scrutiny. CA acted within its rules, which is the most damning thing I can say about the rules. Three good people were hung out for one stupid decision under the harshest spotlight in sport. The institution has paid nothing, and changed nothing. Sandpaper revisited: Read our coverage

A man has been arrested after allegedly carjacking a vehicle in Sydney’s CBD and driving erratically down George Street before hitting a pedestrian and crashing into a police car in front of stunned Thursday night shoppers.

The 36-year-old man appeared covered in blood and was wearing only his underwear when he was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building about 9pm on Thursday.

A man was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building after an alleged carjacking. TNV

Police allege the man bundled a woman aged in her 20s out of her Mazda sedan at the intersection of King and Pitt streets in Sydney’s CBD, then drove along George Street before crashing into a ride-share vehicle near the intersection of Market Street.

The vehicle then allegedly crashed into a marked police car parked near the light rail tracks at the Queen Victoria Building. Footage from the scene shows the Mazda crashed head-on with the vehicle, next to the light rail stop, while the man was treated by police and paramedics on the nearby footpath.
