World.title: Sandpapergate: The tough questions about who knew what that never got asked
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Sandpapergate: The tough questions about who knew what that never got asked Darren Kane Sports Columnist October 9, 2026 — 5:30am

October 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Over the last fortnight, so many of us have been enthralled in a game of “Remember When” regarding a blizzard of rude recollections about the Sandpaper-gate events of 2018 in South Africa. Remember when, indeed … Australia’s Test team is back in South Africa this week, where that imbroglio kicked off eight years and seven months ago. Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were all banned over the scandal. AP Back then, I wrote that the Australian players needed to lawyer-up and demand a fair hearing; such was the schemozzle of their head-spiking. A year later I opined that they’d been bashed up too hard.



In 2022, I dared to write that David Warner’s lifetime leadership ban constituted moral policing ham-fistedly disguised as the metering-out of discipline. Nothing Cricket Australia (CA) has done since gives me the slightest inclination to deviate from these views. There’s my remember when … On the Saturday of the Cape Town Test, Cameron Bancroft was filmed comically shoving sandpaper into his underpants. The next day, CA’s then chief executive James Sutherland fronted the media, without consulting the captain, Steve Smith. Cameron Bancroft stuffs a piece of sandpaper down his trousers in the infamous Test eight years ago. Nine By Tuesday, CA scrambled a two-man squad to arrive in South Africa, to investigate. The probe was completed inside 100 hours. Only selected witnesses had their chains rattled.



By the following day, Smith and Warner had been handed 12-month bans from all cricket, Bancroft nine months. Smith was barred from leadership roles for a further year. Warner was banned from leading for life. By Thursday, they were on their way home. Within days, each had cried on camera, blubbering their scripted “messaging”. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images Within a fortnight, they had accepted everything. Nobody appealed. Smith’s admissions were that he’d been party to a premeditated, orchestrated and juvenile plan to cheat. You can’t remain captain after that. Nobody has sensibly prosecuted the alternate case.



None of the players were charged by CA with wilfully or unfairly changing the condition of the ball under law 41.3 of the Laws of Cricket. That’s the on-field offence, and the only body competent to prosecute it is the International Cricket Council. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith front an infamous press conference at Newlands. Getty Images The ICC dealt with Bancroft under 41.3; he copped a small fine and some demerit points but no suspension. The ICC dealt with Smith for conduct contrary to the spirit of the game; he copped one

Test match and his match fee. That’s it. Warner, supposedly the evil puppet master; the ICC didn’t touch him. And the umpires didn’t even change the ball. The sandpaper failed.



CA instead reached for article 2.3.5 of its Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. That’s the archetypal catch-all: conduct contrary to the spirit of the game, unbecoming, harmful to the interests of cricket, blah blah. Disrepute is of course an elastic concept; it stretches to fit whatever the outrage demands. The players weren’t banned for sandpapering a ball. They were banned for the embarrassment CA suffered when the calamitous scheme was detected, and for the fibbing that followed. Loading They could’ve copped the sanction; admitted the charge but contested the severity before an independent Code of Conduct commissioner; or denied it and appealed. The sanctions were announced as settled fact before any commissioner had been appointed, let alone sitting in judgment.



Each player was frogmarched to a microphone by CA to make admissions, in harrowing circumstances, before any of them had so much as a phone call from a lawyer. I’ve advised plenty of clients to run dead on questions from journalists for this reason; honest answers given under duress become legal potholes. And then there’s the thing nobody at CA will utter aloud: selection of a national cricket team is discretionary. A player who takes his employer to an independent hearing and succeeds in getting a reduced penalty must then present himself to that same employer for selection. Warner and Smith didn’t appeal because they did the calculus: winning the battle meant being banished. That calculation was rational. A right you’re too frightened to exercise isn’t a right.



So some tough questions about who knew what never got asked. How did the bowlers using that ball form no suspicion it was being attacked with an abrasive? Was Cape Town the first time, or just the first time anyone got caught? What did coach Darren Lehmann know, and when? How does Smith’s instinctive blurting about a “leadership group” square with the official narrative? When Bancroft stated in 2021 that the bowlers’ knowledge was “self-explanatory”, CA invited him to provide evidence; the bowlers issued a denial. Since then, nothing.



Compare the process other athletes have been afforded. The 34 Essendon players who sat out the 2016 AFL season after being found guilty of anti-doping rule violations copped a comparable penalty, but they got there via a full hearing before the code’s Anti-Doping Tribunal. Former Bulldogs NRL star James Graham copped 12 matches for biting Billy Slater’s ear in the 2012 grand final. Sandpaper on a ball that the umpires didn’t bother replacing drew a sanction roughly four times longer. CA also announced that any future leadership for Smith and Bancroft would be “conditional on acceptance by fans and the public”. How was that meant to be measured? No disciplinary system in any sport, or any court, conditions the restoration of a person’s standing in a popularity contest. That sentence told you everything about what the window-dressing exercise really was about.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Sandpaper series was radioactive from the start. Then a USB stick was delivered to my room Yes, they broke the rules – they admitted it; they didn’t appeal; and anyway the organisation has since reformed. But CA’s treatment of Warner, Smith and Bancroft in 2018 was shameful. In late 2022 the CA’s Code of Conduct was changed to allow long-term sanctions to be reviewed, only because Warner had asked for his lifetime leadership ban to be revisited. The review panel then insisted on a public hearing that would’ve retried Cape Town from scratch. Warner withdrew from a procedure considered by some to be akin to a lynching. He wasn’t wrong.



The ban was quietly lifted in November 2023, weeks before he retired from Test cricket, at the precise point it no longer mattered. That’s not redemption. That’s an institution abandoning a position it knew wouldn’t survive scrutiny. CA acted within its rules, which is the most damning thing I can say about the rules. Three good people were hung out for one stupid decision under the harshest spotlight in sport. The institution has paid nothing, and changed nothing. Sandpaper revisited: Read our coverage

World.title: After two years and $12.3 million, Wellington's City Gallery is back
World.content:
Davy doesn’t think the public will notice dramatic changes, though they’ve “tried, in the choices that we’ve made, to increase our flexibility so that we’re staying with what art is doing and can continue to show all types of art in the best possible way.”



During its closure the gallery partnered with other institutions, such as the Dowse Art Museum, the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa, and the National Library. Davy says its future is in building those partnerships, platforming Māori and indigenous art with a dedicated programme, and fostering and celebrating women artists. A new neon sculpture by Auckland artist Sean Keer has been commissioned for the gallery’s previously unused sculpture terrace for next year.



"It's that beautiful reminder that out of periods of unsettledness or destruction, beauty and positivity can come,” Davy says.

World.title: Alarm sounded over double risk of AI and quantum threat
World.content:
A global cyber security firm is warning New Zealand enterprises to take action now to protect their digital assets as the dual risks of AI and the year to quantum (Y2Q) are approaching faster than expected.

Y2Q emerged as the next Y2K moment with potential to decrypt virtually all commonly used encrypted device from door locks to data.

Fortinet senior executives were visiting New Zealand this week to share the latest cyber security intelligence with large organisations responsible for critical data and infrastructure, including health, finance, energy and other utility sectors.

The dual technologies will make easy work of decrypting the security of most existing digital devices and systems, somewhere between 2029 and 2030, without upgrading to meet the emerging risks.

"What we are particularly worried about is infrastructure," Fortinet senior vice president Filippo Cassini said.

But the warning was intended for everyone, including big and small businesses, as well as consumers.

AI a "double-edged sword"

Cassini said AI had huge potential for positive growth, but was a double-edged sword.

"It can be used as defence, but it also can be used as weapon," he said.

"And the call for everyone is become more aware of its potential, so that they can use it for good."

Investment drives speed of change

Fortinet vice president of product management Wei Ling Neo said there was no time to waste.

She said investment in AI meant the speed of change was accelerating.

"(It) has been shortened by a lot of investments into quantum computing, which has brought the timeline much closer to 29 and 2030, for when we will have a viable quantum computer that will be able to decrypt the current algorithms that we use."

Data is a liability

Cassini said bad actors were already preparing for Q-Day.

Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) was a widespread surveillance and attack strategy where cyber criminals collect encrypted data today and store for Q-Day, when decryption becomes possible.

"I think a lot of organisations today are very focused on AI and not really inventorying the type of infrastructure, the type of data they're handling," she said.

"The timeline is getting shorter and shorter for them to be ready, to protect against quantum threat."

Legacy systems containing outdated or archived data will need to be protected or purged.

That will come with a cost either way, but should be given a high priority considering current regulations requiring organisations to safeguard sensitive data.

Software upgrades essential

The upgrades would be costly for businesses, but also for consumers who might find there were no software updates available to protect their equipment.

Cassini said consumers should assess their own risks and be sure to buy digital devices with software upgrades.

"I think they should be looking at how safe and upgradable it is," he said.

"It's a little bit of extra money, but I think it's worth it."

World.title: Are tighter KiwiSaver rules stopping weight loss surgeries?
World.content:
A bariatric surgeon says about half of his initial consults with patients now do not proceed to surgery - and a more stringent KiwiSaver approach may be to blame.

Sean Liddle, a general and bariatric surgeon practising in Northland said there were a few reasons why about half of his initial consults with clients did not end in surgery.

Some patients chose to have surgery offshore, where the cost could be lower, he said.

Sometimes it was financial constraints.

Audio player for " Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/personal-finance/1798627%2Fare-tighter-kiwisaver-rules-stopping-weight-loss-surgeries

Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 9m

"An increasing proportion of patients rely on withdrawing KiwiSaver funds to help finance treatment. Anecdotally, the criteria and approval process for KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals appear to have become more stringent, and I am seeing a higher number of applications being declined.

"This may be preventing some patients from proceeding with surgery despite an initial interest."

Christine Liggins, founder of Debtfix, which is now managing KiwiSaver withdrawal applications for a number of KiwiSaver providers, said some had changed the way they assessed applications for weight loss surgery, and were only paying the initial deposit.

They then paid the rest once evidence of the surgery was provided.

"This likely stopped some because they had to spend the money on the bariatric surgery," she said.

Whereas previously, she said some people might have ended up not using the money for the intended purpose.

"Which is why I am advocating for the funds to be paid directly to the source of the hardship rather than deposited in someone's account."

David Callanan, general manager of corporate trustee services at Public Trust, said surgery was cited in a relatively small number of hardship withdrawal cases.

"The most common reasons for people applying to withdraw are living costs, overdue bills and loans, and overdue mortgage or rent.

"We encourage people to contact their KiwiSaver provider for guidance on applying for a KiwiSaver significant financial hardship withdrawal to cover medical costs."

Greg Smith, investment specialist at Generate, said the rules around accessing KiwiSaver for bariatric surgery had become better understood through industry guidance and complaints rulings, particularly around the difference between significant financial hardship and serious illness.

"Under the serious illness provisions, the threshold is extremely high. Obesity and related health conditions may be serious, but applicants generally need to show they are permanently unable to work or face an imminent risk of death. Bariatric surgery is often viewed as a treatment intended to improve health and restore functioning, which is why many applications on this ground are declined.

"Under the significant financial hardship provisions, the focus shifts from medical need to financial need. Applicants need to demonstrate not only that the surgery is necessary, but also that they have exhausted other reasonable options to pay for it, such as savings, insurance, finance, or other resources. So if surgeons are seeing fewer patients proceed to surgery after an initial consultation, it may be because people have become more aware that KiwiSaver withdrawals are not automatic, and that meeting the legal tests can be difficult. But I wouldn't characterise that as KiwiSaver providers becoming tougher. It's more that supervisors are applying the statutory requirements, and recent rulings have clarified just how strict those requirements are."

World.title: Han Jiang ordered to pay $100,000 after meth lab contaminated Auckland rental
World.content:
An Auckland rental was polluted so badly by a large-scale methamphetamine lab that it needed to be decontaminated five times.

The interior had to be completely refurbished, and the home failed to sell after it became known locally as "the meth house".

Now the Tenancy Tribunal has ordered former tenant Han Jiang to pay her landlord the maximum sum of $100,000 after she manufactured methamphetamine in the home, rendering it uninhabitable.

The landlord incurred $104,254.45 in costs and more than $59,000 in rent loss when Jiang was arrested and sentenced to three years in prison after a police search that found an active, large-scale, clandestine lab containing equipment, material and precursor substances capable of making methamphetamine.

Hotplates, air stills, glass jars, measuring jugs, funnels, disposable gloves, breathing apparatus, frying pans, tubing, syringes and glassware were also found.

A glass meth pipe. (File photo) RNZ / Peter de Graaf

In several areas of the house, there were 20-litre containers of liquids, including toluene, large amounts of caustic soda, methamphetamine crystals and $124,835 in cash.

When the landlord had the home tested for meth contamination days after the raid in May 2024, the highest level of methamphetamine detected in a room was 3360 micrograms (µg) per 100sq cm. This was the highest reading the tribunal had seen.

The landlord, whose name is suppressed, applied to the tribunal for meth testing and decontamination costs, rent loss, police raid damage, reinstatement costs and power bills. He claimed a total loss of $163,374.55.

Tribunal adjudicators Rex Woodhouse and Toni Prowse said in their joint decision that the law did not allow them to make an order of more than $100,000.

The landlord, a large and established property management firm, accepted the limitation and confirmed that it still wanted the claim dealt with by the tribunal.

The tenant is in prison and arrangements were made for her to attend the hearing by audiovisual link, but she did not appear.

The tribunal understood that she chose not to attend, and the case was heard in her absence.

Home decontaminated five times

The tenancy began in March 2024. Two months later, a police raid uncovered meth manufacturing in the property.

The landlord had the premises tested for contamination. A report from Analytica Laboratories recorded 20 specific samples tested on May 28, 2024.

The highest level of methamphetamine detected was 3360µg/100sq cm, ranging down to 53.2µg.

The landlord noted that these were the highest levels it had seen, and the person who conducted the testing also said they were the highest he had seen in a home.

The landlord hired Extreme Cleaning Solutions (ECS) to decontaminate the house.

Three rounds of treatment were needed before the levels were low enough for ECS to issue a Decontamination Contractor Clearance Certificate.

Where manufacturing is suspected, contamination levels must be lowered to 1.5μg/100sq cm.

After the certificate was issued, the landlord began repairs and remedial work.

The landlord told the tribunal that it painted the interior of the entire house, installed a new benchtop and appliances in the kitchen, replaced light fittings and switches, replaced ventilation systems, heat pumps and extraction fans, and soft furnishings such as curtains, blinds and carpets.

The work was completed by November 18, 2024, and the landlord advertised the property for rent.

The property manager said it was difficult to relet, as potential tenants were put off by its past.

She told the tribunal that tenants were finally found in January 2025.

The 'meth house' stigma

Before the tenants moved in, the landlord ordered another methamphetamine test, which again showed contamination above 1.5µg/100sq cm in several rooms.

Further decontamination work was done, and a certificate was reissued.

The house was then put up for sale. There was little interest, which the landlord attributed to its stigma as a "meth house".

In August 2025, further testing was done and, of the eight samples, two returned results above 1.5µg and more decontamination was completed.

Samples taken in October were less than 1.5µg, and the house was considered fit to relet.

"We accept that the tenant's manufacture of methamphetamine contaminated these premises," Woodhouse said.

"Because the methamphetamine contamination was more than 1.5μg/100sq cm, the premises were uninhabitable, or to put that another way, unclean and/or intentionally damaged."

The landlord told the tribunal that Jiang had paid rent until June 4, 2024.

The landlord sought rent compensation from then until December 12, 2025, minus 90 days when the house was for sale, totalling $59,120.10, which was ordered to be paid in full.

The landlord was also successful in all but one of its other remedial work claims, which would have come to $60,900.38.

Given the tribunal's cap, it could award remediation costs of only $40,879.90.

The landlord incurred costs of $3566.75 to repair police damage, including damage to doors, blinds and gate, but the tribunal ruled that these costs should sit with the tenant because they related to police actions to enforce the tenant's breach.

"We recognise that the landlord seeks further orders. However, given ... we have reached the ceiling of our jurisdiction, we decline to make further orders," Woodhouse said.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Genre-bending Canadian writer Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize
World.content: Much of Carson’s early career was dominated by her work in classics – she studied for her bachelor’s, master’s and doctorate degrees at the University of Toronto and also received a diploma in classics from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Although she published an essay and her Ph.D. thesis in her thirties, it wasn’t until she was 42 years old that her first book of poems “Short Talks” was published. Three more works followed before “Autobiography of Red” marked her out as a critical favourite.

World.title: Three Fiji police officers charged with alleged murder of fellow constable
World.content:
Three Fiji police officers will appear in court on Friday after being charged with the alleged murder of one of their own earlier this year.

Fiji's Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) confirmed on Thursday that it had sanctioned charges against the three men in relation to the death of Constable Peniasi Racagi.

Racagi's body was discovered floating at sea off a beach in Lami town, located approximately 15 minutes west of the capital Suva.

Racagi, 24, was based at the Lami Police Station.

The Fiji Police Force confirmed elements of foul play following a post-mortem and a homicide investigation was launched.

"The Acting Director of Public Prosecutions has sanctioned charges against three police officers in relation to the death of Lami Police Constable Peniasi Racagi," the ODPP statement said.

The three officers have been jointly charged with murder contrary to Section 237 of Fiji's Crimes Act.

"It is alleged that the three police officers murdered Constable Peniasi Racagi in February this year following an altercation," the ODPP statement said.

In a statement, Fiji Police said that based on the ODPP's advice, Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu has directed the formal laying of charges against the three police officers.

World.title: Immigration catches up with overstayer who lived under alias for 38 years
World.content:
An overstayer who used a forged passport when he arrived 38 years ago and lived under a false identity has lost his attempt to appeal deportation.

But Lafaele Laoa, 60, has still not returned to Samoa after a three-month deadline to do so expired last week.

Laoa used the assumed name of Olive Mao when he arrived in 1988, and despite trying to locate him, Immigration New Zealand did not find him until police shared information with them in 2024.

He had a list of previous convictions from 1992 to 2013, and 10 alleged family harm incidents between 2009 and 2020.

"He made no effort during his prolonged stay here to regularise his status, other than his request for ministerial intervention in 2024 after being placed in immigration custody and with deportation imminent," said the immigration and protection tribunal.

"The number of family harm episodes (including two five-day police safety orders) indicates that he perpetrated violence fairly regularly in the last 11 years of his relationship with his second partner."

Laoa was detained in custody because authorities could not establish his identity, and he had no passport to be deported.

Leaving Samoa

Laoa told a psychiatrist that he met his first partner when he came to New Zealand in 1987 and she became pregnant. He returned here after their son was born the following year, using the identity of a friend's brother. He resumed his relationship and they went on to have three daughters.

His former partner took custody of their children when the relationship ended and he lived with another woman for 20 years.

He had convictions from 1992 to 2013, which were classed as less serious and had been 'clean-slated'.

Laoa requested ministerial intervention about his deportation, saying he used the alias because he did not want to be away from his family in New Zealand.

"He said that he had applied for a visa under his real name but that this had been declined so he applied again under another person's name, Olive Mao."

A family dispute over land meant he had nowhere to live in Samoa if he went back.

Apia, the national capital of Samoa. RNZ / Koroi Hawkins

The tribunal heard he was caring for his sister, who had end-stage renal failure, and that while his three daughters were in Australia, his son and most close family remained in New Zealand.

Laoa had apologised for the family harm incidents, where he was recorded as the alleged aggressor, but also accused his partner of calling the police unnecessarily and not telling the full truth.

His lawyer said his criminal offending occurred more than a decade ago, and it should not be taken into account in a deportation appeal about overstaying.

The tribunal disagreed

The appeal tribunal (IPT) said that his 38-year stay in New Zealand was an exceptional humanitarian circumstance - however, it found that his lengthy unlawful stay and use of a false identity would make his deportation neither unjust or unduly harsh.

"The tribunal has determined that [his sister] can be reasonably expected to be cared for by her own children and other members of her family and that she can access state support," it said in its written decision.

"He has little or no connection to either of his previous partners or his children, three of whom are not even in New Zealand."

It acknowledged he could face challenges readjusting to Samoa, but said it was difficult to "reconcile the appellant's concern for his own future with the violent treatment he meted out to another person".

The tribunal said he spoke Samoan and had lived there until he left for New Zealand when he was in his 20s, 38 years ago.

"While that is an extremely long time, the appellant is returning as an older man who in all likelihood will have a village to return to and, if not, four adult children and other relatives to financially contribute to his living expenses.

Deported, but still here

"The tribunal orders that the deportation of the appellant be delayed for a period of three months, commencing on the date of this decision. This is because [his sister's] family will need to make alternative arrangements for their mother's care while they are at work and they and/or the appellant's children will need time to pool funds for the cost of [his] return and his immediate needs on arrival at least."

That three-month period ended on 29 September.

"Immigration New Zealand (INZ) can confirm that Lafaele Laoa has not departed New Zealand and remains here unlawfully," national compliance manager Fadia Mudafar told RNZ.

"We are engaging with Mr Laoa and his representative regarding his departure from New Zealand. If he does not leave voluntarily, further compliance enforcement action may be considered.

"This case has been subject to a number of legal processes, including consideration by IPT. With those processes now concluded, Immigration Compliance will progress the next steps."

Where to get help: Family Violence

World.title: Police puzzled by grisly discovery in Wellington pedestrian tunnel
World.content:
Police want to hear from anyone who has information about a large pool of human blood discovered in a Wellington pedestrian tunnel over the weekend.

Police were called to Coutts Street in Rongotai on Sunday night at 10.40pm after the blood was found. The scene was cordoned off while police conducted a scene examination.

Detective Senior Sergeant Steve Wescott said testing shows it was human blood but they didn't locate anybody in the nearby area.

Police are now asking for the public's help to identify anyone who may have been involved.

"If there is a person involved, our priority is to check on their welfare," Wescott said.

Police want to hear from anyone who was in the area near the tunnel, which runs under the Wellington Airport from Coutts Street, Rongotai, to Miro Street in Miramar, on Sunday evening prior to 10.40pm.

World.title: South Africa vs Australia Test series, everything you need to know
World.content:
Australia is back in South Africa for one of the most eagerly anticipated Test series in recent history.

It has been eight long years since Australia last toured South Africa in red-ball cricket, in a series that will forever be remembered for its ignominy.

Sandpapergate is what that contest will be remembered for, but even before that, it was crossing a red line in despicable behaviour unbecoming of the sport.

Here's everything you need to know ahead of the three-Test series.

When are the Test matches?

Newlands is one of the world's most picturesque cricket grounds. (Getty Images: Dave Rogers)

The two teams will play three Tests.

The first is at Kingsmead in Durban from October 9 to 13.

The second is at St George's Park in Gqeberha from October 18 to 22.

And Newlands in Cape Town will host the third from October 27 to 31.

What time are the Test matches?

The Durban Test starts at 6:30pm AEDT and will likely run through to 2am AEDT.

That AEDT time relates to New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania.

In Queensland, the action begins at 5:30pm.

In South Australia, at 6pm.

In the Northern Territory, at 5pm.

And the first ball will be bowled at 3:30pm in Western Australia.

How can I watch the Test series?

Unless you're lucky enough to be on the Kingsmead hill like Wiaan Mulder, you'll have to watch on Fox Sports or Kayo. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Darren Stewart)

The entire series is live on Fox Sports and Kayo.

ABC Sport will also have live radio commentary on the ABC Listen App or online.

You can also follow every ball in our live blog on the ABC Sport website.

Who is playing in the series?

Australia's squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey (wk), Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Sam Harper (wk), Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Matthew Kuhnemann, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Nic Maddinson, Michael Neser, Matt Renshaw, Steven Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster.

South Africa's squad: Temba Bavuma (c), Marques Ackerman, David Bedingham, Corbin Bosch, Gerald Coetzee, Tony de Zorzi, Simon Harmer, Marco Jansen, Keshav Maharaj, Aiden Markram, Wiaan Mulder, Senuran Muthusamy, Anrich Nortje, Dane Paterson, Kagiso Rabada, Ryan Rickelton (wk), Tristan Stubbs (wk), Kyle Verreynne (wk).

Australia's record against South Africa

Australia has historically had great success against the Proteas in South Africa. (Getty Images: Morne de Klerk)

Australia has won 54 of the 102 Test matches between the two teams, with 21 draws and 27 defeats since their first meeting in 1902.

On South African soil, Australia also has a winning record, with 29 victories against 16 defeats and nine draws.

Australia has won six of the 11 Tests played at St George's in Durban, including winning each of the last three Tests it has played there, while South Africa has won three with two draws.

The two teams also drew a Test at the city's old Lord's ground in 1921, before the venue's demolition in 1922.

South Africa has a much better record at St George's Park in Gqeberha though, winning four of the seven matches played there, including the last two.

Before 2021, Gqeberha was Port Elizabeth, but is now known by its Xhosa name, and this is the first time Australia will play in the city under its new name.

Australia will play in Gqeberha for the first time. Australia's previous trips to St George's Park came when the city was known as Port Elizabeth. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Australia has a great record at Newlands though, winning 10 of the 14 Tests played in the shadow of Table Mountain. However, it has only won one of its last four Tests at the ground considered one of the most beautiful in the world.

The two teams last played a Test in June 2025, when South Africa shocked Australia at Lord's to win the World Test Championship.

In the 2022/23 summer of cricket, Australia claimed a 2-0 Test series victory over South Africa on home soil.

The last time Australia played a Test series in South Africa was 2018, and it's safe to say things were … complicated.

The fiery 2018 series

Cameron Bancroft and Steven Smith were hauled over the coals for the ball tampering scandal. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

It is fair to say the 2018 series was combative, fiery, febrile and chaotic.

Australia won the first Test at Kingsmead in Durban, but not before David Warner and Quinton de Kock almost came to blows in a stairwell at the end of the fourth day.

South Africa won the second Test in Gqeberha, but man of the match Kagiso Rabada, who took 5/96 and 6/54, was subsequently banned for barging into Steve Smith after dismissing him in the first innings.

Rabada was then handed a reprieve after an appeal involving one of South Africa's highest-profile lawyers, freeing him to play the next two matches.

The third Test was in Cape Town where, in the shadows of Table Mountain, Australia's descent into the dark arts was exposed.

Sandpaper gate scandal explained Cameron Bancroft was charged with ball tampering in Cape Town — here's how the dark day for Australian cricket unfolded.

On the third day, host broadcaster Supersport captured Cameron Bancroft rubbing the ball with a square of sandpaper to help encourage the prodigious reverse swing that had featured throughout the series thus far.

While South Africa romped to a 322-run win and a series lead, the full extent of Australia's cheating was exposed, leading to a moral reckoning about the team's approach back home, with then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull leading the criticism of the offending players.

Smith, Bancroft and Warner were all sent home in disgrace, and an under-manned Australian team was thumped by 492 runs at the Wanderers in Johannesburg.

What's happened since?

South Africa stunned Australia at Lord's to win the World Test Championship. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Australia has toured South Africa twice since the 2018 Test series, in 2020 and 2023 for limited-overs matches, with Smith and Warner both involved.

The two teams also just completed a three-match ODI series, which South Africa won 2-1.

The Proteas also toured Australia for a Test series in 2022/23, Australia winning 2-0 with a draw in the third Test in Sydney.

South Africa are the current World Test champions, beating Australia in the final in 2025, but haven't played a match in this format for 11 months.

By the time the first ball is bowled in Durban, it will have been 641 days since South Africa last played a Test on home soil.

Australia, the world number-one-ranked Test team, is coming off a humbling defeat to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Hopefully the febrile atmosphere of eight years ago has dissipated.

Because, unencumbered by the extracurricular issues, the cricket should be of the highest quality.

World.title: Katie Lynch wants to see AFL 'harness the momentum' of Pride Round
World.content:
The Gold Coast Suns' Katie Lynch says Pride Round comes at exactly the moment needed every season.

Two weeks out from the men's season finishing and a month before the women start finals, it provides an injection of enthusiasm, celebration and joy.

"A different energy comes into the competition on Pride Round," Lynch told ABC Sport.

"Because so many of our players connect with the movement and understand the power of the round for the community and who we represent," Lynch told ABC Sport.

However, Lynch would like to see that movement grow beyond the AFLW competition and across the whole AFL, to include not just the men's teams but all club staff and fans of the game.

Katie Lynch and Lily Mithen wanted the Suns' Pride guersney to represent celebration of the queer community. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

The dedicated league-wide Pride Round was introduced annually in 2021.

It celebrates inclusion and diversity over two weeks, while honouring the contributions of the LGBTQ+ community to the game and providing a platform for education on queer issues, particularly those entwined with the game.

"I think that can be perhaps transferred across more of the whole code essentially," Lynch said.

"A pride round in the men's would be awesome to see, and I know from my experience, it's nothing but a positive experience, and so I can see that going enormously well and being enormously helpful for the entire code."

AFLW has had a dedicated league-wide Pride Round since 2021. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Some LGBTQ+ Australian Rules fans and community members have felt the pang of exclusion from the sport in recent years.

The AFL is cracking down on homophobic language in the game, with CEO Andrew Dillon stressing "homophobia has no place in Australian football", at any level or under any circumstances, which has come as a reaction to the prevalence of slurs.

In the past three years, there have been 10 cases of AFL-listed players or coaches sanctioned for homophobic language, including Suns players Max Knobel this year and star defender Wil Powell in 2024.

Inaugural AFLW player Aliesha Newman designed the official match ball for Pride Round 2026. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

When put to Lynch whether an extended Pride Round would help in this regard, she said the game of Aussie Rules had always been excellent at creating a space for people to connect, converse and interact, and that Pride Round was an incredible vehicle to do that around LGBTQ+ issues and experiences.

"We know that the players and the code have significant ability to influence, of course, and we've seen that probably have a negative effect on our fans more recently," she said.

"So I think for me, it's how do we shift that dial to come back the other way?

"And that's why I talk about things like visibility and representation."

She said it was also a great opportunity to connect more fans to the game, and have them feel seen within it.

This year Lynch helped design the club's Pride guernsey alongside her teammate Lily Mithen and good friend and tattoo artist Mady Peters.

It resembles patchwork tattoos and stickers, including a tramp stamp on the back, which Lynch says is proof they had a lot of fun putting it together.

Katie Lynch with Mady Peters, who helped craft the Pride guernsey. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

But more than that, Lynch said it felt special to have her friend Peters "who doesn't even know what a drop punt is" now have an attachment to the game of AFLW through the Pride movement, where she is represented as a queer person.

Lynch said she noticed the boost in attendance during Pride Round, including within her own friend group.

"My friends are great, very supportive of me … but if they're going to come to a game, it's Pride Round," she said.

" Pride Round has the power to bring people, even loose fans of AFL, to the game … and not only to experience the joy of it but they're there because they feel like they belong there. "

Pride Round is a big celebration every year in the AFLW. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

She wants that "special feeling" to reach even further.

"That's what I've felt, particularly this year, is the support for us and this Pride Round has been enormous, and it's growing," she said.

"The opportunity now is to harness the momentum we've got and use it in a growth capacity.

"We'll probably never know the enormity of pride and visibility, particularly as players … I feel there's so much impact that I don't see, but I know is there."

World.title: The duality of Australia's newest cricket captain Sophie Molineux
World.content:
There are two sides to Sophie Molineux.

The everyday version. Quiet, composed, down-to-earth. Calmly answering questions, even the difficult ones, unfazed.

Those level-headed qualities come in handy when she's on the field, allowing her to think clearly and execute at critical points in the game.

Then there's Molineux's alter ego. The outgoing, bubbly personality that her teammates know well and us outsiders get a glimpse of every now and then.

Katy Perry performs on stage with Sophie Molineux at the MCG in 2020. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Whether it be dressing up as 80's icon Jane Fonda in neon lycra to lead a stretch session on tour, opening the batting in a game of street cricket outside the Old Mates pub in New York, or celebrating hard after a T20 World Cup win … It's fun and it's rather infectious.

In 2020, Molineux danced on stage with Katy Perry at the MCG. In 2026, she channelled Shane Warne on the Lord's balcony, holding a stump aloft as a beer was poured over her head.

During her six months in the job as the nation's newest captain, this contrast has made a real impact to the team environment. And it speaks volumes that two of her peers that watched from the sidelines in July as Australia reclaimed the T20 crown were filled with pride.

Loading Instagram content

Instead of feeling bitter they'd been left on the bench while the rest of the side beat England in the final by seven wickets, Grace Harris and Megan Schutt reflected on how much this victory meant to the entire group. The first with Molineux in charge.

"That was good fun," Harris remarked.

"It's not unlike Soph to get amongst the celebrations and it's great to see an Aussie captain kind of relax a bit too — you've got to enjoy the wins.

"To go through the World Cup and not even look like losing was really cool and a real answer to the criticism we've had in recent times," Schutt added.

"It was a euphoric feeling for Soph. There were so many people that doubted the decision to make her captain, when we knew internally why she was picked for that role. To be able to put it to them a bit felt good and we're so proud of her.

"Following the game when the crowd had dispersed, it was late at night, and we were sitting on the ground with the trophy basically having a gratitude session for the last six weeks.

"It felt really deserving for Soph."

Molineux has suffered a range of injuries during her career. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

When it was announced that skipper Alyssa Healy would retire in March and Molineux would be her successor, even the most diehard cricket fans were shocked.

Most had thought the experience of vice-captain Tahlia McGrath or all-rounder Ash Gardner would put them next in line. McGrath had even filled in for Healy 15 times previously. Perhaps even 24-year-old Annabel Sutherland would have been a good pick, as a long-term nod to the future?

All three had certainly played more international matches than Molineux, whose career has been hampered by a string of injuries since her debut in 2018. Due to serious foot, knee and shoulder issues, Molineux had only accumulated a total 58 caps when she was appointed.

Social media was rife with criticism. Were others more worthy? Would she be able to stay fit and be a consistent presence in the team?

Those concerns are still a question mark now, as a hip injury rules Molineux out of the ODI series beginning on Friday against Bangladesh on home soil. The selectors are hopeful she'll be back to play the three T20Is scheduled at North Sydney Oval against New Zealand in late October.

Vice captain Tahlia McGrath was an obvious choice as the next skipper, having already filled in the role when Alyssa Healy was unavailable. (Getty: Matt Roberts)

"I was aware of the criticism, and I understood completely why it came and why people wouldn't have expected my appointment," Molineux tells ABC Sport.

"I would have loved to have played another 100 games for Australia by now but that hasn't been my journey and I can't change that.

"I wouldn't even want to change that because through those injuries and setbacks I learned a whole lot about myself — what's important to me and a big part of that was leading.

"Making sure that whatever environment I was in, that I could contribute and make others feel safe. It set me up, in a way, to be able to do this job.

"At the same time, I was pretty determined to prove it all wrong, and it probably fuelled me to nail the preparation for the T20 World Cup."

Australia lifts the ICC Women's T20 World Cup for a seventh time. (Getty: Alex Davidson)

After two consecutive semi-final exits at ICC tournaments, there was extra pressure on Australia to perform. Despite this, Molineux excelled.

The left-arm orthodox bowler finished in the top three wicket-takers (11 in 7 innings with best figures of 2/6) and was credited by her teammates for spearheading their most consistent and dominant campaign yet.

Which is saying something, as this was their seventh T20 title. The result felt like vindication for her family too, who have supported her through every one of her setbacks.

Loading Instagram content

"They ride it with you, the highs and the lows," Molineux said.

"Throughout the World Cup they were in the stands watching and for them to be able to experience it was really special to me.

"They were the first ones to the games and the last ones to leave.

"I'm forever grateful for my family's support and Mum and Dad were so excited and happy when I was appointed as captain … Their opinions to me were most important."

As the summer of cricket approaches, with next year's Women's Ashes on the horizon, we wonder, what kind of leader does Molineux want to be?

"I just want to be authentic. I want to be me," she responds.

"I've played under some amazing captains in Meg Lanning and Alyssa Healy. They were strong players who wanted to take the team on their shoulders and lead through their actions. I've learned a lot from them, but I don't want to lose too much of who I am.

"I am from country Victoria. I play cricket because I love the challenge and the people. The memories and the experiences. So, I don't really want to lose that sense of fun.

"Although the job can be serious at times, it's getting that balance right."

This article was written for the ABC Cricket Magazine, available online, or in local newsagents from November.

World.title: Matildas coach backs Mary Fowler's absence from friendlies
World.content:
Coach Joe Montemurro has said the Matildas support Mary Fowler's decision to miss upcoming friendlies for personal circumstances and is adamant they have the creative players available to cover her.

Fowler, 23, withdrew this week from the squad to play world number three Germany on Saturday (AEDT) and Haiti on Wednesday.

"It's really important that we create an environment that is important for the player, and as the circumstances are private, I'm not going to elaborate," Montemurro said.

Fowler out of Matildas internationals Mary Fowler will be replaced by Leah Davidson for the upcoming friendlies, with the Matildas star withdrawing due to personal circumstances.

"But yes, absolutely, discussions were had with Mary, with the club (Manchester City), and with the relative people, and we believe that we've made the right decision and I think everyone's in support of the situation."

There has been speculation that Fowler has returned to Australia to support her partner, Nathan Cleary, which Football Australia has not confirmed.

The Penrith rugby league star required emergency surgery after suffering a career-threatening badly broken leg in the Panthers' NRL preliminary final loss in late September.

Players opting out of windows for personal reasons is not rare, especially given the intense schedules of club and international football.

"At the end of the day, we're all human. You can't always base your life around football," Australian goalkeeper Mackenzie Arnold said.

"I have never personally been in that experience, so I don't really know how to put it into words.

"But I would say if I had that situation that I felt the need to go home and I asked the coach for that and I had full trust in him that he was going to give me that permission — then of course, it's important.

"But I think the the bottom line is, at the end of the day we're all human, so if we need to make that decision, then that's what we need to go with."

The Matildas are without three of their best creative outlets — Fowler, Kyra Cooney-Cross and Katrina Gorry — for this window.

But Montemurro backed Australia's "very, very talented" midfield depth.

Montemurro name-dropped Vittsjo gun Dani Galic, Nottingham Forest midfielder Alana Murphy and uncapped Valerenga playmaker Hana Lowry.

"They're names I want you to remember, because I really do believe that they're going to be the next generation of midfielders," he said.

AAP

World.title: Kai Allen shines as Ford gets engine change for Bathurst
World.content:
Kai Allen has fired the first warning shot ahead of Sunday's Bathurst 1000 with the fastest time across today's two practice sessions.

In perfect conditions at Mount Panorama, Allen topped the time sheets in the first practice session of the weekend with a time of 2:05.5460, more than three-tenths better than the next fastest.

The blistering time for Allen, who drives a Ford for Grove Racing, comes after Supercars confirmed the engine in all Ford competitors would be changed for this weekend.

Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

Barometric pressure testing before last year's Bathurst 1000, and again before this weekend, found the Ford engine lost power at high altitude.

A change to the engine, developed by Triple Eight Race Engineering, which is Ford's homologation team, has been approved by Supercars to level the playing field this weekend.

There will be no change to the Toyota or GM (Chevrolet) engines.

"As you're aware, Supercars have conducted Barometric engine testing over the last 12 months and recently completed a further test," a note to teams read.

"The results of this test have been provided to the Homologation Teams following which consultation has taken place.

"The testing has identified a power loss on the Ford at lower Barometric pressure and as such Supercars have approved a change of ESD developed by the Ford Homologation team to correct this for the Bathurst event only."

Six of the top 10 cars from Thursday's first session were Fords, with Chevrolets making up the other four spots, including PremiAir's Jayden Ojeda who was second fastest with a 2:05.8737.

The fastest Toyota belonged to reigning Supercars champion Chaz Mostert who was 17th fastest for the number 1 Walkinshaw TWG Racing.

While Allen shone, it was not all smooth sailing for Grove Racing with Matthew Payne, last year's Bathurst 1000 winner, being called in early after his team found power steering fluid on the garage floor.

Lochie Dalton, driving for the Chevrolet number 99 Erebus Motorsport, topped the co-drivers practice session later on Thursday with a 2:05.874.

Again, only Fords and Chevrolets were in the top 10. Again, Walkinshaw TWG Racing's number 1 was the fastest Toyota, with co-driver Fabian Coulthard at the wheel.

There will be two more practice sessions on Friday ahead of qualifying.

World.title: Dropped Aussie opener out of Sheffield Shield match with concussion
World.content:
Jake Weatherald's wretched run has continued, with the discarded Test opener forced out of the start of the domestic cricket season with concussion.

Weatherald was subbed out of South Australia's opening game against Victoria at Junction Oval on Thursday, before the start of day two.

He crashed into the picket fence while chasing the ball on Wednesday during Victoria's first innings.

Weatherald then faced only faced six balls at the end of day one before Victorian debutant Harry Hoekstra had him caught behind for a duck.

It is understood Weatherald had delayed symptoms, prompting the decision on Thursday morning to take him out of the game.

Matthew Gilkes took Weatherald's place in the SA line-up.

Weatherald was dropped from the Test team in August after their shock first-Test loss to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Hoekstra also top-scored with 45 at number nine as Victoria rallied to reach 244 in their first innings.

South Australia resumed at 1-4 and were 5-185 approaching tea.

Opener Henry Hunt made 71 before David Moody bowled him in a crucial breakthrough for the fourth wicket.

Jake Lehmann was 52 not out and Hoekstra had continued his fine debut with three wickets.

AAP

World.title: 'Live on forever': Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on
World.content:
Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

It is just that this year's Great Race feels a bit more special, with Australian motorsport marking 20 years since the nine-time Mount Panorama conqueror's tragic death.

A long-time protege of Brock, seven-time Bathurst 1000 winner Lowndes will line up for his 33rd bid at claiming the holy grail of Australian motorsport.

Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

The 52-year-old will share the number 15 Team 18 wildcard with Super2 racer Bayley Hall after Triple Eight Racing Engineering ditched Chevrolet for Ford last year.

Lowndes has paired with rookies since former Triple Eight teammate Jamie Whincup's retirement in 2021, a move that helps the three-time Supercars champion pass on Brock's legacy.

"I'm somewhat gone full circle," Lowndes said today.

"Bayley, we did a track walk the other day, and I literally recalled everything that Peter taught me; from Turn 1, from Hell Corner, all the way around to Murray's Corner.

"For me, I'm hopefully passing on that legacy in some way … it is a milestone year. There's no doubt about that."

Peter Brock, pictured in 2004, won the Bathurst 1000 a record nine times. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Ask Lowndes what he remembers of Brock's counsel, and he will condense his knowledge of the track's 23 corners into a minute: advice like doing all your braking over Skyline or looking for the kink on the inside of the Elbow for your turn-in point.

"Peter was more than just a teammate," Lowndes said.

"His legacy will live on forever. He was bigger than the sport in some regards.

"He was just very much a person that could capture people's attention, hold their attention, but also inspire them for greatness.

"Those are the parts that I miss 20 years on."

Just weeks after Brock died in 2006, Lowndes roared to an emotional Bathurst 1000 win with an up-and-coming Jamie Whincup to pay tribute to his great mate.

Just weeks after Peter Brock's death, Craig Lowndes (left) and Jamie Whincup won the Bathurst 1000 in 2006. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Mark Horsburgh)

"History shows that the gap at the end of the day was 0.5, and that was Brock's number for a long time," Lowndes said.

Whincup added: "The minute's silence, I'll never forget that."

"You generally got someone on the hill yell out or whatnot, but that day, even the birds stopped chirping.

"It was my first (Bathurst) win for the team and a memory that I'll take to the grave."

Seven-time champion Whincup won't be on the grid for the first time since his 2002 debut, making way for Nick Percat to link up with title contender Broc Feeney, and allowing him to focus on his duties as Triple Eight team principal.

Feeney and Percat will be smarting after a horror outing at last month's The Bend 500, finishing 24th out of 26 cars at the Bathurst 1000 curtain-raiser.

The Triple Eight star has never won the 1,000km epic and is second in the standings behind last year's race winner and Grove Racing star Matt Payne.

World.title: NZ Rugby goes to court over PNG 'Chiefs' name
World.content:
Rugby union officials have launched New Zealand High Court proceedings to prevent the National Rugby League's (NRL) new Papua New Guinea-based franchise from using the "Chiefs" name in New Zealand.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) said the move was an effort to protect the brand of the Waikato-based Chiefs, who have played in the Super Rugby competition across Australasia since rugby union turned professional in 1996.

The NRL, which is Australia-based but has one team in the New Zealand city of Auckland, announced the expansion of the league to Papua New Guinea in 2024.

The island nation's Prime Minister James Marape unveiled the name "Chiefs" the following year.

James Marape (front, second from right) announced the PNG Chiefs' name in October 2025. (Supplied: NRL)

NZR said attempts to engage the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) over the issue had been unsuccessful and it was seeking an interim and final injunction against the use of the name before the Papua New Guinea team was officially launched later this month.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said in a statement today.

"We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand."

Action branded 'hypocritical'

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys said the complaint was hypocritical given the New South Wales rugby league team had used the "Blues" brand for more than half a century before the Auckland Blues Super Rugby franchise was launched 30 years ago.

"We will defend this vigorously," he said.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

Super Rugby Chiefs chief executive Simon Graafhuis told Pacific Beat that he was confident of a resolution, adding that he would prefer the NRL team to change its name.

"Peter V'landys is the head honcho [and] is pretty adamant he's not going to do that. IP law is pretty clear. I think we're on pretty solid ground. So it could be an interesting ride," he said.

"We're open to working with them [the NRL]. This is all about protecting our brand that's taken 30 years to generate value and that's what's important to us at this stage.

"This week we had a request from a funeral celebrant to see if our logo could be used on a headstone. It's just a reminder of what it actually means to our community and yeah, absolutely worth fighting for."

Mr Graafhuis said a drastically different colour scheme would not be enough to satisfy the club that the PNG team was not infringing on its name and trademark.

"I suppose it'll come down to the courts, won't it? The longer this goes on, the higher the costs, but also the bigger the damages. So, hopefully we're all keen to avoid that one," he said.

IP Australia, the government agency that administers rights to trademarks, has examined the PNG Chiefs' case and given it an initial acceptance, triggering an "opposition period".

Any party that opposes the application has two months to lodge an appeal.

Rugby league split from rugby union in the late 19th century in a dispute about amateurism.

PNG Chiefs face 'danger of brand confusion' over team name Australia's intellectual property agency tells PNG's rugby league franchise that its chosen name, the Chiefs, risks being confused with the name of a Super Rugby club.

While union is the more popular game globally, league rules the roost on Australia's eastern seaboard and has been making great strides in New Zealand.

Papua New Guinea is the only country in the world where rugby league is the most popular sport.

The new team has already signed a slew of top NRL players ahead of its first season in 2028, and will be backed by hundreds of millions of dollars in funding from the Australian government, which is looking to shore up its influence in the Pacific Islands.

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific," Mr Lancaster said.

"We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."

The ABC has contacted IP Australia and Mr Lancaster for comment.

Reuters/ABC

Tech.title: Paramount is making a Cyberpunk 2077 film
Tech.content: Cyberpunk 2077 is heading to the big screen. Deadline reports that CD Projekt Red’s popular sci-fi video game franchise is being adapted into a live-action film by Paramount Pictures. There’s no details just yet on when the film might premiere. But Deadline says that Lorenzo di Bonaventura, who is known for producing the Transformers films, will be a producer on the movie.

Tech.title: Tim Cook says ‘I’m not meddling’ in the new Apple CEO’s business
Tech.content:
Tim Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September, handing over the top job to former hardware chief John Ternus and taking an executive chairman role. Cook’s still a visible representative of the company, having been recently photographed attending a state dinner at the White House. But in an interview with The Independent, Cook says he’s “not meddling” in Ternus’ work.

“First of all, John and I have an incredible level of trust in each other,” Cook said. “The relationship must be based on trust, and the communication must be frequent and significant. But other than that, what I’m focused on right now is worldwide policy. And the interface with governments around the world matters because there are lots of things where we’re trying to advance or advocate for change. There’s a significant amount of work in that, and I’m doing that and helping John in any way he sees fit. I’m not meddling. I’m not a meddler.”

Cook also said he’s told Ternus to “make it your own job. Put your time in the things that you can add the most value to around the company. And that means don’t mimic me. Just like I didn’t mimic Steve. We all have different strengths.” (Ternus told staff that, based on advice from Cook, “I need to spend my time where I can add the most value for Apple,” Bloomberg recently reported.)

In the interview, Cook discussed how he wanted to make the leadership transition to Ternus “the best transition ever, a textbook example that people could look back to and learn from.” The transition “actually started years ago,” according to Cook, and he said that “I think everything has gone sort of exactly the way I had envisioned it.” Ternus introduced the iPhone Duo just days after taking over, and Cook said that he “wanted John to have some wind at his back.”

Playground Games first revealed earlier this year that Forza Horizon 6 would be arriving on PS5 in 2026, but the launch is now being pushed back. I reported last month that there would be a delay to early next year, and Forza Horizon 6 is now officially debuting on January 26th, 2027.

Tech.title: USA Today becomes the latest publisher to sue OpenAI
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

USA Today Co., along with the several local newspapers it owns, is suing OpenAI over claims that the company copied “hundreds of thousands” of articles to train its AI models, as reported earlier by Reuters. In a filing on Thursday, the publisher asks for damages of more than $250 million, alleging OpenAI’s unauthorized use of its content “has done real and continuing” harm to its outlets.

“OpenAI’s commercial success rests on large-scale copyright infringement,” USA Today Co.’s lawsuit claims. It alleges that OpenAI never asked for permission to use its content, instead “took” USA Today’s content to “build products worth hundreds of billions of dollars.” The Tennessean, Indy Star, The Columbus Dispatch, The Oklahoman, and several other local outlets are also included in the lawsuit.

OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Tech.title: SpaceXAI backs Omarchy, the controversial Linux distro, with $1.5 million in compute
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If Elon Musk and SpaceXAI were going to back any Linux distro, it seems obvious they’d back Omarchy. Today it was announced that SpaceXAI would be joining the Omacom Foundation, which oversees Omarchy, as a Founding Corporate Patron and donating $1.5 million worth of Grok tokens to David Heinemeier Hansson’s Linux project. According to Hansson’s blog post announcing the partnership, the tokens will primarily be used to accelerate development, review code, and patch bugs.

Hansson is the Danish entrepreneur known for creating Ruby on Rails and co-founding the company behind Basecamp. But he’s also becoming known for promoting anti-immigration policies through racist blog posts. In a July post, he compared immigrants to wolves and said, “When wolves get out of control, you shoot them.”

1Password previously found itself in hot water for contributing to Omarchy, as has Cloudflare. When asked about its contributions to Hansson’s Linux distro by Nilay Patel on the Decoder podcast, Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said he didn’t think it was his job to “police different people’s political beliefs.”

Tech.title: Older Pixel watches are losing free cellular access to several safety features

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Google announced through a short community post today that the LTE versions of the Pixel Watch 2 and 3 are losing free access to Safety Signal that allowed features like Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, and Safety Check to work through cellular networks without the need for a carrier plan. The connectivity was included as part of a Google Health Premium subscription, but after December 12th the free access will end requiring users to pay for a mobile plan to continue to use Safety Signal on an LTE network.

Existing users with free access will be notified through notifications and an email. The Safety Signal features will still be available without a mobile plan during a 30-day transition period starting when the email is sent, but access ends after the mid-December cutoff.
