Tech.title: Anthropic bans ‘abusive or cruel behavior’ toward Claude
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

Anthropic is making changes to its usage policy for the first time in over a year to reflect new and high-risk cases of misuse — including election interference, weapons development, surveillance, and health and financial uses. But one of the most significant changes prohibits “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward Claude.

Last August, the company announced it would allow Claude to end conversations with “persistently harmful or abusive” users as part of its research into “model welfare.” The new update says that terminating conversations is still the “primary enforcement mechanism”; Anthropic did not provide a comment on whether there would be further enforcement mechanisms, such as potential user bans. Anthropic wrote that the new policy update “is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.”

Beyond the model welfare change, Anthropic has also gathered several “scattered” existing restrictions into a new ban on deceptive commercial or political campaigns, addressing the growing issue of AI-generated propaganda. It restricts “efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts.” Its election section also prohibits voter deception and election disruption, including spreading misinformation “about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout,” Anthropic wrote.

Terminating conversations is still the “primary enforcement mechanism.”

Anthropic said that though its usage policy has always publicly banned weapons development using Claude, the company has seen multiple attempts to use Claude to develop guidance for and control software for weapons — so the new usage policy expands the ban to include “ software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles.” And since the company’s last threat intelligence report suggested that people were using Claude-powered surveillance more and more to identify and track “political dissidents”, the company has made its surveillance bans clearer.

“Tracking people without their consent is prohibited, whether it happens in real time or through analysis of previously collected data,” Anthropic wrote. “Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process. We also prohibit Claude from being used to build or improve tools designed for surveillance.”

Anthropic states that these rules may be modified for “contracts with certain governmental customers … if, in Anthropic’s judgment, the contractual use restrictions and applicable safeguards are adequate to mitigate the potential harms.” The company has previously contracted with the US military.

Anthropic has seen multiple attempts to use Claude to develop guidance for and control software for weapons.

Anthropic also added a new rule that when Anthropic’s AI models are “connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury,” then a “qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed.” (It’s not clear if that operator must be human or not.) This reflects the growing trend of AI labs investing in robotics and other hardware to give AI systems physical embodiments and may offer hints at Anthropic’s future partnerships in that field.

Over the past year, Anthropic has repeatedly flirted with the idea that its AI models could be conscious in some way. “Questions about potential internal experience, consciousness, moral status, and welfare are serious ones that we’re investigating as models become more sophisticated and capable,” Kyle Fish, who leads the company’s model welfare research, told The Verge in February. That same month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on a podcast, “We don’t know if the models are conscious.”

Other parts of the AI industry have been expressly against such ideas. This past September, Microsoft AI’s code of conduct made headlines for taking a firm stance on AI welfare, with a draft posted by Mustafa Suleyman reading, “The idea of model welfare is wrong. AI’s should not have rights or legal personhood.” But at some point, the document changed to have a more measured take: “Whilst the science of AI consciousness is far from settled … We reject the pursuit of legal personhood, or the idea that models might deserve welfare, or be entitled to rights.”

Tech.title: Watch the trailer for ‘The Altruists,’ Netflix’s show about the FTX scandal
Tech.content:
In Brief

It’s a great time to be alive if you follow tech news and love messy drama. We’re not just getting a Nathan Fielder documentary about Elizabeth Holmes this fall. Netflix’s “The Altruists,” which follows Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison through the scandal that crushed FTX and landed them in prison, is coming out on November 19.

It’s just in time for Thanksgiving, assuming that another infamous Sam doesn’t ruin our holiday plans again.

Here’s the trailer, starring Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison:

We can’t say we ever expected that the ethical disconnects behind effective altruism were going to pique the interest of Hollywood, but hopefully, Netflix will do the strangeness of this story justice.

“From the very beginning, I was so fascinated by both Sam’s and Caroline’s real stories,” co-showrunner Graham Moore said in an interview with Netflix this summer. “Those are both characters I could not have possibly made up had I tried — I’m not nearly a good enough writer to create characters as fascinating as either Sam Bankman-Fried or Caroline Ellison.”

Tech.title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed
Tech.content:
They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews.

He can even write a little Python, he says.

The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more.

In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about.

“I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?”

No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral.

The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.”

He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space.

As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.)

“I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said.

In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in L.A., where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making.

Ben Affleck (Hollywood star & Artists Equity CEO) talks about how he fine-tunes open video models by unfreezing weights and trained only the last cinematic layer so a film crew can hit real production standards.



for context, Ben Affleck founded InterPositive in 2022, a 16-person… pic.twitter.com/xIOvD0xMyt — Rohan Paul (@rohanpaul_ai) October 1, 2026

The actor used the technique himself in his movie “Animals,” where AI aided in the post-production process.

At one point, he also weighed in on the concerns around AI and its world-ending potential. His worries, however, were much more rational.

“When I worry about AI, I worry about my kids in school. I worry about the 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over [the movie] business in any meaningful way. I think it’s going to be additive,” Affleck said.

Tech.title: Popular AI leaderboard Arena nearly doubles valuation to $3.1B valuation in 10 months
Tech.content:
Arena, which originated in 2023 as a research project at UC Berkeley that crowdsourced rankings of AI models, has raised a $200 million Series B round at a $3.1 billion valuation, it said on Thursday.

This comes after the company said it reached $100 million in annualized run-rate revenue in June.

The round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures, with Salesforce Ventures, 01 Advisors, Dell Technologies Capital, Endeavor Catalyst, a16z, Felicis and others joining in. Arena previously announced a $150 million Series A in January at a $1.7 billion post-money valuation. At the time, its annualized revenue was $30 million, it said. So that means its valuation has nearly doubled in about 10 months.

Arena provides a crowdsourced platform that is free for consumers to use. People enter prompts or request vibe-coded projects and then rate which model does it better. Arena claims it has tens of millions of monthly visitors.

In September of last year, it introduced its commercial product, AI Evaluations, a service that provides model labs and enterprises with detailed performance analytics based on its community feedback. The timing proved impeccable. This year, AI labs realized that their models were gaming benchmarking tests, finding ways to rack up good scores without truly earning them. At the same time, enterprises wanted help determining which model works best for their own internal needs rather than relying only on standardized benchmarks.

“AI is advancing faster than our ability to evaluate it, and static benchmarks break down once models recognize they’re being tested,” the company said in its funding announcement. “The world needs a neutral third party to measure how safe and aligned AI actually is once it’s in the hands of real people. Arena is stepping into that role today,” it added.

To that end, Arena has also added a new category to its leaderboard: alignment. This is where it ranks models based on issues like unauthorized action (taking actions it wasn’t asked to take); false attribution (wrongly crediting statements or facts to the wrong source); and what it calls “deceptive completion” (lying about completing tasks that it didn’t do).

Currently, a slate of OpenAI’s models are at the top of its preliminary alignment leaderboard, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable in sixth and ninth place, respectively.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s revenue is reportedly $20 billion less than previously projected
Tech.content:
In Brief

A little over a week ago, it was reported that OpenAI’s annualized revenue was approaching $70 billion, a figure that would have made it competitive with Anthropic’s reported run rate. Now, however, the AI lab is said to have told investors that the real revenue is some $20 billion lower than that.

The Financial Times reports that the company has told investors that its annualized revenue is “approaching $50 billion.” The publication also notes that the previous figure of $70 billion was based on information that had previously been shared with investors by OpenAI. That figure was devised via “attempts by OpenAI’s own investors to produce a direct comparison with Anthropic’s annualised revenues,” per the FT.

It’s worth pointing out that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently — with Anthropic counting sales made by its cloud partners. OpenAI doesn’t do this.

TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for comment.

The issue of OpenAI’s revenue has troubled the company, as it attempts to justify the gargantuan investments being made on its behalf; the AI giant raised $122 billion during a March funding round alone. The company’s leaked 2025 financials earlier this year showed it had made about $13 billion but spent significantly more. OpenAI’s IPO, which was previously rumored to be materializing this year, has been pushed off until early 2027.

Tech.title: Google brings agentic AI to Gemini, starting with businesses
Tech.content:
At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface.

The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots.

The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work.

Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers.

Image Credits:Google

According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these.

Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals.

By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future.

The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others.

It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network.

Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress.

Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person.

The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack.

Image Credits:Google

The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers.

Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control.

Tech.title: Anthropic changes usage policy to ban model abuse and election interference
Tech.content:
In Brief

Anthropic updated its usage policy on Thursday, codifying new prohibitions on election interference, weapons software, and surveillance. But perhaps the most attention-getting change is a new prohibition against prolonged verbal abuse of the model, which is now expressly forbidden.

Since an update in August, Claude has been trained to end conversations with “persistently harmful or abusive user interactions” — but the new policy explicitly bars users from pursuing those conversations.

“The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose,” the post explains. “It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.”

The change comes after Anthropic has sought out collaborations with prominent religious scholars — in some cases, seeking to convince them that Claude could be conscious or have a soul.

Separate sections of the usage policy forbid users from engaging in broadly deceptive campaigns, such as using Claude to run fake accounts or fabricated news outlets. The policy also includes rules against deceiving voters or disrupting elections, collected in a section titled “Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes.”

Tech.title: OpenAI’s math solutions aren’t meeting the field’s standards yet
Tech.content:
When OpenAI released hundreds of claimed solutions to some of the world’s hardest math problems this week, the frontier lab said that it had consulted an advisory group of elite mathematicians to avoid the controversy that came with the last time one of its models solved a long-standing problem in the field.

But OpenAI fell short of those standards, particularly where the mathematicians emphasized the need for human understanding of a mathematical result. That’s especially concerning after a new paper highlighted gaps between the natural language and formally expressed solution to a million-dollar problem ostensibly solved by OpenAI’s models.

The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), hosted by Princeton University’s Institute for Advanced Studies, is made up of nine prominent researchers at institutions around the world.

The organization released guidelines for frontier labs solving math problems at the end of September. In a statement on the latest set of proofs, the AGMAI said that “it is ultimately up to the mathematical community to assess the extent to which our recommendations were followed successfully.”

However, the organization’s first request was “to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.” OpenAI’s release explicitly says that it is evaluating its proprietary models using open research problems in mathematics.

The advisory group did not respond when asked by TechCrunch for a more thorough evaluation of OpenAI’s latest proof release. The lab clearly followed some of its principles, including releasing results as soon as possible and including information about how the models reached their conclusions. But not for all of them: Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model’s chain of thought.

For papers that people don’t understand, the mathematicians suggested the proofs should be formalized — but just 42% of the proofs released by OpenAI had not undergone this process.

Ultimately, it’s still not clear that OpenAI is taking “responsibility for ensuring that human understanding will follow” when releasing its proofs, in accordance to the AGMAI principles. AGMAI suggested that OpenAI should help fund the work of human mathematicians who will be required to make the lab’s solutions meaningful in any real way.

“Problems are being solved autonomously by AI prompters who have no interest in the broader field itself once their initial target is ‘solved’, and do not understand the AI output well enough to answer questions on the result, give talks, or otherwise interact with the rest of the field,” Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician who has criticized OpenAI’s approach, wrote on social media after the release.

That problem is exemplified by a paper released this week by mathematicians at the University of Cambridge and King’s College in London that questions the way frontier labs are approaching these challenges.

When AI models solve mathematical problems, they first create a “natural language” explanation, then try to express that result in Lean, a programming language that in theory confirms the accuracy of the proof by compiling it as code.

However, there may be problems with the way the models translate their natural language proofs into code; this paper documents at least two discrepancies between the natural language proof and the Lean code behind the solution OpenAI has offered to a problem derived from the Navier-Stokes equations that describe the complex behavior of fluids.

These discrepancies don’t necessarily disprove either solution, but they do raise questions on whether we can simply rely on models to formalize their own solutions without human involvement. That’s one reason that AGMAI asked OpenAI to “include machine-readable metadata correlating the natural language and formal artifacts,” something that the frontier lab did not do with these releases.

“Because of the phenomenon of mistranslations — as highlighted in this paper — the NL proof by OpenAI and

other autoformalised Lean proofs should not prima facie be trusted without the same peer review process and

scrutiny that other proofs are subjected to,” the authors of the “lost in translation” paper conclude.

Mathematicians stress that when new results are discovered by humans, they take responsibility for them and engage with the broader community through papers, talks, and seminars. That process increases understanding of the solutions, finds strategies that can be used to solve other problems, and allows the new knowledge to be applied in practical fields.

When a model is prompted to solve a hard problem and spits out a solution, “there is not human understanding of them at the point of release, and now the work begins,” Harvard University mathematics professor Melanie Wood told TechCrunch.

Tech.title: A startup founder who served time in prison is looking to court an untapped market: ex-cons
Tech.content:
Richard Bronson, an entrepreneur who recently launched a startup called Commissary Club, has an unusual background for a founder: in a previous life, he spent time in prison.

In the 1980s, Bronson worked for the notorious Stratton Oakmont — the corruption-riddled brokerage firm that was run by Jordan Belfort, the “Wolf of Wall Street” whose story became a 2013 film. The firm collapsed in the mid-1990s under the weight of misconduct accusations.

Bronson was a partner at Stratton but left after a year to start his own firm in South Florida. He was quite successful in that venture, until he wasn’t.

“I built a $100 million business taking these small cap companies public,” Bronson told TechCrunch. “Some of the success, however, came through breaking the law — securities laws — and ultimately, as I knew inevitably would happen, I had to pay the price. I lost everything, and most significantly, my freedom. And I was sent to federal prison for a couple of years.”

Bronson has been out of prison for a long time now, but he has never forgotten the struggles he had when he initially emerged from prison.

“Nobody would hire me, despite all of my education and work experience and everything else. I was like completely radioactive,” he said.

Bronson’s experience after prison helped inform his current startup, an employment-focused social media platform called Commissary Club, which takes its name from the store inside a prison where inmates buy snacks and toiletries. The site is specifically marketed to ex-cons and uses AI to help them navigate the often confusing process of finding employment and housing after they reenter the world.

“I could not help but notice how little assistance was available to people coming out of prison,” said Bronson. “If it was this bad for me, what about the guys I was in prison with who had very little education and very little job experience? What were their chances?”

Commissary Club also has a social component, which Bronson said he added because he knows how isolating the post-prison experience can be. “It’s almost like Facebook,” he said, “where people can not only find jobs, and get the help with the jobs and the housing and access to benefits, but they find the other missing ingredient that’s existentially important to them that isn’t satisfied elsewhere. They find community.” Judging by the site, Commissary Club also appears primed to become a referral network, and it offers a way for users to find dates.

For now, Bronson’s startup is a team of two — just him and his co-founder, Roman Kissin, who Bronson called the technical mind (or “the brains”) behind the project. Kissin previously worked for eBay and IBM and, between 2022 and 2025, he served as the CTO of LexisNexis, according to his LinkedIn profile.

The site is free at first, then switches to paid. Users get “the first 10 applications for free, and then we bundle the next at $149 for 10 applications, or $14.99 each,” Bronson told TechCrunch. Some may balk at that for-profit model, and for people just out of prison, it may be a tough sell.

Yet Bronson sees it as a win-win — a business that can help a community that few others are trying to help.

“People immediately assume, ‘Oh, is this a nonprofit?’ And the answer is no,” said Bronson. “There’s a strong mission component, certainly,” he continued, “and I have devoted my life, when I came out of prison, to helping my brothers and sisters with records. Part of it is because I just felt so remorseful for the shit that I had done. I still wake up every day regretting choices I made.

“But we’re going after a huge, huge market that nobody — I mean nobody — does anything about,” said Bronson. “People talk about AI taking away employment and people losing jobs. I look at it differently. We’re building AI that creates employment for people that society left behind.”

Bronson’s Commissary Club was selected for TechCrunch’s storied pitch competition Startup Battlefield 200, taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt October 13-15 in San Francisco.

Tech.title: Trump Administration Cuts Off Access to a Major Immigration Program for Workers at Microsoft and Adobe
Tech.content:
The Trump administration will no longer allow Microsoft and other tech companies to participate in a program that allows H-1B visa holders to apply for green cards, one of the most common pathways for skilled foreign workers seeking permanent residency in the United States.

In addition to Microsoft, administration officials said on Thursday that software giant Adobe and IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata will be suspended from the PERM program, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification program. PERM is a key step for H-1B visaholders to gain permanent residency, requiring employers to prove that there are no American workers who would be suitable for the applicant's permanent job opportunity.

Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said that the agency is investigating whether these companies committed fraud, undercutting American workers by hiring foreign employees.

Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, singled out Microsoft. "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said in a press conference.

In a statement provided by Microsoft representative Kaitlin Haskins, the company said it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," adding that it develops its workforce by "strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world."

Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.

The suspension marks a victory for tech workers who have complained about unfairly losing out on jobs to immigrant workers.

Jobs Now, an advocacy group composed of US citizens working in big tech, celebrated Vance’s announcement on its X account with a video of dancing crabs. The group publicizes otherwise difficult-to-find PERM job postings and says it helped Americans apply to nearly 500,000 jobs across 7,000 employers between last January and this past July.

The organization and its members have also filed complaints against tech companies about alleged abuse of the PERM system, and have called for a number of changes to the employment immigration system. “Every job in America should be offered to an American first, no exceptions,” the group told WIRED in an unsigned statement.

This isn't the first time tech companies have been targeted over PERM. Earlier this year, OpenAI and a company it acquired agreed to settle accusations from the Trump administration about violating rules for the program. Apple reached a similar deal in 2023.

Tech.title: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Alexa Tablet 11, Alexa Tablet 8: Specs, Features, Price
Tech.content:
The era of Amazon's Fire tablets—cheap slate computers ranging from $60 to $280—is over.

All of the Fire tablets are being replaced by the all-aluminum Amazon Alexa Tablet. These tablets will, in a first for Amazon, run official Android and have full access to the Google Play Store. The lack of proper app support was always a sticking point for the Fire tablets, which ran a custom version of Android and had a much more limited app library.

The new Alexa Tablet series comes in three models: the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro ($500), Alexa Tablet 11 ($330), and Alexa Tablet 8 ($230), with the numbers corresponding to the display size. Amazon is also offering kids' editions of the latter two devices at the same prices. These include bumper cases for extra protection, a one-year, worry-free guarantee to replace the device if it breaks, and a year of Amazon Kids+ service to fill the tablet with age-appropriate content.

As for Fire tablets, Amazon says it will stop shipping the devices in the next month or two. It will support them for four years from the last ship date. Amazon is committing to at least four years of software updates for the new Alexa tablets, which will launch with Android 16 and will receive Android 17 early in 2027. Preorders for the new Alexa Tablets are open now, and they'll begin shipping on October 14.

Premium Tablets

From left to right: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, the Alexa Tablet 11, and the Alexa Tablet 8. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

The experience is largely the same on all three tablets, with aluminum builds designed to mimic the new aluminum Kindles. The MediaTek Dimensity 8189 chip powers the two smaller tablets, whereas the 12-inch device gets a little more power from the MediaTek Dimensity 8400.

Tech.title: The New Alexa Tablets Feel Like a Blueprint for an Amazon Phone
Tech.content:
Is Amazon making a smartphone? A Reuters report from earlier this year revealed details about a device codenamed Transformer under development, with Amazon's Alexa+ AI assistant as the focus of the experience.

With Amazon announcing a complete rebrand of its tablet line on Thursday—killing the cheap Fire Tablets and replacing them with premium Alexa Tablets that finally run Android with access to the Google Play Store—we now have a blueprint for what an Android-powered Amazon phone could look like.

Amazon's souped-up Alexa+ assistant is front and center on the tablets. There's a persistent “Ask Alexa” widget on the home screen that lets you call on the assistant to ask it questions—you can say “Alexa” to trigger it, too. But Alexa+ now finally has what Amazon calls On-Screen Intelligence. Like Google's Gemini on Android phones or Apple's Siri on iPhones, which can read your screen and answer contextual questions, Alexa now has the same functionality (if you opt in).

Tech.title: How Massive Is Elon Musk’s Trillion-Dollar Fortune? Spend It Yourself
Tech.content:
On any given day, Elon Musk is worth about a trillion dollars. This does not mean that he has a trillion dollar bills sitting in an old-timey vault in a dusty basement somewhere; his wealth is mostly tied up in shares of SpaceX and Tesla. But if he were to cash those out, sell Neuralink and the Boring Company, and scrounge together some extra change, his checking account would hit 13 digits.

“Trillionaire” is an easy enough word to say. It’s fun, even! Rolls off the tongue. But research has shown that the human brain has a very hard time comprehending the actual size and scope of large numbers. “Trillion” sounds like a short hop from “billion,” after all, even though it is in fact 1,000 times bigger. And even if you are somehow able to wrap your mind around that immense scale, it still feels abstract, no matter how many times you compare it to the area of Central Park or the weight of a fleet of trucks. Maybe a better way to visualize a trillion dollars, then, is through what you can actually buy with it.

Spend Elon Musk’s Money What’s it like to be the richest man in the world? Find out for yourself.

WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal, the proprietor of the consistently delightful website Neal.fun, to do just that. Spend Elon Musk’s Money is a new visualization that lets you, well, spend Elon Musk’s money, on anything from Big Macs to aircraft carriers to the Las Vegas Sphere. It keeps a tally as you go, so you can actually see how far a trillion dollars gets you these days, and it shows the items you’ve bought in a physical space.

WIRED spoke with Agarwal about this new project, why it feels so relevant now, and the state of building things on the web. You can read that interview below, and waste a few hours on Spend Elon Musk’s money right here.

Tech.title: Life Is Asymmetric. The Scientists Who Figured Out Why Won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Tech.content:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai for discovering a solution to the enigma of nature’s chemical asymmetry, a finding that opened up new avenues for manipulating the reactions used in manufacturing pharmaceuticals and other materials.

Some molecules are chiral, meaning a molecule has two forms that are mirror images of each other but not identical, like your left and right hand. One of the most mysterious chemical phenomena in biology is that living organisms contain almost exclusively one of the two forms. This is known as homochirality.

Both versions of the molecules—each called an enantiomer—have similar physical properties but can behave differently. The Nobel Committee used a simple analogy to explain this: A locksmith can create two mirror-image keys, but “only one of them fits the lock—and the lock can be damaged if your customers try to unlock it with the other key.”

In the development of new drugs that use, for example, amino acids or sugar molecules as a basis, homochirality poses a problem: While one of the enantiomers of these chiral molecules produces the desired therapeutic effect, the other can cause unnecessary and, at times, harmful side effects. Scientists can’t always easily control which version of the molecule they get out of their synthesis.

The discovery of chiral molecules dates back to the time of Pasteur, who found two enantiomers that reacted very differently when exposed to bacteria. Since then, various researchers have attempted to replicate homochirality in the laboratory with the goal of understanding its spontaneous origin and applying this knowledge to the design of controlled reactions for various purposes. However, early experiments yielded equal amounts of the two variants, failing to reproduce the selectivity observed in nature.

Tech.title: WIRED’s Midterms Races to Watch
Tech.content:
The midterm elections are a month away and the candidate pool has never been more WIRED. Races are being run—and likely decided—on Silicon Valley funding, data center debates, AI regulation, extremism, and more. From the contests that will decide the Senate to less attention-grabbing ones that will decide who controls voting in key swing states in 2028, these are the candidates and races we think are most worth watching closely in the weeks to come, and which we'll be keeping an eye on.

Texas’ 10th Congressional District: Chris Gober (R) vs. Caitlin Rourk (D)

WHAT MAKES THIS A WIRED RACE: DOGE, Musk, America PAC, AI lobby

Former America PAC lawyer Chris Gober is running to represent Texas’ newly gerrymandered 10th district. Gober served as counsel for the Texas Republican congressional delegation for the 2025 redistricting effort that saw a new, gerrymandered map created for the 2026 midterms—one that was meant to create five new Republican congressional districts.

In addition to representing Musk’s PAC, Gober’s law firm, Lex Politica, has also represented Elevate New Mexico, a limited liability company that ran an advertising campaign supporting a controversial data center project in the state, as well as the Danube Institute USA, a think tank aligned with Hungary’s former right-wing leader Viktor Orban.

According to reporting from The New York Times, Gober was one of several lawyers who advised on the structure of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in the weeks leading up to President Donald Trump’s inauguration.

The 10th district also includes Grimes County, where SpaceXAI and Tesla have said they plan to open a 100-million-square-foot “terafab” facility to manufacture semiconductors. In addition to his legal work, Gober’s LinkedIn lists him as general counsel for a lobbying group called Maven Advocacy Partners, the client base of which includes several defense tech startups. (Its name appears to be a reference to the Department of War’s Project Maven, which is supported by tech companies like Palantir and Anduril.) Gober also appears to run another company called Maven Defense Solutions. Both the company and the lobbying group share an address with his law firm, Lex Politica, and his campaign office.

Gober’s campaign has received $747,550 from the American Mission PAC, a right-leaning super PAC that has itself received funding from Leading the Future, a PAC focused on promoting AI-friendly candidates and policies. Leading the Future has raised over $140 million from Silicon Valley billionaires like OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale, as well as the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz.

Tech.title: Goodbye, Fire Tablet: Amazon’s New Alexa Tablet Is a Flashy Portable Entertainment Hub
Tech.content:
A new lineup of Amazon tablets has been announced, and the devices are designed for both work and play. Amazon Alexa Tablets combine cloud-based device syncing functionality, onboard AI capabilities and the entirety of Amazon’s media catalog, making them something akin to on-the-go entertainment hubs.

Each of the three Alexa Tablet models has an aluminum chassis, which will protect what’ll be some of the thinnest devices Amazon has ever released. More importantly, Fire OS and the Amazon Appstore are going away. Instead of a custom, forked operating system, the Alexa Tablets will run Android 16 at launch, and will upgrade to Android 17 in early 2027. That means these devices will offer full Play Store functionality, giving you access to plenty of apps that haven’t previously been compatible with Amazon tablets.

But the software capabilities are what I suspect will be the real draw. If you use an Amazon account on your computer, phone, TV or other device, it will automatically sync up with the Alexa Tablets. A dynamic tab on the home screen allows you to quickly pick up movies, shows, books and games wherever you left off. There’s also an algorithmic “For You” layout that shows you other content you might enjoy based off of what you’re currently enjoying, like a streaming model that pulls together every form of media in one place.

More from CNET

Avid readers will be able to access their Audible and Kindle libraries in one place, and a new Kindle mode also silences notifications, turns down blue light and enhances battery life. I got a firsthand look at the e-ink and color paper modes at an in-person event in New York and was impressed with how the pages looked on-screen. The texture of the display is sufficiently papery, too. (TCL’s Nxtpaper devices may soon be given a run for their money.)

The Alexa Plus AI assistant may not be the speediest helper, but it has all of your Amazon account’s personal information at its virtual fingertips. Tyler Graham/CNET

Each Alexa Tablet is deeply integrated with Alexa Plus AI, allowing you to converse with it and pull answers from Amazon’s Silk browser on the fly. Opting into on-screen intelligence allows the generative model to see what’s on the display. It can answer questions about images in a browser, locate listings for specific products shown in a social media video and more. During the product demonstration, Alexa Plus took upwards of half a minute to respond to complicated prompts, but the onboard model responded accurately to verbal requests about managing a personal calendar and finding nearby restaurants based on dietary restrictions.

Kevin Keith, vice president of Amazon’s devices team, told me that the new lineup of Amazon Alexa Tablets will supersede the Fire Tablets entirely. The company will wind down production of its old product and sell the remaining stock over the next few months. Once those Fire tablets sell out, Amazon has committed to providing at least four years of software support, including security and operating system updates.

The Amazon Alexa Tablet lineup

The cloud syncing, Kindle mode and Alexa Plus on-screen intelligence features are packaged into every Alexa Tablet, but these devices aren’t all built the same. The three models have different hardware and peripheral capabilities. Here’s what you can expect from the first wave of Alexa Tablets.

The flagship tablet includes deep AI integration and multiwindowing functionality. It blends work and entertainment capabilities into one device. Tyler Graham/CNET

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro

Amazon’s new flagship tablet feels like a true jack of all trades. It’s an entertainment hub, an ereader and a personal AI assistant that can be converted into a work laptop using a few simple peripherals.

The most premium configuration has a whopping 16GB of memory, which will help with a more demanding workload for folks who routinely use the device’s multiwindowing capabilities or more complex Play Store applications.

This feels like the platonic ideal of a hybrid device. It’s more portable than a laptop, but has all your favorite mobile apps. It’s powerful enough for some light gaming but you can use it to read a new book, too. It’s not specialized for any particular task, but it can do a bit of everything. Its launch price is also cheaper than most budget laptops to boot.

The Alexa Tablet 11 may not be quite as large as the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, but it dwarfs the Alexa Tablet 8. Tyler Graham/CNET

Amazon Alexa Tablet 11

This middle-of-the-road Alexa Tablet is likely for people who want the entertainment hub functionality of the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro but are willing to make some compromises to save some money.

The 11-inch model is still able to use a keyboard, but it doesn’t have a physical pogo pin connection. You can still use the stylus to draw on-screen, but there’s less space to do so. More importantly, you’re losing out on the higher storage options available on the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro.

This might not be a portable workstation, but it’s a solid entertainment hub nonetheless: You still get high resolution and all of Amazon’s media is in one place. If you’re looking for a better bargain on a “fun” tablet, the Alexa Tablet 11 could end up being the perfect middle-ground for you.

The diminutive Alexa Tablet 8 has the same built-in device cloud syncing and Alexa Plus capabilities as the rest of the lineup, but I wouldn’t expect this model to serve as an entertainment hub or work device.

Even though it has full Play Store access, it has less memory and storage space than the more expensive Alexa Tablets. I reckon most people will use this 8.7-inch tablet as a pocket-size ereader in the new and improved Kindle mode, with its additional capabilities serving as a bonus.

The Amazon Kids tablets have been redesigned, too

Just like the regular Fire Tablets, the Fire Kids lineup is going the way of the dodo. But it’s being replaced with two Alexa Tablets that are also built specifically for children. Keith told me the design philosophy for these tablets was to bring them more in line with devices for adults while maintaining safety features and parental controls.

“We know kids want a tablet, not a toy, so we add the same hardware as the Alexa Tablet,” he said. “We ship it with a bumper, a completely different UI and software built just for kids.”

Younger children will benefit from the new 8.7-inch tablet, which has a soft, foam cover around the chassis, while a sleeker 11-inch model will come with a more form-fitting, kid-proof case.

The devices come with the generative-AI Storybuilder tool, which lets kids verbalize stories and see custom visuals for them. This is paired off with its own set of parental controls and a parental dashboard that provides weekly insights on tablet usage. Every Amazon Kids tablet comes with a one-year subscription to Amazon Kids Plus.

The full lineup of Amazon Alexa Tablets is available for preorder now, and will begin shipping out across the US on Oct. 14.

Tech.title: Is That Picture AI? Google’s SynthID Detector Launches to Identify AI-Generated Media
Tech.content:
AI slop is getting so good that it’s not always easy to distinguish a photorealistic forgery from a real photo. It’s no longer as easy as looking for the six-fingered renderings of just a year ago. Beyond looking for subtle clues, spotting AI images often comes down to a gut feeling that something simply looks off.

Now there’s another tool to help identify fakes, and it works with AI-edited audio and video, too. Google has opened its SynthID Detector to the public, so anyone with a Google, Apple or ChatGPT account can upload media to determine whether it’s been saved with a SynthID tag indicating manipulation using generative AI.

Google introduced SynthID in 2023 and, in late 2025, made it possible to query Google Gemini about whether images were created using Google’s AI. At the Google I/O annual developer conference this past May, the tool expanded to include detecting video and audio content in Google Chrome and Google Search.

More from CNET

The standalone SynthID Detector tool currently detects media generated by Google, OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao. Not yet named is Apple, which announced it would support SynthID at its recent fall event announcing the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

A spokesperson for Google, in an email to CNET, emphasized that working with other companies is crucial when it comes to identifying AI-generated content because no single company can solve the problem alone. They also said there’s no specific date for Apple support, but that it will be available soon.

Even so, the SynthID Detector seems already wired for Apple’s content. I uploaded a photo shot with an iPhone 18 Pro and edited using Apple’s Reframe tool, and it successfully detected the embedded SynthID tag. For an untouched iPhone-captured photo, the detector correctly did not detect a tag.

The original photo, captured with an iPhone, underwent a slight perspective shift using Apple’s Reframe tool, which then embedded a SynthID tag that was recognized by Google’s SynthID Detector. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Images generated from prompts using ChatGPT were correctly flagged as including AI-generated content

This photo was entirely AI-generated from a prompt in ChatGPT. Although the SynthID tag was detected, the janky pattern of leaves on the ground gives it away, too. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

To probe the level of Apple support in the tool, I created an entirely AI-generated image in Apple’s Playground app using ChatGPT’s image generation model, but the SynthID Detector did not identify it as AI-generated. It’s likely the Playground app does not yet have SynthID tagging wired in.

Apple’s Playground app was used to generate this variation, which was created with ChatGPT, but the detector found no SynthID metadata. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

I also tested some photos captured using a Google Pixel 11 Pro. The company takes a two-pronged approach to image veracity on its own devices: embedding C2PA (or Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) metadata in every image it creates to verify the accuracy of the original capture, and adding a SynthID when an image has been edited using AI.

I edited the original photo with a Pixel 11 Pro XL in Google Photos by asking Gemini to create a night version with an aurora, shown at right. The SynthID Detector correctly noted the SynthID tag in the edited version.

Although Apple is adopting SynthID, it has not signed onto C2PA. Instead, it’s using its own Reference Image technology to store a cryptographically verified original of an image. Those shots must be captured in the Reference mode in the iPhone’s Camera app, though.

It’s also encouraging to see Google handle the media in a sensible way. When you first visit the site, you must agree to terms of service that spell out that media files you upload are processed in real time and then deleted after the results are displayed. A digital signature of the media is mapped to your user identifier and then deleted after 24 hours.

OpenAI has its own verification tool, but it only looks for OpenAI watermarks; the AI-generated samples I tested with Google’s tool came up negative on OpenAI’s site.

Any tool that helps determine genuine content is welcome, but as usual, the responsibility falls on the viewer to make that determination — if not by noticing on sight, then by making the effort of downloading the media, loading the tool and uploading it. The upside is that tracking technology such as SynthID is finally making its way into more media and paving the way for more widespread detection of AI slop.

Tech.title: Utah Now Allows AI to Scan Your Face and Prescribe Acne Medication
Tech.content:
Robot medical help is fairly common in sci-fi, ranging from Baymax in Big Hero 6 to the surgical bots in Star Wars that put Anakin Skywalker into Darth Vader’s infamous black armor. Now, a subscription service in Utah has deployed the first AI doctor capable of prescribing medication.

Healthcare startup Nolla Health focuses primarily on skincare and acne treatment, and subscriptions cost $5 per month. According to Bloomberg, a patient uses an app to scan their face and fills out forms giving their medical history. AI software then analyzes the patient’s face and generates an acne severity score. If the scan and medical information indicate it, the patient receives a prescription for one of eight approved treatments.

The pilot program is slated to last one year, Bloomberg reports. The first 100 prescriptions will be overseen by a board-certified physician before being sent to pharmacies. If that works, the next phase will allow the AI to fully treat 400 patients, with a physician reviewing the bot’s decisions weekly. The third phase involves the physician auditing at least 10% of written prescriptions once per month.

More from CNET

In an email to CNET, Nolla Health co-founder and CEO Luis Wenus said the company is “showing how AI can responsibly expand access and help someone get personalized treatment in minutes instead of long waits or going without care altogether.”

Michelle McOmber, CEO of the Utah Medical Association, told CNET in an email that Nolla Health didn’t need the association’s approval to run this pilot program. The Office of AI Policy had a brief conversation with the association’s president, a dermatologist, who had the subcommittee of the Utah Medical Licensing Board review the plan and provide comments.

The Office of AI Policy is part of the Utah Department of Commerce and is tasked with guiding responsible AI policies in the state.

McOmber told CNET that this “very limited and very specific” use of AI is acceptable, but that the Utah Medical Association “would not be in favor of it being used for anything else at this time as it is.”

AI isn’t ready for more responsibility

Studies report that doctors, surgeons and mental health professionals are among the least likely professions to be replaced by AI. Even so, many medical professionals agree that the use of AI in the medical field is inevitable, either as a tool to assist human physicians or for simpler tasks, such as diagnosing acne or other skin conditions.

Some of those same medical professionals believe that AI in medicine is moving too quickly.

“We think people are trying to go too fast in using and relying on AI in healthcare,” McOmber said. “We do believe that AI, as a tool, can help physicians in different ways and that it will be used and even should be used.”

McOmber says human physicians should always be involved in patient care, whether it’s writing prescriptions or examining patients to diagnose conditions. AI in its current form is best for such simple tasks as gathering useful medical information and histories from patients, she says.

“Care decisions ultimately should rest with the physician in consultation with the patient,” McOmber says. “AI, if used inappropriately, can be very dangerous in healthcare.”

Tech.title: Your New Apple Watch and AirPods Still Fall Short on Repairability, iFixit Teardowns Reveal
Tech.content:
If you’re one of the lucky people who, over the past month, managed to acquire one of the latest Apple Watch models or the AirPods 5, there’s something about your new piece of tech you should know — they’re not easy to repair.

That might not seem like a problem right now – they’re new, after all. But over time, you might wish to swap out their batteries to prolong their lifespans. It’s not impossible, but none of the wearables Apple debuted last month are a quick fix.

Repairability advocacy group iFixit regularly tears down new consumer devices and assigns them a score out of 10, based on how easy they are to repair. On Tuesday, it gave the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 marks of 4 out of 10 on the repairability scale, with the AirPods 5 gaining a score of just 2 out of 10 in a similar exercise last week.

More from CNET

On the surface, it looks like the AirPods have come out worse in this experiment than the Apple Watches, but it really depends on perspective. Apple has actually made improvements to the AirPods since the last model, which scored 0 out of 10, so these two additional marks point to the company making moves toward increased repairability.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is marginally easier to repair than its predecessor – thanks to an adhesive pull tab that releases the battery – although iFixit still describes this as “modest gains.” Meanwhile, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is no easier to repair than the three previous generations, which all also scored 4 out of 10.

“Apple still hasn’t fixed the biggest problem with Watch repair: battery repair,” iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens said over email. “You have to slice open very stubborn adhesive and risk damaging the fragile display to get to the battery of both new Apple Watches.”

Furthermore, iFixit says that it believes Apple is failing to comply with right-to-repair regulations in 10 US states. In Oregon, for example, companies are required to make the same parts, tools and documentation available to repair and DIY shops as they use to fix products in-house. “To do repairs, we need parts, tools, and manuals, and Apple has never made them available for Apple Watch,” says Wiens.

Back in June, Wiens told me that this was a “fixable design problem” with the Apple Watch. It doesn’t require Apple to make any upgrades to the device – instead, it requires the company to actively aid in the growth of the wider repair ecosystem.

Apple didn’t comment on iFixit’s findings and conclusions. Previously, a spokesperson for the company said that it meets the requirements of Minnesota’s right-to-repair law specifically, and that it’s the first smartphone maker to support a push for federal right-to-repair regulation.

Right-to-repair regulation differs from state to state, but it’s motivated by one unifying idea: making it easier and cheaper for people to have their tech repaired, usually by giving them more choice to go through the original manufacturer, a third-party repair company of their choice or doing it themselves at home.

The benefit of repairability is that it extends the lifecycle of our products, reducing electronic waste and saving us from having to keep splashing out on replacement tech.

How does Apple compare to the competition?

In iFixit’s assessment of the new Apple Watches, it concludes that the company needs to do better. It highlights Google’s Pixel Watch as an alternative product that shows how repairability can be done right.

I can speak to this personally, having successfully disassembled and reassembled the Pixel Watch earlier this year. Was it tricky? Yes. Did it take twice as long as I thought it would? Again, yes. But the point is that I was able not just to remove the battery, but replace the entire screen. This is why iFixit awarded the Pixel Watch a repairability score of 9 out of 10.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

What I learned from delving into the world of wearables repairability is that smartwatches and headphones need to be designed with repair in mind from the get-go – it can’t simply be retrofitted around an existing device. It’s no easy feat to guarantee repairability when you also don’t want to compromise a device’s durability and waterproofing. It’s especially hard to do without trade-offs.

The Pixel Watch might be the gold standard for repairability right now, but the industry is hardly rushing to play catch-up. Apple might be languishing near the bottom of the heap, but it’s not a massive outlier.

There are also benefits to the way Apple does things. By keeping certain repairs in-house, the company retains quality control over the devices it’s fixing and returning to people. But giving people the power to choose how to repair tech they already own is increasingly a consumer right, and ultimately, even tech giants must comply with regulations.

Apple has made great strides in recent years to make its devices more repairable (even if the iPhone 18 Pro is also pretty tricky to repair). The company’s products also tend to last a long time and have great resale value. It has a great track record of making consumer-friendly breakthroughs that make people attached to their Apple devices. But repairability is one feature the company has yet to prove it’s mastered.

Tech.title: The Surface Laptop Ultra Is Here: Microsoft and Nvidia Built a Premium Computer for the AI Age
Tech.content:
After months of teasers, Microsoft officially gave the Surface Laptop Ultra the two things it needed: a release date and a price. You’ll like one and hate the other. Let’s get into everything Microsoft announced at its Oct. 7 Windows and Surface event.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is anything but a surprise. Microsoft first unveiled the device this spring at Computex, and since then, it popped up at Microsoft’s Build software conference and IFA. The 15-inch laptop is powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip and platform. This computer is a workhorse, meant for developers, creators and others who need a lot of horsepower to power through their work. It also comes with a magnetic USB-C charging cord, new for Microsoft.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is available for preorder now, and devices will begin shipping on Friday, Oct. 16.

Pricing for the Ultra is going to depend a lot on how much memory you need in your laptop. The base model with 24GB of RAM, a 512GB SSD and a lower-end RTX Spark N1X processor (the version with the 18-core CPU and 5,120-core GPU) starts at $2,600. But upgrade to the 32GB model, with 1TB SSD, and you’ll pay $3,300. The most expensive model, with 128GB of RAM, goes all the way up to $5,900. And that’s before shipping and taxes.

If the pricing didn’t give it away already, this laptop is not an affordable, everyday option. It’s not meant to be: It’s the flagship member of the Surface lineup, aimed at hardcore workers who need or want a device that can handle a lot of AI compute-intensive tasks or a lightweight system that can handle GPU-intensive work.

“We built it for developers and creators pushing the limits of performance, who want portability with exceptional craft,” Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s Windows chief, said at the event on Wednesday.

A big part of Microsoft’s sales pitch is the ability to run AI models and agents locally on device. There are some advantages to using local AI models. You keep all the information more secure within your hardware — no outsourcing to the cloud — and after the initial setup costs, it can be cheaper to run. Both of those points are appealing to businesses that need to keep their data private and avoid hefty bills from “AI tokenmaxxing” employees (people who use a lot of AI).

To truly get the most use out of local AI, you need a device that can handle your generative and agentic tasks without eating more memory than you’ve got or taking forever. That’s where Nvidia comes in with its RTX Spark. It’s a new Arm-based system-on-chip platform that brings Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU architecture — sometimes used in AI data centers — to Windows laptops.

We’ll have to wait and see just how well the Surface Laptop Ultra handles in our full testing. For now, check out CNET’s best laptops of 2026.
